Technically, the axiom does not indicate how to find the choice; it simply postulates its existence.
key_problems: Independence from ZF: AC is neither provable nor disprovable in ZF.
Paradoxical consequences (Banach–Tarski) raise philosophical questions about the nature of mathematical existence.
In constructivist mathematics, AC is rejected, which requires rebuilding many areas.
axiom_of_choice.fun_fact: The statement 'the Tychonoff product of compact spaces is compact' is equivalent to the axiom of choice, although the connection is far from obvious. Likewise, 'every ring with a unit contains a maximal ideal' is also equivalent to AC.

formulas.description: Formal statement of the axiom of choice
formulas.latex: \forall X (\emptyset \notin X \implies \exists f: X \to \bigcup X \text{ such that } \forall A \in X, f(A) \in A)
formulas.meaning: X is a family of nonempty sets, ⋃X is the union of all elements of X, f is a choice function assigning to each A ∈ X an element from A.

catalysis.name: catalysis
catalysis.mini: Reaction accelerator that is not consumed itself — like a matchmaker bringing molecules together to create new bonds.
catalysis.practical_application: Catalytic converters in cars transform toxic exhaust gases into safe nitrogen and water.
catalysis.description_popular: Catalysis is the increase in the rate of a chemical reaction under the action of a substance that is not part of the final products. The catalyst lowers the activation energy (energy barrier), opening an alternative reaction pathway. It can be homogeneous (in the same phase as the reactants) or heterogeneous (usually a solid in a liquid or gaseous medium).
catalysis.fun_fact_popular: The same catalyst can accelerate both the forward and reverse reactions — it does not shift the equilibrium, only helps to reach it faster.
catalysis.description_simple: Catalysis is when a special substance (catalyst) helps a chemical reaction proceed faster or at a lower temperature, but is itself not consumed. Like a bridge connecting two shores, it provides a path with less effort.
catalysis.history_simple: The word 'catalysis' was proposed by Jöns Berzelius in 1836, observing the acceleration of reactions in the presence of certain substances.
catalysis.how_it_works_simple: The catalyst offers molecules a new route where less push energy (activation energy) is needed to start the reaction. Molecules dock on its surface, weaken their bonds, and transform into products faster.
catalysis.description: Catalysis is a process underlying most industrial chemical technologies and biological systems. The mechanism of heterogeneous catalysis includes adsorption of reactants on the active sites of the catalyst surface, their chemical activation (weakening of intramolecular bonds), migration, reaction, and desorption of products. Homogeneous catalysis is often realized through the formation of an intermediate complex of the catalyst with the substrate, which then decomposes releasing the product and regenerating the catalyst. Enzymatic catalysis in living organisms is distinguished by exceptional selectivity and regulability. The rate of a catalytic reaction usually follows the Arrhenius equation with a reduced effective activation energy. The most important indicators of a catalyst are activity (TON, turnover frequency), selectivity, and stability (service life). Modern directions: nanocatalysis, photocatalysis, electrocatalysis for water splitting.
catalysis.history: The term 'catalysis' was introduced by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1836 to describe reactions accelerated in the presence of substances that themselves do not change. In 1895, Wilhelm Ostwald gave a quantitative definition of a catalyst as a substance that accelerates a reaction but does not shift equilibrium. In the early 20th century, Paul Sabatier discovered hydrogenation on metallic nickel, for which he received the Nobel Prize. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed catalytic synthesis of ammonia, revolutionizing agriculture. Further development of enzymatic catalysis is associated with the names of Michaelis, Menten, Briggs and Haldane. Today, catalysis permeates petrochemistry, energy, and environmental protection.
catalysis.how_it_works: The catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. In heterogeneous catalysis, chemisorption plays a decisive role — the formation of chemical bonds between the reactants and the active sites on the surface. This weakens certain interatomic bonds in the reactant molecules, facilitating their breaking. Then the adsorbed particles interact, forming products that desorb, freeing the sites. For example, in ammonia synthesis on an iron catalyst, N₂ and H₂ molecules dissociate into atoms, which requires high energy without a catalyst. The reaction rate is often described by the Arrhenius equation: k = A exp(-Ea/RT), where Ea is the activation energy. The catalyst lowers Ea. In enzymes, an additional role is played by the complementarity of the active site to the substrate (lock-and-key model) and stabilization of the transition state.
key_problems: Design of catalysts with predictable activity and selectivity without empirical trial and error.
Creation of stable and cheap catalysts based on common elements instead of platinum for fuel cells.
Understanding mechanisms of catalyst deactivation and development of regeneration methods.
catalysis.fun_fact: A zeolite catalyst (aluminosilicate) in oil cracking has a specific surface area of up to 1000 m²/g — in one teaspoon, the unfolded surface is comparable to a football field.

formulas.description: Arrhenius equation for the reaction rate constant
formulas.meaning: k — reaction rate constant, A — pre-exponential factor (collision frequency), E_a — activation energy (minimum energy required for reactants to start the reaction), R — universal gas constant (R ≈ 8.314 J/(mol·K)), T — absolute temperature (in Kelvin)

spin_foam.name: spin foam
spin_foam.mini: Spin foam is a 'quantum foam' of spacetime, where geometry, like the edges of a crystal lattice, is woven from discrete quanta of area, giving birth to a world without primordial smoothness.
spin_foam.practical_application: The theory aims to describe the quantum nature of gravity, replacing continuous spacetime with microscopic 'building blocks' that could constitute a black hole or the Universe itself.
spin_foam.description_popular: Spin foam is a formalism of loop quantum gravity, where spacetime is represented not as a continuous background, but as an evolving network of boundary surfaces (simplices), each face of which is labeled by quantum numbers — spins. These spins determine the area of the face in Planck units.
spin_foam.fun_fact_popular: If a 'quantum microscope' existed, at the scale of 10⁻³⁵ meters (Planck length), space would look like a bubbling foam with changing topology.
spin_foam.description_simple: At tiny, ultra-small scales, space ceases to be smooth like paper and becomes like a foam of soap bubbles. Each 'bubble' or face of this foam has a quantized size — spin (a property similar to rotation, but without a classical analogy).
spin_foam.history_simple: The idea grew out of John Wheeler's foam model in the 1950s, and the modern incarnation — spin foams — was developed in the 1990s by Carlo Rovelli, Lee Smolin, and others.
spin_foam.how_it_works_simple: Just as molecules in a crystal form a lattice, spin 'cubes' connect, forming quantum geometry. At very high energies, this pattern might manifest, perhaps inside black holes or at the beginning of the Big Bang.
spin_foam.description: Spin foam is a covariant formulation of quantum geometry within loop quantum gravity. It describes the quantum state of the gravitational field as a superposition of histories, represented by a two-dimensional complex (foam) of vertices, edges, and faces, where each face carries a representation of the SU(2) group — spin. The transition amplitude between states is given by a sum over all foams, which is the quantum analog of the path integral.
spin_foam.history: The roots of the idea go back to John Wheeler, who in 1955 suggested that at Planck scales, spacetime turns into a 'quantum foam' due to fluctuations. In the 1990s, Carlo Rovelli and Lee Smolin, developing loop quantum gravity, turned this into a precise mathematical structure of spin foams, where amplitudes are computed using representation theory. John Baez also made significant contributions, connecting foams with topological quantum field theory.
spin_foam.how_it_works: Spin foam is built from 4-simplices (four-dimensional analogs of tetrahedra), whose faces are colored by spins. Spacetime arises as the history of merging and splitting of these quantum cells. The transition amplitude is computed according to rules similar to Feynman's, but with discrete spatial quanta. It resembles a crystal lattice, where defects and vibrations are interpreted as particles. The formalism leads to a discrete spectrum of areas and volumes and eliminates singularities, for example, in black holes and the Big Bang.
key_problems: How to incorporate matter fields into spin foams and obtain the Standard Model?
How to prove that the macroscopic limit of spin foam gives smooth spacetime with general relativity?
How to connect spin foam to observable effects, for example, in the cosmic microwave background?
spin_foam.fun_fact: In some models, spin foam turns out to be dual to tensor networks, which gave rise to the hypothesis of the holographic nature of gravity: our three-dimensional sensations may be a projection of a two-dimensional quantum foam on the boundary.

formulas.description: Area of a face in spin foam
formulas.meaning: A — area of the face; γ — Immirzi parameter (dimensionless constant of order 1); l_p = √(ħ G/c³) ≈ 1.616×10⁻³⁵ m — Planck length; j — spin of the face (half-integer, j = 0, 1/2, 1, …).

hadron.name: hadron
hadron.mini: Hadrons are particles assembled from quarks, like a mosaic of pieces. Protons and neutrons inside the atomic nucleus are the most well-known hadrons.
hadron.practical_application: Understanding hadrons explains the structure of matter and allows studying the forces inside atomic nuclei, which is applied in nuclear energy and medical imaging (PET scanning).
hadron.description_popular: Hadrons are a class of subatomic particles that participate in the strong interaction. They are not fundamental but consist of quarks held together by gluons (carriers of the strong interaction). The name comes from the Greek 'hadros' meaning massive, reflecting their relatively large mass compared to leptons (e.g., electrons). Hadrons include protons and neutrons (baryons, fermions with half-integer spin), as well as mesons (bosons with integer spin). Inside a hadron, quarks are bound so tightly that free quarks are not observed—this is the property of confinement.
hadron.fun_fact_popular: Although the proton appears stable, some theories predict that it could decay over an unimaginably long time—more than 10³⁴ years. Such decay has not yet been observed.
hadron.description_simple: Hadrons are tiny particles that make up almost everything around us: they form atomic nuclei. Their peculiarity is that they are not elementary but assembled from even smaller parts—quarks, glued together by a 'glue'—a special strong interaction (the strongest interaction in nature, holding quarks together). Imagine quarks as glowing beads, and the strong interaction as a thread that keeps them from flying apart. Hadrons come in two types: baryons—made of three quarks (like the proton and neutron), and mesons—made of a quark and an antiquark (unstable particles).
hadron.history_simple: The idea that hadrons consist of more fundamental particles arose in the 1960s. Physicists Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig independently proposed the existence of quarks. Later experiments at accelerators confirmed their reality.
hadron.how_it_works_simple: Quarks inside a hadron are never alone—they are always confined within. Attempting to tear a hadron apart requires enormous energy and leads to the creation of new quarks, which immediately form new hadrons. It's like trying to break a magnet: instead of two halves, you get two whole magnets.
hadron.description: A hadron is a composite particle formed from quarks and gluons bound by the strong interaction, described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Quarks possess color charge—an analogue of electric charge for the strong interaction—and gluons are the carriers of this interaction and themselves carry color charge, leading to self-interaction and confinement. Hadrons are divided into baryons (three quarks, fermions) and mesons (quark-antiquark, bosons). There are also exotic hadrons: tetraquarks, pentaquarks, and glueballs. The mass of a hadron significantly exceeds the sum of the masses of its constituent quarks due to the energy of gluon fields (the Higgs mechanism provides only a small part). The internal structure of hadrons is studied in deep inelastic scattering experiments. At high energies, QCD exhibits asymptotic freedom: quarks behave as nearly free particles.
hadron.history: The concept of hadrons became established by the mid-20th century as the number of discovered particles grew rapidly. In 1961, Murray Gell-Mann and Yuval Ne'eman proposed a classification of hadrons based on the SU(3) group, leading to the prediction of the Ω⁻ baryon. In 1964, Gell-Mann and, independently, George Zweig introduced the quark hypothesis. Experimental confirmation of quarks was obtained in the late 1960s in electron-proton scattering experiments at SLAC. The development of QCD in the 1970s (Gross, Wilczek, Politzer) explained the dynamics of the strong interaction.
hadron.how_it_works: Hadrons arise due to confinement: the color charges of quarks are attracted by gluons so strongly that the potential energy grows linearly with distance. When attempting to separate quarks, the gluon field string breaks, producing a quark-antiquark pair from the vacuum, leading to hadronization—the formation of jets of hadrons. This is described by the laws of QCD, in which asymptotic freedom and infrared slavery are important. Hadron masses are calculated using lattice QCD. The Pauli principle explains why baryons have an antisymmetric color wave function: the three quarks must be of different colors.
key_problems: Nature of confinement: mathematically rigorous proof of color confinement
Precise calculation of hadron masses from first principles of QCD
Search for exotic hadrons and glueballs
Proton spin puzzle: how quarks and gluons form its spin 1/2
hadron.fun_fact: In the proton, the mass of the quarks accounts for only about 1% of its total mass. The remaining 99% is the energy of the gluon field, according to mass-energy equivalence (E = mc²).

virtual_particle.name: virtual particle
virtual_particle.mini: A virtual particle is like a fleeting borrowed grain of energy in the boiling ocean of quantum vacuum, vanishing faster than a glance but still managing to transmit a force.
virtual_particle.practical_application: Explains how electric charges interact (via messenger photons) and why empty space actually seethes with energy.
virtual_particle.description_popular: Virtual particles are quantum fluctuations of fields (quantum fields are fundamental entities describing particles as excitations) that briefly appear in the vacuum due to energy uncertainty. They do not exist as real free particles but mediate interactions and alter the properties of the vacuum.
virtual_particle.fun_fact_popular: The energy of virtual particles affects the spectrum of the hydrogen atom — this is called the Lamb shift, measured with incredible precision.
virtual_particle.description_simple: In the quantum world (the realm of very small things), even emptiness is not empty. Particles constantly appear and vanish for brief moments, like bubbles in boiling water. These particles are virtual: they exist so fleetingly that they cannot be seen directly, but their influence is palpable.
virtual_particle.history_simple: The idea emerged in the 1920s-30s with the development of quantum electrodynamics and was formally described in the 1940s by Richard Feynman and others.
virtual_particle.how_it_works_simple: Two ships exchange swift rowers who burst from the water and return. The rowers are unseen but push the ships. Similarly, virtual particles carry forces between ordinary particles: for example, virtual photons make a magnet attract.
virtual_particle.description: Within quantum field theory, virtual particles are internal lines in Feynman diagrams, corresponding to mathematical terms in perturbation expansions. They are quantum fluctuations of underlying fields, governed by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle (ΔE·Δt ≥ ħ/2 — it is impossible to precisely know both energy and time simultaneously), allowing energy to be borrowed from the vacuum for a short time to create particle-antiparticle pairs.
virtual_particle.history: The concept grew from work in quantum electrodynamics (QED). Paul Dirac introduced the theory of radiation and absorption in 1927, and the idea of virtual particles was formalized in the late 1940s by Richard Feynman, Julian Schwinger, and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga, for which they received the Nobel Prize. The term was likely coined by Wheeler. John Wheeler also investigated quantum foam, where virtual particles account for the foam-like geometry at Planck scales.
virtual_particle.how_it_works: According to the uncertainty principle, vacuum fluctuations of fields give rise to virtual pairs. In QED, virtual photons mediate the electromagnetic interaction between charged particles: each vertex in a Feynman diagram represents an act of emission or absorption of a virtual particle. They may be 'off mass shell' (their energy-momentum does not satisfy E² = p²c² + m²c⁴), unlike real particles. Effects of virtual particles manifest in vacuum polarization, the Lamb shift, the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron, and, macroscopically, in the Casimir effect, where an attractive force arises between two closely spaced conducting plates due to the difference in density of virtual photons outside and inside.
key_problems: How to explain the cosmological constant if the vacuum energy from virtual particles is predicted to be 120 orders of magnitude larger than observed?
What is the role of virtual particles in quantum gravity, especially near black holes, where they may contribute to Hawking radiation?
Can virtual and real particles be experimentally distinguished at ultra-short time scales?
virtual_particle.fun_fact: In strong electromagnetic fields (e.g., near nuclei with large charge), virtual electron-positron pairs can become real — this is the 'Schwinger mechanism' of particle creation, predicted in 1951.

formulas.description: Energy-time uncertainty principle
formulas.meaning: ΔE — energy uncertainty; Δt — time uncertainty; ħ = h/(2π) ≈ 1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s — reduced Planck constant.

diffraction.name: diffraction
diffraction.mini: Waves bending around obstacles, like sea swell passing between pier supports.
diffraction.practical_application: Thanks to diffraction, spectrometer gratings work, splitting light into colors for analyzing the chemical composition of stars.
diffraction.description_popular: Diffraction is the deviation of waves (light, sound, water) from straight-line propagation when encountering an obstacle or opening. It becomes noticeable when the slit size is comparable to the wavelength. In the case of light, it produces an interference pattern — a set of bands of varying brightness.
diffraction.fun_fact_popular: If you look through a thin fabric at a street lamp, you can see rainbow streaks — that's also diffraction on the threads.
diffraction.description_simple: If you throw a stone into a pond, the water circles bend around blades of grass. It's the same with light: passing through a narrow slit, it spreads out to the sides and creates alternating light and dark bands.
diffraction.history_simple: The phenomenon was first described by Francesco Grimaldi in 1665, and explained as a wave property of light by Thomas Young in 1801.
diffraction.how_it_works_simple: When a wave meets the edge of an object or a slit, it bends and interferes with itself. Where the crests coincide, the light is amplified (bright band), where they don't align, it cancels out (dark band).
diffraction.description: Diffraction is a fundamental wave phenomenon inherent to all types of waves: electromagnetic, sound, water waves. It occurs when a wave interacts with an inhomogeneity in the medium — for example, the edge of an opaque screen, a slit, an aperture, or a periodic structure. According to the Huygens-Fresnel principle, each point on the wavefront becomes a source of secondary spherical waves, and the resulting field at the observation point is the superposition of these secondary waves. The interference of secondary waves leads to a spatial redistribution of intensity. A distinction is made between Fresnel diffraction (in the near zone) and Fraunhofer diffraction (in the far zone, where parallel rays arrive). Mathematically, diffraction is described by the Fresnel-Kirchhoff integral. The phenomenon is widely used to study the structure of matter: X-ray diffraction on crystals (X-ray crystallography), electron diffraction, neutron diffraction. The resolution limit of optical instruments is also determined by diffraction.
diffraction.history: The first systematic description of light diffraction was given by the Italian physicist Francesco Grimaldi in a posthumous work of 1665, introducing the term itself. The wave nature of light, capable of explaining diffraction, was championed by Christiaan Huygens (1690). In 1801, Thomas Young demonstrated interference from two slits, confirming the wave theory. Augustin-Jean Fresnel in 1818 presented a rigorous mathematical theory, solving the problem of diffraction at an edge. Later, in 1912, Max von Laue and colleagues discovered X-ray diffraction in crystals, which earned him the Nobel Prize. William Lawrence Bragg and his father William Henry Bragg developed a method for deciphering crystal structures from diffraction patterns. Joseph von Fraunhofer invented the diffraction grating and used it for spectroscopy.
diffraction.how_it_works: Diffraction is a consequence of wave superposition. When part of the wavefront is blocked by an obstacle, secondary waves from the open areas interfere, creating a complex pattern. For periodic structures such as a diffraction grating or crystal lattice, the condition for reinforcement is described by Bragg's law: nλ = 2d sin θ, where n is the diffraction order, λ is the wavelength, d is the interplanar spacing, and θ is the grazing angle. This law underlies X-ray crystallography. For gratings with many grooves, the intensity is concentrated in narrow peaks, allowing diffraction to be used in spectrometers to measure wavelengths with high precision.
key_problems: Accurate calculation of diffraction fields for complex three-dimensional objects without simplifications remains computationally intensive.
Development of X-ray diffraction methods for studying disordered structures (liquids, amorphous solids) with time resolution.
diffraction.fun_fact: The diffraction grating of hummingbird feathers creates an iridescent coloration that changes with viewing angle; in technology, similar structures (photonic crystals) are used in optical fibers.

formulas.description: Bragg's law for diffraction on a crystal
formulas.meaning: n is the diffraction order (integer), λ is the wavelength of the incident radiation, d is the interplanar spacing in the crystal lattice, θ is the grazing angle (between the incident beam and the crystal plane)

fluctuation.name: fluctuation
fluctuation.mini: Fluctuation is a random deviation of a system from equilibrium: like ripples on water without wind or a burst of laughter in a quiet audience, a reminder that calm is only a statistical illusion.
fluctuation.practical_application: Without quantum fluctuations, galaxies would not have formed, and electronic circuits constantly suffer from thermal noise — voltage fluctuations due to random electron motion.
fluctuation.description_popular: Fluctuation is a spontaneous deviation of a macroscopic parameter (temperature, density, energy) from its equilibrium value. In closed systems, it is smaller the more particles there are, but in the micro-world, quantum fluctuations are fundamental: even absolute zero does not freeze the zero-point oscillations of fields.
fluctuation.fun_fact_popular: The cosmic microwave background radiation is an 'imprint' of quantum fluctuations of the early universe, magnified by inflation to sizes that gave birth to galaxies.
fluctuation.description_simple: In any large collection of objects (molecules, people, money) there is always variability: here and there, a clustering or thinning arises. This is fluctuation — a temporary departure from the average. In physics, fluctuations can be thermal (related to temperature) and quantum (unavoidable, according to the laws of the micro-world).
fluctuation.history_simple: Systematic study began in the 19th century: Robert Brown discovered Brownian motion (1827), and Ludwig Boltzmann and Josiah Gibbs created statistical mechanics, which explained these fluctuations.
fluctuation.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a beach with people: on average, everyone is lying evenly, but sometimes clusters form around the ice cream vendor. So it is with molecules in the air: in a room, pressure is constant, but in a microscopic volume, density jumps — these are fluctuations.
fluctuation.description: Fluctuation is a temporary random deviation of a physical quantity from its average value, described by statistical distributions. In equilibrium statistical mechanics, fluctuations are related to the system's susceptibility (fluctuation-dissipation theorem). In quantum field theory, vacuum fluctuations are inevitable due to the uncertainty principle and manifest as virtual particles.
fluctuation.history: The concept took hold in the 19th century: after Robert Brown's observations (1827) of the chaotic motion of pollen in water, Albert Einstein in 1905 quantitatively described Brownian motion, proving the existence of molecules. Ludwig Boltzmann had earlier laid the foundations for the statistical interpretation of thermodynamics, linking entropy to probability, and thus to fluctuations. In the quantum realm, the formalism was developed in the mid-20th century.
fluctuation.how_it_works: In thermodynamic systems, the probability of a fluctuation is exponentially suppressed, as prescribed by the Boltzmann distribution (P ~ e^{-ΔE/kT}). In quantum mechanics, even the ground state of a harmonic oscillator has non-zero energy, causing zero-point fluctuations of coordinate and momentum, which follows from Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. In cosmology, quantum fluctuations of the vacuum inflaton field, stretched to macroscopic scales, became the seeds of the large-scale structure of the universe, observed through anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background.
key_problems: How to explain the exact value of the amplitude of primordial fluctuations that led to our observable universe?
How to link quantum fluctuations to dark energy — is it a consequence of vacuum fluctuations or something else?
Can quantum fluctuations be experimentally controlled for ultra-precise measurements, for example, in gravitational wave detectors?
fluctuation.fun_fact: Fluctuations in the quantum Hall effect manifest as fractional charge: electrons together with fluctuations create collective quasiparticles with charge e/3, e/5, etc.

formulas.description: Boltzmann distribution for energy fluctuations
formulas.meaning: P — probability of a fluctuation with excess energy ΔE; k_B ≈ 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K — Boltzmann constant; T — absolute temperature in kelvins.

formulas.description: Zero-point energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator
formulas.meaning: E₀ — minimum oscillation energy; ħ = h/(2π) ≈ 1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s — reduced Planck constant; ω — angular frequency of the oscillator.

quintessence.name: quintessence
quintessence.mini: Quintessence is a hypothetical form of dark energy that can change over time. If dark energy is a sea, then quintessence is a wave that waxes and wanes.
quintessence.practical_application: Helps understand why the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate and predict its ultimate fate — whether it will be a Big Rip or eternal cooling.
quintessence.description_popular: Quintessence is a hypothetical form of dark energy with variable density, described by a scalar field. Unlike Einstein's cosmological constant (Λ), which is unchanging, quintessence can evolve in time and space. The equation of state of such energy is characterized by the parameter w = p/ρ (ratio of pressure to density), which for quintessence lies in the range -1 < w < -1/3. When w = -1, it is indistinguishable from Λ, and values close to -1/3 lead to a slowdown of the acceleration. Observations have not yet confirmed deviations of w from -1, but allow for subtle dynamics.
quintessence.fun_fact_popular: The name 'fifth element energy' refers to the ancient Greek notion that the heavens consist of a special substance — ether, or quintessence. Modern physics may be bringing this idea back on scientific grounds.
quintessence.description_simple: Quintessence is a special energy that fills space and causes the Universe to expand faster and faster. Unlike ordinary dark energy, which is considered constant (like a steady hum), quintessence can weaken or strengthen in different places and at different times. It's as if the air in a room became denser or thinner, affecting the movement of objects. The idea came from particle physics: there is a field (an invisible substance, similar to a magnetic field) that slowly changes and creates repulsive gravity.
quintessence.history_simple: The word 'quintessence' goes back to ancient philosophy — the fifth element after earth, water, air, and fire. In cosmology, it was revived in 1998 when astronomers discovered that the expansion of the Universe was accelerating. Scientists suggested that this was not due to a constant cosmological constant, but to a dynamic field, named quintessence.
quintessence.how_it_works_simple: Quintessence is like a spring that slowly unwinds. As the field 'rolls' down the energy slope, its pressure is negative, and it acts like antigravity, pushing galaxies apart. If the field freezes, acceleration stops; if it continues to change, the Universe may face the tearing apart of matter.
quintessence.description: Quintessence in cosmology is a model of dark energy based on a scalar field ϕ with canonical kinetic term and potential V(ϕ). The action for such a field in curved spacetime yields an energy-momentum tensor that, for slowly varying field, provides negative pressure, causing accelerated expansion of the Universe. The Friedmann equation for the scale factor a(t) is modified with quintessence, and the field dynamics determine the evolution of dark energy. Possible potentials include exponential V(ϕ) ∝ exp(-λϕ) or inverse power-law V(ϕ) ∝ ϕ^(-α). The difference from models with a cosmological constant lies in the absence of the 'coincidence' problem (why are the densities of matter and dark energy comparable today) thanks to tracking mechanisms. Observational constraints from supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and baryon acoustic oscillations currently agree with w ≈ -1, but future missions may detect small deviations.
quintessence.history: After the discovery of the accelerated expansion of the Universe in 1998 by groups led by Saul Perlmutter, Adam Riess, and Brian Schmidt, the question arose about the nature of dark energy. Although the cosmological constant was the simplest explanation, theorists including Paul Steinhardt and Robert Caldwell proposed models of a dynamic scalar field — quintessence. The term became established in the literature as a contrast to the static Λ. The idea is supported by attempts to link dark energy with the inflationary field in the early Universe.
quintessence.how_it_works: The dynamics of quintessence obey the Klein-Gordon equation in an expanding Universe: ϕ̈ + 3Hϕ̇ + dV/dϕ = 0, where H is the Hubble parameter. The braking due to expansion causes the field to roll slowly, preserving the potential energy, which dominates and creates negative pressure. The energy density and pressure of the field: ρ_ϕ = ϕ̇²/2 + V(ϕ), p_ϕ = ϕ̇²/2 - V(ϕ). When V(ϕ) ≫ ϕ̇², we get p_ϕ ≈ -ρ_ϕ, which leads to acceleration. Quintessence models must solve the fifth force problem, since field variations could manifest in laboratory experiments, so it is usually assumed that the field interacts very weakly with matter.
key_problems: Nature of the scalar field: elementary particle or modification of gravity?
Measuring the time dependence of parameter w with high precision
Preventing unwanted interactions with matter (fifth force)
Explaining initial conditions and coincidence with the current matter density
quintessence.fun_fact: Some quintessence models predict that as the Universe expands, the field may stop accelerating and even change sign, causing collapse. This is called 'frozen quintessence'.

formulas.description: Equation of state for quintessence
formulas.meaning: w — equation of state parameter, p — pressure, ρ — energy density; for quintessence -1 < w < -1/3

spectrometer.name: spectrometer
spectrometer.mini: Rainbow meter: breaks light into colored stripes and uses them to determine the composition of distant stars.
spectrometer.practical_application: In medicine, mass spectrometers detect traces of drugs in blood, while optical spectrometers test water quality by identifying contaminants.
spectrometer.description_popular: A spectrometer is an instrument for measuring the distribution of electromagnetic radiation by wavelength or frequency. Main components: an entrance slit, a dispersive element (prism or diffraction grating), focusing optics, and a detector (CCD array, photomultiplier). Spectrometers are distinguished by range: ultraviolet, visible, infrared, X-ray, etc. A spectrograph is an instrument that records the entire spectrum simultaneously. Key characteristics are spectral resolution and light throughput.
spectrometer.fun_fact_popular: Every chemical element leaves a unique “fingerprint” in the spectrum—a set of bright lines. This is how astronomers determined that the Sun and other stars are composed mainly of hydrogen and helium.
spectrometer.description_simple: A spectrometer is an instrument that, like a prism, splits light into colors. But it doesn't just show a rainbow: it precisely measures how much of each color is in the light. This way we can find out what the light source is made of—sodium gives yellow, hydrogen gives red and blue-violet.
spectrometer.history_simple: The first prototype of a spectrometer was a glass prism used by Isaac Newton in 1666 to decompose sunlight. Later, Joseph von Fraunhofer added a diffraction grating and saw dark lines in the Sun's spectrum.
spectrometer.how_it_works_simple: Light passes through a narrow slit and hits an element that separates it by wavelength—this could be a prism (refracts violet more strongly) or a diffraction grating (reflects different colors at different angles). The detector records how much light arrives at each microscopic section. This constructs the spectrum—a graph of brightness versus wavelength.
spectrometer.description: A spectrometer is a measuring instrument that allows quantitative analysis of the spectral composition of electromagnetic radiation. In general, it includes a radiation source (external or built-in), a dispersive system, an optical scheme for forming a parallel beam and focusing, a detector, and a data processing system. The basis of operation is the conversion of the intensity-wavelength dependence into a spatial distribution, which is recorded by a multi-element photodetector. Dispersion can be achieved by refraction in a prism (refractive) or by diffraction on a periodic structure. Modern spectrometers use concave holographic gratings, which allow combining dispersion and focusing onto a flat detector. Absolute wavelength calibration is performed using reference sources (gas-discharge lamps with known lines). Spectrometers are classified by detection principle (scanning, with a stationary detector; single-beam, double-beam), by modulation type (dispersive, interference—Fourier spectrometers), by spectral region. Mass spectrometers measure not wavelengths but masses of charged particles, but also belong to analytical instruments. Astronomical spectrometers are often coupled with telescopes and have high resolution (R = λ/Δλ up to 100,000 and above) for studying stellar atmospheres, the interstellar medium, and the redshift of galaxies.
spectrometer.history: The history of the spectrometer began with the experiments of Isaac Newton in 1666, who decomposed sunlight with a prism. Newton introduced the term “spectrum,” calling the colored stripe a “ghost” (spectrum). In 1814, Joseph von Fraunhofer, replacing the prism with a diffraction grating of his own making, discovered dark lines in the solar spectrum (Fraunhofer lines) and measured their wavelengths. This laid the foundation for astrospectroscopy. In 1859, Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen created the first spectroscope with a gas burner and prism, linking spectral lines to chemical elements. In the 20th century, the development of electronics led to photoelectric registration. Today, space observatories are equipped with spectrometers operating from X-ray to infrared ranges (for example, the STIS instrument on the Hubble telescope).
spectrometer.how_it_works: The principle of an optical spectrometer: the radiation under study passes through an entrance slit to a collimator, which forms a parallel beam. Then the beam hits a dispersing element—for example, a reflective diffraction grating with rules. According to the diffraction condition d(sin α ± sin β) = mλ, where d is the grating period, α and β are the angles of incidence and diffraction, m is the order, light of different wavelengths is deflected at different angles. Then a focusing mirror forms images of the slit in monochromatic light on the detector (CCD line or array). The signal intensity from each pixel is proportional to the photon flux of the corresponding wavelength. Calibration converts pixel number into wavelength. An alternative type is the Fourier spectrometer: it uses a Michelson interferometer, where the interferogram (intensity dependence on path difference) is measured, and the spectrum is recovered by Fourier transformation. The advantage is high resolution and light throughput.
key_problems: Reducing the size of spectrometers to chip format (microspectrometers) while maintaining high resolution for portable devices.
Noise suppression and increasing dynamic range for detecting exoplanet atmospheres via transit spectroscopy.
Creating spectrometers for far ultraviolet and X-rays with angular resolution sufficient for spectroscopy of individual sources in clusters.
spectrometer.fun_fact: The spectrometer on the Cassini probe discovered water geysers on Enceladus by analyzing scattered light; its resolution allowed distinguishing water vapor lines from ammonia and methane impurities.

fourier_transform.name: Fourier transform
fourier_transform.mini: A mathematical 'translator' from the language of time to the language of frequency: it decomposes a complex signal into simple sine waves, like breaking down a musical chord into individual notes. Any intricate dance becomes the sum of smooth swayings.
fourier_transform.practical_application: Image compression (JPEG), noise filtering in audio, signal analysis in MRI and radar, digitization of music — everywhere where it is necessary to isolate frequencies or remove interference.
fourier_transform.description_popular: The Fourier transform is an integral transform that maps a function of a real variable (often time) to a function of a complex variable (frequency). It decomposes the signal into an orthogonal basis of harmonic oscillations. The result (spectrum) shows the amplitude and phase of each frequency component. The inverse transform allows reconstructing the original signal. Thanks to the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), the algorithm works very quickly and is used everywhere in signal processing.
fourier_transform.fun_fact_popular: In quantum mechanics, the momentum representation of the wave function is the Fourier transform of its coordinate representation. The Heisenberg uncertainty principle arises from the properties of the Fourier transform: the narrower the signal in time, the wider its spectrum.
fourier_transform.description_simple: The Fourier transform decomposes a complex wave into simple components. Imagine that your voice is a soup of different sounds: a low hum and a high whistle. The Fourier transform takes this 'soup' and tells how much hum, how much whistle, and how much hiss there is. It does this by comparing the original signal with pure sine waves (smooth waves) of all possible frequencies (frequency — number of oscillations per second). Thus, from an audio recording, you can find out the notes, and from a photograph — smooth transitions and sharp contours.
fourier_transform.history_simple: French mathematician Joseph Fourier proposed this idea in 1807 while studying how heat propagates in solids. He realized that any temperature distribution could be represented as a sum of simple waves. Later, the method began to be applied everywhere — from music to quantum physics.
fourier_transform.how_it_works_simple: Imagine that from a footprint in the sand you need to guess which waves left it. The Fourier transform acts like a detective: it alternately tries on waves of different lengths and strengths to the footprint. Where the match is good, a big 'clue' appears. In a computer, this is done by multiplying the signal by test sinusoids and summing the results. The result is a spectrum — a graph showing which frequencies are present.
fourier_transform.description: For an absolutely integrable function f(t), the direct Fourier transform is defined as f̂(ω) = ∫₋∞∞ f(t) e^{-iωt} dt, where t is time, ω is angular frequency. Inverse: f(t) = (1/2π) ∫₋∞∞ f̂(ω) e^{iωt} dω. There are variants for periodic functions (Fourier series) and discrete sequences (Discrete Fourier Transform, DFT). The Fast Fourier Transform algorithm (Cooley–Tukey, 1965) allows computing the DFT in O(n log n) operations. Properties: linearity, shift gives a phase factor, differentiation ↔ multiplication by iω, convolution ↔ product. Generalizations: multidimensional FT, windowed FT, wavelets, Fourier analysis on groups. In physics, the FT connects coordinate and momentum spaces, ensuring the uncertainty principle.
fourier_transform.history: Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier in 1807 (published in 1822) in a memoir on heat propagation showed that an arbitrary function can be expanded into a trigonometric series. The idea met resistance from Lagrange and Laplace, who doubted the convergence of the series. Later, Dirichlet (1829) clarified the conditions. In the 20th century, Laurent Schwartz extended the transform to generalized functions (Dirac delta function). Today it is the basis of harmonic analysis.
fourier_transform.how_it_works: Mathematically, the kernel e^{-iωt} acts as a 'probe': for each frequency ω, we compute the correlation of the signal with a harmonic oscillation of that frequency. The integral measures the 'similarity'. Thanks to the orthogonality of sinusoids, the decomposition is invertible without loss. The Fast Fourier Transform uses the symmetry of complex roots of unity, reducing the computation of a large matrix to a series of small ones. In quantum mechanics, the wave function in momentum representation is the Fourier transform of the coordinate wave function, and the relation Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2 follows directly from the properties of the FT.
key_problems: Not all functions have a Fourier transform in the classical sense — a generalization to distributions is required.
Gibbs phenomenon: at points of discontinuity, the Fourier series produces overshoots whose amplitude does not decrease with increasing number of terms (about 9% of the jump).
Interpretation of negative frequencies in physical applications is not always intuitive.
Non-stationary signals require windowed FT or wavelets for adequate analysis.
fourier_transform.fun_fact: The Fourier transform of a finite function (equal to zero outside a finite interval) is an analytic function on the entire complex plane — this is the Paley–Wiener theorem.

formulas.description: Direct Fourier transform
formulas.meaning: f(t) — original function (usually time), ω — angular frequency, i — imaginary unit, e — base of the natural logarithm.

formulas.description: Inverse Fourier transform
formulas.meaning: From the spectrum f̂(ω), the original function f(t) is reconstructed. The factor 1/(2π) normalizes the transform.

genomics.name: genomics
genomics.mini: The genome is an instruction manual for a living organism, written in each of its cells. Genomics is a way to read this manual from start to finish, like reading an entire book rather than individual sentences.
genomics.practical_application: Genomics allows predicting hereditary diseases, creating personalized medicines, and tracking the evolution of viruses such as SARS-CoV-2.
genomics.description_popular: Genomics is a field of molecular biology that studies the structure, function, evolution, and mapping of genomes. Unlike genetics, which focuses on individual genes, genomics considers the entire genetic material of an organism as a unified system. Modern high-throughput sequencing methods enable rapid and inexpensive determination of billions of nucleotide sequences.
genomics.fun_fact_popular: If you printed the human genome as a book, you would need about 3,000 volumes of 1,000 pages each—and all of that fits into a cell nucleus the size of a thousandth of a millimeter.
genomics.description_simple: Genomics studies the complete set of hereditary information (genome) of a living being. Imagine an organism as a huge library, and genes as individual books. Genomics doesn't just read one book; it reads the entire library at once to understand how they are connected. Terms in parentheses: genome is the complete set of DNA with all instructions; DNA is the molecule that stores the genetic code.
genomics.history_simple: The first complete genome (of a bacteriophage virus) was sequenced in 1977. The human genome was deciphered by 2003 as part of the international Human Genome Project.
genomics.how_it_works_simple: Scientists break DNA into small pieces, read their sequence (sequencing), and assemble them back like a giant puzzle. Then, using computers, they search for 'word-genes' in this text and try to understand their functions.
genomics.description: Genomics is an interdisciplinary science at the intersection of biology, computer science, and statistics, dealing with the comprehensive analysis of complete genomes. It includes structural genomics (determining the spatial organization of genes), functional genomics (studying expression and regulation), comparative genomics (comparing genomes of different species), and epigenomics (investigating changes that do not affect the DNA sequence). Key technologies include next-generation sequencing (NGS), microarrays, and mass spectrometry. Genomics has revolutionized medicine, agriculture, and evolutionary biology.
genomics.history: The term 'genome' was proposed by Hans Winkler in 1920, but the practical emergence of genomics began in the 1970s with the invention of DNA sequencing methods by Frederick Sanger and Walter Gilbert. In 1990, the Human Genome Project started and was completed in 2003 with the full sequence of the euchromatic portion. Since then, sequencing costs have dropped a millionfold, ushering in the era of personal genomics.
genomics.how_it_works: The process includes sample collection, DNA extraction, fragmentation, sequencing (determining the order of nucleotides), bioinformatic assembly, and annotation (identifying gene locations and regulatory elements). Analysis relies on sequence alignment algorithms, homology searches, and protein function predictions.
key_problems: Complete deciphering of the functional significance of non-coding DNA (previously considered 'junk').
Understanding how interactions of thousands of genes determine complex traits (multifactorial nature).
Ethical issues regarding privacy of genetic information and germline editing.
Creating accurate predictive models of phenotype from genotype.
genomics.fun_fact: The human genome contains about 3.2 billion nucleotide base pairs, but protein-coding regions (exons) make up only about 1.5% of the total length. The rest consists of mobile genetic elements, introns, and repetitive sequences, which actively participate in regulation.

hormone.name: hormone
hormone.mini: Hormones are the body's chemical couriers: the brain and glands send them through the blood to remotely control organ function.
hormone.practical_application: Hormones are used to make insulin for diabetics, birth control pills, and adrenaline to stop anaphylactic shock.
hormone.description_popular: Hormones are biologically active substances produced by endocrine glands and carried via the bloodstream. They act in extremely low concentrations (nanograms per milliliter) and regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction, and mood. They are classified into peptide, steroid, and amino acid derivative hormones, which bind to receptors on the surface or inside target cells.
hormone.fun_fact_popular: Oxytocin, the 'cuddle hormone', is released in mothers during breastfeeding and in lovers during touch, enhancing feelings of trust.
hormone.description_simple: Hormones are signaling substances. Glands, like post offices, release hormones into the blood—'letters' with an address. Each cell with a matching receptor (lock) receives the letter and acts according to instructions.
hormone.history_simple: The first hormone—adrenaline—was isolated by Japanese Jokichi Takamine and American John Abel in 1901.
hormone.how_it_works_simple: The hormone travels through the blood until it finds a cell with a special receptor protein. The binding of the hormone to the receptor triggers a cascade of chemical reactions inside the cell, causing it, for example, to speed up the heartbeat or store glucose.
hormone.description: Hormones are chemical messengers that provide humoral regulation. Synthesized by specialized cells (often in glands), they are secreted into the blood and act on target cells via high-affinity receptors. The hormone-receptor interaction triggers intracellular signaling cascades: adenylate cyclase, phosphoinositide, tyrosine kinase pathways, which alter enzyme activity or gene expression. Hormone concentrations are regulated by feedback mechanisms, such as the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.
hormone.history: Claude Bernard's experiments (1855) showed that the liver releases glucose into the blood, laying the foundations of endocrinology. In 1901, J. Takamine and J. Abel independently crystallized adrenaline. Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin in 1921, saving millions of lives. Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally in the 1970s revealed the structure of hypothalamic releasing hormones.
hormone.how_it_works: Steroid hormones penetrate the plasma membrane and bind to nuclear receptors, regulating gene transcription. Peptide hormones and catecholamines bind to membrane receptors, activating G-proteins or enzymatic cascades, leading to the formation of second messengers (cAMP, IP3, Ca²⁺). This achieves signal amplification: one hormone molecule can trigger the synthesis of thousands of target enzyme molecules. Negative feedback maintains homeostasis: for example, thyroid hormones inhibit thyrotropin production.
key_problems: Molecular mechanisms of insulin resistance in obesity
Off-target effects of hormonal drugs and their long-term consequences
Individual variability of hormonal background for personalized medicine
hormone.fun_fact: Growth hormone in children at night actually enhances bone growth, and its peak occurs during deep sleep—hence the phrase 'grow while you sleep'.

neurotransmitter.name: neurotransmitter
neurotransmitter.mini: A molecular courier that delivers messages between nerve cells, like a postman delivering letters to addresses.
neurotransmitter.practical_application: Brain function, emotions, movement — everything depends on neurotransmitters; imbalances underlie depression, Parkinson's disease, and other disorders.
neurotransmitter.description_popular: Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that transmit signals between neurons, and from neurons to muscle or gland cells. They are synthesized in the neuron, packaged into vesicles (bubbles), and released into the synaptic cleft in response to an electrical impulse. The molecules diffuse to the postsynaptic membrane and bind to receptors, causing either excitation or inhibition. This process underlies all functions of the nervous system.
neurotransmitter.fun_fact_popular: Some neurotransmitters, such as oxytocin, act not only in the brain but throughout the body — it stimulates uterine contractions during childbirth and milk ejection, as well as forming the bond between mother and child.
neurotransmitter.description_simple: A neurotransmitter is a substance that one nerve cell (neuron) releases to transmit a signal to another cell. It can be compared to a key: it only fits a particular lock (receptor) on the surface of the receiving cell. When the key is inserted, a chain of events is triggered in the cell. Different neurotransmitters perform different tasks: for example, dopamine is linked to pleasure and motivation, serotonin to mood, acetylcholine to muscle movements.
neurotransmitter.history_simple: The idea of chemical signal transmission in the nervous system was first proven by Otto Loewi in 1921. He conducted an experiment with frog hearts and showed that one heart could slow down another through a fluid, releasing a then-unknown substance — later named acetylcholine.
neurotransmitter.how_it_works_simple: Imagine two people throwing a ball: the neurotransmitter is the ball. One neuron throws the ball into the gap between cells (the synaptic cleft), and the other catches it with a special glove (receptor) and knows what to do next.
neurotransmitter.description: Neurotransmitters are endogenous chemicals that transmit signals across the synapse from one neuron to another or to an effector cell. They belong to various classes: amino acids (glutamate, GABA), monoamines (dopamine, serotonin), peptides (endorphins), and others. Synthesis occurs in the neuron cell body or presynaptic terminal; after packaging into vesicles and exocytosis triggered by Ca2+ ions, the neurotransmitter binds to specific receptors (ionotropic or metabotropic), initiating intracellular signaling cascades. Inactivation occurs via reuptake, enzymatic degradation, or diffusion. The balance of different neurotransmitter systems determines complex behavior and cognitive functions.
neurotransmitter.history: The concept of chemical transmission arose from Otto Loewi's experiments (1921), which demonstrated humoral transmission in the frog vagus nerve. Later, Henry Dale identified acetylcholine. In the 1950s, the discovery of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine expanded the understanding of synaptic transmission. Current research focuses on the role of neurotransmitters in plasticity, learning, and mental illnesses.
neurotransmitter.how_it_works: The process includes: 1) synthesis and loading into vesicles, 2) action potential opening calcium channels, 3) vesicle fusion with the membrane and release of the neurotransmitter, 4) diffusion across the cleft, 5) binding to receptors, 6) postsynaptic response, 7) inactivation. Autoreceptors and reuptake transporters play important roles. Disruptions at any step lead to neurological pathologies.
key_problems: How is information encoded in the patterns of neurotransmitter release?
What is the exact mechanism of action of many neuropeptides?
How do neurotransmitters interact with the brain's immune system (microglia)?
neurotransmitter.fun_fact: A single synaptic vesicle contains about 5000 molecules of neurotransmitter, yet only a few hundred are needed for recognition by the postsynaptic cell — the rest serves as a reliability buffer for transmission.

synapse.name: synapse
synapse.mini: A microscopic gap between nerve cells where an electrical signal turns into a chemical one, like a handshake between two partners.
synapse.practical_application: Synapses are information processing points in the brain; their plasticity underlies learning and memory, and failures lead to neurodegeneration.
synapse.description_popular: A synapse is a specialized structure that ensures signal transmission between neurons. It consists of a presynaptic terminal (where neurotransmitter is packaged in vesicles), a synaptic cleft (about 20–40 nanometers wide), and a postsynaptic membrane with receptors. The arrival of a nerve impulse triggers calcium ion influx, causing exocytosis of vesicles and release of the mediator, which diffuses to the receptors. The strength of a synapse can change — this is called synaptic plasticity.
synapse.fun_fact_popular: The human brain has about 100 trillion synapses — more than the number of stars in our galaxy.
synapse.description_simple: A synapse is the point of contact between two neurons where signal transmission occurs. There is a small gap that the signal crosses with the help of chemicals (neurotransmitters). Like on a factory conveyor belt: one workshop passes a part to the next, but there is a gap between them, and the part is thrown over by a courier. Excitatory synapses (speed up the receiving neuron) and inhibitory synapses (slow it down) are distinguished.
synapse.history_simple: The term 'synapse' was introduced by Charles Sherrington in 1897, combining the Greek words for 'connect' and 'together'. He realized that neurons are not fused but only touch. Later, the structure of the synapse was observed using an electron microscope.
synapse.how_it_works_simple: An electrical impulse runs along the neuron like a wave, reaches the end and says: 'Time to send the package!'. Vesicles with neurotransmitter burst, spilling their contents into the gap. The neighboring neuron catches the molecules, and a signal is born again.
synapse.description: A synapse is an intercellular contact consisting of a presynaptic terminal, synaptic cleft, and postsynaptic density. Chemical and electrical synapses are distinguished. In chemical synapses, neurotransmitter vesicles undergo a cycle of exo- and endocytosis; the SNARE protein complex plays a key role. Electrical synapses (gap junctions) provide direct electrical communication through connexons. Postsynaptic receptors are divided into ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channels) and metabotropic (G-protein coupled). Long-term potentiation and depression are the main mechanisms of synaptic plasticity.
synapse.history: Charles Sherrington introduced the concept of the synapse in 1897, based on reflex studies. Earlier, Ramón y Cajal showed that neurons are individual cells that contact each other. In the 1950s, electron microscopy confirmed the existence of the synaptic cleft. Pharmacological and electrophysiological research in the second half of the 20th century revealed the diversity of mediators and transmission mechanisms.
synapse.how_it_works: When the action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open. Ca²⁺ ions enter the terminal and trigger a cascade: vesicles merge with the membrane via SNARE proteins, releasing their contents into the cleft (quantal secretion). The mediator diffuses and binds to postsynaptic receptors, which opens ion channels, changing the membrane potential. Mediator remnants are removed by enzymes or reuptake. In electrical synapses, current passes directly through connexons. Modulation of synaptic transmission underlies cognitive processes.
key_problems: How exactly does synaptic plasticity encode memory at the molecular level?
What is the role of glia in modulating synapses?
Can age-related decline in synaptic density be reversed?
synapse.fun_fact: The total area of synaptic contacts in one cubic millimeter of cerebral cortex exceeds several square centimeters.

gamma_radiation.name: Gamma radiation
gamma_radiation.mini: The most energetic kind of light, invisible to the eye, born in the most explosive and hottest points of the Universe — from supernova explosions to black holes.
gamma_radiation.practical_application: In medicine — sterilization of instruments and cancer treatment; in astronomy — the search for dark matter and the study of extreme processes.
gamma_radiation.description_popular: Gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength less than 0.01 nm and photon energy above ~100 keV. It occupies the highest-energy part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Processes generating gamma rays include nuclear reactions, annihilation (mutual destruction) of particles and antiparticles, and the interaction of high-energy particles with magnetic fields. The Earth's atmosphere is opaque to gamma rays, so they are mainly detected by space observatories.
gamma_radiation.fun_fact_popular: Gamma-ray bursts are the most powerful explosions in the Universe: in a few seconds they release as much energy as the Sun will emit in its entire life. One such burst, recorded in 2008, was visible to the naked eye despite a distance of 7.5 billion light-years!
gamma_radiation.description_simple: Gamma rays are invisible waves, similar to light but much more energetic and dangerous. Their energy is so great that they can pass through thick layers of metal and damage living cells. They are formed when atoms decay (for example, in nuclear explosions) or when hot gas in space is accelerated to unimaginable speeds.
gamma_radiation.history_simple: Gamma radiation was discovered in 1900 by French physicist Paul Villard, who noticed that radioactive radium emits rays that are not deflected by a magnet and have enormous penetrating power. Later, Ernest Rutherford named them gamma rays.
gamma_radiation.how_it_works_simple: Gamma radiation is a stream of tiny light particles (photons) with a very short wavelength. When an atomic nucleus transitions from an excited state to a calm one, it ejects excess energy in the form of a gamma quantum. In space, powerful gamma-ray bursts occur during the collision of neutron stars or the collapse of massive stars.
gamma_radiation.description: Gamma radiation (γ-radiation) is shortwave electromagnetic radiation with photon energy typically exceeding 100 keV, corresponding to a wavelength shorter than 0.01 nm. It arises from transitions between energy levels of atomic nuclei (nuclear spectroscopy), annihilation of particle-antiparticle pairs (e.g., the electron-positron line at 511 keV), bremsstrahlung of relativistic particles, and in astrophysical accelerators — supernova remnants, accretion disks of black holes, and gamma-ray bursts. On Earth, gamma radiation is obtained using radioisotope sources (Co-60, Cs-137), nuclear reactors, and accelerators. Detection is carried out with scintillation, semiconductor, and Cherenkov detectors.
gamma_radiation.history: Gamma rays were discovered in 1900 by Paul Villard during the study of radioactive radiation from radium: he noticed a component with extremely high penetrating power, unaffected by magnetic deflection. In 1903, Ernest Rutherford named this radiation gamma rays, by analogy with alpha and beta particles. In the 1920s, Arthur Compton investigated the scattering of gamma quanta on electrons (the Compton effect), confirming the corpuscular properties of radiation. Since the mid-20th century, astronomical observations began: in the 1960s, the Vela satellites detected gamma-ray bursts, and later telescopes such as Compton, Fermi, and Integral discovered thousands of sources.
gamma_radiation.how_it_works: Gamma radiation obeys the Planck–Einstein equation: E = hν, linking photon energy to frequency. It is emitted during the relaxation of excited nuclei: a nuclide in an excited state X* → X + γ. In astrophysics, non-thermal mechanisms are common: synchrotron radiation of relativistic electrons in magnetic fields, inverse Compton scattering, where high-energy electrons transfer energy to photons, and bremsstrahlung. For gamma-ray bursts, models have been developed: the collapsar (hypernova) for long bursts and the merger of compact objects for short ones. Interaction of gamma quanta with matter occurs via the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, and electron-positron pair production (the latter dominates at energies >1.022 MeV). These processes also determine detection methods.
key_problems: Origin of cosmic gamma-ray bursts: detailed mechanism of jet and radiation generation
Nature of gamma radiation from the Galactic center (excess at energies 1-3 GeV, possibly from dark matter annihilation)
Identification of sources of high-energy gamma quanta of teraelectronvolt energies (pevatrons) in the Milky Way
Development of compact and effective detectors for nuclear medicine and security
gamma_radiation.fun_fact: Due to the Compton effect, gamma rays lose energy when scattering on electrons, and this dependence allowed the creation of Compton telescopes that reconstruct the direction to the source. The Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope detects about one gamma-ray burst per second, and the most distant one detected occurred when the Universe was less than 500 million years old.

formulas.description: Planck–Einstein equation relating the energy of a gamma quantum to its frequency
formulas.meaning: E — photon energy, h — Planck constant (h ≈ 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s), ν — frequency of the electromagnetic wave (for gamma radiation ν > 3×10¹⁹ Hz).

formulas.description: Threshold energy for electron-positron pair production by a gamma quantum in the field of a nucleus
formulas.meaning: E_thr — minimum energy of the gamma quantum for pair formation, m_e — electron mass (m_e ≈ 9.109×10⁻³¹ kg), c — speed of light in vacuum (c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s); the product 2m_e c^2 ≈ 1.022 MeV.

neuron.name: neuron
neuron.mini: A conductor cell that transmits electrical discharges along a neural circuit. Like a relay, it closes if the incoming signal exceeds a threshold.
neuron.practical_application: Artificial neural networks, inspired by the work of neurons, recognize faces, translate texts, and drive cars. Understanding neurons has allowed treating epilepsy and Parkinson's disease through brain stimulation.
neuron.description_popular: A neuron is an electrically excitable cell, the basis of the nervous system. The neuron's membrane uses ion channels to create a potential difference (resting potential around -70 mV). Upon excitation, sodium channels open, sodium ions enter, and the potential becomes positive—this is the action potential. It propagates along the axon at speeds up to 120 m/s. At synapses, the electrical signal is converted into chemical: neurotransmitters (e.g., glutamate) are released and bind to receptors of the next neuron, continuing the relay.
neuron.fun_fact_popular: The conduction speed along some axons exceeds 400 km/h. And the total number of synapses in the brain is estimated at a quadrillion (10^15).
neuron.description_simple: A neuron is a cell of the brain and nervous system that can receive and send signals. It has a body and processes: short ones (dendrites) catch signals, a long one (axon) transmits them further. The signal runs like an electric wave (impulse). Between neurons there are gaps (synapses), where the signal jumps using chemical substances (mediators).
neuron.history_simple: Spanish doctor Santiago Ramón y Cajal in the late 19th century used staining (Golgi method) to see individual neurons. He proved that the nervous system consists of cells, not a continuous web.
neuron.how_it_works_simple: When a neuron receives enough signals from neighbors, the charge inside it rapidly changes, and an impulse runs along the axon. At the end of the axon, chemical messengers are released that excite or inhibit the next neuron. Thus, information is transmitted from the sensory organs to the brain and back to the muscles.
neuron.description: A neuron is the fundamental structural and functional unit of the nervous system, specialized for generating and conducting electrical signals. It consists of a soma (body), a dendritic tree, and an axon ending in synaptic terminals. The cell membrane contains passive and active ion channels that maintain the membrane potential. The action potential is a universal electrical signal that propagates without attenuation thanks to the regenerative activation of voltage-gated sodium channels. Myelination of the axon (by Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes) dramatically speeds up conduction via the saltatory mechanism—jumping between nodes of Ranvier. At synapses, depolarization opens calcium channels, Ca²⁺ triggers exocytosis of vesicles with neurotransmitters. Postsynaptic receptors (ionotropic and metabotropic) convert the chemical signal back into an electrical one. Spatial and temporal summation of synaptic potentials determines whether an action potential will occur. Neurons are classified by neurotransmitter (glutamatergic, GABAergic, etc.), structure (unipolar, bipolar, multipolar), and function (sensory, motor, interneurons).
neuron.history: In 1873, Camillo Golgi developed a method for staining nervous tissue with silver nitrate (the Golgi stain), which made it possible to see neurons in their entirety. Santiago Ramón y Cajal, using this method in the 1880s, detailed the histology of the nervous system and formulated the neuron doctrine—the idea that the nervous system is composed of discrete cells. Their opposition to the reticular theory ended in the 20th century with the invention of the electron microscope, which confirmed the synaptic cleft. In 1952, Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley created a mathematical model of the action potential in the giant squid axon, laying the foundations of computational neuroscience.
neuron.how_it_works: The functioning of a neuron is determined by the laws of electrochemistry. The membrane separates ions: more Na⁺ outside, more K⁺ inside. The sodium-potassium ATPase (Na⁺/K⁺ pump) actively transports 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, creating ion gradients. The resting potential is close to the potassium equilibrium potential, described by the Nernst equation: E_K = (RT/F) ln([K⁺]out/[K⁺]in). Upon stimulation, voltage-gated sodium channels open, Na⁺ enters, depolarizing the membrane; when the potential reaches a threshold (~-55 mV), more sodium channels open—a positive feedback loop generates the spike. Then sodium channels inactivate, potassium channels open, expelling K⁺ and returning the potential to rest. The refractory period ensures unidirectional impulse propagation. At synapses, the action potential activates calcium channels, Ca²⁺ enters, causing vesicle fusion with the membrane and release of the neurotransmitter. The neurotransmitter diffuses to receptors; excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate) open sodium channels, inhibitory ones (GABA) open chloride or potassium channels, shifting the potential closer to the equilibrium. Synaptic plasticity (long-term potentiation) underlies memory.
key_problems: How exactly does synaptic plasticity encode long-term memory?
The role of glial cells in information processing.
Mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's).
Complete description of ion channels and their regulation.
How do cognitive functions emerge from the activity of individual neurons?
neuron.fun_fact: The giant squid axon reaches 1 mm in diameter—hundreds of times thicker than human; it was used for the first measurements of ionic currents.

formulas.description: Nernst equation for the equilibrium potential of an ion—balance between diffusion and electric field.
formulas.meaning: E_ion – equilibrium potential (V); R – universal gas constant, R ≈ 8.314 J/(mol·K); T – absolute temperature (K); z – ion charge (dimensionless); F – Faraday constant, F ≈ 96485 C/mol; [ion]_out, [ion]_in – ion concentrations outside and inside the cell.

immunity.name: immunity
immunity.mini: Immunity is an army of defenders inside us that remembers every enemy and strikes more accurately each time.
immunity.practical_application: Vaccination trains the immune system to recognize real viruses, and cancer immunotherapy teaches it to attack tumors.
immunity.description_popular: Immunity can be innate and acquired. Innate immunity reacts instantly and identically to any threat: skin and mucous membranes create a barrier, macrophages and neutrophils phagocytize (engulf) intruders, and the complement system punches holes in bacterial membranes. Acquired (adaptive) immunity starts slower but acts precisely: lymphocytes recognize specific antigens, after which B cells turn into plasma cells and release antibodies, and killer T cells destroy infected cells. This response leaves memory cells, ensuring a rapid reaction upon repeated contact.
immunity.fun_fact_popular: Breast milk contains ready-made antibodies that protect the infant from infections in the first months of life, while its own immunity is still immature.
immunity.description_simple: Immunity is the body's defense system against microbes and viruses. White blood cells (leukocytes) stand guard in the blood and tissues – they are like border guards. Upon detecting a stranger, they either immediately engulf it or produce special protein tags (antibodies) that help other defender cells find and destroy the enemy.
immunity.history_simple: English doctor Edward Jenner in 1796 noticed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not get smallpox. He made the world's first vaccination: he took fluid from a cowpox blister and introduced it to a boy – thus vaccination was born.
immunity.how_it_works_simple: When an unfamiliar microbe enters the body, the immune system studies its special characteristics (antigens) and starts producing antibodies that fit these characteristics exactly, like a key fits a lock. The antibodies cling to the enemy and neutralize it. Some memory cells remain alive for years, so that upon a repeat encounter, the reaction is immediate – this is the secret of immunity after illness or vaccination.
immunity.description: The immune system is a complex defense network that distinguishes 'self' from 'non-self'. It is based on recognition of antigens (foreign molecular structures) via lymphocyte receptors. Innate immunity (macrophages, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, the complement system, cytokines) provides an immediate response and activates the adaptive arm. Adaptive immunity is realized through clonal selection: from a vast repertoire of lymphocytes with unique receptors, those that recognize a specific antigen are selected and multiplied. T helper cells (CD4+) coordinate the response, T killer cells (CD8+) destroy infected cells, B cells differentiate into plasma cells and produce antibodies of five classes (IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, IgD). Central tolerance (in the thymus and bone marrow) eliminates autoreactive lymphocytes.
immunity.history: Since ancient times, it was observed that those who recovered from the plague did not get reinfected. Edward Jenner scientifically justified vaccination in 1796. Louis Pasteur in the 1880s created vaccines against chicken cholera and rabies. Ilya Mechnikov (1882) discovered phagocytosis, Paul Ehrlich (1891) – humoral immunity and antibodies. In 1959-62, Macfarlane Burnet and Peter Medawar uncovered the mechanisms of immunological tolerance. In 1975, Susumu Tonegawa showed how immunoglobulin genes rearrange to create billions of antibody variations.
immunity.how_it_works: The process begins with the capture of an antigen by dendritic cells, which migrate to lymph nodes and present antigen fragments on MHC II molecules to T helper cells. Activated T helpers secrete interleukins, stimulating the proliferation of B cells and their maturation into plasma cells that release millions of antibody molecules into the bloodstream. T killer cells recognize foreign peptides on MHC I of infected cells and induce apoptosis via the perforin-granzyme mechanism. Some B and T cells are preserved as memory cells (sometimes for life), ensuring a secondary response. Key molecules: antibodies (immunoglobulins), T-cell receptors (TCR), major histocompatibility complex (MHC), cytokines (interleukins, interferons).
key_problems: Etiology of autoimmune diseases and ways to safely suppress them
Creation of effective vaccines against chronic infections (HIV, malaria)
Evasion of tumors from immune surveillance and overcoming immunosuppression of the microenvironment
immunity.fun_fact: The immune system can recognize a single foreign molecule among a million self molecules thanks to the hypervariable regions of antibodies.

antibody.name: antibody
antibody.mini: Antibody — like a molecular watchdog: recognizes a stranger by its unique smell (antigen) and latches onto it to mark it for destruction.
antibody.practical_application: Antibodies are used in therapy (e.g., against COVID-19), in diagnostic tests (pregnancy tests), and in scientific experiments to detect proteins.
antibody.description_popular: Antibodies are glycoproteins of the immunoglobulin superfamily, produced by plasma cells (activated B-lymphocytes). Each antibody consists of two heavy and two light chains linked by disulfide bonds, and has a variable region for antigen recognition and a constant region that determines effector functions. There are five classes: IgM, IgG, IgA, IgE, IgD. Binding to an antigen can directly block infectivity, as well as opsonize the pathogen, activate complement and natural killer cells (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity). Monoclonal antibodies are a key tool in biotechnology and medicine.
antibody.fun_fact_popular: The human body can produce more than a billion different antibodies, although the number of genes is relatively small — diversity is achieved through the shuffling of genetic segments.
antibody.description_simple: An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein produced by the immune system. It works like a lock that is opened by only one key: each pair of ends of the Y-shaped structure recognizes only one specific antigen (foreign molecule). After binding to the antigen, the antibody either neutralizes it or attracts other cells to destroy the intruder.
antibody.history_simple: Antibodies were discovered by Emil von Behring in 1890 when he used blood serum to treat diphtheria. Later, the structure of antibodies was deciphered by Gerald Edelman and Rodney Porter.
antibody.how_it_works_simple: When a foreign agent (e.g., a virus) enters the body, specialized cells recognize it and begin producing antibodies. They act like 'Velcro', sticking to the surface of the virus and preventing it from entering cells, and also serve as tags for scavenger cells.
antibody.description: Immunoglobulins are a family of Y-shaped proteins that provide humoral immunity. Basic structure: a tetramer of two identical heavy chains (H) and two light chains (L). Each chain contains a variable domain (V) and constant domains (C).
