An antibody has two antigen-binding fragments (Fab), each comprising VH, VL and CL/CH1, and one crystallizable fragment (Fc), responsible for interaction with Fc receptors and complement. Generation of diversity occurs through V(D)J recombination, somatic hypermutation, and gene conversion. Affinity maturation in germinal centers increases the strength of antigen binding. Monoclonal antibodies are produced by hybridoma technology or recombinant methods (phage display). Bispecific antibodies, conjugates with toxins and radionuclides expand therapeutic possibilities.
antibody.history: Antibody-based immunity was discovered by Emil von Behring and Shibasaburo Kitasato in 1890 with the demonstration of passive immunization against diphtheria toxin using serum. In 1959, Gerald Edelman and Rodney Porter independently determined the structure of antibodies, for which they received the Nobel Prize. The invention of monoclonal antibody technology by César Milstein and Georges Köhler in 1975 opened the era of therapeutic antibodies.
antibody.how_it_works: Antigen recognition is based on non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, electrostatic, hydrophobic) between the hypervariable regions (CDRs) of the antibody and the antigenic epitope. Binding alters the antibody's conformation, and through the Fc fragment effector mechanisms are initiated: complement-dependent cytolysis (C1q is recruited to the Fc, triggering the cascade), antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (FcγRIII on NK cells), opsonization of phagocytes. Different isotypes perform specialized functions: IgG is the main one in blood, IgA in mucous membranes, IgE in allergies and parasites. The principle of genetic recombination and selection underlies adaptive recognition.
key_problems: Creating universal broad-spectrum antibodies against rapidly mutating viruses
Preventing immunogenicity of therapeutic antibodies
Targeted delivery of antibodies into cells to affect intracellular targets
Understanding the role of autoantibodies in neurodegenerative diseases
Using antibodies to cross the blood-brain barrier
antibody.fun_fact: Immunoglobulin G is the smallest of the antibodies, but it can cross the placental barrier, providing passive immunity to the fetus. The 'Trojan' antibody technology uses bispecific antibodies to transport therapeutic molecules across the blood-brain barrier by binding to the transferrin receptor.

ultraviolet_radiation.name: ultraviolet radiation
ultraviolet_radiation.mini: Invisible neighbor of violet — light whose energy burns skin, kills microbes, and makes some substances glow.
ultraviolet_radiation.practical_application: Tanning beds and sterilization of instruments in hospitals; checking the authenticity of banknotes by the glow of marks.
ultraviolet_radiation.description_popular: Ultraviolet radiation occupies the spectrum from 10 to 400 nm, divided into near (UVA, 315–400), middle (UVB, 280–315), far (UVC, 100–280), and vacuum ultraviolet. The main natural source is the Sun, but only UVA and a little UVB reach the surface; UVC is completely absorbed by the ozone layer. UV radiation initiates chemical reactions (e.g., vitamin D synthesis) and can cause many materials to fluoresce.
ultraviolet_radiation.fun_fact_popular: Medical quartz lamps emit UVC that destroys viral DNA, so air in operating rooms can be disinfected with light.
ultraviolet_radiation.description_simple: Ultraviolet (UV) is radiation, like light, but with shorter waves (distance between wave crests) that our eyes cannot see. It carries more energy than visible light, so it can damage cells. It is the sun's UV rays that cause tanning and burns. Bees, unlike us, see in ultraviolet, so flowers are painted with bright patterns for them.
ultraviolet_radiation.history_simple: UV was discovered by German physicist Johann Wilhelm Ritter in 1801, when he noticed that chemical reactions proceed faster beyond the violet edge of the rainbow. Later, James Maxwell described all electromagnetic waves with a unified theory.
ultraviolet_radiation.how_it_works_simple: UV is emitted by the Sun and artificial lamps. Its energy is absorbed by DNA molecules (the substance of heredity), causing mutations (changes in DNA), so nature created a protective ozone layer in the atmosphere. In sterilization lamps, special gases emit UV during discharge, which kills bacteria.
ultraviolet_radiation.description: Ultraviolet radiation is electromagnetic waves with lengths from ~10 nm to 400 nm, having photon energy of 3–124 eV. In this range, quanta can break chemical bonds, cause the photoelectric effect, and ionize atoms (starting from the extreme ultraviolet). UV is strongly absorbed by the Earth's atmosphere thanks to the ozone layer (Hartley band), which protects the biosphere. In astrophysics, the UV range carries information about hot stars, the interstellar medium, and the exospheres of planets.
ultraviolet_radiation.history: In 1801, Ritter, working with a prism, determined that beyond the violet part of the spectrum there are rays that accelerate the decomposition of silver chloride. At the end of the 19th century, it was realized that UV is part of a unified electromagnetic spectrum, whose theory was created by Maxwell. In the 20th century, the development of quantum mechanics led to the understanding of the photoelectric effect caused by UV (Einstein, 1905). The creation of efficient semiconductor UV LEDs based on gallium nitride (Nakamura's work) opened up compact radiation sources.
ultraviolet_radiation.how_it_works: According to the Planck–Einstein formula, the energy of a photon E = hν determines the ability of UV to cause chemical processes. The photoeffect is explained by Einstein's equation E_k max = hν – W, where W is the work function. In astrophysics, the spectrum of hot stars obeys Wien's displacement law λ_max = b/T (T > 10000 K gives a peak in UV). UV telescopes on satellites (e.g., GALEX) use multi-mirror systems to focus hard radiation, since ordinary lenses absorb UV.
key_problems: Lack of cheap and durable far UV (UVC) sources
Increase in skin cancer incidence due to ozone layer depletion
Development of optics for vacuum UV that can work without absorption
ultraviolet_radiation.fun_fact: Ultraviolet 'sees' what is hidden from the eyes: under its rays, old paintings reveal the artist's corrections, and at a crime scene invisible traces appear.

formulas.description: Energy of a UV photon (Planck–Einstein equation)
formulas.meaning: E — photon energy, h ≈ 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s — Planck constant, ν — radiation frequency, c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s — speed of light, λ — wavelength

formulas.description: Einstein's equation for the photoelectric effect
formulas.meaning: E_k max — maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electron, h — Planck constant, ν — frequency of incident UV, W — work function of the material (energy needed to detach an electron)

formulas.description: Wien's displacement law for the peak of thermal radiation
formulas.meaning: λ_max — wavelength of maximum emission, b ≈ 2.898×10⁻³ m·K — Wien's constant, T — temperature of the black body

rna.name: RNA
rna.mini: RNA is a working copy of instructions from DNA, a single-stranded molecule that carries information and participates in protein synthesis.
rna.practical_application: RNA-based technologies, such as mRNA vaccines, enable rapid development of protection against new viruses.
rna.description_popular: RNA is a long chain (polymer) of nucleotides (building blocks). It is usually single-stranded, and uses ribose as its sugar (instead of deoxyribose, as in DNA), and contains uracil instead of thymine. RNA types differ by role: messenger (mRNA) — carries instructions from DNA to ribosomes (cellular protein synthesis machines); transfer (tRNA) — delivers amino acids for protein assembly; ribosomal (rRNA) — forms the ribosomes themselves. There are also regulatory RNAs (e.g., microRNAs that fine-tune protein production) and catalytic RNAs (ribozymes capable of accelerating chemical reactions).
rna.fun_fact_popular: Some viruses, such as HIV or SARS-CoV-2, use RNA as their genetic material, and their variability is due to the high error rate (mutations) during RNA copying.
rna.description_simple: RNA is like a tape with written text copied from DNA. It uses the same base letters, but U (uracil) instead of T (thymine). It is more flexible and short-lived than DNA. There are different types of RNA: messenger (mRNA) — carries the instructions; transfer (tRNA) — brings amino acids; ribosomal (rRNA) — builds the protein.
rna.history_simple: RNA was discovered in 1961 when scientists realized that a messenger was needed to transfer information from DNA. Later it was found that some viruses store genetic information as RNA.
rna.how_it_works_simple: When a cell needs a protein, a copy in the form of mRNA is read from the required section of DNA. This mRNA leaves the nucleus (the cell's DNA storage) into the cytoplasm (the cell's interior), where the ribosome (protein factory) assembles the protein by attaching amino acids brought by tRNA.
rna.description: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) is a linear polymer consisting of ribonucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds. Each nucleotide includes ribose, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base: adenine (A), uracil (U), guanine (G), cytosine (C). Unlike DNA, RNA is usually single-stranded and can adopt complex three-dimensional structures, which determines its catalytic properties. Major types: messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), ribosomal RNA (rRNA), as well as regulatory (microRNAs, small interfering RNAs) and catalytic (ribozymes). RNA synthesis (transcription) is carried out by RNA polymerases. In eukaryotes, mRNA undergoes processing: capping, polyadenylation, and splicing. RNA can serve as the genome in many viruses (retroviruses, coronaviruses). The RNA world theory suggests that RNA was the first molecule capable of storing information and catalyzing chemical reactions.
rna.history: RNA was first isolated in 1868 by Friedrich Miescher, but its role remained unclear for a long time. In 1939, it was shown that RNA participates in protein synthesis. In 1961, mRNA was discovered, and in 1965, the structure of tRNA was deciphered. In the 1980s, the catalytic properties of RNA (ribozymes) were discovered, strengthening the RNA world hypothesis. With the discovery of RNA interference in the 1990s, the development of RNA-based technologies began, including mRNA vaccines.
rna.how_it_works: RNA is synthesized in the nucleus during transcription: RNA polymerase unwinds a DNA segment and builds a complementary RNA strand. In eukaryotes, the primary pre-mRNA transcript undergoes splicing (removal of introns) and modifications. Mature mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm, where it binds to a ribosome. The ribosome—a complex of rRNA and proteins—moves along the mRNA and, with the help of tRNAs carrying amino acids, synthesizes a polypeptide chain. Each tRNA has an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon. The process is regulated by various factors, and small regulatory RNAs can suppress gene expression by degrading mRNA or blocking translation.
key_problems: The precise origin of RNA in prebiotic conditions
Details of splicing mechanisms
The role of epitranscriptomic modifications
rna.fun_fact: The length of the largest known RNA—titin protein mRNA—is about 100,000 nucleotides, and its synthesis time can exceed an hour.

crispr.name: CRISPR
crispr.mini: CRISPR is molecular scissors that can cut DNA at a precisely specified location, allowing editing of the genetic code.
crispr.practical_application: CRISPR technology is used to treat hereditary diseases, create pest-resistant plants, and modify animals for research.
crispr.description_popular: CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) is a bacterial immune system turned into a universal tool for genetic engineering. It consists of two components: a guide RNA (sgRNA) complementary to the target DNA segment, and the Cas endonuclease (most often Cas9). The complex scans DNA, recognizes the target site by complementarity, and creates a double-strand break. Repair of the break via non-homologous end joining leads to insertions/deletions, disabling the gene; homologous recombination with a donor template allows precise changes to be made. This technology is significantly simpler and cheaper than previous methods.
crispr.fun_fact_popular: With CRISPR, pigs resistant to African swine fever have already been created, and human embryo genes have been edited to correct a mutation causing heart disease.
crispr.description_simple: CRISPR is a tool for editing genes (hereditary instructions). It works like a 'find and replace' function in text: a scientist specifies the desired DNA sequence (like a word), and the Cas enzyme finds it in the genome and cuts it. Then the cell repairs the break itself, making changes or inserting a new fragment. It’s as if a proofreader in a printing house cut out a typo and pasted in the correct letter.
crispr.history_simple: The CRISPR/Cas system was discovered by Francisco Mojica and other scientists studying bacterial defense mechanisms. In 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier adapted it for gene editing.
crispr.how_it_works_simple: A guide RNA (a molecular guide) directs the Cas protein to the desired location in the DNA. The protein cuts both strands, and the cell initiates emergency repair. Scientists can add a template with the correct sequence, and the cell will copy it during repair.
crispr.description: CRISPR/Cas9 is an adaptive system based on RNA-guided DNA cleavage. Originally, it is part of the adaptive immunity of bacteria and archaea: they integrate sequences from invading viruses into their CRISPR locus, then use transcribed RNA copies to recognize and destroy phage DNA upon reinfection. For gene editing, Cas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes or other variants (Cas12a, Cas13, Cas9 nickases) are used. Specificity is determined by the length of the guide RNA and the presence of a PAM (protospacer adjacent motif) — a short sequence near the target site. After creating a break, the cell initiates repair mechanisms: NHEJ (non-homologous end joining) and HDR (homology-directed repair). Off-target effects are possible, minimized by engineered Cas variants with increased accuracy. The technology is used for gene knockout, transcriptional activation/inhibition, epigenetic editing, and diagnostics (SHERLOCK, DETECTR).
crispr.history: The idea of genome editing with nucleases evolved from zinc fingers and TALEN, but the discovery of CRISPR was a revolution. Francisco Mojica in 1993 discovered repetitive sequences in the archaeal genome, later their function in immunity was elucidated. In 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier reprogrammed the system for laboratory use. Feng Zhang and colleagues in 2013 first applied CRISPR for editing eukaryotic genomes. For this, Doudna and Charpentier received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.
crispr.how_it_works: The mechanism is based on complementary binding of RNA to DNA and subsequent hydrolysis of phosphodiester bonds. Cas9 contains two nuclease domains: HNH cleaves the strand complementary to the RNA, and RuvC cleaves the non-complementary strand. The guide RNA consists of crRNA (containing a spacer complementary to the target) and tracrRNA, necessary for binding to Cas. Combining them into a single sgRNA simplified use. The DNA break triggers a cellular response: NHEJ quickly ligates the ends, introducing insertions/deletions, which often inactivates the gene; HDR requires the presence of donor DNA and occurs less frequently, but allows precise editing. Specificity is limited by the thermodynamic stability of the hybrid and the possibility of mismatched binding, but engineered Cas mutations (HiFi-Cas9) reduce off-target cleavage.
key_problems: Increasing delivery specificity and minimizing off-target modifications
Ethical limitations of human embryo editing
Controlling DNA repair to increase homologous recombination efficiency
Delivery to non-dividing cells and tissues in vivo
Understanding long-term consequences of genome modification
crispr.fun_fact: The CRISPR/Cas system can be used not only for cutting, but also for DNA methylation or attaching fluorescent labels, turning it into a tool for observing chromatin in real time.

stem_cell.name: stem cell
stem_cell.mini: A creator cell that can turn into other cells of the body, like clay from which any shapes can be molded.
stem_cell.practical_application: Stem cells repair damaged tissues and organs — they are used to treat leukemia, burns, and test new drugs.
stem_cell.description_popular: Stem cells are distinguished by two properties: self-renewal (unlimited division without loss of potential) and potency — the ability to differentiate into specialized types. Totipotent cells (zygote) can create an entire organism; pluripotent (embryonic) — all tissues except extraembryonic membranes; multipotent (adult) — a limited set of cells. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are obtained by activating certain genes in mature cells.
stem_cell.fun_fact_popular: More than 80 diseases, including some types of cancer and anemia, are successfully treated with umbilical cord blood stem cells.
stem_cell.description_simple: Stem cells are cells without a specialty but with an outstanding ability: they can divide and become any other cells of the body (neurons, muscles, bones). There are two main types: embryonic (obtained from early embryos — embryos at an early stage of development), which can give rise to a whole organism, and adult (in bone marrow, skin), which repair individual damages. Just as a cook can make both bread and pancakes from one dough, a stem cell generates different tissues.
stem_cell.history_simple: In the 1960s, Ernest McCulloch and James Till discovered hematopoietic stem cells in mice. Then human embryonic stem cells were isolated (1998), and in 2006 Shinya Yamanaka created induced stem cells by reprogramming ordinary adult cells.
stem_cell.how_it_works_simple: When dividing, stem cells create one twin copy (self-renewal) and one cell that begins to specialize under the influence of chemical signals. For example, in the bone marrow, signals cause descendants to become red or white blood cells.
stem_cell.description: Stem cells are characterized by asymmetric division, in which one daughter cell retains stemness and the other enters the path of differentiation. Pluripotent stem cells maintain the expression of key transcription factors OCT4, SOX2, NANOG, forming an autoregulatory network. Their differentiation into three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) and further into specialized cells is regulated by signaling pathways (Wnt, BMP, Notch, FGF). The microenvironment (niche) through extracellular matrix components and paracrine factors determines the balance between quiescence, self-renewal, and commitment. The iPSC technology (Shinya Yamanaka, 2006) is based on transient overexpression of the genes Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc, reverting somatic cells to a pluripotent state. Hematopoietic stem cells are clinically used for bone marrow transplantation, and methods of cell therapy for regeneration of myocardium, neurons, and pancreatic β-cells are being developed.
stem_cell.history: The idea of stem cells dates back to the work of Ernst Haeckel (1868) and August Weismann (1885). Experimental confirmation was provided by Canadian hematologists Ernest McCulloch and James Till, who discovered spleen colony-forming units — hematopoietic stem cells of the mouse in 1963. The isolation of human embryonic stem cells by Martin Evans (1981 for mouse, 1998 for human) and the creation of induced pluripotent stem cells by Shinya Yamanaka (2006, Nobel Prize 2012) opened the era of regenerative medicine.
stem_cell.how_it_works: The molecular machinery of pluripotency includes mutually reinforcing transcription factors OCT4, SOX2, NANOG, which bind their own promoters and each other's promoters, and also repress differentiation genes through recruitment of polycomb repressor complexes. Signaling molecules of the niche (SCF, Notch ligands, Wnt) activate intracellular cascades that alter the epigenetic landscape of DNA methylation and histone modifications, switching the cell from a naive to a primed state of pluripotency. Differentiation proceeds as a sequential loss of potencies with parallel activation of tissue-specific genes. Upon transplantation, stem cells are subject to the risk of teratoma formation, therefore methods of directed in vitro differentiation with subsequent purification of target populations are being developed.
key_problems: How to avoid tumor (teratoma) formation during stem cell transplantation?
Is it possible to completely reverse cellular aging?
Ethical limitations of using embryonic stem cells.
stem_cell.fun_fact: In 2013, mini-brains were grown from stem cells — organoids the size of a pea, spontaneously generating neural activity similar to an embryonic brain.

bioinformatics.name: bioinformatics
bioinformatics.mini: Bioinformatics is a 'translator' from the language of biology to the language of mathematics and back. It helps find meaning in mountains of biological data, just as a decoder reads encrypted messages.
bioinformatics.practical_application: Thanks to bioinformatics, scientists can find bacterial antibiotic resistance genes in a matter of days and develop new vaccines by analyzing protein sequences.
bioinformatics.description_popular: Bioinformatics is an interdisciplinary field that develops methods and software tools for understanding biological data. It combines computer science, statistics, mathematics, and engineering to analyze and interpret high-throughput experimental data (genomics, proteomics, metabolomics). Key tasks include genome annotation, protein structure prediction, evolutionary analysis, and systems biology.
bioinformatics.fun_fact_popular: The world's largest database of genetic sequences (GenBank) doubles roughly every 18 months and now contains trillions of nucleotides—more than the number of stars in the Milky Way.
bioinformatics.description_simple: Bioinformatics bridges biology and computer science. If a genome is a huge text, bioinformatics is the software that reads, compares, and finds errors in that text. It uses computers to store, search, and analyze biological data (DNA sequences, protein structures, etc.). Note: sequencing is reading the order of 'letters' in DNA.
bioinformatics.history_simple: Bioinformatics emerged in the 1960s with the first computer programs for protein sequence analysis, but it truly flourished in the 1990s with the start of the Human Genome Project.
bioinformatics.how_it_works_simple: Just as a search engine finds similar phrases in different books, bioinformatics algorithms compare genes from different organisms to identify common functions or ancestors.
bioinformatics.description: Bioinformatics is a scientific discipline that encompasses the creation and application of computational algorithms, statistical models, databases, and visualizations to solve biological problems. It includes sequence analysis (alignment, motif search, phylogenetics), structural bioinformatics (protein folding prediction, molecular docking), systems biology (modeling of gene networks, metabolic pathways), and the processing of single-cell and metagenomic data. Machine learning, especially deep neural networks (AlphaFold), has revolutionized the prediction of three-dimensional protein structures.
bioinformatics.history: The roots of bioinformatics go back to the 1960s, when Margaret Oakley Dayhoff created the first protein sequence data bank and amino acid substitution matrices. In the 1970s, the Needleman–Wunsch and Smith–Waterman sequence alignment algorithms were developed. The Human Genome Project (1990–2003) provided a powerful impetus, requiring the assembly and annotation of an entire genome. In the last decade, progress has accelerated thanks to cloud computing and artificial intelligence.
bioinformatics.how_it_works: A typical bioinformatics pipeline includes: preprocessing of raw data (e.g., adapter trimming and quality control in sequencing), alignment to a reference genome or de novo assembly, variant calling, gene mapping, and functional analysis. Statistical methods (Bayesian inference, hidden Markov models) play a central role.
key_problems: Accurate prediction of the function of uncharacterized proteins from sequence and structure.
Integration of heterogeneous data (genomics, proteomics, metabolomics, clinical records) into unified predictive models.
Analysis of vast amounts of single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics data.
Creation of complete computational models of an entire cell or organism.
bioinformatics.fun_fact: One of the early successes of bioinformatics in the 1980s was the discovery of the v-sis oncogene in simian sarcoma virus by comparing its sequence with the human platelet-derived growth factor gene; this showed how the virus 'stole' a cellular gene and turned it into a cancer-causing one.

evolution.name: evolution
evolution.mini: Species do not remain unchanged — they adapt to the environment, like clay changing shape under fingers. Those with favorable random changes survive and reproduce.
evolution.practical_application: Understanding evolution helps create vaccines against rapidly mutating viruses and explains bacterial resistance to antibiotics. Plant and animal breeding is accelerated evolution under human control.
evolution.description_popular: Biological evolution is the change in heritable characteristics of populations over generations. Its main mechanisms: mutations (DNA changes), gene recombination during sexual reproduction, gene flow (exchange of individuals between populations), genetic drift (random fluctuations in gene variant frequencies), and natural selection. Natural selection directs evolution: traits that increase fitness (the ability to survive and reproduce) gradually spread. Population separation (geographic barriers) can lead to speciation.
evolution.fun_fact_popular: The octopus eye and the human eye are structured very similarly but developed independently — this is an example of convergent evolution: similar conditions produce similar solutions.
evolution.description_simple: Evolution is the gradual change of living beings from generation to generation. Imagine a flock of sparrows: some have slightly stronger beaks, others weaker. In a hungry year, birds with strong beaks can crack more seeds, survive, and leave more chicks with similar beaks. After many years, the beak of the entire population becomes stronger. This is natural selection (nature 'chooses' the fittest). Random changes — mutations (errors in genes) — provide the material for selection.
evolution.history_simple: The idea of evolution was proposed by Charles Darwin after a round-the-world voyage. In 1859, he published the book 'On the Origin of Species,' where he proved that all species are related by common descent and change through natural selection.
evolution.how_it_works_simple: In every population, there are different variants of traits (variation). Those that help survive and leave more offspring become more common over time. The environment filters out less successful variants. Thus, millions of years ago, fish developed fins, and land animals developed legs.
evolution.description: Evolution in biology is the process of change in the genetic composition of populations over time, leading to adaptation, speciation, and biodiversity. The modern synthetic theory of evolution integrates Darwinism, Mendelian genetics, and population genetics. Mutations are the source of genetic variation; recombination and sexual reproduction create new allele combinations. Natural selection acts on phenotypes, changing allele frequencies in the gene pool. Genetic drift is especially important in small populations. Microevolution (changes within species) and macroevolution (origin of new species and taxa) are connected. Modern methods of molecular phylogenetics allow reconstructing evolutionary trees by comparing DNA sequences.
evolution.history: The idea of species transformation dates back to antiquity, but scientific substantiation emerged in the 19th century. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently formulated the concept of natural selection; Darwin published it in 1859 in 'On the Origin of Species.' Gregor Mendel discovered the laws of heredity in 1865, which later formed the basis of genetics. In the early 20th century, the synthesis of Mendelism and Darwinism led to the formation of the synthetic theory of evolution (S.S. Chetverikov, J.B.S. Haldane, R. Fisher, S. Wright). The discovery of the DNA structure (1953) and the development of molecular biology provided a direct mechanism for heredity and mutations.
evolution.how_it_works: The evolutionary process is based on four main factors: mutations, recombination, genetic drift, and natural selection. Mutations randomly change the DNA sequence; most are neutral or harmful, but some confer an advantage. Recombination during meiosis shuffles paternal and maternal chromosomes, creating new allele combinations. Genetic drift causes random changes in allele frequencies, especially in small populations. Natural selection increases the frequency of alleles that enhance fitness in a given environment. Mathematically, this is described by the Hardy-Weinberg law, which shows equilibrium in the absence of evolutionary forces. Speciation often occurs through geographic isolation, where accumulated differences lead to reproductive incompatibility.
key_problems: The origin of life and the transition from non-living to living.
Rates of evolution: gradualism vs. punctuated equilibrium.
The role of horizontal gene transfer in bacteria.
Evolution of complex structures, such as the flagellum.
Interaction of evolution and development (evo-devo).
Mechanisms for maintaining genetic variation.
evolution.fun_fact: Humans and bananas share about 60% of genes — a result of a common evolutionary ancestor that lived hundreds of millions of years ago.

formulas.description: Hardy-Weinberg law — a model describing the equilibrium of allele frequencies in an ideal population (without evolutionary forces).
formulas.meaning: p — frequency of the dominant allele; q — frequency of the recessive allele; p + q = 1; p² — proportion of homozygous dominant genotypes; 2pq — proportion of heterozygotes; q² — proportion of homozygous recessive genotypes.

gene.name: gene
gene.mini: A gene is a recipe written in DNA for creating a protein that determines a certain trait of an organism, such as eye color.
gene.practical_application: Genetic tests allow predicting predisposition to diseases, and gene therapy is already correcting defective genes to treat hereditary diseases.
gene.description_popular: A gene is a segment of DNA containing information about the structure of a polypeptide chain (protein) or functional RNA. Each gene has a specific location on a chromosome (a compact packaging of DNA). It consists of exons (coding regions) and introns (non-coding inserts removed during splicing—a cutting process). Gene expression is its transformation into function: first transcription (copying the gene into messenger RNA), then translation (converting the nucleotide sequence into an amino acid chain). Regulatory sequences control when and in which cells a gene is active. Alleles are variants of the same gene that determine, for example, different eye color.
gene.fun_fact_popular: Genetically, humans and bananas are 60% identical because many basic genes necessary for cell life are highly conserved across different species.
gene.description_simple: A gene is a section of the DNA molecule (a long chain storing hereditary information). It contains instructions for building a specific protein (the main building and working material of the cell). Proteins make us who we are: they shape facial features, height, hair, and also control all processes in the body. Genes are passed from parents to children—that's why we have common traits with mom and dad. The human body contains about 20–25 thousand genes.
gene.history_simple: The concept of the gene appeared in the late 19th century thanks to Gregor Mendel's experiments with peas, although he did not use the word itself. The term 'gene' was proposed by Danish botanist Wilhelm Johannsen in 1909. And the deciphering of the DNA structure by Watson and Crick in 1953 showed how genes are physically arranged.
gene.how_it_works_simple: A gene works like a program. First, a copy is made from it—an RNA molecule (similar to DNA but more mobile). Then RNA goes to ribosomes—the 'assembly machines' of the cell. The ribosome reads the instructions and links amino acids into a chain, creating a protein. This protein then performs its function: it becomes part of a muscle, a hormone, or an enzyme that speeds up chemical reactions.
gene.description: A gene is a section of the DNA molecule that serves as a template for the synthesis of a functional product: a protein or non-coding RNA (tRNA, rRNA, miRNA, etc.). The exact definition of a gene continues to evolve with the development of genomics; it includes not only coding sequences (open reading frames) but also all regulatory elements: promoters, enhancers, silencers, transcription factor binding sites. Eukaryotic genes have a mosaic structure: exons alternate with introns, and alternative splicing allows one gene to encode several different proteins. The human genome contains about 3.1 billion nucleotide pairs, of which only about 1.5% code for proteins, the rest being non-coding DNA performing regulatory functions. Mutations in genes can lead to changes in protein structure or disruption of regulation, which underlies many hereditary diseases.
gene.history: The origin of the concept of the gene is associated with the work of Gregor Mendel (1866), who described discrete hereditary factors. The term 'gene' was introduced by Johannsen in 1909 to denote the unit of heredity. In 1910, Thomas Morgan proved that genes are located on chromosomes. The unraveling of the nature of the gene as a segment of DNA belongs to molecular biology of the 1940s–1950s, culminating in the discovery of the double helix by Watson and Crick in 1953. Erwin Schrödinger in his book 'What is Life?' (1944) predicted that hereditary information should be stored in an 'aperiodic crystal,' which stimulated the search for the structure of DNA.
gene.how_it_works: The mechanism of gene action involves several stages. Transcription initiation begins with the binding of RNA polymerase to the promoter. With the participation of transcription factors, it unwinds the double helix and synthesizes pre-mRNA complementary to the template DNA strand. Processing includes capping, polyadenylation, and splicing—removal of introns and joining of exons. Mature mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm, where the ribosome, with the help of tRNAs carrying amino acids, carries out translation: the sequence of nucleotide triplets (codons) determines the sequence of amino acids in the protein. Post-translational modifications give the protein its final shape and activity. Regulation of gene expression occurs at all these stages and is critically important for cell differentiation and response to the environment.
key_problems: the role of non-coding DNA in evolution and development
complete understanding of genome regulation and epigenetics
accurate prediction of protein structure from gene sequence
safe and precise in vivo gene therapy
gene.fun_fact: The largest human gene is the dystrophin gene; it contains 2.4 million nucleotide pairs and is associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy; its transcription takes about 16 hours.

sequencing.name: sequencing
sequencing.mini: Reading the genetic code letter by letter, like deciphering a cipher written with DNA molecules.
sequencing.practical_application: Medical diagnostics of hereditary diseases, creation of personalized medicine, tracking virus evolution, forensics.
sequencing.description_popular: Sequencing is the determination of the nucleotide sequence of DNA or RNA. Modern methods include Sanger sequencing (with dideoxynucleotides and capillary electrophoresis) and high-throughput technologies (NGS), such as Illumina (synthesis with reversible terminators), pyrosequencing, and nanopore sequencing. The principle is based on base complementarity and detection of a signal from the incorporation of each nucleotide into the growing chain.
sequencing.fun_fact_popular: The first complete sequencing of the human genome took 13 years and cost nearly $3 billion; now it is done in a day and for less than $1000.
sequencing.description_simple: Sequencing is a way to find out the order of 'letters' in a DNA or RNA molecule. There are only four letters: A, T, G, C (adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine). Imagine a very long string of beads of four colors—sequencing allows you to record the sequence of colors. Today, special machines do this, and they can read an entire human genome in a day.
sequencing.history_simple: Sequencing methods began to be developed in the 1970s. Frederick Sanger invented a method for which he received the Nobel Prize—he used termination of DNA synthesis at random points, and then reconstructed the sequence from the lengths of the fragments. Later, faster technologies emerged—so-called next-generation sequencing.
sequencing.how_it_works_simple: DNA is like a book written in invisible ink. The sequencer 'develops' the text: it copies the fragment many times, and then reads, letter by letter, the signal given by each added letter—for example, a flash of a certain color.
sequencing.description: Sequencing is a set of methods for determining the linear sequence of nucleotides in a polymer nucleic acid molecule. It includes fragment library preparation, amplification (PCR or clonal on a solid phase), synthesis of the complementary strand with detection of each step. The Sanger method uses dideoxynucleotide triphosphates that terminate synthesis; separation of fragments by length gives the sequence. NGS platforms (Illumina, Ion Torrent, Pacific Biosciences, Oxford Nanopore) differ in chemistry and type of detected signal—fluorescence, pH, electric current. Bioinformatics processing assembles short reads into contigs and aligns them to a reference genome.
sequencing.history: In 1977, Sanger proposed an enzymatic method for DNA sequencing using dideoxy analogs; simultaneously, Maxam and Gilbert developed a chemical method. In the 1990s, automation with capillary electrophoresis accelerated the process. The breakthrough was the advent of NGS in the 2000s (454, Solexa/Illumina), which allowed parallel sequencing of millions of fragments. The latest technologies (PacBio, Nanopore) read single molecules in real time.
sequencing.how_it_works: General scheme: DNA is fragmented, adapters are ligated to the ends. In Illumina technology, fragments hybridize on a flow cell and are amplified by bridge PCR, forming clusters. Then sequencing-by-synthesis occurs: reversible terminators with fluorophores are added, after each cycle an image is taken, the terminator is removed, and the cycle repeats. Image analysis converts signal intensity into a nucleotide sequence. In nanopore sequencing (Oxford Nanopore), a DNA strand is passed through a protein pore and the change in ionic current, specific for each nucleotide, is measured.
key_problems: How to make sequencing cheaper and faster for routine use at the point of care?
How to improve reading accuracy in regions with repeats and modifications?
How to directly sequence RNA and proteins at molecular resolution?
sequencing.fun_fact: Sequencing the DNA of a mammoth preserved in permafrost allows studying its genetics and even discussing the possibility of resurrecting the species.

moon.name: Moon
moon.mini: The nearest celestial body, the eternal satellite of Earth, which with its gravity raises the oceans and illuminates the night sky with reflected sunlight.
moon.practical_application: Stabilizes Earth's rotation axis, causing tides that affect navigation, coastal ecosystems and potentially used for tidal energy.
moon.description_popular: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and the fifth largest satellite in the Solar System. It formed about 4.5 billion years ago, likely from debris ejected into orbit after a collision between Earth and a Mars-sized body. Its surface is covered with impact craters, and the dark areas — the lunar maria — are solidified basaltic lava plains. The lack of atmosphere leads to extreme temperature variations: from +127°C during the day to -173°C at night.
moon.fun_fact_popular: From Earth, only one side of the Moon is visible due to tidal locking (gravitational synchronization of rotation), but that doesn't mean the far side is always dark — day and night alternate there just like on the visible side. The first images of the far side were taken by the Soviet probe Luna 3 in 1959.
moon.description_simple: The Moon is a large rocky ball that orbits Earth. It shines because it reflects sunlight. Its surface is covered with craters from meteorite impacts and dark plains that were once mistaken for seas.
moon.history_simple: People have observed the Moon since ancient times. In 1609, Galileo Galilei first pointed a telescope at it and saw mountains and craters. Later, scientists realized that the craters were formed by impacts.
moon.how_it_works_simple: The Moon is kept near Earth by gravity. It completes a full orbit around Earth in about 27 days. It always faces us with the same side because it rotates on its axis at the same rate. The Moon's gravity causes tides in the oceans.
moon.description: The Moon is a rocky planetary body with a radius of 1737 km, orbiting Earth in an elliptical orbit with an average distance of 384,400 km and eccentricity of 0.0549. Its average density is 3.34 g/cm³, significantly lower than Earth's, indicating a low iron content. The Moon is differentiated into a crust, mantle, and possibly a small liquid outer core. The surface is divided into two main types of terrain: light highlands, heavily cratered, and dark maria, filled with basaltic lavas. The composition is similar to Earth's mantle, supporting the giant impact hypothesis. Tidal interaction with Earth slows Earth's rotation and moves the Moon away by about 3.8 cm per year.
moon.history: Ancient civilizations worshipped the Moon and used its phases for calendars. In 1609, Galileo Galilei used a telescope to sketch lunar mountains and craters, disproving the idea of perfect celestial spheres. In 1665, Robert Hooke in 'Micrographia' described lunar craters in detail and suggested their impact origin. The space race began in the 20th century: in 1959, Luna 2 reached the surface, and in 1969, Apollo 11 made the first manned landing. Analysis of returned samples revealed a striking similarity to Earth rocks, strengthening the impact hypothesis. Modern missions like LRO and Chang'e continue to map the Moon and search for water ice in polar craters.
moon.how_it_works: The motion of the Moon is described by Kepler's laws and the law of universal gravitation. The orbit is perturbed by the Sun and planets, leading to librations that allow us to see slightly more than half the surface. The main feature is tidal locking: due to tidal forces, the Moon always faces Earth with the same side, as its rotation period around its axis equals its orbital period. This results from the dissipation of tidal friction energy. The Moon's gravitational influence on Earth causes tides, which slow Earth's rotation and transfer orbital momentum to the Moon, increasing its distance.
key_problems: Origin of the Moon: although the giant impact hypothesis dominates, questions remain about the isotope composition being identical to Earth's
Presence of water in polar craters and the possibility of its extraction for future bases
Internal structure: does a liquid core exist, and how does it generate a residual magnetic field
Nature of lunar swirls and magnetic anomalies
moon.fun_fact: Lunar laser ranging, begun with the installation of corner reflectors by Apollo astronauts, allowed measuring the distance to the Moon with millimeter precision and revealed that it is receding from Earth at about 3.8 cm per year — roughly the same rate as human fingernails grow.

formulas.description: Law of universal gravitation describing the force of attraction between Earth and the Moon
formulas.meaning: F is the gravitational force, G is the gravitational constant (G ≈ 6.674×10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²)), M_Earth is the mass of Earth (≈ 5.97×10²⁴ kg), M_Moon is the mass of the Moon (≈ 7.35×10²² kg), R is the distance between the centers of Earth and the Moon (≈ 3.84×10⁸ m).

formulas.description: Distance to the Moon by laser ranging method
formulas.meaning: d is the distance from the telescope to the corner reflector on the Moon, c is the speed of light in vacuum (c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s), Δt is the round-trip travel time of the laser pulse.

protein.name: protein
protein.mini: Protein is a molecular machine built from a chain of amino acids that performs almost all work in the cell: from oxygen transport to protection against microbes.
protein.practical_application: Proteins are part of food, enzymes in laundry detergents, and their design using AI opens the way to new drugs.
protein.description_popular: Proteins are large molecules built from one or more chains of amino acids (polypeptide chains). Amino acids are connected by special bonds (peptide bonds). From 20 types of amino acids, a unique sequence is formed that determines how the chain folds into a three-dimensional shape. Proteins perform many tasks: they act as catalysts (enzymes that speed up chemical reactions), transporters, building materials, signaling molecules, and defenders (antibodies).
protein.fun_fact_popular: Spider web is almost pure fibroin protein, which surpasses steel of the same weight in tensile strength.
protein.description_simple: Protein is like beads, where each bead is an amino acid. There are only 20 types, but they can be arranged into an infinite variety of forms. The folded chain becomes a protein with its function. For example, hemoglobin carries oxygen, and keratin makes hair strong.
protein.history_simple: The word 'protein' comes from egg white, which coagulates when heated. In the 19th century, chemists began studying the composition of proteins, and in the 1950s, the first spatial structure of a protein was deciphered.
protein.how_it_works_simple: A gene in DNA encodes the sequence of amino acids in a protein. The cell assembles the protein on a ribosome (a molecular machine for protein assembly), like on an assembly line. Then the chain folds itself into the required three-dimensional shape, which determines its function.
protein.description: Proteins are linear polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. The order of amino acids is determined by the genetic code. The folding of the polypeptide chain into the native three-dimensional conformation occurs spontaneously and is determined by the amino acid sequence (Anfinsen's hypothesis). Structural hierarchy: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helices, β-sheets), tertiary (overall folding), and quaternary (assembly of subunits). Proteins perform catalytic (enzymes), structural (collagen, keratin), transport (hemoglobin), protective (antibodies), signaling (receptors, hormones), and motor (myosin) functions. Their dysfunction underlies many diseases. Structure determination methods include X-ray crystallography, NMR, and cryo-electron microscopy.
protein.history: The concept of proteins as a special class of substances emerged in the 18th century. In 1838, Jöns Jacob Berzelius proposed the term 'protein'. In 1902, Franz Hofmeister discovered that amino acids are linked by peptide bonds. The primary structure of a protein (insulin) was deciphered by Frederick Sanger in 1953. The spatial structure of myoglobin was determined in 1958 by John Kendrew using X-ray crystallography, whose methods were developed by William Lawrence Bragg. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AlphaFold) has revolutionized protein structure prediction.
protein.how_it_works: Proteins are synthesized on ribosomes during translation. Genetic information from mRNA is read by codons; tRNA delivers the corresponding amino acid. The growing polypeptide chain often undergoes post-translational modifications (phosphorylation, glycosylation, etc.), which affect protein activity and localization. Protein folding often occurs with the help of molecular chaperones. Misfolding leads to aggregation and diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's disease). Proteins can interact with other molecules with high specificity, forming complex networks of signaling pathways.
key_problems: Complete understanding of the protein folding mechanism
Prediction of protein functions de novo
Creation of artificial proteins with desired properties
protein.fun_fact: The largest known protein is titin (about 34,350 amino acids), which works as a molecular spring in muscles.

metabolism.name: metabolism
metabolism.mini: Just as a stove burns wood for heat, your body 'burns' food to live and move.
metabolism.practical_application: Metabolism determines how many calories you burn at rest — this is the foundation of diets and workouts.
metabolism.description_popular: Metabolism combines two streams of reactions: catabolism (breakdown of complex substances with energy release) and anabolism (synthesis of compounds necessary for the body with energy expenditure). Basal metabolism — the minimum energy expenditure to sustain life — accounts for about 60–75% of daily calorie consumption. Metabolic rate depends on age, gender, muscle mass, thyroid hormones, and genetics.
metabolism.fun_fact_popular: The hummingbird has one of the fastest metabolisms among vertebrates: its heart beats up to 1,200 times per minute, and it must eat every 10–15 minutes or it will die of exhaustion.
metabolism.description_simple: Metabolism is all the chemical transformations in the body that turn food into energy and building blocks. Your cell is a tiny factory: some workers (enzymes — protein catalysts) break down a sandwich into bricks, others assemble muscles from them or send fuel to the 'stoves' (mitochondria — the cell's power plants) so you can run and think.
metabolism.history_simple: The concept of 'metabolism' was introduced in the 19th century by the German physiologist Theodor Schwann, but the foundations were laid by alchemists observing fermentation. Later, scientists discovered that enzymes are involved in all reactions.
metabolism.how_it_works_simple: After eating, digestion breaks down proteins, fats, and carbohydrates into small molecules. Blood carries them to cells, where enzymes speed up reactions: some break down molecules to release energy, others create new substances for growth and repair.
metabolism.description: Metabolism is a set of enzymatic reactions forming branched metabolic pathways. Glucose catabolism starts with glycolysis, continues in the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, where energy is stored as ATP. Anabolism uses intermediate metabolites to synthesize amino acids, lipids, nucleotides. Regulation occurs through transcriptional control of enzyme expression, allosteric modulation, and hormonal signals (insulin, glucagon, adrenaline). The central element is ATP — the universal energy carrier. Metabolic networks exhibit emergent properties: the flow of substances is redirected depending on the cell's needs, and feedback loops maintain homeostasis.
metabolism.history: The term 'metabolism' comes from the Greek 'metabole' — change. Study began with the work of Jan Baptist van Helmont (17th century), but systematic research emerged in the 19th century: Theodor Schwann formulated cell theory, and Claude Bernard introduced the concept of homeostasis. In the 20th century, Hans Krebs discovered the citric acid cycle, and Fritz Lipmann described the role of ATP. Modern metabolomics studies thousands of metabolites simultaneously.
metabolism.how_it_works: Metabolism is carried out through enzymatic reactions, the rates of which are described by Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Key pathways such as glycolysis and the Krebs cycle act as 'hubs' linking catabolism and anabolism. The electron transport chain in mitochondria creates a proton gradient used by ATP synthase to synthesize ATP — this process is called oxidative phosphorylation. Hormones (insulin, glucagon, adrenaline, thyroxine) coordinate metabolic fluxes through signaling cascades. At the organism level, Kleiber's law relates metabolic rate to body mass.
key_problems: How exactly do the genome and epigenome tune metabolic networks in different tissues?
Is it possible to purposefully speed up metabolism without harming health?
What is the role of the microbiome in host metabolism?
metabolism.fun_fact: The slowest metabolism in nature is probably in tardigrades in a state of cryptobiosis: their metabolic rate drops to 0.01% of normal, allowing them to survive in outer space.

formulas.description: Kleiber's law relates metabolic rate to body mass
formulas.meaning: B is the animal's metabolic rate (W), B_0 is a constant depending on the taxonomic group (for mammals about 3.4 W/kg^(3/4)), M is body mass (kg).

enzyme.name: enzyme
enzyme.mini: Enzymes are tiny molecular machines inside cells that speed up chemical reactions by millions of times. Without them, life would stop: digestion, breathing, DNA copying—all depend on enzymes.
enzyme.practical_application: Enzymes are used in laundry detergents to remove stains at low temperatures, in cheese and bread production, and in medicines to dissolve blood clots.
enzyme.description_popular: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly of protein nature, that accelerate biochemical reactions by lowering the activation energy (the energy barrier that must be overcome to start a reaction). They have high substrate specificity and work under mild conditions (temperature, pressure, pH) typical of living systems. Enzyme activity is regulated by inhibitors and activators.
enzyme.fun_fact_popular: The enzyme catalase, found in our liver, breaks down hydrogen peroxide at a rate that, if working at full power, could fill more than half a million liters of water with bubbles in one second.
enzyme.description_simple: An enzyme is a protein (special molecule) that works like a key in a lock. Each enzyme fits only its specific substance (substrate) and helps it quickly turn into something else. For example, the enzyme in saliva (amylase) begins breaking down starch into sugars right in the mouth.
enzyme.history_simple: The first enzyme—diastase (amylase)—was isolated from malt by French chemist Anselme Payen in 1833. The term 'enzyme' was proposed by Wilhelm Kühne in 1878.
enzyme.how_it_works_simple: An enzyme acts like a skilled assembler: it captures a molecule, weakens a specific bond in it, and that molecule breaks apart or joins with another, while the enzyme itself remains unchanged and ready to help again.
enzyme.description: Enzymes are globular proteins (except for some RNA catalysts—ribozymes) that function as biocatalysts with exceptional efficiency and selectivity. Their catalytic activity is due to the presence of an active site—a unique three-dimensional structure complementary to the transition state of the substrate. Many enzymes require cofactors (metal ions) or coenzymes (vitamin derivatives). The kinetics of enzymatic reactions is described by the Michaelis-Menten model.
enzyme.history: The history of enzyme study began with work on fermentation: Louis Pasteur in the 1850s believed enzymes were inseparable from living cells, while Eduard Buchner in 1897 proved the possibility of cell-free fermentation (Nobel Prize 1907). James Sumner in 1926 first crystallized an enzyme (urease) and proved its protein nature. In the 1960s, the three-dimensional structures of the first enzymes were determined using X-ray crystallography.
enzyme.how_it_works: The enzyme binds the substrate in the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex, stabilizes the transition state, lowering the activation energy. After the reaction, the product is released, and the enzyme returns to its original state. The Michaelis-Menten kinetic equation describes the dependence of velocity on substrate concentration.
key_problems: Prediction of catalytic activity and substrate specificity from amino acid sequence de novo.
Design of enzymes with desired properties (protein engineering) for industry and medicine.
Full understanding of the mechanisms of enzyme regulation in the cellular context (allostery, post-translational modifications).
Creation of efficient artificial enzymes (synzymes) based on non-protein scaffolds.
enzyme.fun_fact: Some enzymes achieve 'catalytic perfection' — their rate is limited only by substrate diffusion. For example, acetylcholinesterase converts acetylcholine with a rate constant on the order of 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹, making it one of the fastest enzymes.

formulas.description: The Michaelis-Menten equation describes the rate of an enzymatic reaction as a function of substrate concentration.
formulas.meaning: where v is the initial reaction rate, V_max is the maximum rate, [S] is the substrate concentration, K_m is the Michaelis constant (equal to the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of V_max).

cell.name: cell
cell.mini: A cell is a living brick from which all organisms are built; inside it, like in a miniature city, work is in full swing: some parts extract energy, others build proteins, and still others remove waste.
cell.practical_application: Understanding the cell is the foundation of medicine: from developing antibiotics to growing organs from stem cells.
cell.description_popular: The cell is the elementary structural and functional unit of living things, capable of self-reproduction. It is separated from the environment by a plasma membrane, which regulates the transport of substances. In eukaryotes (organisms whose cells have a defined nucleus), the interior contains a nucleus containing DNA packaged into chromosomes (tightly coiled DNA threads). The cytoplasm is filled with organelles: mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, ribosomes synthesize proteins based on RNA templates (messenger molecules that copy DNA fragments), the endoplasmic reticulum transports substances, the Golgi apparatus sorts and packages proteins, lysosomes provide intracellular digestion.
cell.fun_fact_popular: There are about 37 trillion cells in the adult human body, but approximately the same number of bacterial cells live inside us, and they are important for health.
cell.description_simple: A cell is the tiniest part of a living organism that can live, feed, and reproduce on its own. It can be compared to a tiny factory surrounded by a fence-membrane (envelope). Inside, there is the nucleus — the 'director's office,' where the blueprints of the entire organism are stored (DNA — molecules with hereditary information). Around the nucleus floats cytoplasm (a jelly-like fluid), and within it work the organelles (little 'machines'): mitochondria produce energy, ribosomes assemble proteins (the main building materials), and lysosomes digest waste.
cell.history_simple: The first person to see cells was Robert Hooke in 1665, while examining a cork through a homemade microscope. He called them 'cells' because they resembled monks' cells.
cell.how_it_works_simple: The cell receives nutrients through the membrane, like through a checkpoint. Then mitochondria convert them into energy, which other parts use to work. DNA in the nucleus gives instructions to ribosomes on how to assemble proteins. When the cell grows, it divides in two — this is how an organism grows and renews itself.
cell.description: The cell is the fundamental unit of life, bounded by a plasma membrane and containing the genetic apparatus that ensures its reproduction. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria and archaea) — without a membrane-bound nucleus — and eukaryotic cells — with a nucleus containing linear DNA packaged by histones into chromatin — are distinguished. The eukaryotic cell contains numerous membrane-bound and non-membrane-bound organelles: mitochondria with their own circular DNA, converting energy from nutrients into ATP; rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes (free and bound), the Golgi complex, lysosomes, peroxisomes, and the cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments), which provides shape and movement. Plant cells additionally contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis, a large central vacuole, and a cell wall made of cellulose. The cell life cycle includes phases: G1, S (DNA replication), G2, and mitosis (nuclear division) or meiosis (formation of gametes).
cell.history: The term 'cell' was introduced by Robert Hooke in 1665, observing cork slices. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek soon described living cells, including bacteria and spermatozoa. In the 19th century, Theodor Schwann and Matthias Schleiden formulated the cell theory: all organisms consist of cells. Rudolf Virchow supplemented it with the statement 'every cell arises from a cell.' Electron microscopy in the mid-20th century revealed the ultrastructure of the cell.
cell.how_it_works: Cell functioning is based on the flow of genetic information: DNA → RNA → protein. Transcription (copying a section of DNA into mRNA) occurs in the nucleus, then mRNA exits into the cytoplasm, where ribosomes carry out translation, assembling the polypeptide chain according to the genetic code. Energy metabolism is provided by mitochondria through the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation using a proton gradient. Transport of substances across the membrane is regulated by passive diffusion, facilitated transport, and active transport, including Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Cell division is controlled by cyclin-dependent kinases, and apoptosis (programmed cell death) eliminates damaged cells.
key_problems: complete understanding of the mechanisms of aging and cellular senescence
artificial creation of a living cell from non-biological components
control of stem cell differentiation for regenerative medicine
overcoming cancerous transformation without damaging healthy cells
cell.fun_fact: The largest cells are egg cells: an ostrich egg cell reaches 15 cm in diameter. The longest are neurons, for example, a motor neuron from the spinal cord to a toe can be over a meter long.

pcr.name: PCR
pcr.mini: Molecular photocopier: allows billions of exact copies of a desired DNA fragment to be made from a tiny sample.
pcr.practical_application: Foundation of COVID-19 tests, paternity establishment, and criminal detection from a drop of blood.
pcr.description_popular: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is an enzymatic method of amplification (multiple copying) of DNA in a test tube (in vitro). It allows selectively synthesizing a huge number of copies of a given DNA fragment, using a thermostable DNA polymerase (an enzyme that withstands high temperatures) and temperature cycling. The method revolutionized molecular biology, medicine, and forensics.
pcr.fun_fact_popular: The sensitivity of PCR is such that theoretically a single molecule of DNA can be detected in a sample. That is why coronavirus tests could detect infection at the earliest stages.
pcr.description_simple: PCR is a method that helps scientists and doctors multiply a specific piece of DNA (carrier of hereditary information) in a test tube. It works like a biological copying machine: it takes a short DNA segment and creates many copies of it by heating and cooling the mixture.
pcr.history_simple: The method was invented by American biochemist Kary Mullis in 1983. The idea came to him during a nighttime drive, and for this discovery he received the Nobel Prize.
pcr.how_it_works_simple: A DNA sample, special building blocks for constructing new copies (nucleotides), a builder enzyme (polymerase), and short primers that indicate which exact segment to copy are added to a test tube. Then the mixture is repeatedly heated and cooled: during heating the two DNA strands unwind, during cooling the primers attach to the desired sites, and the polymerase completes the missing halves. Each cycle doubles the number of copies.
pcr.description: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a method of exponential amplification of specific DNA sequences, based on repeating cycles of denaturation, primer annealing, and elongation using a thermostable DNA polymerase (usually Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus). Each cycle theoretically doubles the amount of target fragments, allowing 2^n copies after n cycles. In practice, efficiency is below 100%, but a billion-fold increase is still achieved. PCR underlies many applications: from sequencing and genotyping to quantitative analysis (qPCR) and pathogen detection.
pcr.history: The concept of DNA amplification via repeated replication cycles was proposed by Kary Mullis in 1983 while working at the biotechnology company Cetus Corporation. The idea came to him during an evening drive along a California highway. The first experiments using the Klenow fragment (unstable at high temperatures) were labor-intensive, as the enzyme had to be added after each denaturation cycle. The key breakthrough was the use of thermostable Taq DNA polymerase, isolated from thermophilic bacteria of Yellowstone, which allowed automation of the process. In 1993, Mullis received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Since then, the method has been continuously improved: real-time PCR (qPCR), digital PCR, and other variants have emerged.
pcr.how_it_works: The process consists of three main stages: (1) Denaturation at ~95°C — breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary DNA strands to form single-stranded templates. (2) Primer annealing at ~50–65°C — specific binding of short oligonucleotide primers to complementary sites on the templates. (3) Elongation at ~72°C — thermostable DNA polymerase synthesizes a new DNA strand starting from the 3' end of the primer, using deoxynucleotide triphosphates (dNTPs) as building blocks. The cycles are repeated 25–40 times in a thermal cycler. A key parameter is specificity, ensured by primer design and optimization of the annealing temperature. The quantitative version (qPCR) uses fluorescent probes to monitor product accumulation in real time, allowing determination of the initial template quantity.
key_problems: Increasing accuracy and reducing amplification errors when working with long fragments
Eliminating contamination by products of previous reactions
Developing faster and cheaper methods for point-of-care diagnostics
Integration with other technologies such as CRISPR diagnostics
pcr.fun_fact: The first thermostable Taq polymerase was isolated from bacteria living in Yellowstone hot springs at temperatures around 70°C. This eliminated the need to add enzyme after each cycle and automated PCR, ultimately leading to the creation of programmable thermal cyclers — devices without which modern genetics is unthinkable.

formulas.description: Theoretical number of copies of the target fragment after n PCR cycles with an initial template amount N0
formulas.meaning: N — final number of copies, N0 — initial number of templates (original DNA molecules), n — number of amplification cycles (assuming 100% efficiency).

microorganism.name: microorganism
microorganism.mini: Tiny living creatures, invisible to the eye, that are everywhere: in the air, water, on the skin. They were the first to colonize the Earth and control the cycle of substances.
microorganism.practical_application: Bacteria and fungi produce antibiotics, bread, yogurt, and also decompose garbage; without them, the planet would drown in waste.
microorganism.description_popular: Microorganisms are the dominant form of life on Earth in terms of biomass and diversity. They include prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) without a nucleus and eukaryotic microbes (fungi, algae, protozoa). Metagenomics has shown that 99% of microbial species cannot be cultured in the laboratory. The human microbiome contains about 100 trillion bacteria — 10 times more than our own cells, and encodes 300 times as many genes as our genome.
microorganism.fun_fact_popular: The microbe Deinococcus radiodurans withstands a radiation dose 3000 times higher than the lethal dose for humans; it is used to clean up radioactive waste.
microorganism.description_simple: Microorganisms are the smallest organisms that can be seen only with a microscope. Among them are bacteria, unicellular fungi (yeasts), archaea (ancient single-celled organisms similar to bacteria but with a different structure) and protozoa like amoebas. Viruses are also often classified as microbes, but they lack cells and are not alive in the usual sense — they only reproduce inside other cells. Most microbes are harmless, and many are beneficial, participating in digestion or producing oxygen.
microorganism.history_simple: The discoverer of microbes is considered to be Antonie van Leeuwenhoek — in the 17th century, he saw 'animalcules' in a drop of water through a homemade microscope. Later, Louis Pasteur proved that they cause fermentation and disease, and Robert Koch isolated the causative agents of tuberculosis and cholera.
microorganism.how_it_works_simple: Microbes live in communities — biofilms on teeth or stones. They feed by absorbing dissolved substances through their membrane, and reproduce by dividing in half. Some can form spores — tough capsules that withstand heat, cold, and even space.
microorganism.description: Microorganisms are microscopic organisms representing all three domains of life: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. They exhibit colossal metabolic diversity: photoautotrophs (cyanobacteria), chemolithotrophs (oxidizing sulfur or iron), and organotrophs. Bacteria reproduce by binary fission but exchange genetic material through conjugation, transformation, and transduction, which accelerates adaptation. Quorum sensing allows populations to coordinate gene expression, for example, for biofilm formation or bioluminescence. Archaea often inhabit extreme conditions: thermophiles at 120°C, acidophiles at pH 0, halophiles in salt lakes. Microorganisms close the biogeochemical cycles of carbon, nitrogen, sulfur, and phosphorus, and their total biomass is estimated at hundreds of gigatons.
microorganism.history: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1676) first described 'animalcules' using lenses of his own making. In the 19th century, Christian Ehrenberg introduced the term 'bacteria', and Pasteur and Koch laid the foundations of medical microbiology. Sergei Winogradsky discovered chemosynthesis, and Martinus Beijerinck isolated nitrogen-fixing bacteria and discovered viruses. In the 20th century, electron microscopy and molecular biology (16S rRNA sequencing) radically changed the systematics, revealing the scale of unexplored diversity.
microorganism.how_it_works: The structural organization of prokaryotes lacks membrane-bound organelles; the genetic apparatus is represented by circular DNA in the nucleoid. Population growth in a closed environment is described by a curve: lag phase, exponential phase, stationary phase, and death phase. Growth kinetics follow the Monod equation: μ = μ_max * S/(K_s + S), where μ is the specific growth rate, μ_max is the maximum rate, S is the substrate concentration, and K_s is the half-saturation constant. Many species form dormant forms — endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium), resistant to radiation, desiccation, and boiling temperature. Horizontal gene transfer and high mutation rate make microorganisms an ideal model for studying evolution in real time.
key_problems: What is the contribution of microorganisms to the origin of multicellularity?
How can the microbiome be used to treat autoimmune diseases?
Are there alternative biochemistries, for example, based on silicon, in other worlds?
microorganism.fun_fact: The largest microorganism — the bacterium Thiomargarita magnifica — is visible to the naked eye and reaches 2 cm; it challenges the notion that bacteria are necessarily microscopic.

modified_gravity.name: modified gravity
modified_gravity.mini: When the rules of gravity are rewritten at large distances — as if the force of a fall changed not only with height, but with the scale of the entire cliff.
modified_gravity.practical_application: Description of galaxy rotation without adding invisible mass; an alternative model for dark matter.
modified_gravity.description_popular: Modified gravity — a class of theories proposing to change the law of gravitation on scales of galaxies and clusters, in order to explain the observed rotation without hypothetical dark matter. In standard cosmology, dark matter adds the missing mass; in alternative approaches, the geometry of spacetime or the potential itself is revised. The best-known model is MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics), introducing a threshold acceleration a₀ ≈ 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ m/s², below which the gravitational force transitions to a different regime.
modified_gravity.fun_fact_popular: MOND accurately predicted the rotation curves of many galaxies, but it has not yet succeeded in explaining cluster collisions, as in the case of the Bullet Cluster.
modified_gravity.description_simple: Ordinary gravity (Newton's law, later refined by Einstein) says that the farther objects are from each other, the weaker they attract. But on the outskirts of galaxies, stars move too fast, as if something is pushing them. Modified gravity is the idea that at very large distances, the law of gravity changes, becoming stronger, so dark matter (invisible substance) is not needed.
modified_gravity.history_simple: In the 1930s, Fritz Zwicky noticed that galaxies in clusters move strangely. Later, in the 1970s, Vera Rubin confirmed this for spiral galaxies. Then physicists (for example, Mordehai Milgrom) proposed changing the very formula of gravity.
modified_gravity.how_it_works_simple: Imagine that the force of gravity at large distances does not behave as 1/distance², but differently — for example, it weakens more slowly. Then stars on the outskirts are attracted more strongly, and their speed is explained without invisible particles. One popular version is MOND, where at very small accelerations the force becomes larger than usual.
modified_gravity.description: Modified gravity theories generalize Einstein's general theory of relativity (GTR) or Newtonian mechanics on large scales to explain the dynamics of galaxies and cosmological acceleration without invoking dark matter and dark energy. Instead of adding unknown forms of matter-energy within GTR, these theories change the gravitational interaction: for example, replacing the inverse-square potential with a potential having a logarithmic or power-law change. MOND (Milgrom, 1983) postulates that at accelerations below the fundamental constant a₀, Newton's second law takes the form F = m μ(a/a₀) a, where μ(x) ≈ 1 for x ≫ 1 and μ(x) ≈ x for x ≪ 1. Relativistic generalizations like TeVeS (Tensor-Vector-Scalar gravity) by Bekenstein include additional fields.
modified_gravity.history: The problem of missing mass was first noticed by Zwicky in 1933 in the Coma Cluster: the velocity dispersion of galaxies indicated a mass many times greater than the visible. In the 1970s, Vera Rubin systematically measured flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies, which were traditionally interpreted as evidence of a massive dark halo. In 1983, Mordehai Milgrom proposed MOND, which reproduced these curves without dark matter, introducing a single constant. Jacob Bekenstein in 2004 developed TeVeS — a relativistic extension of MOND, consistent with lensing and cosmology.
modified_gravity.how_it_works: In the Newtonian limit F = G M m / r², but when a ≪ a₀ (typical value for galaxy outskirts) the effective force in MOND becomes F ≈ m a₀ / √(a/a₀) = m √(a₀ a). For a test body at distance r from central mass M, this yields v ≈ (G M a₀)^(1/4) — constant rotation velocity, explaining flat curves. In relativistic versions, the field equations are modified: instead of standard Einstein equations, additional metrics or scalars are introduced. The equivalence principle is usually preserved in the weak field. On galaxy cluster scales, even modified gravity often requires some amount of ordinary dark matter (e.g., sterile neutrinos).
key_problems: Explaining all observed phenomena without dark matter (colliding clusters, CMB anisotropy)
Creating a complete relativistic theory consistent with GTR and cosmology
Predicting the existence and properties of additional fields and their detection
modified_gravity.fun_fact: The constant a₀ is surprisingly close in order of magnitude to c · H₀ / (2π), hinting at a connection between gravity and the expansion of the Universe.

formulas.description: Modified force in MOND for small accelerations
formulas.meaning: F — gravitational force, m — mass of the test body, a₀ ≈ 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ m/s² — Milgrom constant, a_N = G M / r² — Newtonian acceleration (G ≈ 6.674×10⁻¹¹ m³/(kg·s²) — gravitational constant, M — mass of the gravitating object, r — distance to it)

formulas.description: Rotation velocity on galactic outskirts in MOND
formulas.meaning: v — orbital speed, G — gravitational constant, M — mass of the galaxy inside the radius, a₀ — Milgrom constant

dna.name: DNA
dna.mini: DNA is a molecular instruction for living organisms, written with four chemical letters on a twisted spiral staircase.
dna.practical_application: By reading DNA, we treat hereditary diseases, create GMOs, and solve crimes.
dna.description_popular: DNA is a long chain molecule (polymer) consisting of two strands of nucleotides (building blocks) twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide contains one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), cytosine (C). The strands are held by weak chemical bonds (hydrogen) between pairs A–T and G–C, which complement each other like a key to a lock (they are complementary). The sequence of bases encodes hereditary information. In organisms with a cell nucleus (eukaryotes), DNA is packaged into chromosomes.
dna.fun_fact_popular: The total length of DNA in all human cells is about 10 billion kilometers — enough to stretch a thread to Pluto and back several times.
dna.description_simple: DNA resembles a very long rope ladder twisted into a spiral. Its rungs are pairs of chemical compounds (nitrogenous bases) that act like letters: A, T, G, C. The sequence of these letters provides instructions for building an organism, like a page in a book. Each cell in the body contains the same book, but reads only the necessary pages.
dna.history_simple: The double helix structure was discovered in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick, using X-ray crystallography data (a method that reveals the arrangement of atoms by shining X-rays on crystals) obtained by Rosalind Franklin.
dna.how_it_works_simple: During cell division, the double helix unwinds, and each strand builds a partner from the floating base-letters around. This produces two identical copies — cells inherit the same instruction.
dna.description: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is a biopolymer composed of nucleotides. Each nucleotide includes deoxyribose (a sugar), a phosphate group, and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G), or cytosine (C). Two antiparallel polynucleotide chains are twisted into a right-handed helix with a diameter of about 2 nm and a helical pitch of 3.4 nm (10 base pairs per turn).
