The chains are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds), G with C (three bonds). This structure was discovered in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick using X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. DNA stores genetic information as a code where nucleotide triplets (codons) correspond to amino acids. DNA replication occurs in a semi-conservative manner with the involvement of multiple enzymes (DNA polymerase, helicase, etc.).
dna.history: The idea that hereditary information is transmitted through molecules arose in the early 20th century. In 1944, Oswald Avery demonstrated that DNA is the carrier of genetic information in bacteria. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick, based on the X-ray diffraction images of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, proposed the double helix model. An important contribution to the development of X-ray crystallography methods was made by William Lawrence Bragg, whose work enabled the deciphering of biomolecular structures. Erwin Schrödinger, in his book 'What is Life?' (1944), predicted the existence of an 'aperiodic crystal' as the carrier of heredity.
dna.how_it_works: DNA works through the central dogma of molecular biology: information is transferred from DNA to RNA (transcription) and then to protein (translation). Transcription is performed by RNA polymerase, which synthesizes messenger RNA (mRNA) based on a DNA template. The resulting mRNA exits the nucleus and binds to a ribosome, where protein synthesis occurs. The nucleotide sequence is read in triplets (codons), each codon specifying one amino acid. The genetic code is universal for all living organisms. Regulation of gene expression is carried out through promoters, enhancers, and epigenetic modifications (e.g., DNA methylation).
key_problems: The question of the origin of DNA in the primordial soup remains unsolved
The problem of DNA folding within the volume of the nucleus
The mechanisms of aging related to DNA damage are not fully understood
dna.fun_fact: Sequencing the first complete human genome (the Human Genome Project) took 13 years and cost 3 billion dollars; today, a human genome can be deciphered in a day for less than 1000 dollars.

virus.name: virus
virus.mini: A virus is like a USB drive with malicious code: it inserts into a cell and reprograms it to produce its own copies.
virus.practical_application: Viruses cause diseases (influenza, COVID-19) but are also used as vectors for gene delivery in gene therapy.
virus.description_popular: A virus is a nanoscale infectious agent that parasitizes cells. Its genetic material – DNA or RNA – is packed into a protein capsid; some viruses have a lipid envelope. The virus is incapable of independent metabolism and reproduction – it necessarily uses the resources of the host cell. After penetration, viral genes integrate into the cellular machinery, forcing it to synthesize viral proteins and replicate the viral genome. Assembly of new virions occurs in the cytoplasm or nucleus, after which they exit, destroying the cell or budding off.
virus.fun_fact_popular: Some viruses can integrate their genetic material into the host DNA and remain there for years without causing symptoms (like the herpes virus).
virus.description_simple: A virus is a tiny particle that can enter a living cell and reproduce only inside it. It consists of genetic material (instructions in the form of DNA or RNA) in a protective shell (protein capsule). Outside a cell, the virus is inactive, like a seed without soil. When it penetrates a cell, it forces it to produce new viruses, which then exit and infect other cells.
virus.history_simple: Viruses were discovered by Russian scientist Dmitry Ivanovsky in 1892 while studying tobacco mosaic disease. He showed that the disease passes through filters that trap bacteria.
virus.how_it_works_simple: The virus attaches to the cell like a key to a lock, then penetrates inside. There it releases its genes, and the cell begins to execute them, like a worker given false instructions, assembling viral parts instead of its own. Eventually the cell dies, and the viruses spread.
virus.description: A virus is an obligate intracellular parasite, representing a nucleoprotein structure. Unlike cellular organisms, viruses lack ribosomes and energy metabolism systems. Its life cycle includes adsorption on the cell surface, penetration (endocytosis or membrane fusion), uncoating (release of the genome), gene expression (transcription and translation using the cellular machinery), genome replication, assembly of virions, and release from the cell. Classification of viruses is based on the type of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded), capsid symmetry, and presence of an envelope. Some viruses (retroviruses) use reverse transcription for integration into the host genome. Viruses infect all forms of life, from bacteria (bacteriophages) to humans.
virus.history: The history of virus discovery begins with the work of Dmitry Ivanovsky (1892), who demonstrated that the causative agent of tobacco mosaic passes through bacterial filters. Later, Martinus Beijerinck (1898) confirmed this and introduced the term 'virus' (liquid living poison). In 1935, Wendell Stanley crystallized the tobacco mosaic virus, proving its particulate nature. With the development of electron microscopy and molecular biology, the structure and replication mechanisms of viruses were established.
virus.how_it_works: Viral parasitism at the molecular level is based on molecular mimicry and the use of cellular receptors. For example, the influenza virus binds via hemagglutinin to sialic acid on the cell surface, enters the endosome, where low pH activates membrane fusion. RNA-genome viruses replicate using RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which they either encode or carry with them. Retroviruses (HIV) use reverse transcriptase to synthesize DNA from an RNA template, which then integrates into the host chromosome via integrase. Virus release can occur by lysis (cell destruction) or budding, when the virus captures a portion of the cell membrane as an envelope.
key_problems: Mechanisms of virus transmission from animals to humans and pandemic prediction
Development of universal antiviral drugs and broad-spectrum vaccines
Understanding the role of endogenous retroviruses in evolution and their impact on immunity
Control of viral reservoirs in the body (e.g., HIV latency)
virus.fun_fact: Viruses are the most numerous biological entities on Earth; there are about 10^30 of them in the ocean, and if lined up, this chain would stretch for 100 million light-years. Bacteriophages destroy about 20% of the bacterial biomass in the ocean daily, influencing global biogeochemical cycles.

bacterium.name: bacterium
bacterium.mini: Bacterium is a microscopic factory: inside it, the work of thousands of molecular machines boils without interruption.
bacterium.practical_application: Bacteria ferment yogurt and kefir, produce insulin for diabetics, and help extract useful minerals from low-grade ores.
bacterium.description_popular: Bacteria are prokaryotic (lacking a nucleus) single-celled organisms of microscopic size (0.5–5 μm). Their circular DNA is concentrated in the nucleoid. The cell wall made of peptidoglycan gives shape (cocci, bacilli, spirilla) and protects against osmotic shock. They feed in various ways: photosynthesis (cyanobacteria), fermentation, respiration with or without oxygen. Plasmids – small circular DNA – often carry antibiotic resistance genes and are transferred between bacteria.
bacterium.fun_fact_popular: The total mass of bacteria on Earth exceeds the mass of all plants and animals combined.
bacterium.description_simple: Bacteria are the smallest living creatures, made of a single cell. Unlike the cells of our body, they have no nucleus: their genetic information (DNA) floats directly in the cytoplasm. Most bacteria are harmless – without them there would be no cheese or sourdough bread.
bacterium.history_simple: The first to glimpse bacteria was Robert Hooke in 1665, examining a thin slice of cork under a microscope, and they were described in detail by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek a decade later.
bacterium.how_it_works_simple: The bacterium grows faster and faster until it divides in two. In warm milk, it does this every 20 minutes, which is why yogurt thickens overnight. Many bacteria are equipped with a flagellum – a tiny propeller that rotates and pushes the cell forward.
bacterium.description: Bacteria are a domain of prokaryotes characterized by the absence of a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles. Sizes range from 0.2 to 750 μm (Thiomargarita namibiensis). Metabolic diversity is enormous: chemolithoautotrophs oxidize inorganic substances, phototrophs use light, organotrophs use organic matter. The cell envelope of gram-positive bacteria contains a thick layer of peptidoglycan with teichoic acids, while gram-negative have a thin layer and an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharides. The bacterial flagellum is a unique rotational nanomotor powered by a proton or sodium gradient. Bacteria reproduce by binary fission; generation time under optimal conditions for E. coli is 20 minutes. Genetic exchange via conjugation, transformation, and transduction facilitates rapid adaptation. Biofilms – structured communities encased in an extracellular matrix – enhance antibiotic resistance.
bacterium.history: In 1665, Robert Hooke described the cellular structure of cork and later drew microorganisms, but the true discoverer of bacteria is considered to be Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1676), who created lenses with 300x magnification. Louis Pasteur in the 1860s disproved the theory of spontaneous generation and proved that bacteria cause fermentation. Robert Koch (1876–1882) identified the causative agents of anthrax, tuberculosis, and cholera, and formulated Koch's postulates. Alexander Fleming in 1928 discovered penicillin. Carl Woese in 1977, based on analysis of 16S rRNA, separated archaea, dividing prokaryotes into two domains.
bacterium.how_it_works: The exponential growth phase is described by the formula N(t)=N₀·2^(t/g). In stationary phase, stress-resistance genes are turned on. Chemotaxis: a network of signaling proteins (CheA, CheY) controls the direction of flagellar rotation, enabling bacteria to swim along gradients of attractants. Quorum sensing: using autoinducers (e.g., AHL in gram-negatives), bacteria assess their density and coordinate behavior – synchronously switching on bioluminescence or virulence genes. Transcription of operons (e.g., lac operon) is regulated by repressors and inducers.
key_problems: Spread of multidrug resistance genes
Role of the gut microbiome in obesity and mental disorders
Development of bacterial biosensors for environmental pollution monitoring
bacterium.fun_fact: Deinococcus radiodurans survives after irradiation with a dose of 5000 Gy (5 Gy is lethal for humans) thanks to multiple genome copies and an extremely powerful DNA repair apparatus.

formulas.description: Exponential growth of a bacterial population
formulas.meaning: N(t) – population size at time t, N₀ – initial population size, g – generation time (doubling time). For Escherichia coli g ≈ 20 minutes in optimal medium at 37°C.

xray_radiation.name: X-ray radiation
xray_radiation.mini: X-rays are light so energetic that they pass through soft materials but are blocked by dense ones, like a swarm of bullets piercing paper but getting stuck in stone.
xray_radiation.practical_application: In medicine, it shines through the body to reveal fractures; at airports, it scans luggage without opening.
xray_radiation.description_popular: X-ray radiation is part of the electromagnetic spectrum with wavelengths from 0.01 to 10 nanometers, corresponding to photon energies from ~100 eV to ~100 keV. It penetrates materials more easily the lower their density and atomic number. In astronomy, X-rays are emitted by hot gas with temperatures of millions of degrees, for example in stellar coronae, accretion disks of black holes, and supernova remnants.
xray_radiation.fun_fact_popular: X-ray telescopes on satellites capture radiation from neutron stars; one such object can shine in X-rays as brightly as a million suns.
xray_radiation.description_simple: X-ray beams are a type of invisible radiation, similar to light but with much higher energy. While ordinary light can be stopped by a sheet of paper, X-rays pass through skin and muscle but are absorbed by bones. That's why bones appear white on an image. In hospitals, the beam is directed through the body, leaving a shadow on film or a digital detector.
xray_radiation.history_simple: Discovered in 1895 by German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen when he noticed that unknown rays exposed a photographic plate even through black paper. For this he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
xray_radiation.how_it_works_simple: Inside an X-ray tube, electrons are accelerated by high voltage (voltage is the difference in electric potential) and slam into a metal target. The sudden deceleration produces X-ray photons (radiation particles).
xray_radiation.description: X-ray radiation consists of electromagnetic waves with energies ranging from tens of electronvolts to several hundred keV. It is generated by the deceleration of charged particles (bremsstrahlung) or by electron transitions in inner atomic shells (characteristic radiation). X-ray photons ionize matter and interact via the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, and electron-positron pair production (at energies >1.022 MeV). Their high penetrating power makes them indispensable in condensed matter physics, materials science, and medicine.
xray_radiation.history: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays on November 8, 1895, while experimenting with cathode rays. He noticed the glow of a barium platinocyanide screen even when the tube was enclosed and called the rays unknown (X). In 1901, Röntgen was awarded the Nobel Prize. In 1912, Max von Laue and colleagues demonstrated the wave nature of X-rays through diffraction on crystals, which led to the development of X-ray crystallography. Arthur Compton in 1923 explained the scattering of X-rays by electrons (Compton effect), confirming the particle properties of radiation. William Lawrence Bragg and his father derived Bragg's law, becoming founders of crystallography.
xray_radiation.how_it_works: When fast electrons collide with the anode in an X-ray tube, the sudden deceleration produces bremsstrahlung with a continuous spectrum, bounded by the minimum wavelength λ_min = hc/(eU), where U is the tube voltage. Electrons also eject inner-shell electrons from the anode atoms; when vacancies are filled, quanta are emitted with energies characteristic of the material, giving a line spectrum. According to Bragg's law, X-ray reflection from crystal planes follows the condition nλ = 2d sin θ, which is used for structure analysis. Compton scattering is described by the wavelength shift Δλ = (h/(m_e c))(1 - cos θ).
key_problems: Creating compact, high-brightness coherent X-ray sources
Difficulty of focusing hard X-rays due to weak refraction
Reducing radiation dose in medical imaging without loss of quality
xray_radiation.fun_fact: Röntgen discovered the rays by accident but hid the details of his experiment, fearing error; he titled his first report 'On a New Kind of Rays,' and only later were they called X-rays.

formulas.description: Minimum wavelength of bremsstrahlung
formulas.meaning: λ_min — minimum wavelength, h ≈ 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s — Planck constant, c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s — speed of light, e ≈ 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C — electron charge, U — accelerating voltage

formulas.description: Bragg's law for crystal diffraction
formulas.meaning: n — order of reflection (integer), λ — X-ray wavelength, d — interplanar spacing in the crystal, θ — glancing angle

formulas.description: Wavelength shift in Compton scattering
formulas.meaning: Δλ — increase in wavelength of scattered radiation, h — Planck constant, m_e ≈ 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg — electron mass, c — speed of light, θ — photon scattering angle

mutation.name: mutation
mutation.mini: A mutation is a typo in the genetic instruction that can lead to a defect in cell function or, conversely, to a useful innovation.
mutation.practical_application: Mutations underlie evolution and the diversity of life, and their study helps understand the causes of cancer and create new plant varieties.
mutation.description_popular: A mutation is a permanent change in the nucleotide sequence (the building blocks of DNA) of DNA, arising from replication errors (DNA duplication), recombination (exchange of segments between chromosomes), or under the influence of mutagens (factors that cause mutations). Point mutations affect a single base pair; their types: substitution (missense — amino acid substitution, nonsense — stop codon appearance), insertion or deletion, often leading to a reading frame shift (alteration of codon grouping). Chromosomal mutations are larger rearrangements: deletions (loss of segments), duplications (doublings), inversions (180° rotation), translocations (relocations). Genomic mutations change the number of chromosomes (aneuploidy — abnormal number, polyploidy — multiplication of the entire set). Mutations can be somatic (in non-reproductive cells, not transmitted) or germinal (in reproductive cells, inherited). Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but in rare cases increase fitness, becoming material for natural selection.
mutation.fun_fact_popular: In humans, each germ cell carries on average about 100 new mutations not present in the parents, making us all a bit mutant.
mutation.description_simple: A mutation is a random change in DNA (the molecule with hereditary information). When copying a huge book, sometimes a letter is omitted or replaced. So it is with DNA: one "letter" (nucleotide) can change, and sometimes this changes the meaning of the instruction. If a mutation occurs in a gene responsible for an important protein, it can cause a disease. But sometimes mutations are harmless or even beneficial — for example, allowing faster running or better milk digestion.
mutation.history_simple: The term "mutation" was proposed by Dutch botanist Hugo de Vries in 1901 after observing sudden changes in evening primrose plants. Later, in 1927, Hermann Muller demonstrated that X-rays can cause mutations, for which he received the Nobel Prize.
mutation.how_it_works_simple: When a cell divides, it copies its DNA. Sometimes mistakes occur during copying — these are spontaneous mutations. Mutations can also be caused by external factors — chemicals, radiation. The altered DNA sends an incorrect command to the ribosome, which may produce a defective protein. If the mutation occurs in a germ cell, it will be passed on to offspring.
mutation.description: A mutation is a sudden, heritable change in genetic material not associated with ordinary recombination. Mechanisms of occurrence include DNA polymerase errors during replication, depurination, deamination of cytosine to uracil, exposure to reactive oxygen species, UV radiation (formation of thymine dimers), ionizing radiation (strand breaks), and chemical mutagens (alkylating agents, base analogs). Repair systems (excision, mismatch repair, homologous recombination, non-homologous end joining) correct many damages, but not all. Mobile genetic elements (transposons) can also cause mutations by inserting into genes. The spectrum of mutations ranges from neutral synonymous substitutions to gross disruptions of protein structure affecting fitness.
mutation.history: The concept of mutations as discrete changes dates back to Hugo de Vries, who in 1901–1903 described them in evening primrose, using the term "mutation" to denote sudden heritable deviations. Thomas Morgan and his school, working with fruit flies in the 1910s, established the connection between mutations and chromosomes. In 1927, Hermann Muller experimentally proved the mutagenic effect of X-rays, laying the foundations of radiation genetics. In the mid-20th century, the discovery of the structure of DNA allowed a transition to molecular understanding of mutations.
mutation.how_it_works: At the molecular level, mutations arise as a result of chemical changes in nucleotides or errors in template synthesis. For example, deamination of cytosine converts it to uracil, which during replication is read as thymine, replacing a C-G pair with T-A. Sources of spontaneous mutations include tautomeric shifts of bases, leading to mispairings during replication. Induced mutations occur after DNA attack by exogenous agents. If the repair system fails, the change becomes fixed in the next replication cycle. Consequences depend on the type of mutation and its location: mutations in promoter regions alter gene expression levels; nonsense mutations truncate the protein; mutations in splice sites disrupt intron removal; epigenetic changes do not affect the DNA sequence but can be heritable. The evolutionary significance of mutations is as the primary source of genetic variation for natural selection.
key_problems: prediction of functional effect of de novo mutations
creation of precise methods for in situ repair of mutant genes
interaction of mutations and epigenetics in carcinogenesis
role of mutations in the evolution of complex adaptations
mutation.fun_fact: The spontaneous mutation rate in humans is about 10⁻⁸ per nucleotide per generation, but in some hypermutable genome sequences it is increased thousands of times.

brain.name: brain
brain.mini: A living computer made of billions of cells, transforming sensations into actions. It turns bursts of electricity into music, love, and dreams.
brain.practical_application: Neural interfaces allow paralyzed people to control prostheses with the power of thought. Neuroimaging (MRI) diagnoses tumors and strokes, and a deep understanding of the brain leads to the treatment of depression and Alzheimer's disease.
brain.description_popular: The brain is the central organ of the nervous system, integrating sensory information, controlling movement, and supporting higher functions (consciousness, thinking, speech). It consists of the cortex (folded surface), subcortical nuclei, cerebellum, and brainstem. The cortex is divided into lobes: frontal—planning and personality, parietal—touch and spatial awareness, temporal—hearing and memory, occipital—vision. Inside the brain are ventricles filled with cerebrospinal fluid. The main processing unit is the neural network; information is encoded by the frequency of impulses and patterns of activity. The most important learning mechanism is long-term potentiation (strengthening of synapses) in the hippocampus.
brain.fun_fact_popular: The brain uses about 20% of all oxygen and calories consumed by the body, yet it weighs only 2% of body weight—an energy-hungry organ.
brain.description_simple: The brain is the main control organ of the body, consisting of nerve cells (neurons) and supporting cells. It works like a biological processor: it receives signals from the eyes, ears, skin, processes them, and issues commands. Thanks to the brain, we think, remember, feel joy, and learn. Different parts of the brain are responsible for different tasks: the back of the head for vision, the frontal part for planning.
brain.history_simple: Ancient Greeks believed that thoughts originated in the heart, but Hippocrates suspected the role of the brain. In the 19th century, physician Paul Broca identified the speech area in the left hemisphere. In the 20th century, the electroencephalograph (recording electrical waves) and tomographs were invented, showing the brain in action.
brain.how_it_works_simple: Neurons communicate via electrical impulses and chemicals. They form networks: for example, the visual network recognizes faces, the motor network controls movements. The brain continuously reorganizes connections between neurons—this is called neuroplasticity and underlies learning. When you memorize a poem, some synapses (junctions between neurons) are strengthened.
brain.description: The human brain is the most complex biological object. It includes: the cerebral cortex (neocortex) with six layers of neurons, responsible for sensory perception, motor commands, and associative functions; the limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus)—emotions, memory; basal ganglia—motor control and learning; thalamus—relay station; hypothalamus—regulation of homeostasis and endocrine functions; brainstem—vital centers for respiration and circulation; cerebellum—coordination of movement and cognitive functions. Neurons form a dense network: in the cortex, each neuron is connected to thousands of others. Brain activity is studied using electroencephalography (EEG), magnetoencephalography (MEG), functional MRI (fMRI), and positron emission tomography (PET). Neuroplasticity—the ability to change synaptic strength and structure under the influence of experience—is a key property that persists into adulthood. Cognitive functions are distributed, but some areas are specialized: Broca's area (speech production), Wernicke's area (speech comprehension), fusiform gyrus (face recognition).
brain.history: The first ideas about the brain are found in the works of Hippocrates and Galen. In the 19th century, phrenology (a pseudoscience about the connection between skull shape and character) gave way to scientific research: Paul Broca in 1861 demonstrated the link between damage to the left frontal lobe and speech impairment. Carl Wernicke described the area for speech comprehension. In the early 20th century, Korbinian Brodmann divided the cortex into 52 areas based on cytoarchitectonics, and Wilder Penfield created maps of the sensory and motor cortex through electrical stimulation. In the second half of the 20th century, non-invasive imaging methods emerged, and at the end of the century, functional MRI allowed us to see brain activity in real time.
brain.how_it_works: The brain processes information in parallel and in a distributed manner. Sensory signals travel through the thalamus to primary cortical areas, then to association areas where features are combined into coherent percepts. Higher-order association areas (prefrontal cortex) are involved in decision making, working memory, and goal setting. The motor system is hierarchical: association areas plan the action, premotor cortex and cerebellum construct the movement program, motor cortex activates spinal motor neurons. In learning and memory, synaptic plasticity plays a key role: strengthening or weakening of transmission. Long-term potentiation (LTP) in the hippocampus depends on activation of NMDA receptors and Ca²⁺ influx, triggering phosphorylation cascades and protein synthesis. Neuromodulators (dopamine, serotonin) regulate global states (attention, motivation, sleep). Sleep is necessary for memory consolidation: during slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus 'replays' daytime activity sequences.
key_problems: Neural basis of consciousness—the 'hard problem' of Chalmers.
How is information encoded in the population activity of neurons?
Complete mapping of the human connectome.
Mechanisms of neurodegenerative and psychiatric diseases.
How do cortical and subcortical systems interact?
The origin of creativity and imagination.
brain.fun_fact: The brain has no pain receptors, so surgery can be performed while the patient is conscious; the patient reports sensations while the surgeon stimulates different areas.

dimensionality_reduction.name: dimensionality reduction
dimensionality_reduction.mini: Compress voluminous data into a simple map, like a geographical atlas turns the three-dimensional world into two-dimensional pages, preserving the essentials.
dimensionality_reduction.practical_application: Accelerating image search, compressing medical images, visualizing complex relationships, for example, in genetics.
dimensionality_reduction.description_popular: The process of transforming data from a high-dimensional feature space to a low-dimensional one with minimal loss of significant information. Used both for visualization (projecting onto 2D or 3D) and as preprocessing before machine learning to reduce computational complexity and avoid the 'curse of dimensionality' (degradation of algorithm performance as the number of features grows).
dimensionality_reduction.fun_fact_popular: Principal component analysis (PCA) is often used to compress facial images: a 10,000-pixel snapshot can be transmitted with just a hundred numbers, and the face remains recognizable.
dimensionality_reduction.description_simple: Data often has many features — for example, a photograph has millions of pixels. Dimensionality reduction is a way to preserve the most important information by removing the superfluous. It's as if an artist drew a portrait with just a few lines, but the person can still be recognized.
dimensionality_reduction.history_simple: In the early 20th century, Karl Pearson invented principal component analysis — the first tool for such compression. Later, many other methods appeared.
dimensionality_reduction.how_it_works_simple: The method finds new, simpler coordinates for the data, so that important differences between objects are not lost. It's like looking at the shadow of an object: a shadow is flat (lower dimensionality), but it's often clear what the object is.
dimensionality_reduction.description: A set of mathematical methods that map points from an n-dimensional vector space to an m-dimensional one, where m < n, while preserving certain structural properties. Linear methods (PCA, SVD, factor analysis) construct a projection that maximizes variance or minimizes reconstruction error. Nonlinear methods (t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders) better preserve local neighborhoods and cluster structure, which is important for visualization. In machine learning, dimensionality reduction addresses feature selection and feature extraction tasks, combating multicollinearity, overfitting, and computational costs.
dimensionality_reduction.history: Principal component analysis (PCA) was proposed by Karl Pearson in 1901; later independently developed by Harold Hotelling in the 1930s. In the 1960s–70s, multidimensional scaling methods appeared. The t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) algorithm was introduced by Laurens van der Maaten and Geoffrey Hinton in 2008, revolutionizing visualization. UMAP (2018) improved global structure preservation and speed.
dimensionality_reduction.how_it_works: Linear PCA method: compute the covariance matrix of the data; its eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues form a new orthonormal basis; projecting onto the first m eigenvectors gives the reduced representation. Nonlinear autoencoder: a neural network with a bottleneck is trained to reconstruct the input; the hidden representation in the bottleneck serves as a low-dimensional code. t-SNE models the probabilities that a point is a neighbor of another in the original and target spaces, minimizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence between them.
key_problems: Choosing the optimal dimensionality m is often heuristic
Difficulty in interpreting latent variables of nonlinear methods
Preserving global structure under strong compression
Scalability to very large data (millions of points)
dimensionality_reduction.fun_fact: In the 2009 Netflix Prize competition, the winning team BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos used SVD (singular value decomposition) for dimensionality reduction of the ratings matrix, which brought them success.

formulas.description: Projection of data onto the first m principal components
formulas.meaning: Z — data matrix in reduced dimensionality (N×m), X — original centered data matrix (N×n), W_m — matrix of m eigenvectors of the covariance matrix X^T X, corresponding to the m largest eigenvalues

eeg_seizure_detection.name: EEG seizure detection
eeg_seizure_detection.mini: Just as a lightning detector catches flashes in the sky, algorithms search for epileptic bursts in the brain's electrical signals.
eeg_seizure_detection.practical_application: Helps doctors detect epilepsy faster by analyzing long EEG recordings; used in wearable devices for seizure prediction.
eeg_seizure_detection.description_popular: Electroencephalogram (EEG) records the total electrical activity of brain neurons using electrodes on the scalp. An epileptic seizure manifests as abnormal synchronous discharges, which on EEG look like sharp bursts (spikes) and slow waves. Detection algorithms analyze the multichannel signal, extracting characteristic patterns whose frequency and shape differ from background activity.
eeg_seizure_detection.fun_fact_popular: Some algorithms can predict a seizure minutes before it starts by analyzing gradual changes in EEG that are invisible to the naked eye.
eeg_seizure_detection.description_simple: EEG (electroencephalogram) is a recording of brain electrical activity, looking like many wavy lines. During an epileptic seizure, these lines change sharply, becoming 'sharp' like mountain peaks. Seizure detection is a computer program that, like a trained eye, finds such peaks among ordinary waves.
eeg_seizure_detection.history_simple: The first automatic detectors appeared in the 1970s; over time they became smarter thanks to machine learning (the computer learns from examples).
eeg_seizure_detection.how_it_works_simple: The program looks at the EEG recording, measures wave height and frequency. If it sees sharp jumps, it marks them as a possible seizure. Modern methods also consider hidden patterns that a human might miss.
eeg_seizure_detection.description: EEG seizure detection is automated recognition in a multichannel time series of electrographic patterns characteristic of epileptic activity: spikes, sharp waves, spike-wave complexes. Modern approaches include classical machine learning methods based on extracted features (power in frequency bands, entropy, wavelet coefficients), as well as deep neural networks (convolutional, recurrent) trained directly on raw data. The task is complicated by high signal variability between patients and artifacts (movements, muscle activity).
eeg_seizure_detection.history: The first automatic seizure detectors appeared in the 1970s and were based on simple threshold rules for amplitude and duration. In the 1990s, frequency analysis methods and neural networks began to be used. With the growth of computing power and the availability of large labeled databases (e.g., the Temple University Hospital project) in the 2010s, there was a leap to deep learning, allowing performance on par with expert clinicians.
eeg_seizure_detection.how_it_works: The system receives a multichannel EEG signal (usually 16-64 leads), digitized at 200-500 Hz. Preprocessing algorithms remove artifacts (filtering, independent component analysis). Then either predefined features are extracted (e.g., power spectral density in delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma bands, fractal dimension, synchronization), or the signal is directly fed into a neural network. The classifier outputs the probability of a seizure for a sliding window (typically 2-10 seconds). At the postprocessing stage, smoothing and thresholding are applied to eliminate false positives. Some systems use transfer learning to adapt to a specific patient.
key_problems: High inter-patient variability of seizure patterns
Lack of labeled data due to the labor-intensive expert annotation
Variety of artifacts masking true activity
Need for real-time operation for warning devices
eeg_seizure_detection.fun_fact: Modern detectors on public datasets achieve sensitivity above 90% and less than one false positive per hour, but in clinical practice performance often drops by half due to non-ideal recording conditions.

formulas.description: The simplest feature is the signal energy in a window
formulas.meaning: E is the signal energy in the time window, N is the number of samples in the window, x_i is the amplitude value of the signal at the i-th moment

stochastic_modeling.name: Stochastic modeling
stochastic_modeling.mini: A world recreated by the rules of chance, like rolling dice to predict the weather, stock market surges, or the evolution of galaxies.
stochastic_modeling.practical_application: Predicting the spread of infections, modeling crowd movement, calculating power plant reliability.
stochastic_modeling.description_popular: A method for studying complex systems by constructing a mathematical model that includes random variables and probabilistic transitions, and then numerically reproducing it many times (Monte Carlo method). Stochastic modeling is indispensable when the analytical solution of equations is too cumbersome or unknown, but the statistical properties of elementary events are available. It is used in physics, biology, finance, and epidemiology for risk and uncertainty assessment.
stochastic_modeling.fun_fact_popular: Physicists already in the mid-20th century modeled the movement of neutrons in a nuclear reactor using random numbers — this is how the Monte Carlo method appeared, named after the casino.
stochastic_modeling.description_simple: Stochastic modeling is an imitation of reality that takes randomness into account. Unlike exact calculations, it acknowledges that we don't know everything and adds an element of surprise, like flipping a coin in a game. It is used when a phenomenon is too messy for strict formulas.
stochastic_modeling.history_simple: Early ideas of random processes appeared in the 19th century in gambling, then developed rapidly in the 20th century for the needs of physics (Brownian motion — the chaotic jiggling of pollen in water) and economics.
stochastic_modeling.how_it_works_simple: A computer model is created, which is run over and over with different random parameters (for example, wind speed). Each run is one scenario of the future. After thousands of such simulations, a cloud of possible outcomes is obtained, from which it is clear what is most likely to happen and what is rare.
stochastic_modeling.description: Construction and simulation of the dynamics of a system described by probabilistic laws, for example, random processes (Markov chains, Wiener process) or stochastic differential equations (SDEs). The goal is to generate an ensemble of trajectories, from which mean values, variances, and probabilities of rare events are estimated. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods allow sampling from complex posterior distributions in Bayesian inference. Agent-based modeling assigns random behavioral rules to a multitude of individual entities, leading to emergent collective effects.
stochastic_modeling.history: The formal foundations were laid in the early 20th century by the works of A. A. Markov, A. Einstein (Brownian motion), and N. Wiener. The Monte Carlo method was invented by Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann in the 1940s for the Manhattan Project. With the growth of computers, stochastic modeling became a standard tool in all sciences, including climatology (ensemble forecasts) and computational biology.
stochastic_modeling.how_it_works: A probabilistic model is defined: for example, the SDE dX_t = μ(X_t,t)dt + σ(X_t,t)dW_t, where W_t is a Wiener process (a continuous random process with independent normal increments). A numerical scheme (Euler–Maruyama) generates discrete increments by adding Gaussian white noise. By repeating the simulation N times, we obtain N trajectories, from which histograms, confidence intervals, etc. are constructed. The convergence of the method is on the order of 1/√N.
key_problems: Computational expensiveness for rare events (huge N required)
Choosing an adequate stochastic model when data is incomplete
Model verification and validation when the real system is non-stationary
The curse of dimensionality for multidimensional processes
stochastic_modeling.fun_fact: The Monte Carlo method helped win a backgammon tournament by training the TD-Gammon program in the 1990s, which became a milestone in reinforcement learning.

formulas.description: Stochastic differential equation (SDE) in Itô form
formulas.meaning: dX_t is the infinitesimal increment of process X at time t, μ is the drift coefficient (deterministic tendency), σ is the diffusion coefficient (noise amplitude), dW_t is the increment of a Wiener process, having the properties: E[dW_t]=0, E[(dW_t)^2]=dt

braess_paradox_in_biology.name: Braess's paradox in biology
braess_paradox_in_biology.mini: Sometimes a new path worsens the overall picture, as if adding a new branch in the tree of blood vessels made the heart work harder.
braess_paradox_in_biology.practical_application: Understanding this paradox helps biologists design optimal systems in synthetic biology and better explain strange failures in the body's natural networks.
braess_paradox_in_biology.description_popular: Braess's paradox occurs in networks with selfish or decentralized route choice. The classic example is road traffic: opening a new street can increase travel time for each driver. In biology, this phenomenon is observed in transport networks (vascular systems, mycelium), in metabolic pathways, and even in population genetics. Adding a new 'channel' or regulatory mechanism that seems beneficial to each element actually reduces overall performance due to overload of bottlenecks.
braess_paradox_in_biology.fun_fact_popular: The slime mold Physarum polycephalum has no brain, but it builds an efficient transport network. When scientists artificially created additional connections, the network degraded instead of improving — a pure Braess's paradox.
braess_paradox_in_biology.description_simple: Braess's paradox is when adding something beneficial actually ruins everything. In biology, this happens in networks: for example, in the slime mold Physarum polycephalum, which builds transport routes. If you create an additional tunnel, nutrients will be delivered more slowly to the edges. It's like how an extra wire in a complex electrical circuit causes a short circuit.
braess_paradox_in_biology.history_simple: The paradox was discovered by the German mathematician Dietrich Braess in 1968 while studying traffic flow. Later, scientists found that similar problems exist in biological and chemical systems.
braess_paradox_in_biology.how_it_works_simple: Ant trail: if you build a new bridge that seems shorter but creates a jam at the exit, it becomes harder for everyone to get food. Similarly, in cellular networks, an 'extra' connection redirects flows suboptimally because each part of the network selfishly chooses its own path.
braess_paradox_in_biology.description: Braess's paradox is a counterintuitive property of network systems with non-cooperative equilibrium, where adding a resource (edge) worsens overall efficiency if each agent locally optimizes their cost function. In biology, the paradox has been described for transport networks (plant vascular networks, neural connections), metabolic pathways, population models, and ecological systems. It demonstrates that evolutionarily developed networks can avoid 'redundant' connections precisely because of such a non-optimal equilibrium.
braess_paradox_in_biology.history: Dietrich Braess, a German mathematician, formulated the paradox in a 1968 paper for transportation planning. However, there were anticipations by Ailing and others. In biology, the paradox began to be actively discussed in the 2000s after experiments with Physarum polycephalum networks and metabolic models. Early microscopic observations of biological structures by Robert Hooke laid the foundation for studying networks, although the paradox was not realized by him.
braess_paradox_in_biology.how_it_works: Consider a network where flow Q must pass from A to B. There are two paths: through node 1 and through node 2. Travel time on an edge depends on the flow f: T(f). Suppose selfish agents minimize their time, and Nash equilibrium is reached when the time on all used paths is equal. If a new edge is added connecting nodes 1 and 2 with zero travel time, initially it seems attractive. But in the new equilibrium, all agents use the new edge, redistributing flow so that the overall average time increases. Mathematically, this is expressed through a system of nonlinear equilibrium equations. In biological networks, the role of 'time' is played by flow resistance or metabolic cost. Principles of dissipation minimization are applied, but taking into account selfishness at the level of cells or organisms.
key_problems: Determining conditions under which biological networks avoid Braess's paradox
Evolutionary pressure against redundant connections
Application for designing stable artificial biological systems
braess_paradox_in_biology.fun_fact: In one experiment with Physarum polycephalum, scientists added a bridge between two parts of the network, and instead of increasing nutrient flow, long-distance transport collapsed — the network switched to local consumption, reminiscent of traffic jams.

formulas.description: Nash equilibrium for a two-route network with Braess's paradox (simplified travel time)
formulas.meaning: T(f) — travel time on the edge depending on flow f, a — time at zero flow (constant), b — delay coefficient (sensitivity to congestion)

formulas.description: Equilibrium condition with equal path times
formulas.meaning: T(f_i) — time on edge i, the sum of times on two paths from A to B must be equal in equilibrium

medical_image_segmentation.name: medical image segmentation
medical_image_segmentation.mini: Like coloring a black-and-white photo to highlight organs or tumors, segmentation breaks a medical scan into meaningful regions.
medical_image_segmentation.practical_application: Outlining tumor boundaries on MRI for radiation therapy planning or measuring organ volumes on CT.
medical_image_segmentation.description_popular: Medical image segmentation automatically divides a scan into anatomical or pathological structures. Modern methods, especially deep learning architectures like U-Net, process images at multiple scales, capturing both fine details and overall context. The output is a probability map for each pixel—the chance of belonging to one class or another (tumor, liver). Training requires large annotated datasets, which are often augmented artificially (rotations, flips).
medical_image_segmentation.fun_fact_popular: The U-Net architecture, shaped like the letter 'U', won the ISBI cell tracking challenge in 2015 and now underlies most medical segmentation tools.
medical_image_segmentation.description_simple: A map where countries are colored differently. Medical image segmentation does this automatically for X-rays, MRI, or CT scans. Algorithms (sets of rules for the computer) analyze brightness and textures and assign each pixel (a tiny square of the image) to a specific organ. This helps doctors see precise shapes and sizes without tracing outlines manually.
medical_image_segmentation.history_simple: Early methods in the 1970s used simple rules, such as thresholding (cutoff by brightness). In the 1980s, more flexible models appeared, like active contours. In the 2010s, deep learning (artificial intelligence mimicking brain cells) brought huge improvements, and the U-Net architecture in 2015 became the standard.
medical_image_segmentation.how_it_works_simple: The computer looks at the image and learns from examples where a doctor has already marked the areas. It uses a neural network (a multi-layered computing system) to predict which organ each pixel belongs to. Imagine a chef who, after looking at photos, learns to cut a cake into equal pieces based on visual cues.
medical_image_segmentation.description: Medical image segmentation is the process of delineating regions of interest in 2D or 3D scans. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn hierarchical features: early layers detect edges, deep layers identify complex shapes. Advanced models follow an encoder-decoder scheme with skip connections (U-Net, V-Net) to combine low-level and high-level features. Loss functions include Dice coefficient or cross-entropy. Uncertainty estimation is an active area to flag potential errors.
medical_image_segmentation.history: Threshold-based segmentation emerged in the 1970s. In 1988, Kass et al. proposed active contour models that optimize energy functions to find boundaries. With deep learning, the U-Net architecture (Ronneberger et al., 2015) revolutionized the field, enabling end-to-end training on limited data. Subsequent improvements include attention mechanisms and transformer-based models. Leading conferences: MICCAI, MIDL.
medical_image_segmentation.how_it_works: A CNN is trained on images with pixel-wise annotations. U-Net compresses the image into a bottleneck through convolutional and pooling layers, then expands it back with transposed convolutions. Skip connections concatenate high-resolution encoder features with the decoder, preserving fine details. The final layer uses softmax (for multiple classes) or sigmoid (for binary cases). Dice loss (1 - 2|X∩Y|/(|X|+|Y|)) handles class imbalance. Post-processing (connected components, CRF) refines boundaries.
key_problems: Generalization across different scanners and protocols
Scarcity and cost of annotations
Quantitative estimation of uncertainty
Efficiency of 3D segmentation
medical_image_segmentation.fun_fact: In a Kaggle lung segmentation competition, the winning solution based on an ensemble of U-Nets achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.99, nearly matching expert performance.

formulas.description: Dice similarity coefficient
formulas.meaning: X — set of pixels in the predicted segmentation, Y — set of pixels in the ground truth segmentation, |·| — set cardinality

quantum_like_models.name: quantum-like models
quantum_like_models.mini: The brain processes uncertainty much like a particle can be in several states at once—until the moment of choice.
quantum_like_models.practical_application: Helps create more flexible AI algorithms that can handle contradictory data.
quantum_like_models.description_popular: Quantum-like models transfer the mathematical apparatus of quantum mechanics (e.g., Hilbert spaces—abstract vector spaces for states, operators—ways of measurement, probability amplitudes—quantities whose squared modulus gives probability) to the description of cognitive processes, social interactions, or biological systems. They do not claim that the brain is literally quantum but use a convenient formalism to account for contextuality, inconsistency, and question order.
quantum_like_models.fun_fact_popular: These models have explained decision-making paradoxes, such as violations of classical probability laws in surveys.
quantum_like_models.description_simple: Some complex systems, such as the brain or society, behave as if they follow the rules of quantum physics (where superposition—being in multiple states at once—and entanglement—instant connections between particles—are possible). Similar mathematical techniques are used to describe, say, fluctuations in public opinion.
quantum_like_models.history_simple: The idea of applying quantum formalisms to psychology and economics began to develop in the late 20th century.
quantum_like_models.how_it_works_simple: Like a coin spinning in the air is both heads and tails at once, so a person deciding exists in a 'superposition' of options.
quantum_like_models.description: Quantum-like models apply the structure of quantum theory—states in Hilbert space, superpositions, probability interference, entanglement—to model phenomena where classical probabilistic approaches fail: order effects in surveys, violations of the law of total probability, context-dependent judgments. They do not postulate a physical quantum nature but use mathematical isomorphism.
quantum_like_models.history: Pioneering work in this area was done by mathematicians and cognitive psychologists such as D. Aerts and A. Khrennikov starting in the 1990s. They showed that many 'irrational' human decisions are well described by quantum-like probabilities. Later, the field was taken up by quantum information specialists. David Deutsch contributed to quantum computing, providing tools; John Archibald Wheeler reflected on the participation of the observer, which resonates with quantum-like approaches.
quantum_like_models.how_it_works: The state of an agent is described by a vector in Hilbert space (a complex vector space with an inner product). Choices are represented by projection operators. The probability of an outcome is given by the squared modulus of the projection (Born rule). Context influences like a change of basis. This allows quantum-like effects: interference (when the sum of probabilities does not reduce to the classical sum) and violation of distributivity. The principle of superposition and interference of states is applied.
key_problems: Testing whether quantum-likeness is truly necessary or if classical models with nonlinearity suffice
Lack of a unified physical basis for quantum effects in macroscopic systems
Difficulty in interpreting quantum-like probabilities in psychology
quantum_like_models.fun_fact: When modeling public opinion polls, the quantum representation can predict results more accurately than a naive probability model because a question can change the respondent's state, similar to a quantum measurement.

formulas.description: Born rule for the probability of transition from state |ψ⟩ to state |φ⟩
formulas.meaning: P is probability, |ψ⟩ is the initial state (vector in Hilbert space), |φ⟩ is the final state, ⟨φ|ψ⟩ is the inner product (probability amplitude)

formulas.description: Expansion of a state in a basis
formulas.meaning: |ψ⟩ is the state vector, c_i are complex amplitudes, |e_i⟩ is an orthonormal basis (set of mutually exclusive states)

active_contour_model.name: active contour model
active_contour_model.mini: An active contour is like an elastic band that automatically wraps around an object in an image.
active_contour_model.practical_application: Segmentation of cell boundaries in microscopy or outlining organs in ultrasound images.
active_contour_model.description_popular: Active contour models (snakes) are a boundary-based segmentation method. A deformable spline, defined parametrically as v(s) = (x(s), y(s)), evolves under the influence of internal forces (elasticity, bending) and external forces (image gradients, intensity). Minimization of total energy (E = ∫ (E_int + E_ext) ds) leads to convergence at object boundaries. Extensions such as geodesic active contours use level sets to handle topology changes.
active_contour_model.fun_fact_popular: Snakes work iteratively: they start from an initial guess and can 'get stuck' if the start is far from the true boundary, much like a blind person feeling their way around an object.
active_contour_model.description_simple: To find the outline of a cell under a microscope, a computer can take a rough curve and gradually pull it towards the edges of the cell. This method, called an active contour or 'snake', works like a rubber band that minimizes energy: it strives to be smooth while lying on brightness transitions. The algorithm (a step-by-step procedure) moves the curve until it locks onto the target.
active_contour_model.history_simple: Proposed by Michael Kass, Andrew Witkin, and Demetri Terzopoulos in 1988. Their paper 'Snakes: Active Contour Models' spawned an entire direction in computer vision. It was initially applied to medical images and object tracking in video.
active_contour_model.how_it_works_simple: The contour is defined by a set of points. The computer calculates an energy (a number indicating how well the contour fits). Internal energy keeps the curve smooth, like a spring that resists bending. External energy pulls the curve towards edges, like gravity. The algorithm moves the points downhill on the energy landscape until they reach a minimum.
active_contour_model.description: Active contour models iteratively deform an initial curve to minimize an energy functional. Internal energy ensures smoothness and regularity; external energy attracts to high-gradient regions. The Euler–Lagrange equation gives the force balance. It is implemented via gradient descent or dynamic programming. Variants include geometric active contours (based on level sets)—they naturally handle topology changes—and region-based models (Chan–Vese), which use intensity statistics.
active_contour_model.history: Kass, Witkin, and Terzopoulos (1988) formulated the snake model. In 1995, Caselles et al. proposed geodesic active contours, linking curve evolution to energy minimization via level sets. Chan and Vese (2001) created a gradient-free region-based model based on the Mumford–Shah functional. Active contours influenced many segmentation methods before the era of deep learning dominance.
active_contour_model.how_it_works: The curve is defined parametrically: v(s) = (x(s), y(s)). Energy: E = ∫₀¹ (α|v'(s)|² + β|v''(s)|²) + E_ext(v(s)) ds. The first term controls tension, the second stiffness. External energy is typically –|∇I|² for edge attraction. The snake is optimized variationally: ∂v/∂t = αv'' – βv'''' – ∇E_ext. Discretization yields a system of equations solved iteratively. Level set methods: the curve is the zero level of a function φ, evolution: ∂φ/∂t = g|∇φ| div(∇φ/|∇φ|) + ∇g·∇φ.
key_problems: Sensitivity to initial guess
Inability of parametric snakes to change topology
Convergence to local minima
Difficulties with blurred or broken boundaries
active_contour_model.fun_fact: The original snake paper demonstrated lip tracking in video, leading to early applications in facial animation.

formulas.description: Energy functional of the snake
formulas.meaning: v(s) — parametric curve (s ∈ [0,1]), α — tension coefficient, β — stiffness coefficient, E_ext — external energy (typically a function of the image gradient)

phylogenetic_network.name: phylogenetic network
phylogenetic_network.mini: Like intertwined tree branches, evolutionary lines do not always diverge — sometimes they merge, forming a network of interwoven connections.
phylogenetic_network.practical_application: Phylogenetic networks help track the spread of viruses (e.g., COVID-19) and identify hybrid plant species for breeding.
phylogenetic_network.description_popular: A phylogenetic network is a model of evolutionary relationships that, in addition to branching (speciation), accounts for reticulation events: horizontal gene transfer, hybridization, recombination. Unlike a phylogenetic tree, the network contains nodes with multiple parent ancestors, making it more suitable for describing the evolution of prokaryotes, viruses, and some plants.
phylogenetic_network.fun_fact_popular: Up to 10% of the human genome may be of viral origin, and network models help trace these unusual genetic connections.
phylogenetic_network.description_simple: A phylogenetic network is a diagram showing kinship relations between species, like a family tree, but with 'bridges' between branches. These bridges mean that genes could be transferred directly from one species to another (horizontal gene transfer) or that populations interbred (hybridization). Unlike a simple tree, the network better reflects the tangled history of life.
phylogenetic_network.history_simple: The idea arose in the late 20th century when scientists realized that ordinary evolutionary trees do not explain all cases. With the development of genetics and computers, networks began to be constructed from the 1990s.
phylogenetic_network.how_it_works_simple: Evolution is like a river delta: the main flow splits into branches, but branches can reconnect. So here: species diverge, but sometimes exchange genetic material, creating a network instead of a tree.
phylogenetic_network.description: A phylogenetic network is a graph structure representing evolutionary relationships between taxa, allowing for reticulation events (horizontal gene transfer, hybridization, introgression, recombination). Mathematically, it can be either a rooted or unrooted graph, often with variations: split networks, recombination networks, overlay networks. Algorithms for their construction are based on optimality methods (least squares, maximum likelihood, Bayesian inference) and combinatorial approaches (split decomposition, neighbor-net). Unlike trees, networks can model non-vertical transmission of hereditary information, which is critical for understanding the evolution of prokaryotes and viruses.
phylogenetic_network.history: The concept of phylogenetic networks arose in response to discrepancies between gene trees and species trees. In the 1980s, Walter Fitch realized the need to account for horizontal transfer, and in the 1990s, with the development of sequencing methods and computer power, the first algorithms for network construction appeared (e.g., the split decomposition algorithm of Bandelt and Dress, 1992). Pioneers of computational phylogenetics included David Swofford, Joseph Felsenstein, and later David Bryant, Daniel Huson, and others who developed modern methods.
phylogenetic_network.how_it_works: Construction of a phylogenetic network begins with the choice of an evolutionary model and data (usually DNA sequences). Algorithms estimate distances or likelihoods and search for a topology that minimizes the number of reticulations or maximizes likelihood. Networks can be explicit — where reticulation nodes denote specific transfer events — or implicit, showing alternative evolutionary scenarios as intertwined structures (e.g., split networks). Validation and network selection are often performed using information criteria (AIC, BIC) and bootstrap.
key_problems: Development of efficient algorithms for large datasets with hundreds of genomes.
Distinguishing true phylogenetic signal from noise and incomplete lineage sorting.
Integration of fossil data into network models.
Quantitative assessment of uncertainty and statistical support for individual reticulations.
phylogenetic_network.fun_fact: There are 'viruses of viruses' — virophages (e.g., Sputnik) that parasitize giant viruses, and network models help untangle these three-way evolutionary relationships.

post_transcriptional_regulation.name: Post-transcriptional regulation
post_transcriptional_regulation.mini: Quality control at the cell's factory: RNA copies of genes are checked, cut, tagged, or destroyed after synthesis to precisely tune protein production.
post_transcriptional_regulation.practical_application: Explains how cells adapt to stress without changing DNA; underlies RNA vaccines and small interfering RNA therapy.
post_transcriptional_regulation.description_popular: Post-transcriptional regulation encompasses all changes and the fate of RNA molecules after transcription (RNA synthesis on a DNA template). These include: splicing (removing non-coding introns and joining exons), alternative splicing (creating different protein variants from one gene), capping, polyadenylation, base editing, transport from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, localization, control of stability and translation rate (protein synthesis). This is critical for dynamic cellular adaptation to environmental conditions and underlies many diseases.
post_transcriptional_regulation.fun_fact_popular: The same gene can yield over 38,000 protein variants through alternative splicing—like assembling different sentences from the same set of words.
post_transcriptional_regulation.description_simple: Genes are instructions in DNA. To make a protein, the cell first creates an RNA copy (ribonucleic acid) of the gene. Post-transcriptional regulation controls the fate of this RNA after copying: the cell can cut out extra pieces (splicing), attach a protective cap (cap) and tail (poly-A), send it for storage, or quickly destroy it. Thus, the cell decides how much and when a protein will be synthesized.
post_transcriptional_regulation.history_simple: For a long time, it was believed that the main control was turning genes on and off at the DNA level. In the 1990s, it was discovered that regulation at the RNA level is no less important. A key discovery—microRNA (small regulatory molecules) in 1993 in the worm C. elegans—showed that cells actively manage RNA after transcription.
post_transcriptional_regulation.how_it_works_simple: It’s like a postal service: the gene is a letter, RNA is a copy of the letter that is carried to the ribosome for protein synthesis. Regulation can delay the courier, change the text (RNA editing), tear up the letter, or redirect it to another address—this way the cell controls message delivery.
post_transcriptional_regulation.description: Post-transcriptional regulation is a set of molecular mechanisms that control the processing, transport, stability, and translation of RNA after its synthesis by RNA polymerase. Key processes: 1) capping of the 5' end with 7-methylguanosine for protection and translation initiation; 2) splicing—removal of introns by the spliceosome or autocatalytically (ribozymes); 3) editing (cytidine to uridine or adenosine to inosine substitution) altering the sequence; 4) polyadenylation of the 3' end, affecting stability and export; 5) transport by mRNP complexes through nuclear pores; 6) regulation of translation involving microRNAs, siRNAs, RNA-binding proteins, and localization in specific compartments (e.g., in neurons). Each step is finely tuned by signaling pathways, ensuring plasticity of gene expression without altering the genome.
post_transcriptional_regulation.history: Until the 1970s, regulation of gene expression was largely associated with transcription (the Jacob and Monod operon model). In 1977, Phillip Sharp and Richard Roberts independently discovered introns and splicing in adenoviruses, and in the 1980s, Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman proved the catalytic activity of RNA (ribozymes). In 1993, Victor Ambros and colleagues described the first microRNA, lin-4 in C. elegans, demonstrating the regulatory function of small RNAs. Later, mechanisms of RNA interference (siRNA) and editing (APOBEC enzymes) were discovered. These works shifted the paradigm from linear information transfer DNA→RNA→protein to a complex network of post-transcriptional control, recognized as key in development, immunity, and pathology.
post_transcriptional_regulation.how_it_works: Post-transcriptional mechanisms modulate the fate of the transcript through the formation of ribonucleoprotein complexes. The cap-binding complex attracts elongation factors, the spliceosome recognizes splicing sites by consensus sequences, and the poly(A)-binding protein stabilizes mRNA. MicroRNAs within RISC partially pair with the 3' untranslated region of mRNA and repress translation or cause deadenylation and degradation. Localization is achieved by cytoskeleton-dependent transport and anchoring. Disruptions of these processes underlie many diseases: from spinal muscular atrophy (splicing mutation in SMN1) to cancer (global splicing imbalance).
key_problems: How to predict the exact pattern of alternative splicing in different tissues and developmental stages?
What is the complete map of non-coding RNA interactions in neurodegenerative diseases?
Mechanisms of dynamic assembly and disassembly of RNA-protein granules (stress granules, P-bodies) and their role in cellular memory.
post_transcriptional_regulation.fun_fact: Some viruses, such as HIV, use their own Rev protein to bypass nuclear control and export unspliced mRNAs, effectively hijacking the cell's post-transcriptional machinery.

decision_making.name: decision making
decision_making.mini: Choosing one option out of several when the outcomes are not always clear. It's like choosing a path in the fog: we rely on fragmented data and gut feeling.
decision_making.practical_application: It is used everywhere: from everyday purchases to financial management and artificial intelligence strategies. By learning to model this process, we create smart assistants capable of advising or making decisions.
decision_making.description_popular: Decision making is a cognitive process of choosing among alternatives, studied in psychology, neuroscience, economics and mathematics. Classical theories (expected utility) assume a rational agent maximizing benefit. However, experiments have revealed heuristics (simplified rules) and biases: people are subject to the framing effect, avoid losses more than they seek gains, and are time-inconsistent. Modern models include quantum-like formalisms to describe context dependence and violations of the law of total probability.
decision_making.fun_fact_popular: If people always acted rationally, lotteries would not exist because the expected value of a ticket is always less than its price.
decision_making.description_simple: This is how we choose: for example, what to eat for breakfast or whether to go to the movies. Scientists study why sometimes the choice is obvious and other times we struggle. It turns out that emotions, past experience, and even the order in which we receive information influence the decision. Simple mathematical models (like counting pros and cons) do not always work because people are not computers.
decision_making.history_simple: Back in the 17th century, Blaise Pascal discussed bets and probabilities. Then economists built a coherent theory of rational choice, but in the 20th century psychologists showed that people systematically deviate from rationality.
decision_making.how_it_works_simple: The brain weighs different desires: 'I want something sweet' and 'I need something healthy'. A 'tug-of-war' occurs between them, and the strongest at that moment wins.
decision_making.description: Decision making refers to the process of choosing between alternatives under uncertainty, risk, or certainty. Decision theory combines normative models (how one should act) and descriptive models (how people actually act). The normative approach dates back to the von Neumann-Morgenstern axioms, where rationality is defined by consistency of preferences. Descriptive models (Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory) introduce a value function that reflects diminishing sensitivity and loss aversion. In quantum decision models, the agent's state is represented as a superposition, and the outcome is measured, explaining question order effects and interference effects.
decision_making.history: Decision analysis began with Pascal and Fermat in the 17th century in correspondence about gambling problems. In the 20th century, von Neumann and Morgenstern formalized expected utility theory. Later, Herbert Simon introduced the concept of bounded rationality. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky experimentally demonstrated systematic biases, for which Kahneman won the Nobel Prize. David Deutsch contributed to quantum computing, which provided tools for quantum-like decision models.
decision_making.how_it_works: Classical approach: a utility function U(x) assigns a number to each outcome, and the action maximizing expected utility E[U(x)] = ∑ P_i U(x_i) is chosen. Prospect theory replaces this with weighted value: V = ∑ π(p_i) v(x_i), where π(p) is the decision weight, v(x) is the value function, concave for gains and convex for losses. In the quantum model, the state |ψ⟩ in Hilbert space evolves unitarily until a 'question' which is described by a projector, and the probability of the answer is given by the squared modulus of the amplitude. The principle of superposition and Born's rule are applied.
key_problems: How to combine normative prescriptions with descriptive biases into a single model
The neurobiological basis of rationality violations
Predicting decisions in dynamically changing contexts
decision_making.fun_fact: The endowment effect shows that people are willing to buy a mug for $5, but to sell their own they want at least $10, which contradicts the standard economic model.

formulas.description: Expected utility
formulas.meaning: EU — expected utility, p_i — probability of outcome i, U(x_i) — utility of outcome x_i (subjective value)

formulas.description: Prospect theory (simplified)
formulas.meaning: V — subjective value of the decision, π(p_i) — probability weight (distorted probability), v(Δx_i) — value function of the change relative to the reference point (Δx_i — gain or loss)

horizontal_gene_transfer.name: horizontal gene transfer
horizontal_gene_transfer.mini: Bacteria exchange genes like people exchange text messages: quickly, directly, and without kinship. This is how antibiotic resistance can instantly spread among different species.
horizontal_gene_transfer.practical_application: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) specifically explains the rapid emergence of superbugs in hospitals and enables the creation of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) for agriculture.
horizontal_gene_transfer.description_popular: Horizontal gene transfer is the process of transferring genetic material between cells of the same generation, bypassing vertical inheritance (from parents to offspring). It is widespread among prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) and less common in eukaryotes. It plays a key role in microbial adaptation, especially in acquiring antibiotic resistance and the evolution of virulence.
horizontal_gene_transfer.fun_fact_popular: Genes responsible for toxins in many dangerous bacteria (for example, Vibrio cholerae) were originally brought in by horizontal transfer from harmless ancestors or viruses.
horizontal_gene_transfer.description_simple: Horizontal gene transfer is the transfer of genetic information between organisms that are not parent and offspring. Bacteria exchange genes like people exchange text messages: quickly, directly, and without kinship. You receive an SMS with a useful tip and apply it immediately — that's how bacteria acquire resistance genes, new enzymes, and even entire blocks of DNA.
horizontal_gene_transfer.history_simple: It was first suspected in 1928 when scientist Frederick Griffith, in an experiment with pneumococci, observed the transformation of harmless bacteria into deadly ones. Later, in 1944, Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty proved that it is DNA that is transferred.
horizontal_gene_transfer.how_it_works_simple: Bacteria use several methods of 'communication': they can capture free DNA from the environment (transformation), receive genes via a carrier virus (transduction), or connect via a tube for direct exchange (conjugation). All this is like different communication channels.
horizontal_gene_transfer.description: Horizontal (lateral) gene transfer (HGT) is the non-reproductive transfer of genetic material between cells, often phylogenetically distant. Molecular mechanisms: natural transformation (uptake and integration of exogenous DNA), conjugation (transfer of plasmids via type IV pili), transduction (by bacteriophages), and gene transfer agents (GTAs) — virus-like particles. In eukaryotes, cases are known involving endocytosis, viral integration, and intercellular contacts. The scale of HGT is enormous: up to 20% of the genome of a typical bacterium may have foreign origin.
horizontal_gene_transfer.history: Griffith's classic experiment (1928) on pneumococcal transformation first demonstrated the possibility of trait transfer between bacteria. In 1944, Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty identified the transforming agent as DNA. Conjugation was described by Lederberg and Tatum in 1946. Transduction was discovered by Norton Zinder and Joshua Lederberg in 1952. With the development of genomics in the 1990s, it became clear that HGT is not an exception but the norm for the microbial world.
horizontal_gene_transfer.how_it_works: In natural transformation, bacteria in a state of competence bind double-stranded DNA, cleave it, transport a single-stranded fragment inside, and integrate it into the chromosome by homologous recombination. Conjugation is initiated by contact via pili, cleavage of the plasmid at oriT, and transfer of single-stranded DNA to the recipient. Transduction begins with erroneous packaging of a bacterial DNA fragment into the phage capsid during lysogenic induction. Evolutionary consequences include genome mosaicism, rapid spread of adaptive alleles, and conflict with phylogenetic signals.
key_problems: Quantitative assessment of the frequency of HGT in natural ecosystems.
Identification of ancient HGT events and their role in macroevolution.
Study of HGT in multicellular organisms: how widespread and functional it is.
Creation of models that account for HGT for accurate phylogenetic reconstruction.
horizontal_gene_transfer.fun_fact: Tardigrades (water bears) are record holders among animals for capturing foreign genes — up to 17% of their genome comes from bacteria, fungi, and plants.

contrastive_learning.name: Contrastive Learning
contrastive_learning.mini: Training by comparing similar and dissimilar — that's how contrastive learning works. Instead of memorizing labels, a neural network learns to capture the essence, distinguishing a cat from a dog even if they weren't named.
contrastive_learning.practical_application: Face recognition without labels, searching for similar photos in large archives, improving diagnoses from medical images when labeled data is scarce.
contrastive_learning.description_popular: Contrastive learning is an approach in machine learning that allows building high-quality data representations without labels (self-supervised learning). It relies on the concept of contrastive loss: the model attracts representations (embeddings) of semantically close objects (positive pairs) and repels representations of unrelated ones (negative pairs). For example, in images, positive pairs are different views (augmentations) of the same photo, while negatives are all other images in the mini-batch. This way, the neural network learns to extract invariant features, ignoring irrelevant variations in lighting, rotation, scale. The method underpins many modern recognition systems, where it often outperforms supervised learning when labels are scarce.
contrastive_learning.fun_fact_popular: OpenAI's CLIP system, trained contrastively on image-text pairs, can generate images from descriptions even though it was never directly taught artistic style — it simply captured the correlations.
contrastive_learning.description_simple: Contrastive learning is a method where a computer program (neural network) is trained to find similarities and differences between objects. It is shown pairs of examples: some pairs are alike (e.g., two photos of the same person), others are different (photos of different people). The program tries to make similar objects end up close together in its 'memory' (feature vector) and dissimilar ones far apart. It's like a 'find the pair' game, but for millions of images.
contrastive_learning.history_simple: The idea of learning by comparisons is old: back in 2006, 'Siamese networks' were used for signature verification. But the modern boom began in 2018–2020 when researchers from Google (SimCLR) and Facebook (MoCo) proposed ways to train large neural networks without human supervision by creating pairs from a single image with different distortions.
contrastive_learning.how_it_works_simple: Take one image and create two new versions — for example, rotate it and change its color. These two versions form a positive pair. Other images in the set serve as negative examples. The neural network converts each image into a vector of numbers. Its task is to reduce the distance between the vectors of the positive pair and increase it for negative pairs. Over time, the vectors start to encode the meaning of the image rather than random details.
