contrastive_learning.description: Contrastive learning is a family of representation learning methods in which the model optimizes a metric space so that semantically similar objects map to nearby points, and dissimilar ones to distant points. Formally, for each anchor example x, a positive example x⁺ is formed, typically via augmentations or context, along with a set of negative examples {x⁻_i}. A loss based on softmax comparison is minimized: the model incentivizes high similarity between x and x⁺ relative to all other pairs. A key innovation in recent years is the use of large mini-batches and memory mechanisms to store negative examples (MoCo) or the elimination of negative pairs via asymmetric architectures (BYOL, SimSiam). Theoretical analysis connects contrastive learning to maximizing mutual information and learning on positive-definite kernels.
contrastive_learning.history: The roots trace back to metric learning: Siamese networks (Bromley et al., 1993) for signature comparison. In 2006, Hadsell and LeCun proposed contrastive loss for learning invariant representations. Revival of interest is linked to progress in self-supervised learning for images: in 2018, the InstDisc model (Wu et al.) used a memory bank; breakthroughs came with MoCo (He et al., 2020) with a queue of negative examples and SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020) with large batch sizes and strong augmentation. These works showed that contrastive pretraining achieves accuracy close to supervised learning, and sometimes surpasses it when fine-tuning on small datasets. The approach was later adapted for video, audio, graphs, and multimodal data (CLIP, 2021).
contrastive_learning.how_it_works: The algorithm includes three stages: (1) stochastic data augmentation creates two independent representations of the same input (e.g., random cropping, color distortion); (2) an encoder (ResNet, ViT) maps them into vectors in a latent space; (3) a projection head (MLP) transforms them into a lower-dimensional space where the contrastive InfoNCE loss is computed: L = -log[ exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) / ∑_{k=1}^{2N} 1_{k≠i} exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ) ], where sim is cosine similarity, τ is a temperature parameter. Optimization reduces the cross-entropy between the distributions of positive and negative pairs. To prevent representational collapse (all vectors degenerating to a single point), mechanisms are employed: negative pairs from a queue (MoCo), stop-gradient and predictor (BYOL), clustering (SwAV). As a result, the latent space acquires semantic structure invariant to the specified transformations.
key_problems: How to choose augmentations that guarantee semantic preservation for arbitrary data types (audio, graphs, video)?
Why some methods (BYOL, SimSiam) work without negative pairs, avoiding collapse — there is no complete theoretical clarity.
Can contrastive learning be extended to continuous output tasks (regression) or time series without quality loss?
Does a universal contrastive pretraining exist that transfers to any downstream task without fine-tuning?
contrastive_learning.fun_fact: In SimCLR experiments, it was found that the best augmentations for photos are random cropping and color distortion, while blurring or rotation degraded results; the optimal combination wasn't obvious even to the creators.

formulas.description: Contrastive InfoNCE loss for one positive example j and 2N-1 negatives (including all others in the mini-batch).
formulas.meaning: L_{i,j} — loss value for the pair (i, j); z_i, z_j, z_k — representation vectors (embeddings) in the latent space (dimensionless, normalized); sim — similarity function, typically cosine similarity: sim(z_i, z_j) = z_i^T z_j / (||z_i|| ||z_j||) (dimensionless, from -1 to 1); τ — temperature parameter (positive number, usually 0.1–0.5), controls the sharpness of the distribution; N — mini-batch size (number of original images, after augmentation we get 2N vectors); 1_{k ≠ i} — indicator function, excluding the pair i=j from the denominator

apparent_diffusion_coefficient.name: apparent diffusion coefficient
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.mini: The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) is a measure of how easily water molecules move in tissues. Like trying to walk through a crowd: the denser the crowd, the less your mobility — similarly, water molecules squeezed by cells move less freely.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.practical_application: In MRI, ADC maps help distinguish cancer (dense cellular structure, reduced diffusion) from healthy tissue or edema, improving diagnostic accuracy without biopsy.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.description_popular: The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) is a quantitative parameter derived from diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI). When DWI is performed with different b-factors (gradient pulse amplitudes), an exponential signal decay curve is obtained. ADC numerically equals the slope of this curve on a semi-log scale and reflects the average diffusion within a voxel (three-dimensional pixel). On ADC maps, areas with restricted diffusion appear hypointense (dark), which correlates with high cellularity of malignant tumors.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.fun_fact_popular: ADC values help not only to detect cancer but also to predict its aggressiveness: the lower the ADC, the higher the Gleason score on biopsy.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.description_simple: The body contains water, and its molecules are constantly in chaotic motion (called Brownian motion or diffusion). In different tissues, this motion is hindered by various obstacles — cell membranes, proteins. They act like a mesh that traps molecules. Where there are many cells packed tightly (as in a tumor), molecules move more slowly. ADC shows this 'apparent' speed because we measure not the true movement of a single molecule but the averaged effect over the observation time. The lower the ADC, the more restrictions, and the more suspicious the tissue.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.history_simple: The method of diffusion-weighted MRI was invented in the 1960s by Edward Stejskal and John Tanner, but it became widely used in medicine in the 1990s thanks to the work of Denis Le Bihan and others. ADC became a standard evaluation parameter.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.how_it_works_simple: The MR scanner takes two images: one without an additional gradient, the second with a strong gradient that 'quenches' the signal from moving molecules. By comparing how much the signal dropped, ADC is calculated. If molecules move freely (as in the bladder), ADC is high. If they are compressed (as in a tumor), the signal persists, and ADC is low.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.description: ADC — apparent diffusion coefficient, calculated by the formula ADC = -ln(S/S0)/b, where S and S0 are signal intensities with and without the diffusion gradient, b is the weighting factor, proportional to the square of the gradient amplitude and duration. In living tissues, diffusion is non-isotropic and restricted by membranes, so ADC reflects not the true self-diffusion coefficient (D0) but the combined effect of all restrictions on the time scale of the MR experiment (~50 ms). ADC decreases with increased cellular density (tumors), ischemia (cellular edema in stroke), abscesses (viscous pus). It increases in necrosis, cysts, edema. In the prostate, ADC <0.6–0.8×10⁻³ mm²/s is suspicious for cancer. Models that account for non-exponential decay are used: intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) separates true diffusion and perfusion, diffusion kurtosis and tensor imaging describe anisotropy.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.history: Diffusion MRI was proposed by Stejskal and Tanner in 1965, using gradient pulses to measure self-diffusion. In 1984, Denis Le Bihan demonstrated its applicability in medicine, obtaining the first diffusion-weighted images of the brain. The term 'apparent diffusion coefficient' emphasized the difference from free diffusion due to tissue barriers. By the 1990s, ADC had become a routine quantitative biomarker in MRI. In the 2000s, the IVIM concept (Le Bihan et al.) allowed separation of the microcirculation contribution. Today, ADC is a key component of multiparametric prostate MRI and brain diagnostics.
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.how_it_works: The DWI sequence includes two strong gradient pulses of equal amplitude G, duration δ, separated by interval Δ. The first pulse encodes the phase of spins according to their position, the second refocuses. If a spin has moved, the phase shift is not compensated, and the signal is attenuated. By measuring the signal at a minimum of two b-values (b = γ²G²δ²(Δ-δ/3), where γ is the gyromagnetic ratio), a plot of ln(S) vs b is constructed. The slope of this plot (absolute value) is the ADC. In practice, a monoexponential model is used, but due to complex microstructure, deviations may occur. The ADC map is computed pixel-by-pixel after model fitting.
key_problems: Standardization of b-values and calculation methods across manufacturers and centers
Variability of ADC due to physiological parameters (temperature, hydration), motion artifacts, and eddy currents from gradients
Limitation of the monoexponential decay model
Difficulty in differentiating hypointense benign changes (e.g., stromal hyperplasia of the prostate) from cancer
Need for fast sequences that reduce distortions
apparent_diffusion_coefficient.fun_fact: ADC maps can be generated with high resolution, but even at standard resolution they are so sensitive that they respond to a 1°C change in tissue temperature — this is being explored for monitoring thermal ablation.

formulas.description: Formula for calculating the apparent diffusion coefficient
formulas.meaning: S — MRI signal intensity with diffusion gradient, S0 — signal intensity without diffusion gradient, b — diffusion weighting factor characterizing sensitivity to diffusion, depends on gradient pulse parameters; ADC units — mm²/s (often expressed as 10⁻³ mm²/s).

molecular_property_prediction.name: molecular property prediction
molecular_property_prediction.mini: How to guess the taste of a dish without tasting it, by the list of ingredients. This is how computers learn to predict the properties of molecules — their toxicity, solubility or drug efficacy — avoiding lengthy laboratory experiments.
molecular_property_prediction.practical_application: Speeds up the development of new materials and drugs, from biodegradable plastics to targeted anticancer agents.
molecular_property_prediction.description_popular: Molecular property prediction is an interdisciplinary field at the intersection of chemistry, physics, and computer science, where computer models are trained on experimental data to estimate the characteristics of molecules without laboratory synthesis. Models can be based on physical laws (quantum mechanics) or on statistical analysis of big data (machine learning). They predict parameters such as toxicity, biological activity, solubility, melting point, and even the color of a substance.
molecular_property_prediction.fun_fact_popular: Modern algorithms can check millions of molecule candidates for a new drug in seconds, whereas synthesizing and testing a single molecule in the lab takes weeks and costs thousands of dollars.
molecular_property_prediction.description_simple: Molecules are tiny combinations of atoms, and each has its own properties: how strong it smells, whether it dissolves in water, whether it can serve as a medicine. Previously, the only way to find out was a laboratory experiment. Now scientists train computer programs (algorithms that find patterns in data) to 'guess' these properties just by looking at the molecule's structure. It's similar to how an experienced chef can tell from a recipe whether the soup will be salty or spicy without tasting every spoonful.
molecular_property_prediction.history_simple: The idea emerged in the mid-20th century along with the development of quantum chemistry (the science that describes the behavior of electrons in molecules). The first mathematical models linking structure and properties were proposed by chemist Corwin Hansch in the 1960s. With the advent of powerful computers and large databases in the 21st century, the method became truly accurate and fast.
molecular_property_prediction.how_it_works_simple: The computer model is fed thousands of examples: for each molecule in the database, its structure and measured property (say, boiling point) are known. The model learns to associate structural features (e.g., number of carbon atoms, presence of certain groups) with the resulting number. After training, it is given a new molecule — and it produces a prediction, like a psychic but based on rigorous patterns.
molecular_property_prediction.description: Molecular property prediction encompasses a wide range of computational approaches to estimate the physicochemical and biological characteristics of molecules. Starting from the fundamental principle that the properties of a substance are determined by its electronic structure (described by the Schrödinger equation), modern methods follow two paths. The first is quantum-chemical calculations (e.g., density functional theory), which allow the computation of energy, dipole moment, absorption spectra based solely on nuclear positions and electron numbers, but require significant computational resources. The second is empirical machine learning models (gradient boosting, neural networks, graph convolutions), trained on experimental data from public databases (PubChem, ChEMBL). In these approaches, a molecule is represented as a set of descriptors (topological, geometric, electrostatic) or directly as a graph, where vertices are atoms and edges are bonds. The trained model captures complex nonlinear 'structure-property' relationships and can generalize to molecules not included in the training set. A key challenge is interpretability: the physical mechanism often remains hidden in the 'black box' of the algorithm.
molecular_property_prediction.history: The roots go back to the 1960s, when Corwin Hansch formulated quantitative structure-activity relationships (QSAR), proposing linear equations linking substituent hydrophobicity to biological activity. In the 1970s–80s, advances in computing made it possible to include quantum-chemical indices and three-dimensional descriptors. A breakthrough came in the 2010s with the emergence of deep learning and GPU availability: models learned to 'read' molecules directly from graph structures, achieving high accuracy in predicting solubility, toxicity, and excited-state energies. Today, property prediction is an integral part of virtual screening in pharmaceutics and the design of new materials.
molecular_property_prediction.how_it_works: At the core of any prediction is the mapping of a molecule into a space of descriptors or a vector representation. The simplest descriptors are atom counts of a certain type, molecular weight, surface area. More complex ones encode information about rings, hydrogen bond donors/acceptors, partial charges (calculated, for example, by the Gasteiger method). In graph neural networks, each atom receives a feature vector, which is iteratively updated by messages from neighboring atoms; the final molecular vector is aggregated and fed to a fully connected layer that outputs a prediction. Training minimizes a loss function, such as mean squared error for continuous properties or cross-entropy for classification. The most important physical laws underlying quantum methods are the Schrödinger equation (time-independent and time-dependent) and the Pauli principle (the exclusion of two fermions occupying the same quantum state). For statistical models, physics is not explicitly required, but feature selection is often motivated by the principle 'like dissolves like': similar molecules have similar properties. Model quality is checked on a hold-out set using metrics (R², RMSE, AUC).
key_problems: Interpretability of black-box models: why does the neural network consider a molecule toxic?
Transfer of predictions to new classes of compounds (generalization ability)
Accounting for environmental conditions (temperature, pressure, solvent) in a single model
Prediction of quantum properties with accuracy comparable to ab initio methods but in fractions of a second
molecular_property_prediction.fun_fact: Graph neural networks used for molecular analysis employ the same architecture as algorithms that detect fake accounts in social networks — in both cases, the structure of connections between nodes plays a key role.

deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.name: deep learning in medical imaging
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.mini: Just as an experienced doctor learns to recognize diseases from scans, a computer program trains on thousands of examples to find tumors or fractures faster and more accurately than a human.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.practical_application: Used in hospitals for automatic analysis of X-rays, MRIs, and CT scans, helping doctors make diagnoses and reducing the risk of error.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.description_popular: Deep learning in medicine uses convolutional neural networks (an architecture inspired by the visual cortex) to analyze radiological images. The model automatically extracts hierarchical features: from edges and textures to complex structures such as tumors. Training requires large labeled datasets where each scan is annotated with a diagnosis.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.fun_fact_popular: Deep learning algorithms can detect lung cancer in a scan several months earlier than an experienced radiologist.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.description_simple: Deep learning is a way to teach a computer to recognize objects in images. Imagine showing a child many photos of cats, and he remembers what a cat looks like. Similarly, a program is trained on medical images: it 'looks' at thousands of images with known diagnoses and learns to find signs of diseases, such as spots on the lungs or cracks in bones.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.history_simple: The ideas of artificial intelligence emerged long ago, but the real breakthrough came after 2012, when powerful computers and large sets of images enabled neural networks to achieve the accuracy of doctors. Today, new models for various tasks appear every month.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.how_it_works_simple: The program consists of layers that, like a sieve, sift through the image: first they find simple lines, then shapes, then whole objects. In medical imaging, this is how organs, vessels, or anomalies are identified. After training, the program can make a preliminary diagnosis on its own.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.description: Deep learning in medical imaging is the application of artificial neural networks with many hidden layers for automatic analysis and interpretation of medical images such as MRI, CT, X-rays, ultrasound, and histological slides. Architectures include convolutional neural networks (CNN) for extracting spatial features, U-Net for segmentation, generative adversarial networks (GAN) for image synthesis and enhancement, and transformers for capturing long-range dependencies. Training is often complicated by the limited size of labeled data, requiring augmentation, transfer learning, and self-supervised methods.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.history: The roots go back to Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958) and LeCun's convolutional networks (LeNet, 1998), but the real explosion occurred after the triumph of AlexNet on ImageNet in 2012. In medicine, the first successes happened in dermatology (skin cancer classification, 2017) and radiology (pneumonia detection, 2017). The FDA approved the first algorithms for clinical practice in 2018. Now it is a rapidly growing field with thousands of publications per year.
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.how_it_works: The process begins with image preprocessing (normalization, registration). The data is then fed into the neural network, where feature maps are formed through alternating convolutions, pooling, and nonlinearities. For classification tasks, the final layers output disease probabilities; for segmentation, masks of organs or pathologies. Optimization is performed via backpropagation with minimization of a loss function (e.g., binary cross-entropy or Dice coefficient). At inference, the model outputs a prediction in a fraction of a second.
key_problems: Lack of high-quality labeled data, especially for rare pathologies.
Generalization problem: models trained on data from one clinic may fail on scans from another due to different equipment and protocols.
Black-box interpretability: doctors find it hard to trust decisions if the model's logic is unclear.
Robustness to adversarial attacks (imperceptible distortions of scans can change the diagnosis).
deep_learning_in_medical_imaging.fun_fact: In 2018, the CheXNet neural network outperformed four radiologists in detecting pneumonia from chest X-rays, training in just one month on 112,000 images.

optical_microscopy.name: optical microscopy
optical_microscopy.mini: A light microscope is a tube with lenses that magnifies tiny objects, making the world of bacteria, cells, and crystals visible. Like binoculars for distant stars, but in reverse—for the very close.
optical_microscopy.practical_application: Used in biology and medicine for cell analysis, in materials science for inspecting microchips, and in forensics for examining fibers and prints.
optical_microscopy.description_popular: An optical microscope forms an image by refracting visible light through a series of lenses. Resolution is limited by diffraction: according to the Rayleigh criterion, two points are distinguishable if the distance between them is at least half the wavelength divided by the numerical aperture of the objective. Modern methods—fluorescence microscopy, confocal, super-resolution (STED, PALM)—overcome this limit, allowing visualization of structures down to single molecules.
optical_microscopy.fun_fact_popular: With an optical microscope, you can not only look but also move objects: laser tweezers can hold and move individual cells or bacteria.
optical_microscopy.description_simple: An optical microscope collects light that passes through the specimen and magnifies it using a system of lenses. The lenses work like a magnifying glass, but much stronger: you can see things hundreds of times thinner than a hair. Special illumination helps highlight transparent details.
optical_microscopy.history_simple: The first microscopes were built in the late 16th century in the Netherlands. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in the 17th century crafted lenses with huge magnification and first saw bacteria and red blood cells. Later scientists improved the design, and today microscopes can distinguish details smaller than the wavelength of light.
optical_microscopy.how_it_works_simple: Light from a lamp passes through a condenser that directs it onto the specimen. The objective lens creates a magnified, inverted image, and the eyepiece further magnifies it for the eye or camera. To see transparent cells, they are stained or phase contrast is used, which turns invisible phase changes into brightness variations.
optical_microscopy.description: Optical microscopy is a set of methods for observing microscopic objects using visible or near-infrared/ultraviolet radiation. A basic brightfield microscope consists of an illumination system (source, condenser), objective, tube, and eyepiece. Image formation is described by Abbe's theory, according to which the microscope acts as a double Fourier analyzer: first a diffraction pattern is created in the back focal plane of the objective, then interference of diffracted beams reconstructs the image. Resolution d = λ/(2 NA) is determined by the wavelength λ and the numerical aperture NA = n sin θ. Modern techniques include: confocal microscopy (suppression of out-of-focus light), two-photon (excitation in the infrared range, depth penetration), super-resolution (STED – stimulated emission depletion, PALM/STORM – single-molecule activation), light sheet (SPIM – reduced photodamage).
optical_microscopy.history: Zacharias Janssen is credited with constructing a compound microscope (1590). Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1674) achieved 300x magnification with single lenses, discovering microorganisms. Robert Hooke in 'Micrographia' (1665) described cells. In 1873, Ernst Abbe developed the theory of image formation and the sine condition. Carl Zeiss and Otto Schott established industrial production of high-quality objectives. In the 20th century, Frits Zernike invented the phase-contrast microscope (1935, Nobel 1953), Marvin Minsky patented the confocal principle (1957). Super-resolution emerged in the 2000s: STED by Stefan Hell (2014 Nobel), PALM by Eric Betzig and Harold Hess.
optical_microscopy.how_it_works: A beam of light from the source is focused by the condenser onto the specimen. Scattered and directly transmitted light is collected by the objective, which forms a primary image in the plane of the field diaphragm. The eyepiece further magnifies it for viewing by eye or transmission to a detector. Contrast in brightfield microscopes arises from absorption or scattering; phase contrast converts a phase shift into an amplitude change. In fluorescence microscopes, the specimen is illuminated at the excitation wavelength, and emitted radiation is separated by a dichroic mirror and filters. In confocal microscopy, a point source and a detector with a pinhole provide optical sectioning. Super-resolution overcomes the diffraction limit by turning off fluorophores at the periphery of the excitation spot (STED) or by precise localization of single photoactivatable molecules (PALM/STORM).
key_problems: Phototoxicity and photobleaching of living samples.
Compromise between resolution, field of view, and depth of penetration.
Difficulty of obtaining high-quality images in deep tissue layers (beyond 1 mm for confocal microscope).
optical_microscopy.fun_fact: The most precise optical microscopes today can distinguish details as small as 20 nm—that is 25 times smaller than the wavelength of blue light. For comparison, the influenza virus is about 100 nm in size.

formulas.description: Resolution limit of the microscope (Abbe criterion)
formulas.meaning: d – minimum resolvable distance, λ – wavelength of light, NA – numerical aperture of the objective (NA = n sin θ, where n is the refractive index of the medium, θ is half the angle of the light cone entering the objective).

prostate_mri.name: prostate MRI
prostate_mri.mini: Prostate MRI is like a detailed satellite image of an area, with different modes highlighting suspicious spots like a thermal camera revealing heat leaks.
prostate_mri.practical_application: It is used for early detection of prostate cancer, biopsy planning, and monitoring disease progression, replacing random tissue sampling with a targeted approach.
prostate_mri.description_popular: Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) of the prostate combines several sequences: T2-weighted images show anatomy, diffusion-weighted images reveal cell density based on water molecule mobility, and dynamic contrast enhancement shows blood supply. Combined analysis allows distinguishing malignant tumors from benign changes with high probability.
prostate_mri.fun_fact_popular: Prostate MRI can detect cancer the size of a pea, which is impossible to feel with a finger, and helps avoid unnecessary biopsies in 30% of patients.
prostate_mri.description_simple: Prostate MRI is a way to look inside the gland without incisions. Just as different filters on a camera (such as black-and-white or thermal) show different aspects of the same object, MRI uses several settings (modes) to see tissue density, water movement within it, and blood flow. Tumors often appear different, like a rotten apple among healthy ones.
prostate_mri.history_simple: The first MRI scanners appeared in the 1970s thanks to the work of Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield. The use of MRI for the prostate began in the 1980s, and by the 2000s it became a precise method with the addition of multiple modes.
prostate_mri.how_it_works_simple: The MRI machine creates a strong magnetic field, causing hydrogen atoms in the body to align like soldiers. Then radio waves briefly disrupt this order, and the atoms return back, emitting a signal. Based on the signal characteristics, the computer constructs an image. Different tissues produce different signals, like different musical instruments sound differently. By adding special pulses, suspicious areas can be 'colored'.
prostate_mri.description: Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging of the prostate is a non-invasive imaging method based on differences in tissue magnetic properties. The protocol necessarily includes T2-weighted imaging for anatomical detail, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with an apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map to assess cell density, and dynamic contrast enhancement (DCE) with intravenous gadolinium contrast to assess vascularization. MR spectroscopy may also be used. Interpretation is based on the PI-RADS scale, which standardizes the assessment of clinically significant cancer risk. High-field scanners (3 Tesla) are preferable to 1.5 T, providing better resolution. Patient preparation includes bowel cleansing, suppression of peristalsis with antispasmodics, and pre-voiding of the bladder.
prostate_mri.history: The roots of MRI go back to 1938, when Isidor Rabi discovered nuclear magnetic resonance. In 1973, Paul Lauterbur obtained the first MR image, and in 1977, Peter Mansfield developed echo-planar imaging, speeding up scanning. For the prostate, the first studies appeared in the 1980s, but it was not until the mid-2000s that the multiparametric approach took shape. In 2012, the European Society of Urogenital Radiology (ESUR) introduced the standardized PI-RADS reporting system, revised in 2015 and 2019. Today, mpMRI is a key step in prostate cancer diagnosis, reducing the number of unnecessary biopsies and improving the detection of aggressive forms.
prostate_mri.how_it_works: A high-strength magnetic field (1.5 or 3 T) aligns the nuclei of hydrogen atoms. A radiofrequency pulse excites them, after which they relax, emitting signals that are encoded by gradient fields and converted into an image. The T2-weighted sequence reflects differences in transverse relaxation time, showing anatomy: the normal peripheral zone is bright, cancer is dark. Diffusion-weighted imaging at different b-values is sensitive to Brownian motion of water; by calculating ADC, a map is obtained where areas of restricted diffusion (high cell density, typical of cancer) appear dark. Dynamic contrast enhancement tracks contrast uptake and washout, revealing zones of neoangiogenesis — tumors 'light up' in the early phases. Combined assessment using the PI-RADS scale minimizes subjectivity.
key_problems: Variability in interpretation between observers (even with PI-RADS not excluded)
Standardization of scanning protocols across different machines
Differentiation of indolent cancer from clinically significant cancer
Artifacts from bowel movement and hip joints
High cost and limited availability of high-field scanners
prostate_mri.fun_fact: Studies show that prostate MRI can be performed without an endorectal coil, greatly improving patient comfort without loss of diagnostic accuracy.

stochastic_gene_expression.name: stochastic gene expression
stochastic_gene_expression.mini: In each cell, genes are not turned on strictly according to schedule, but with elements of randomness — like raindrops that fall sometimes more often, sometimes less often. This explains why twins with identical DNA are not exact copies.
stochastic_gene_expression.practical_application: Understanding stochastic expression helps explain the resistance of cancer cells to therapy and develop more reliable genetic engineering constructs for biotechnology.
stochastic_gene_expression.description_popular: Stochastic gene expression is the variability of mRNA and protein levels in genetically identical cells under the same conditions, caused by random molecular events. The main sources of noise: intrinsic (biochemical fluctuations during transcription and translation) and extrinsic (differences in the number of ribosomes, polymerases, growth factors between cells). This phenomenon underlies cellular heterogeneity and has evolutionary significance, allowing populations to survive in a changing environment.
stochastic_gene_expression.fun_fact_popular: In the same pancreatic tissue, different cells can produce insulin with a hundredfold difference, even with identical glucose stimulation.
stochastic_gene_expression.description_simple: Stochastic gene expression is a random, unpredictable process of turning genes on and off in the cell. There are thousands of genes in a cell, each turning on by itself, like an independent faucet, sometimes a little more, sometimes less, even if conditions are identical. Because of this, the amounts of proteins (gene products) in different cells of the same organism differ.
stochastic_gene_expression.history_simple: In the 1950s, scientists noticed that seemingly identical bacteria reacted differently to lactose: some produced the enzyme, others did not. But only in the 2000s, with the advent of microscopes that allowed looking at individual cells, it became clear how important this randomness is.
stochastic_gene_expression.how_it_works_simple: DNA is a library of recipes, expression is cooking a dish. The activator molecule (the cook) looks for the right recipe. But there are few molecules and they move chaotically (Brownian motion), so the waiting time and the number of proteins produced vary. This results in 'noise' in the cellular kitchen.
stochastic_gene_expression.description: Stochastic gene expression is a fundamental property of gene regulation, related to the discrete nature of molecular events and low copy numbers of key components (genes, mRNA, transcription factors). Mathematically described by the chemical master equation or stochastic differential equations. Noise is quantitatively characterized by the coefficient of variation (CV) or the Fano factor. Intrinsic noise (inherent to the genetic circuit itself) and extrinsic noise (due to fluctuations in the cellular environment) are distinguished. The two-state model (gene active/inactive) is often used to describe transcriptional bursts. Stochasticity plays a role in cellular decision-making (lambda phage, B. subtilis competence), differentiation, and therapy resistance.
stochastic_gene_expression.history: Classical observations of phenotypic heterogeneity in isogenic populations (e.g., fluctuations of β-galactosidase in E. coli, Novick and Weiner, 1957) were long considered an artifact. In the 1990s, with the development of single-cell fluorescence microscopy (e.g., the work of Elowitz and Leibler, 2000), it became possible to quantitatively study noise. Theoretical foundations were laid by Delbrück (1940), and later by Berg (1978), McAdams, Arkin (1997). Modern high-throughput methods (single-cell sequencing) confirm the ubiquity of stochastic expression.
stochastic_gene_expression.how_it_works: Transcription is initiated by the binding of RNA polymerase and transcription factors to the promoter, a stochastic process due to the low probability of molecular collisions in the cell volume. After initiation, mRNA synthesis occurs in bursts, and degradation of mRNA and proteins is exponential, creating Poisson noise. Negative and positive feedback loops in regulatory networks can suppress or amplify noise. Evolutionarily selected circuits—for example, bistable switches—use noise for random cell fate decisions.
key_problems: Predicting phenotype from genotype taking into account stochasticity in multicellular organisms.
Understanding noise transmission through cascades of signaling pathways.
Using noise in synthetic biology to create controlled heterogeneous systems.
Development of computational models integrating stochasticity and spatiotemporal gradients.
stochastic_gene_expression.fun_fact: The HIV genome contains only 9 genes, but through stochastic expression and alternative splicing, the virus 'tries' many strategies, evading immunity.

formulas.description: Intrinsic noise in constitutive expression
formulas.meaning: η²_int — square of the coefficient of variation (CV²) of intrinsic noise; ⟨m⟩ — average number of mRNA molecules per cell (dimensionless quantity); ⟨p⟩ — average number of protein molecules per cell (dimensionless quantity). The formula is approximate for the case without feedback and negligible extrinsic noise component.

neural_network_oscillations.name: Neural Network Oscillations
neural_network_oscillations.mini: The brain is not silence but a pulsating rhythm. Neural network oscillations are waves of electrical activity that run through the brain like ripples on water, and without them, sleep, memory, or attention would be impossible.
neural_network_oscillations.practical_application: Reading brain rhythms (EEG) helps diagnose epilepsy, control prostheses through brain-computer interfaces, and develop therapies for attention disorders.
neural_network_oscillations.description_popular: Neural network oscillations are periodic bursts of total electrical activity of large populations of neurons. They arise due to mutual excitation and inhibition between cells. Rhythms are distinguished by frequency: delta (0.5–4 Hz) — deep sleep, theta (4–8 Hz) — drowsy state, alpha (8–13 Hz) — relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed, beta (13–30 Hz) — active attention, gamma (30–100 Hz) — information processing. These oscillations are not just noise, but a functional tool: they synchronize remote areas for data exchange (the binding problem), as if two computers tuned to a common carrier frequency.
neural_network_oscillations.fun_fact_popular: In newborns, the alpha rhythm is almost absent and only develops by the age of three, while slow waves of deep sleep help 'wash out' toxic proteins accumulated during the day from the brain.
neural_network_oscillations.description_simple: Oscillations (fluctuations) in neural networks are when many nerve cells (neurons) in the brain begin to turn on and off synchronously, creating rhythmic waves. It's like an orchestra where each instrument plays its note, but together they make music. Such rhythms are slow during sleep and fast when solving problems. They help different parts of the brain communicate with each other.
neural_network_oscillations.history_simple: In 1924, psychiatrist Hans Berger first recorded the electrical activity of the human brain by attaching electrodes to the scalp. He saw waves that he called the alpha rhythm. Since then, scientists have found many different rhythms (delta, theta, gamma, and others) and realized that they are connected with our thoughts, emotions, and memory.
neural_network_oscillations.how_it_works_simple: Neurons communicate through electrical impulses. When a large group of neurons sends impulses at about the same time, a wave arises that can be detected from outside. Strong connections between neurons help maintain the rhythm, like a clock pendulum that is pushed in time.
neural_network_oscillations.description: Oscillations in neural networks are a macroscopic phenomenon generated by the collective dynamics of excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Mathematically, they are modeled by systems of differential equations, such as the Wilson-Cowan model (excitation-inhibition) or the Kuramoto model for coupled oscillators. At the micro level, oscillations arise from reverberating activity in closed circuits, pacemaker neurons, and resonant properties of membranes. These rhythms modulate synaptic plasticity, thereby controlling learning and memory. For example, theta rhythm in the hippocampus organizes sequences of place cell activation, while gamma rhythm promotes precise spike synchronization during sensory information processing. Disturbances in oscillations are biomarkers of neurological diseases (epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia).
neural_network_oscillations.history: History began with the invention of electroencephalography. Hans Berger performed the first human EEG recording in 1924, but recognition came only after 1934 when Edgar Adrian repeated the experiments. Berger described alpha and beta rhythms. In the 1930s–50s, William Grey Walter and others studied the delta rhythm in brain tumors. In the 1960s, computer analysis of EEG allowed the extraction of evoked potentials. A breakthrough was the discovery of local field potentials (LFP) and the link between oscillations and cognitive processes: in the 1980s, Wolf Singer proposed the synchronization hypothesis for feature binding. Today, optogenetics and modern imaging methods allow targeted manipulation of oscillations.
neural_network_oscillations.how_it_works: Oscillations are maintained by a balance of excitation (via glutamatergic neurons) and inhibition (via GABAergic interneurons). The key mechanism is reverberating circuits: excitation from one group of neurons activates inhibitory cells, which after a short delay suppress the first group, after which the cycle repeats. The frequency of oscillations is determined by the time constants of synapses and the length of chains. For a global rhythm to arise, synchronization through gap junctions (electrical synapses) and a common synchronizing projection from subcortical structures, such as the thalamus, is necessary. Gamma rhythm (30–80 Hz) is locally generated by pyramidal neurons and fast-spiking interneurons, which create a temporal window for precise spike synchronization. Theta rhythm coordinates the interaction between the hippocampus and cortex, organizing temporal compression of sequences. From the perspective of nonlinear dynamics, the transition to a synchronized state is a phase transition described by order parameters.
key_problems: Are oscillations unequivocally the cause of cognitive processes or an epiphenomenon?
How to measure the information flow transmitted by phase synchronization without confusing correlation with causation?
Is it possible to create neuroprostheses that restore disrupted rhythms in Alzheimer's disease without disturbing normal dynamics?
How to scale models of individual neuronal ensembles to full-scale cortical activity without losing biophysical accuracy?
neural_network_oscillations.fun_fact: Neural oscillations exist even in invertebrates: in honeybees, gamma rhythm (20–50 Hz) is recorded during olfactory learning and likely helps it remember the smell of nectar.

formulas.description: The Wilson-Cowan model (1972) describes the dynamics of the average activity of excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations of neurons. Often leads to oscillations due to mutual coupling.
formulas.latex: \tau_e \frac{dE}{dt} = -E + (k_e - r_e E) f_e(w_{ee} E - w_{ie} I + P_e) \\ \tau_i \frac{dI}{dt} = -I + (k_i - r_i I) f_i(w_{ei} E - w_{ii} I + P_i)
formulas.meaning: E, I — average activities of excitatory and inhibitory populations (dimensionless, typically 0–1); τ_e, τ_i — time constants of decay (ms); k_e, k_i — maximum activities; r_e, r_i — refractoriness parameters; w_ee, w_ie, w_ei, w_ii — connection strengths; P_e, P_i — external inputs; f_e, f_i — sigmoidal response functions (usually logistic)

lateral_gene_transfer.name: horizontal gene transfer
lateral_gene_transfer.mini: Genes can travel not only through inheritance but also directly between different organisms, like files via Bluetooth. This is how bacteria instantly exchange antibiotic resistance.
lateral_gene_transfer.practical_application: Explains the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance among bacteria and is used in genetic engineering to create GMOs.
lateral_gene_transfer.description_popular: Horizontal gene transfer is a mechanism by which genetic information moves between organisms not through sexual reproduction or inheritance from parents. It is especially characteristic of prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea), but also influences the evolution of eukaryotes. Unlike slow mutations, horizontal transfer allows organisms to acquire ready-made genes, enabling rapid adaptation.
lateral_gene_transfer.fun_fact_popular: The human genome contains genes obtained from viruses and bacteria millions of years ago. About 8% of our DNA consists of remnants of ancient viruses that once integrated into the genome of our ancestors.
lateral_gene_transfer.description_simple: Usually children get genes from their parents. But some organisms, such as bacteria, have a way to exchange genes directly with each other, even if they are not relatives. This is similar to how people share recipes: one baker learned a new baking method and passed it to a colleague, even though they are not from the same family. This way bacteria can quickly learn new tricks — for example, not to fear antibiotics (substances that kill bacteria).
lateral_gene_transfer.history_simple: This was first noticed in the 1920s when scientists saw that different strains of pneumococci could exchange properties. Later, in the 1940s, Oswald Avery and his colleagues showed that the transfer occurs through DNA.
lateral_gene_transfer.how_it_works_simple: The donor organism releases a piece of DNA (the carrier of instructions) into the environment, or passes it through contact, or uses viruses as couriers. The recipient picks up this piece and inserts it into its own DNA, acquiring new abilities.
lateral_gene_transfer.description: Lateral (horizontal) gene transfer (LGT or HGT) is the process of transferring genetic material between cells of different taxonomic groups, bypassing reproductive inheritance. The main mechanisms in prokaryotes: transformation (uptake of free DNA from the environment), conjugation (direct contact with transfer of plasmids through pili), and transduction (transfer by bacteriophages). In eukaryotes, it is less studied but has been proven in a number of protists, fungi, plants, and even animals. LGT plays a key role in the spread of virulence factors, metabolic pathways, and resistance to antimicrobial agents, as well as in the evolution of ancient eukaryotes by capturing genes from symbiotic bacteria. Modern phylogenomic methods allow detecting traces of such transfers based on discrepancies between phylogenetic trees of individual genes and species.
lateral_gene_transfer.history: The concept emerged in the early 20th century. Frederick Griffith in 1928 described the transformation of pneumococci but did not know about DNA. Later, in 1944, the experiment by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty proved that the transforming agent is DNA. The study of LGT intensified with the development of genomics, when it became clear that many bacteria have mosaic genomes with foreign regions.
lateral_gene_transfer.how_it_works: At the molecular level, LGT includes several stages: exit of DNA from the donor (active secretion, cell lysis), existence of extracellular DNA (often in complex with proteins), penetration into the recipient (through membrane channels or receptors), and integration into the genome by homologous recombination or via site-specific recombinases. Many mobile genetic elements, such as transposons and integrons, play an intermediary role. The frequency and success of transfer depend on phylogenetic distance, ecological niche, and the restriction-modification systems of the host cell.
key_problems: Prevalence and evolutionary significance of LGT in eukaryotes, especially in multicellular organisms.
Mechanisms of control and regulation of horizontal transfer in natural ecosystems.
Quantitative assessment of the contribution of LGT to adaptation and speciation.
Development of methods to accurately distinguish traces of ancient LGT from artifacts of phylogenetic reconstruction.
lateral_gene_transfer.fun_fact: Some microorganisms are able to absorb DNA from the environment through natural competence — a state in which the cell expresses proteins for binding and transporting DNA, and this ability can be induced by stress or population density through quorum sensing.

ion_channel_noise.name: ion channel noise
ion_channel_noise.mini: Ion channel noise is the random fluctuation of electric current across a cell membrane due to the spontaneous opening and closing of protein pores. Like interference in a radio receiver, this noise superimposes on the useful signal and affects the precision of nerve impulse transmission.
ion_channel_noise.practical_application: Understanding noise helps develop accurate neural network models and explains why the neural code sometimes errs. In nanoelectronics, similar phenomena limit the miniaturization of sensors.
ion_channel_noise.description_popular: Ion channel noise is the stochastic fluctuations of transmembrane current arising from the discrete nature of conductance and the random switching of individual ion channels between open and closed states. The noise amplitude is inversely proportional to the square root of the number of channels, so in small cells or thin neuronal processes it can reach a significant magnitude, comparable to the signal. The spectral density of the noise follows a Lorentzian with a characteristic frequency determined by the channel kinetics.
ion_channel_noise.fun_fact_popular: In retinal photoreceptors, the visual noise from random channel activations sets a fundamental sensitivity limit: we are able to capture just a few photons only because the channel noise is small.
ion_channel_noise.description_simple: In the cell membrane, there are many ion channels, but they do not open simultaneously or on a strict schedule. Each channel behaves like a miniature switch that spontaneously clicks between 'open' and 'closed' states due to thermal motion (constant vibration of atoms). The total ionic current flowing through the cell therefore continuously fluctuates — like a stream into which pebbles are dropped here and there. These small fluctuations are ion channel noise.
ion_channel_noise.history_simple: Noise associated with the opening of single channels was first directly observed by neurobiologists in the 1970s using the patch clamp method, which made it possible to 'see' currents from a single channel. Before that, noise was masked by averaging over many channels.
ion_channel_noise.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a crowd of people running across a square one by one: if many are running, the overall hum is smooth, but when the observer watches only a few, he notices the irregularity. Ion channel noise is the same irregularity, but in the world of proteins. The electric current through a cell is composed of 'bursts' from individual channels. Since channel transitions are random, the current always has irregular fluctuations, and the fewer the channels, the more noticeable the noise.
ion_channel_noise.description: Ion channels conduct current in quanta whose magnitude is determined by the single-channel conductance γ and the electrochemical driving force. The probabilistic nature of state transitions means the current exhibits shot noise and excess low-frequency noise (1/f noise). Shot noise is described by a Poisson distribution for the number of open channels; its spectral density is constant for a signal with rectangular pulses of duration τ, forming a Lorentzian spectrum S(f) ∝ τ / (1 + (2πfτ)²). Low-frequency noise is linked to slow conformational transitions of the protein or diffusional processes in the membrane. In systems with few channels, noise limits the reliability of signal transmission, setting a barrier for stimulus discrimination (signal-to-noise problem). Quantitatively, the variance of the membrane current σ² = N p_open (1-p_open) i², where N is the number of channels, p_open is the open state probability, i is the single-channel current. This formula follows from the binomial distribution of channel states assuming their independence.
ion_channel_noise.history: The first indications of the discrete nature of membrane currents appeared in the classic work of Hodgkin and Huxley (1952), but direct measurements of single-channel noise became possible thanks to the patch clamp technique developed by Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann (1976, Nobel Prize 1991). By analyzing current fluctuations in a microscopic membrane patch, they showed that channels switch randomly, obeying first-order kinetics. The theory of ion channel noise was formalized in the work of Dennis Baylor, Trevor Lamb, and King-Wai Yau (1979) using photoreceptors as an example, where noise imposes fundamental limits on vision.
ion_channel_noise.how_it_works: Each ion channel can be represented as a two-level system with an energy barrier between states. Transitions occur due to thermal fluctuations obeying the Boltzmann distribution: the probability of overcoming a barrier of height ΔG is proportional to exp(-ΔG/kT). Consequently, at physiological temperatures (~310 K), channels flicker chaotically. The current through the membrane I(t) = Σ_k γ_k (V - E_k) s_k(t), where s_k(t) is an indicator function equal to 1 if the k-th channel is open and 0 if closed. Current fluctuations are determined by the correlation function <I(t)I(t+τ)> and in the frequency domain by the power spectral density. For an ensemble of identical independent channels with a single open state, the current noise has binomial statistics, and the current variance σ_I² = N i² p(1-p), where N is the number of channels, i is the current through one channel, p is the open state probability. This is classical shot noise. In real channels, kinetics is more complex: the presence of multiple closed and inactivated states leads to multi-exponential correlations and colored noise. In small neurons, where channel numbers are on the order of hundreds, noise is comparable to the signal amplitude, causing spontaneous action potentials and contributing significantly to stochastic resonance — a phenomenon in which a weak signal is amplified by an optimal level of noise. Laws and principles: Boltzmann distribution (probability of thermal transitions), Nernst equation (driving force), Ohm's law (current-voltage relationship for an open channel).
key_problems: The origin of low-frequency 1/f noise in biological membranes remains incompletely understood.
The effect of noise on in vivo neural network learning: does it aid or hinder plasticity?
Development of methods to reduce noise in implantable neurointerfaces without loss of sensitivity.
ion_channel_noise.fun_fact: In songbird neurons, potassium channels create noise used to generate spontaneous activity necessary for song learning — birds 'improvise' thanks to the atomic Brownian motion of proteins.

formulas.description: Variance of ion channel noise current
formulas.meaning: σ² is the current variance, N is the number of channels, p is the open probability of a single channel, i is the current through one open channel

evidential_neural_networks.name: evidential neural networks
evidential_neural_networks.mini: A neural network that, instead of a single answer, reports how confident it is in it — like a weather forecast with a 70% chance of rain.
evidential_neural_networks.practical_application: Safe medical diagnosis: in addition to detecting a tumor, the network indicates the confidence level, warning the doctor if the prediction is unreliable.
evidential_neural_networks.description_popular: Evidential neural networks output Dirichlet distribution parameters for classification, representing belief masses. The model learns to provide high evidence for the correct class by minimizing a loss function consisting of expected mean squared error and Kullback–Leibler divergence, which penalizes evidence for other classes. This allows quantifying epistemic (model) and aleatoric (data noise) uncertainty and detecting anomalies.
evidential_neural_networks.fun_fact_popular: If an evidential network is shown a completely new type of image, it will honestly indicate high uncertainty, unlike a regular network that might confidently make a mistake.
evidential_neural_networks.description_simple: A regular neural network (a trainable computer system) gives a single definite answer. An evidential network provides a spectrum of possibilities with evidence weights — like a jury where each opinion is weighted. It uses Dempster–Shafer theory (a mathematical framework for reasoning under incomplete data) and tells not only the answer but also the degree of ignorance: when data is insufficient, it honestly admits 'I don't know'.
evidential_neural_networks.history_simple: Dempster–Shafer theory was developed by Arthur Dempster in the 1960s and Glenn Shafer in the 1970s. Evidential neural networks emerged in the 1990s but gained popularity in the 2010s due to attention to AI reliability. Variants like Deep Evidential Regression (Sensoy et al., 2018) brought them into the mainstream.
evidential_neural_networks.how_it_works_simple: Instead of probabilities that sum to one, the network provides evidence for each class. Imagine giving points to candidates: the more evidence, the more points. If the total sum is small, the network admits ignorance. Training penalizes evidence for incorrect classes and encourages evidence for correct ones, and regularization prevents the network from being overconfident without justification.
evidential_neural_networks.description: Evidential neural networks combine Dempster–Shafer evidence theory with deep learning. For classification, the network predicts parameters of the Dirichlet distribution, which is conjugate to the categorical distribution. The sum of evidence S = ∑ α_k, where α_k = e_k + a_k, e_k is the evidence for class k, a_k is a prior value (usually 1). Belief in class k: b_k = e_k / S. Loss function: L = ∑ (y_j – p_j)² + λ_t ∑ p_j log(p_j / α_j), where p_j = α_j / S. This encourages high evidence for the correct class and penalizes conflicting evidence.
evidential_neural_networks.history: Dempster (1967) and Shafer (1976) introduced belief functions. Denoeux (1995) proposed neural network models based on them. In 2018, Sensoy, Kaplan, and Kandemir extended the approach to deep learning with the Dirichlet distribution. Recent work addresses calibration, adversarial robustness, and applications in medicine and autonomous driving.
evidential_neural_networks.how_it_works: The output layer gives K nonnegative values e_k. Dirichlet concentrations α_k = e_k + a_k. Loss function: L_i(Θ) = ∫ ||y_i – p||² (1/B(α_i)) ∏ p_j^{α_{ij}-1} dp + λ_t D_KL( Dir(p; 	ilde{α}_i) || Dir(p; 1) ), where 	ilde{α}_i = y_i + (1 – y_i) ⊙ α_i. This is equivalent to minimizing expected loss and penalizing non-uniform Dirichlet for incorrect classes. Uncertainty is measured by Dirichlet entropy or the sum of evidence.
key_problems: Calibration of predicted uncertainties
Computational costs for sampling or integration
Sensitivity to out-of-distribution data remains an open question
Interpretability of evidential output
evidential_neural_networks.fun_fact: In medical imaging, evidential networks have been used to identify questionable X-rays: they send them for re-analysis, which in some studies reduced false negative diagnoses by 30%.

formulas.description: Dirichlet distribution over class probabilities
formulas.meaning: p is the vector of class probabilities, α_k are concentration parameters (>0) obtained from the network output, Γ is the gamma function

disjunction_effect.name: disjunction effect
disjunction_effect.mini: The disjunction effect is a quirk of our thinking: when a person doesn't know which of two possible events will occur, they often postpone a decision or behave as if both options are unlikely, even if the combined chances are high. It's as if uncertainty paralyzes choice.
disjunction_effect.practical_application: It explains why people don't buy insurance without knowing the exact probability of risks, or why investors wait for clarity even if it means missed profit. It is taken into account in economics, marketing, and political science.
disjunction_effect.description_popular: The disjunction effect is a cognitive bias in which people avoid making a definite choice when the outcome depends on one of uncertain, mutually exclusive events. Formally, it is a violation of Leonard Savage's 'sure-thing principle': if in each possible situation the same option is preferred, then it should also be preferred in the absence of information about which situation has occurred. The effect is especially strong under conditions of prospective (future) uncertainty.
disjunction_effect.fun_fact_popular: In an experiment by Tversky and Shafir, students who knew they had either passed or failed an exam preferred to buy a vacation trip more often than those who had not yet been told the result. Knowledge freed them from choice paralysis.
disjunction_effect.description_simple: Imagine you are offered a concert ticket for tomorrow, but you're not sure if it will rain. If you know for sure it will rain, you might decline; if you know for sure it's dry, you'll buy. But if the forecast is uncertain (50/50), you most likely won't buy the ticket, even though there is a chance of good weather. That's how the disjunction effect works: uncertainty between two events makes us act as if both events are worse than each one individually.
disjunction_effect.history_simple: The effect was discovered by psychologists in the late 20th century while studying decision-making paradoxes. The term 'disjunction effect' was introduced by Amos Tversky and Eldar Shafir in 1992, after they noticed that people violate the 'sure-thing principle' from game theory when the outcome depends on mutually exclusive reasons.
disjunction_effect.how_it_works_simple: Normally, a rational person evaluates each event separately. But in a disjunction (an 'either-or' situation), the brain plays it safe: it focuses on the uncertainty and refuses to act, even if any of the specific outcomes would lead to the same decision. It's like a chess game: knowing your opponent's next move, you'll make yours, but if there are two possible moves, you might get confused and do nothing.
disjunction_effect.description: The disjunction effect is a phenomenon in behavioral economics and cognitive psychology that describes a systematic violation of the sure-thing principle under uncertainty caused by disjunctive events (mutually exclusive possibilities). If upon the occurrence of event A the agent prefers action X over action Y, and the same upon the occurrence of ¬A, then it is rational to prefer X even without knowledge of the state of A. However, real people often refuse X when state A is unknown, demonstrating 'disjunctive ambivalence'. The effect is related to the Ellsberg paradox and can be explained by ambiguity aversion, emotional factors, or an inability to simulate hypothetical events.
disjunction_effect.history: The sure-thing principle dates back to Leonard Savage's (1954) work on the foundations of statistics. The disjunction effect was experimentally identified by Amos Tversky and Eldar Shafir in their 1992 paper 'The Disjunction Effect in Choice Under Uncertainty'. They conducted a series of surveys, including the Hawaii problem (vacation after an exam) and the betting problem (gambling after a coin toss). Later, the effect was replicated in neuroeconomic studies, and in the 2000s, quantum-like models of decision-making emerged, where superposition of states explains violations of classical probability laws.
disjunction_effect.how_it_works: Standard expected utility theory prescribes acting based on weighted probabilities of outcomes. In a disjunction, the agent faces an event space {A, ¬A}. If under both A and ¬A action X dominates, then in a state of ignorance the choice of X should remain. The observed refusal of X is explained by several mechanisms: the hypothesis of considering unconsidered scenarios (people imagine the worst-case development), emotional anticipation (regret over a decision made when the outcome is unknown), or quantum-like superposition of mental states, where utility evaluation interferes and leads to non-classical choice probabilities.
key_problems: What is the exact neurophysiological mechanism of the effect?
Why is the effect weaker in repeated or group decisions?
How to formalize disjunction in a generalized decision theory without loss of predictive power?
disjunction_effect.fun_fact: In quantum decision-making models, the disjunction effect is analogous to wave interference: the state of uncertainty behaves as a superposition (A and ¬A), and 'mental interference' can weaken the probability of choice compared to a collapsed state (known A or ¬A).

gene_expression_noise.name: gene expression noise
gene_expression_noise.mini: Random fluctuations of protein levels in identical cells — like interference in a radio receiver or uneven sprinkling of salt.
gene_expression_noise.practical_application: Explains why bacteria survive antibiotics and why tumors become resistant to therapy; used to create stable synthetic genetic circuits.
gene_expression_noise.description_popular: Gene expression noise — stochastic (probabilistic) fluctuations in mRNA and protein concentrations, caused by the small number of molecules and the random nature of biochemical reactions. Intrinsic noise — the inherent variability of transcription and translation processes due to the discrete nature of chemical events — and extrinsic noise — fluctuations in the numbers of transcription factors, ribosomes, and metabolites common to many genes in the cell — are distinguished. Intrinsic noise is usually measured as the squared coefficient of variation (σ²/μ²), and it is inversely proportional to the average number of molecules.
gene_expression_noise.fun_fact_popular: Bacteria use noise as a strategy: at any time, a few cells in a colony randomly become resistant to an antibiotic, even without encountering it — thus the population hedges against extinction.
gene_expression_noise.description_simple: Even in genetically identical cells in the same environment, the amount of the same protein can vary by orders of magnitude. These random fluctuations are called gene expression noise. The cause: within the tiny volumes of a cell, DNA, RNA, and protein molecules collide and react chaotically, as if you are trying to pick up exactly one grain of sugar with two fingers.
gene_expression_noise.history_simple: Random fluctuations in biochemistry were known as early as the 1950s, but the importance of noise for cell fate was realized only in the 2000s, when methods for tracking individual cells emerged. Key experiments: synchronized bacterial cultures with fluorescent proteins showed that noise can predetermine survival under stress.
gene_expression_noise.how_it_works_simple: Noise arises at every step: first, DNA unstably unwinds, and the enzyme (RNA polymerase) attaches randomly — transcription proceeds in bursts. Then, RNA molecules are short-lived and can degrade before protein synthesis. Protein synthesis (translation) itself is also bursty. The sum of these random events creates noise.
gene_expression_noise.description: Gene expression noise is a fundamental property of genetic systems, determined by the stochastic kinetics of rare molecular events. Mathematically modeled by the chemical Langevin equation or master equation formalism. Intrinsic noise for an unregulated gene is proportional to 1/(average mRNA number), leading to Poisson statistics of products. However, due to regulatory loops and promoter architecture, distributions can deviate (super-Poissonian or sub-Poissonian). Extrinsic noise is often described by small fluctuation expansion (method of moment equations) or through correlation analysis with reporters (dual histograms). Noise plays a dual role: on one hand, it limits the precision of genetic programs; on the other, it creates phenotypic heterogeneity necessary for evolution and differentiation, for example, in the transition of stem cells to specialized ones.
gene_expression_noise.history: The concept of biochemical noise dates back to the work of Max Delbrück (1940s) on mutagenesis. In 1957, Aaron Novick and Milton Weiner experimentally recorded fluctuations of β-galactosidase in E. coli. However, wide recognition came after 2002 with the publication of Elowitz's paper, where using two fluorescent reporters (CFP and YFP) under identical promoters, intrinsic and extrinsic noise were quantitatively separated. Later, studies by Swain and Thatuv (2005–2010) showed the relationship between noise, gene network architecture, and evolutionary fitness. In the 2010s, super-resolution microscopy allowed visualization of individual transcripts in living cells, confirming the bursty nature of transcription (transcriptional bursts).
gene_expression_noise.how_it_works: Noise is generated at all stages of expression: (1) transcription initiation — the promoter randomly switches between active and inactive states due to local chromatin rearrangements and dissociation of activators (bursts); (2) mRNA maturation and degradation — lifetime is determined by stochastic interactions with RNases; (3) translation initiation depends on ribosome collision with mRNA, which is a rare event in the cell volume; (4) protein secretion and degradation are also variable. Combinatorially, these processes amplify variation, and feedback loops (e.g., negative autoregulation) can reduce noise. In eukaryotes, noise is modulated by epigenetic factors and compartmentalization.
key_problems: How do cells maintain precise levels of vital proteins despite high internal noise?
Can we control noise to reprogram cell states (e.g., turn cancer cells into benign ones)?
What is the relationship between expression noise and epigenetic heterogeneity leading to drug resistance?
gene_expression_noise.fun_fact: In humans, genes responsible for the rapid immune response have increased noise — this allows the T-lymphocyte population to more quickly 'feel out' an effective strategy against a new pathogen.

formulas.description: Squared coefficient of variation — dimensionless measure of intrinsic protein expression noise.
formulas.meaning: \eta^2 — expression noise, dimensionless quantity; \sigma^2 — variance of the number of protein molecules in a cell; \mu — mean number of protein molecules in a cell.

pirads_classification.name: PI-RADS classification
pirads_classification.mini: PI-RADS is a scale from 1 to 5, like stars in a hotel review: 1 is excellent, nothing found; 5 is very bad, almost certainly cancer. It helps doctors describe how suspicious the detected areas on prostate MRI are in a unified language.
pirads_classification.practical_application: The PI-RADS classification standardizes MRI reports, reducing interpretation variability and guiding decisions on the need for biopsy: for PI-RADS 1-2, biopsy is usually not needed; for 3, at discretion; for 4-5, mandatory.
pirads_classification.description_popular: The PI-RADS (Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System) is a standardized method for assessing the probability of clinically significant prostate cancer based on multiparametric MRI. Each detected lesion in the transition or peripheral zone receives a score on a 5-point scale. The assessment is based on analysis of T2-weighted imaging (dominant sequence for the transition zone), diffusion-weighted imaging (dominant for the peripheral zone), and dynamic contrast enhancement (which plays a supporting role). The rules for assigning the final score depend on the zone and the presence of certain features: border clarity, size, signal intensity. PI-RADS 3 indicates an uncertain result, PI-RADS 4 and 5 indicate the need for biopsy.
pirads_classification.fun_fact_popular: PI-RADS version 2.1 clarified that lesions smaller than 1 cm in the transition zone cannot receive a score higher than 3, which reduced overdiagnosis.
pirads_classification.description_simple: After a doctor looks at a prostate MRI, they need to describe in words how much each finding resembles cancer. PI-RADS is like an agreement among doctors worldwide on which words to use. Lesions are given scores: 1 — definitely normal, 2 — most likely normal, 3 — unclear (questionable), 4 — suspicious, 5 — very suspicious. When assigning a score, they look at size, shape, brightness in different MRI modes — it's like evaluating a watermelon: if it's small, with a smooth rind and a crisp sound when tapped, it's good; if it's large, with a soft spot and a dull sound, it's bad.
pirads_classification.history_simple: Before 2012, each doctor described results in their own way, leading to confusion. Then a group of experts from the European Society of Urogenital Radiology (ESUR) created the first version of PI-RADS. In 2015 it was improved (version 2), and in 2019 the current version 2.1 came out with even clearer guidelines.
pirads_classification.how_it_works_simple: The doctor examines three main images: T2, an ADC map, and a contrast-enhanced image. For each zone they see, they assign a separate score for each type of image. Then, using special rules (algorithm), these scores are combined into a final score from 1 to 5. For example, if T2 shows a clear dark lesion, on ADC it is also dark, and contrast actively enters it — that is a clear 5.
pirads_classification.description: The PI-RADS v2.1 classification is a detailed semiotic system stratifying the risk of clinically significant cancer (defined as ISUP ≥ 2, i.e., Gleason ≥ 3+4 or volume ≥ 0.5 cm³) based on mpMRI. The assessment is zone-specific: for the peripheral zone, the leading sequence is DWI/ADC, with the DWI score being primary; for the transition zone, T2. Dynamic contrast enhancement is used to clarify uncertain cases (category 2 or 3 on DWI): a positive DCE upgrades the final category to 4. The system requires high-quality scanning (at least 1.5 T) with adherence to minimal technical specifications. PI-RADS 1 — normal, 2 — clearly benign changes, 3 — intermediate risk, 4 — high probability of cancer, 5 — very high probability. Categories are linked to an action plan: PI-RADS ≥3 may be referred for MRI-guided targeted biopsy. Scientific data show that the negative predictive value of PI-RADS 1-2 for excluding clinically significant cancer is 85–95%.
pirads_classification.history: The need for unification arose in the early 2000s with the increasing use of mpMRI. The first PI-RADS version was released by ESUR in 2012 but was imperfect due to convoluted algorithms. In 2015, together with the American College of Radiology (ACR) and the AdMeTech Foundation, version 2 was presented, simplifying the rules and separating the approach for the transition and peripheral zones. In 2019, an interdisciplinary expert group released PI-RADS v2.1, refining criteria for the transition zone (for example, removing the 2+1 score, relaxing requirements for nodule shape), which increased specificity. PI-RADS is recognized as an international standard, and its validation continues in different populations.
pirads_classification.how_it_works:
After obtaining mpMRI images, the radiologist evaluates each finding sequentially:
1. Determine the zone (peripheral or transition) using T2 anatomy.
2. Peripheral zone: primary DWI assessment. DWI score: 1 — no changes, 2 — linear/wedge-shaped vague hypointensity, 3 — focal moderate hypointensity (indistinct, small), 4 — distinctly hypointense lesion <1.5 cm, 5 — distinctly hypointense lesion ≥1.5 cm or with extracapsular extension. For DWI score 3 — assess DCE: if there is focal enhancement occurring earlier than or simultaneously with the peak of normal tissue, then the final PI-RADS category is 4; if negative — 3. For DWI score 4 or 5, the category corresponds to the DWI score regardless of DCE.
3. Transition zone: primary T2 assessment. T2 score: 1 — homogeneous transition zone, 2 — nodules with a clear capsule or chondroid nodules, 3 — moderate inhomogeneity with indistinct margins, 4 — lenticular, irregular, indistinct lesion, 5 — same lesion with invasive features or ≥1.5 cm. For T2 score 2 or 3 — consider DWI: if DWI ≥4 (distinct restricted diffusion <1.5 cm), then the category is upgraded to 3 or 4 respectively. DCE does not affect the transition zone.
Size is measured by the largest diameter on an axial image. If there are multiple findings, an index lesion (the most suspicious) may be given. The report includes a map indicating the PI-RADS score of each finding.
key_problems: Subjectivity in assessing border 'fuzziness' and moderate hypointensity, leading to variability between experts
Insufficient specificity of PI-RADS 3 — a high proportion of false-positive biopsies
Evolution of diagnostic criteria as data accumulates (revision of size thresholds, the role of DCE for the transition zone remains controversial)
Applicability of the system on low-field devices and without an endorectal coil requires additional validation
Need for adaptation to new biomarkers (restosis, radiomics) and artificial intelligence methods
pirads_classification.fun_fact: A 2023 study showed that a neural network trained on tens of thousands of MRIs can assign PI-RADS scores with accuracy comparable to experienced radiologists, but it 'doubts' more often in category 3.

collective_behavior.name: collective behavior
collective_behavior.mini: A flock of birds turns instantly without a leader, water molecules freeze into ice simultaneously — this is collective behavior: simple rules generate complex patterns.
collective_behavior.practical_application: Controlling drone swarms, predicting traffic jams and crowd panic, creating self-organizing materials.
collective_behavior.description_popular: Collective behavior arises in systems of many interacting agents — from animal flocks to swarming particles. The key lies in local interactions: each agent reacts to its surroundings via a simple algorithm, without a global plan. This gives rise to emergent properties — ones not present in individual elements. For example, a school of fish compacts when threatened, creating the illusion of a larger organism; an ant colony finds the shortest path to food via pheromone trails. The transition from chaotic to ordered motion is analogous to a phase transition in physics, where the collective state changes abruptly upon reaching a critical density or coupling strength.
collective_behavior.fun_fact_popular: Fireflies of certain species synchronize their flashes without any conductor: each insect adjusts to the rhythm of its neighbors, and after a few cycles the entire population glows in unison, turning the night forest into a living, flashing cloud.
collective_behavior.description_simple: Collective behavior is when many individual objects (birds, fish, cells, particles) follow simple rules, and together they produce complex motion or structures. It seems as if the group has a collective mind, but in reality each follows only what is nearby. For instance, if each bird in a flock maintains distance from its neighbors and flies in the same direction as they do, the whole flock behaves like a fluid.
collective_behavior.history_simple: Scientists long observed that large groups of living things behave as a single entity. But true understanding came in the mid-20th century with the advent of computers. For example, in 1987 Craig Reynolds created a program with virtual birds (boids) that, following three simple rules, flew like a real flock. This showed that complex collective behavior does not require a leader.
collective_behavior.how_it_works_simple: The foundation lies in rules that each participant follows based on its nearest neighbors.
