Typically these are: maintain distance (avoid collisions), align velocity with neighbors, and move toward the center of the group. When there are many such participants, waves of coordinated motion arise, like in a stadium where spectators stand and sit in sequence, creating a 'wave'.
collective_behavior.description: Collective behavior studies how complex spatial-temporal structures and coherent dynamics emerge from simple local interaction rules among many elements (agents). It is an interdisciplinary phenomenon spanning condensed matter physics, statistical mechanics, biology, sociology, and robotics. Typical examples: formation of crystal lattices upon cooling, convective cells in fluids, synchronization of chemical oscillators, bird flocks, human crowds, neural ensembles. Mathematically it is described by models based on systems of coupled differential equations (e.g., the Kuramoto model for phase oscillators), lattice gases, or agent-based simulations. Key concepts: emergence, self-organization, order parameter, phase transition. Collective behavior often exhibits a critical state where the system is most sensitive to small perturbations (self-organized criticality).
collective_behavior.history: The first scientific descriptions of collective animal behavior appeared in the early 20th century, but the theoretical foundation was laid in physics by many scientists. In the 19th century, Ludwig Boltzmann developed statistical mechanics, showing how microscopic rules for molecules give rise to macroscopic gas properties. This idea was adopted for other systems. In the 1930s–40s, biologists (Julian Huxley, William H. Thorpe) studied synchronization in birds and fish. A breakthrough came with advances in computing: in the 1970s the first simulations emerged (e.g., the Vicsek model for collective particle motion), and in 1986 Craig Reynolds published the famous 'Boids' model, demonstrating that three rules produce realistic flocking behavior. Concurrently, physicists (Stanley Milgram, Serge Galam) investigated crowds, while chemists studied the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction. Today, collective behavior is a rapidly developing field applicable to neuroscience, robotics, and social networks.
collective_behavior.how_it_works: The mechanism is based on positive feedback and nonlinear interactions. Each agent obeys simple local rules, often including short-range repulsion (to avoid collisions), alignment of velocity with the neighborhood average (direction matching), and attraction toward the local group center (maintaining cohesion). At low density or weak coupling, the system is chaotic. Upon exceeding a coupling threshold (strength of attraction or number of neighbors), a phase transition occurs, akin to magnetization: long-range order emerges, and all agents move coherently. This is described by an order parameter, such as the mean orientation vector. In more complex cases, excitation waves, vortices, and clusters form. In neural systems, collective dynamics give rise to oscillations and spike synchronization. The universality of these phenomena is explained by renormalization group methods, showing that many diverse systems belong to the same universality class near a critical point.
key_problems: How is collective behavior encoded in the genome, if individual organisms do not carry a 'plan' for the entire group?
Can sudden regime shifts (e.g., crowd panic) be predicted from local data?
How to scale agent-based models to systems with billions of elements (e.g., social networks) without losing realism?
Are collective quantum effects at room temperature, similar to superconductivity, possible in artificial systems?
collective_behavior.fun_fact: The slime mold Physarum polycephalum, a single-celled organism without a nervous system, forms a network of tubes capable of finding the shortest path through a maze and even mimicking the railway map of Tokyo's metro—all thanks to the collective behavior of its protoplasm.

formulas.description: The Kuramoto model describes the synchronization of a large number of coupled oscillators (e.g., fireflies). The phase of each oscillator θ_i changes under the influence of its natural frequency ω_i and coupling with others.
formulas.meaning: θ_i — phase of the i-th oscillator (dimensionless, rad), t — time (s), ω_i — natural frequency of the i-th oscillator (rad/s, individual for each), K — coupling strength (rad/s, positive constant), N — total number of oscillators

ion_channel.name: ion channel
ion_channel.mini: Ion channels are microscopic gates in the cell membrane that allow electrically charged particles (ions) to pass in or out. Just as a heart valve ensures blood flow in one direction, a channel controls the flow of sodium, potassium, or calcium, creating electrical signals in nerves and muscles.
ion_channel.practical_application: Ion channels are targets for many drugs: painkillers block sodium channels, while medications for epilepsy and arrhythmia stabilize their function. Channel dysfunction causes severe hereditary diseases.
ion_channel.description_popular: Ion channels are transmembrane proteins that form water-filled pores with a diameter of a few angstroms. They provide passive transport of Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻ ions through the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane down the electrochemical gradient. Channel selectivity is determined by the pore size and the arrangement of charged amino acids at the mouth. Channels have two key properties: conductance (the ability to pass an ion current) and a gating mechanism that switches the protein between open, closed, and inactivated states. According to activation type, there are voltage-gated, ligand-gated, and mechanosensitive channels.
ion_channel.fun_fact_popular: A single channel allows up to 100 million ions per second to pass through, yet remains remarkably selective: a potassium channel passes a potassium ion 10,000 times better than a smaller sodium ion.
ion_channel.description_simple: Every living cell is surrounded by a membrane (a very thin fat film) that does not allow charged particles—ions—to pass through. For ions to still be able to enter and exit, there are special channel proteins in the membrane. They work like highly selective tubes: a sodium channel allows only sodium ions to pass, a potassium channel—only potassium ions. Controlling the opening of a channel resembles a door with a combination lock: some channels open in response to a change in electrical voltage across the membrane, others—when a signaling molecule (for example, a neurotransmitter) attaches to them.
ion_channel.history_simple: The first ideas about the existence of pores in the membrane emerged at the beginning of the 20th century when physiologists noticed that the cell membrane allows potassium and sodium ions to pass through differently. The decisive breakthrough occurred in the 1950s thanks to Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley, who mathematically described ion currents in the giant squid axon. They suggested that there were separate pathways for sodium and potassium. Later, in the 1970s–80s, using the patch clamp technique (a microelectrode technique that allows the study of single channels), it became possible to record how a single ion channel opens and closes.
ion_channel.how_it_works_simple: At rest, many channels are closed, maintaining different concentrations of ions inside and outside the cell—like water behind a dam. A stimulus (for example, a nerve impulse) serves as a signal to open the sluice: the channel protein changes its shape, forming a through pore. Ions rush through it according to the concentration gradient (from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration), much like air escaping from a punctured balloon. This flow generates an electric current that transmits the signal further.
ion_channel.description: Ion channels are integral membrane proteins that form an ion-conducting pathway through the hydrophobic barrier of the lipid bilayer. Their structure includes a pore formed by α-helices or β-sheets, and sensory domains that detect the stimulus. The classical model of the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv demonstrates a tetrameric architecture with a central pore and four voltage-sensing domains containing regularly spaced positively charged arginine residues. Upon membrane depolarization, these charges shift in the electric field, causing a conformational rearrangement that opens the gate. Ion selectivity is achieved through a selectivity filter—a narrowing of the pore lined with carbonyl oxygens that precisely coordinate the dehydrated ion of the appropriate size. The kinetics of transitions between states are described by Markov schemes, and the single-channel current obeys Ohm's law on a microscopic scale: i = γ(V – E_rev), where γ is the channel conductance.
ion_channel.history: The concept of selective ion pores originated in the works of Julius Bernstein (1902), but experimental confirmation came with the work of Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley (1952), who, studying the giant squid axon, separated sodium and potassium currents and proposed a mathematical model of excitation. The patch clamp technique, developed by Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann (1976), allowed recording currents through single channels, for which they received the Nobel Prize. The three-dimensional structure of a potassium channel was first deciphered by Roderick MacKinnon in 1998 using X-ray crystallography, confirming the hypothesis of the selectivity filter and gating mechanism.
ion_channel.how_it_works: The functioning of an ion channel is based on the laws of electrostatics and the thermodynamics of irreversible processes. The driving force for ion flow is the electrochemical gradient, determined by the concentration difference (chemical component) and the membrane potential (electrical component). The equilibrium potential for an ion is given by the Nernst equation: E_eq = (RT/zF) ln([X]_out/[X]_in). The selectivity filter uses the principle of complementarity: the pore size and the arrangement of polar groups exactly match the radius of the hydrated or dehydrated ion. For the K⁺ channel, selectivity is explained by the 'stripping' of the hydration shell and stabilization of the ion in the filter cavity by carbonyl atoms, which is energetically unfavorable for the smaller Na⁺, which is coordinated too weakly. The gating mechanism obeys stochastic dynamics: thermal fluctuations lead to random transitions between conformational states, giving rise to the so-called 'shot noise' of the current (ion channel noise). Mathematically, the behavior of an ensemble of channels is described by the Hodgkin–Huxley kinetic equations or, for a single channel, by the distribution of open and closed state durations. The Pauli principle is not relevant, since ions are distinguishable classical particles. A deeper level involves molecular dynamics calculations using the Schrödinger equation for the electron subsystem, but in practice, force fields are used.
key_problems: The detailed mechanism of inactivation of many channels remains a subject of debate.
Ab initio prediction of the structure and dynamics of ion channels for unstructured regions.
Development of highly selective drugs that act only on specific channel isoforms, without side effects.
ion_channel.fun_fact: In the electric organs of some fish (rays, eels), voltage-gated sodium channels synchronize so tightly that they generate a discharge of up to 600 volts—enough to stun a horse.

formulas.description: Nernst equation for the equilibrium potential of an ion
formulas.meaning: E — equilibrium potential, R — universal gas constant, R ≈ 8.314 J/(mol·K), T — absolute temperature, z — ion charge (dimensionless, for K⁺ z = +1), F — Faraday constant, F ≈ 96485 C/mol, [X]_out and [X]_in — extracellular and intracellular concentrations of ion X

brain_cancer_detection.name: brain cancer detection
brain_cancer_detection.mini: Just as an airport scanner finds a prohibited item, algorithms analyze MRI scans and highlight suspicious tissue areas.
brain_cancer_detection.practical_application: Helps doctors diagnose at an early stage, reduces the number of false alarms, and precisely determines tumor boundaries before surgery or radiation.
brain_cancer_detection.description_popular: Brain cancer detection using artificial intelligence includes segmentation (delineation) of tumors on MRI images. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) with the U-Net architecture are most effective, processing 3D volumes and classifying each voxel as healthy tissue, necrosis, edema, or tumor. Models are pre-trained on large datasets (e.g., BraTS) with slice-by-slice annotation. The key challenge is distinguishing glioblastoma from metastases and non-tumor formations (abscess, demyelination). Additionally, radiomics (extraction of multiple quantitative features from images) and diffusion-weighted MRI are used.
brain_cancer_detection.fun_fact_popular: Some algorithms can detect a tumor 6–12 months earlier than a radiologist by analyzing barely noticeable changes in signal intensity on consecutive scans.
brain_cancer_detection.description_simple: Detecting brain cancer is searching for tumors using scans (MRI) or blood tests. A computer program, trained on thousands of examples, compares each brain region to those it has seen before and marks areas that look like cancer. It is similar to how an experienced mushroom picker instantly distinguishes an edible mushroom from a poisonous one by signs invisible to a beginner.
brain_cancer_detection.history_simple: Automatic analysis of medical images began in the 1980s with simple rules (if brightness is above a threshold, it's a tumor). In the 2010s, neural networks (deep learning) emerged that learn complex patterns on their own. Today they surpass humans in speed and accuracy of finding small lesions.
brain_cancer_detection.how_it_works_simple: MRI produces many thin slices of the brain; the program treats each tiny cube (voxel) as a set of numbers: brightness, texture, shape. It looks for combinations that appeared in thousands of annotated tumors. Then it creates a heat map: suspect areas are highlighted in color, like an artist coloring an outline.
brain_cancer_detection.description: Modern computer-aided diagnostic systems for brain cancer integrate multimodal MRI (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR, DWI) and employ deep neural networks for classification, detection, and segmentation tasks. Leading architectures: nnU-Net — a self-adapting 3D U-Net, Swin UNETR with transformers for global context, and ensembles of models with post-processing via conditional random fields. For small datasets, augmentation (rotations, contrast changes) and GAN synthesis are used. Beyond accuracy, prediction uncertainty (Bayesian networks, MC Dropout) and interpretability (Grad-CAM, saliency maps) are evaluated. In the clinic, speed matters — inference within seconds on GPU, as well as compliance with DICOM standards and integration into PACS systems. Promising directions: self-contrastive learning on unlabeled scans and multi-task models that simultaneously predict histology, mutation status, and prognosis.
brain_cancer_detection.history: The development of computer-aided brain cancer diagnosis began with expert systems in the 1980s that used thresholding and texture filters. In 1998, the first CAD package for MRI appeared, and in the 2010s, public BraTS (Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge) competitions accelerated progress. The pivotal moment was the victory of convolutional networks in 2015 (DeepMedic). Since 2018, U-Net-based models and its 3D modifications became the standard. In the 2020s, the FDA approved several AI systems (e.g., icobrain) to assist in clinical decisions, although widespread adoption is hindered by scanner and protocol variability.
brain_cancer_detection.how_it_works: A typical pipeline: (1) preprocessing — intensity normalization, skull stripping, registration to an atlas; (2) an input 3D patch from four channels (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR) is fed into a U-Net encoder that extracts hierarchical features from edges to texture; (3) the decoder restores spatial resolution with skip connections, outputting probability maps for each class; (4) the loss function is usually a combination of Dice Loss and cross-entropy, accounting for class imbalance; (5) post-processing — removal of small false spots using connected components and morphological operations. To increase robustness, activation consistency is checked under small distortions of the input image (test-time augmentation). The integrated system visualizes the segmentation in the clinician's interface, providing quantitative metrics (volume, radiomics).
key_problems: Lack of well-annotated MRI data, especially for rare tumor subtypes and post-surgical changes.
Black box: it is difficult to explain why exactly this voxel was classified as tumor by the neural network — a problem of physician trust.
Early diagnosis of infiltrative gliomas, which in initial stages do not breach the blood-brain barrier and enhance poorly on contrast.
brain_cancer_detection.fun_fact: A 2022 meta-analysis showed that ensembles of neural networks reduce false-positive tumor diagnoses by 30% compared to a single radiologist's report when teleconsultations are unavailable.

formulas.description: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) — a quantitative characteristic of diffusion-weighted MRI reflecting cell density.
formulas.meaning: S — MRI signal intensity with diffusion weighting; S_0 — intensity without diffusion weighting; b — diffusion factor, a constant set by the pulse sequence parameters (usually 1000 s/mm²).

generative_adversarial_networks.name: Generative Adversarial Networks
generative_adversarial_networks.mini: A counterfeiter creates increasingly skillful copies, while an expert learns to spot the trick. Together, they perfect their craft to the point of automatic mastery.
generative_adversarial_networks.practical_application: Generating photorealistic faces, creating clothing designs, enhancing medical images — anywhere that requires plausibly filling in the details.
generative_adversarial_networks.description_popular: GAN is an architecture of two neural networks playing a minimax game: generator G tries to fool discriminator D by creating plausible data, while D learns to spot fakes. Equilibrium occurs when G reproduces the real data distribution so accurately that D can no longer distinguish—its accuracy drops to random guessing (50%). Like an arms race between a counterfeit bill maker and a bank expert, each side raises the bar.
generative_adversarial_networks.fun_fact_popular: The most impressive deepfakes and old film restorations owe their existence to GANs.
generative_adversarial_networks.description_simple: A Generative Adversarial Network is a pair of programs: a generator (forger) and a discriminator (expert). The generator, like an artist, draws an image, and the discriminator compares it to originals and gives feedback. Both learn from each other until the fakes become indistinguishable. This duel hones both skills: the counterfeiter becomes more skillful, and the detector more discerning.
generative_adversarial_networks.history_simple: Invented by Ian Goodfellow and colleagues in 2014. Since then, it has spawned numerous variants for images, video, music, and text.
generative_adversarial_networks.how_it_works_simple: The generator takes random noise (like a set of chaotic brushstrokes) and turns it into an image. The discriminator looks at the picture and issues a verdict: 'real' or 'fake'. The expert's mistake becomes a lesson for the generator—and vice versa.
generative_adversarial_networks.description:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) are generative models where two neural networks optimize opposing loss functions. Generator G(z) maps a latent variable z (usually from a normal distribution) to the data space, while discriminator D(x) estimates the probability that input x is real. The game objective is minimax: min_G max_D V(D,G) = E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))]. With an optimal discriminator, minimizing this functional is equivalent to minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between distributions, leading G to perfect imitation.

A workshop where apprentices compete in forging paintings, and an expert tirelessly seeks differences. In the heat of this competition, skill grows: copies acquire the soul of the original. The process stops when even a trained eye can't spot a difference—and then art itself emerges victorious.
generative_adversarial_networks.history: Proposed by Ian Goodfellow et al. (2014) as a way to train generative models without explicitly modeling the data distribution. The idea traces back to adversarial games and minimax theory. They quickly became popular due to their ability to generate realistic images, sound, and video. Subsequent modifications—DCGAN, StyleGAN, CycleGAN—addressed training instability issues and improved quality.
generative_adversarial_networks.how_it_works: During training, G and D are updated alternately. The discriminator receives a real sample and the generator's output, computes its loss (logistic loss function). The generator adjusts its weights to maximize the discriminator's error—i.e., to make the fake appear real. Gradients from D flow back through G, shaping the latent representation. Problem: vanishing gradients if D is too strong, so non-standard loss functions (e.g., Wasserstein GAN) are often used.
key_problems: Training instability: mode collapse, where the generator produces monotonous examples.
Difficulties in assessing convergence: no reliable stopping criterion.
Ethical concerns: creation of deepfakes and forgeries.
generative_adversarial_networks.fun_fact: One of the first demonstrations of GANs—generating handwritten digits—is now capable of synthesizing a high-resolution human face indistinguishable from a photograph.

formulas.description: GAN minimax loss function
formulas.meaning: G — generator, D — discriminator, x — sample of real data, p_data — distribution of real data, z — latent variable, p_z — distribution of latent variables (usually Gaussian with zero mean and unit variance), E — mathematical expectation, G(z) — generated sample

attention_mechanism.name: attention mechanism
attention_mechanism.mini: A spotlight on stage picks out the main actor at each moment of dialogue. The rest temporarily recedes into shadow.
attention_mechanism.practical_application: Smart cameras that track motion, and translation systems that grasp the meaning of a long phrase, work exactly like that.
attention_mechanism.description_popular: The attention mechanism is a computational technique that allows a model to dynamically weigh the importance of different parts of the input data. Unlike fixed convolutions, attention adapts to each specific example: the word "crane" (water tap or construction machine) will get different surroundings depending on the context. Like a director moving the spotlight from one actor to another, attention redirects light according to the mise-en-scène.
attention_mechanism.fun_fact_popular: The human visual system also has an analogue — selective attention: the brain amplifies the signal from the desired object and suppresses the rest.
attention_mechanism.description_simple: A mechanism that, when processing data, can focus on important details, like a spotlight on stage. When reading a sentence, for each word it determines which other words to pay attention to in order to understand the meaning more precisely. As a result, a new picture is created where the connections between words are highlighted — like a stage where all actors are visible at once, but the lead actor stands out brighter.
attention_mechanism.history_simple: The idea of "attention" in machine learning was proposed in the 1990s, and in 2014–2015 working models for translation appeared (Bahdanau et al.). Later it became a key part of transformers.
attention_mechanism.how_it_works_simple: Each word, as it were, asks all the others: "How important are you to me right now?" The answer is a weight (a numerical score). Then all the words are mixed in the right proportion, creating a refined representation for that position in the sentence.
attention_mechanism.description:
The attention mechanism in neural networks computes a context-dependent representation of a sequence element by aggregating information from all elements with weights that depend on their compatibility. Mathematically, it is a weighted sum of values, where the weights are obtained as the similarity of queries and keys. A generalization is self-attention, where queries, keys, and values are generated from the same source.

A theatrical lighting instrument does not just shine uniformly — it emphasizes dramatic moments. Similarly, attention highlights semantic centers in the input stream, allowing the model to build a hierarchy of significance. The result: instead of a flat sequence, a volumetric understanding emerges, where each element is connected to the others by a dynamic web of beams.
attention_mechanism.history: The concept of attention in AI goes back to ideas from the 1960s about visual search. In neural networks, the first implementations were alignment systems for machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2014). Then the mechanism became modular with "Attention is All You Need" (2017), where it was transformed into a self-contained building block — self-attention in the transformer.
attention_mechanism.how_it_works: Three matrices are computed: queries Q, keys K, values V (linear projections of the inputs). For each query, dot products are calculated with all keys, scaled by √d_k, and transformed via softmax into a probability distribution. These probabilities are used as weights for summing the values. Multi-head attention repeats the procedure several times with different projections, capturing various types of relationships.
key_problems: Quadratic growth of computational complexity with sequence length (the problem of long documents)
Explainability: why did the model focus specifically on these elements?
Plasticity: how to maintain the ability to learn quickly without forgetting?
attention_mechanism.fun_fact: In GPT-3, there are 96 transformer layers, each with multiple attention heads, yielding over 100 billion parameters — a number exceeding the number of neurons in a crow's brain.

formulas.description: Scaled dot-product attention
formulas.meaning: Q - queries, K - keys, V - values, d_k - dimension of keys, softmax - function returning probabilities, √d_k - scaling factor to prevent large softmax arguments

robotics.name: Robotics
robotics.mini: A robot is a mechanical actor that performs a script of movements. Robotics teaches machines to act in the real world.
robotics.practical_application: Robotic arms on assembly lines, da Vinci surgical assistants, rovers on Mars.
robotics.description_popular: A robot does not have to be humanoid. It is any device capable of acting on the physical world according to a program. A food processor is a simple robot: it has a motor (actuator) and a button (command). A modern robotic system is an orchestra conducted by a processor-conductor: each joint-musician plays its part with perfect timing.
robotics.fun_fact_popular: The fastest industrial robot packs up to 200 candies per minute in three shifts without a break, and its positioning repeatability is thinner than a human hair.
robotics.description_simple: A metal 'arm' in a factory moves more precisely than a human welder. Robotics unites hardware and software so that a machine replicates actions conceived by a person. Just as a pianist extracts music from keys, so a programmer imbues movement into servo drives.
robotics.history_simple: The first industrial robot, Unimate, started working in 1961 on a General Motors assembly line – it lifted hot metal parts. Since then, robots have entered manufacturing, medicine, and everyday life.
robotics.how_it_works_simple: A robot resembles a marionette, except the strings are replaced by electrical signals. Sensors are its eyes and ears: a camera recognizes an object, a microphone hears a command. The brain-computer processes signals and sends orders to muscle-motors. The 'see – think – act' loop repeats tens of times per second.
robotics.description: Robotics merges mechanics, electronics, and computer science to build machines with a specified degree of autonomy. It covers the design of manipulators, mobile platforms, exoskeletons, and software agents. Core disciplines: kinematics (geometry of motion), dynamics (forces and torques), trajectory planning, computer vision, and machine learning. Robots are classified by application area (industrial, service, research) and by control type (feedback-based, pre-programmed, with AI elements).
robotics.history: The word 'robot' was coined by Karel Čapek in his play R.U.R. (1920). The engineering field began with teleoperated manipulators for handling radioactive materials in the 1940s. The turning point was George Devol's Unimate – the first programmable manipulator, patented in 1954 and installed on a GM factory floor in 1961. In the 1970s, microprocessors enabled control along complex trajectories. Today, robotics is rapidly merging with artificial intelligence, giving rise to self-learning robots.
robotics.how_it_works: Robot control is hierarchical: the strategic level plans a task (e.g., pick a part from a table), the tactical level breaks it into a sequence of movements, and the executive level generates control signals for actuators. A key tool is the closed feedback loop: sensors (encoders, torque sensors, cameras) continuously report position and forces, and the controller compares actual values with setpoints and adjusts motor currents. For complex tasks like walking, Model Predictive Control is used, which computes the system's behavior several steps ahead.
key_problems: Autonomous operation in unstructured environments: a robot in a home or on a construction site faces an infinite variety of situations
Energy efficiency: building mechanisms that can operate for hours without recharging
Safe human-robot interaction without protective barriers
Transferring skills from simulation to reality (sim-to-real gap)
Soft-bodied robots (soft robotics) – controlling deformable structures
robotics.fun_fact: MIT's cheetah robot reached 7.9 km/h without a tether in 2019, and leaped over a 40 cm obstacle. Its legs mimic animal tendons, storing energy through elastic deformation.

digital_image_processing.name: Digital Image Processing
digital_image_processing.mini: A selfie on your phone instantly becomes brighter and a pimple disappears. It's not magic: every dot of the photo is a number, and the program passes these numbers through mathematical sieves, removing some details and emphasizing others.
digital_image_processing.practical_application: Automatic photo retouching, face recognition in cameras, analysis of medical images (X-rays, MRI), drone navigation, quality enhancement of old photos and videos.
digital_image_processing.description_popular: Digital Image Processing (DIP) is a set of methods for working with raster images (a grid of pixels). Basic operations: changing brightness/contrast, histogram equalization (aligning the distribution of brightness values), filtering (smoothing, sharpening, edge detection). A filter is a mask (a small square of coefficients) that is applied to each point and computes a weighted sum of its neighbors. Convolution is the key operation. More advanced methods rely on the Fourier transform, wavelets, and neural networks. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn to select filters themselves for the task, whether it's face recognition, tumor segmentation, or style transfer.
digital_image_processing.fun_fact_popular: The 'Unsharp Mask' filter, which sharpens photos, actually subtracts a blurred copy: sharpness = original + (original – blur). This trick was invented back in darkrooms for film.
digital_image_processing.description_simple: Digital image processing teaches a computer to see and improve pictures. For it, a photograph is a table of numbers: each cell contains three numbers—how much red, green, and blue. Processing changes these numbers according to rules to make the image sharper, alter colors, or find objects in it. For example, a blurry photo becomes sharp: the algorithm subtracts the average of its neighbors from each pixel, and edges stand out.
digital_image_processing.history_simple: It all began in the 1960s with space programs: images of the Moon were transmitted with interference and needed to be cleaned. That's when the first contrast enhancement methods were invented. Since then, every new camera and every filter in a phone has been a step forward.
digital_image_processing.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a picture as a mosaic of tiny tiles. To find edges, the program compares neighboring tiles: if the brightness jump is large, that's a boundary. To remove noise, it averages similar tiles. Everything boils down to simple arithmetic operations repeated millions of times. Smart algorithms learn from examples: show a thousand cat faces, and the network remembers which pixel combinations form ears and whiskers.
digital_image_processing.description: Digital image processing is a branch of computer science that deals with transforming, analyzing, and synthesizing visual information represented as a discrete function I(x,y), where x,y are pixel coordinates and the value is brightness or a color vector. Main areas: quality improvement (denoising, super-resolution), restoration (blind deconvolution), compression (JPEG, HEIF), analysis (object detection, segmentation, depth estimation). The mathematical toolkit includes linear operators (convolution, Fourier transform), nonlinear filters (median), morphological processing, variational methods (energy functional minimization), and deep learning. Modern approaches rely on U-Net, vision transformers (ViT), diffusion models.
digital_image_processing.history: The starting point was NASA programs correcting images from lunar missions in the 1960s. In the 1970s–1980s, standard filtering algorithms emerged, and JPEG compression (1992) based on the discrete cosine transform. The development of computer vision in the 1990s brought methods for edge detection (Canny), texture analysis, and motion tracking. The revolution of convolutional neural networks began with AlexNet (2012), which won the ImageNet competition, after which deep learning became the primary tool for image analysis, including generative models (GAN, 2014) and diffusion networks (2020s).
digital_image_processing.how_it_works: Basic pipeline: digitization → preprocessing → segmentation → feature extraction → interpretation. Digitization yields a pixel matrix. A filter (e.g., Gaussian blur) computes convolution: I'(x,y) = Σ Σ K(u,v) I(x-u, y-v). For edge detection, Sobel or Laplacian kernels are used. In a CNN, a layer of trainable filters sweeps across the image, creating feature maps; then pooling reduces resolution. Deep networks extract a hierarchy from edges and textures to objects and scenes. In generation tasks, diffusion models gradually add noise and learn to reverse the process, creating realistic images from random noise.
key_problems: Restoring images captured in poor conditions (night, fog, camera shake)
Blind deconvolution: restoring the original image without precise knowledge of the blur function
Ensuring robustness of neural networks to adversarial attacks (imperceptible distortions that fool the model)
Realistic rendering and synthesis of images without artifacts (the problem of 'floating' details in GANs)
Interpretability of deep models: why the network made a decision
digital_image_processing.fun_fact: The very first digital photograph (1957) was a 176×176 pixel square obtained on a scanner built into the SEAC computer. Today, such dimensions are smaller than a desktop icon.

formulas.description: Two-dimensional convolution — the basic operation of many filters
formulas.meaning: I — original image, K — filter kernel (mask of size (2a+1)×(2b+1))

convolutional_neural_networks.name: Convolutional Neural Networks
convolutional_neural_networks.mini: An old roll of negatives: at first only sharp edges appear in the image, then textures, and finally the full portrait. A convolutional network triggers a similar process when it 'looks at' a photo.
convolutional_neural_networks.practical_application: A phone camera that automatically focuses on faces; medical scans where software finds tumors.
convolutional_neural_networks.description_popular: Delicate work: imagine a photographer in a red room developing a film. He places it in a tray, and the image slowly appears on the sheet. The outlines come first—similarly, the first convolutional layer of a CNN (a sliding 3×3 filter) extracts horizontal and vertical lines. The second layer then notices corners and simple textures, and the fifth can recognize a cat's ear. By the end of the process, a meaningful portrait is assembled from abstract feature maps.
convolutional_neural_networks.fun_fact_popular: The GoogLeNet network (2014) contained 'mini-networks' inside, called inception modules, which simultaneously looked at the image with filters of different sizes—as if several magicians examined one photo through magnifying glasses of varying strengths.
convolutional_neural_networks.description_simple: A sheet of photographic paper in a developer tray. Lines appear, then spots, and suddenly—a familiar silhouette. A convolutional neural network (a program that learns to recognize images) does something similar. It runs the image through several filter layers. The first filter catches only edges, the second—corners and simple patterns, and deep layers assemble eyes, wheels, or leaves from them.
convolutional_neural_networks.history_simple: The first successful convolutional networks appeared in the late 1990s: French scientist Yann LeCun taught a program to read handwritten digits from checks. But the real explosion occurred in 2012, when the AlexNet network won an image competition using the computing power of graphics cards.
convolutional_neural_networks.how_it_works_simple: A small matrix of numbers (filter) slides over the image, multiplying its numbers by the pixel brightness, and the output is a feature map (an image showing where the desired feature is). After many such passes, the network understands what is depicted.
convolutional_neural_networks.description: A photo slowly sinks into a reddish solution. A minute later, the outlines of a face emerge from the thick shadow. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a deep learning architecture optimized for processing data with spatial or temporal structure, such as images. It consists of alternating convolutional layers (which apply trainable filters), pooling layers for dimensionality reduction, and fully connected layers for classification. Key properties: local receptive field, weight sharing, and shift invariance. At the end, we pull a finished portrait out of the developer tray—the network has extracted the necessary features and recognized the person.
convolutional_neural_networks.history: The idea of local receptive fields dates back to the work of Hubel and Wiesel on the visual cortex (1959). In 1980, Kunihiko Fukushima proposed the neocognitron, a hierarchical network for pattern recognition inspired by these discoveries. The first practically useful CNN was created by Yann LeCun in 1989 (LeNet) for handwritten digit recognition. With the advent of GPUs and the ImageNet dataset, architectures by Alex Krizhevsky (AlexNet, 2012), and later VGG, ResNet, and EfficientNet, revolutionized computer vision.
convolutional_neural_networks.how_it_works: The convolutional layer computes cross-correlation between the input tensor and filters. Each filter is a small weight tensor (e.g., 3×3×depth), sliding with a specified stride. The formula is: result[x,y] = bias + sum over i,j,k input[x+i, y+j, k] * filter[i,j,k]. Then nonlinearity (typically ReLU). The pooling layer (max pooling) replaces a window with the maximum value, reducing size. Deep networks can learn a hierarchy of features from simple gradients to complex objects.
key_problems: Adaptation to scale and rotation variations without data augmentation
Interpretability of internal representations
High computational cost of training large architectures
Need for precise tuning of hyperparameters (depth, filter sizes)
Tendency to overfit with small data size
convolutional_neural_networks.fun_fact: In one of the first visualizations of AlexNet filters, researchers found that the highest-level filter responded to human faces, even though the network was never specifically trained for that.

formulas.description: Convolution operation for one filter
formulas.meaning: S(i,j) — output feature map; I — input image; K — convolution kernel (filter); m, n — indices over the kernel's spatial dimensions

transformers.name: transformers
transformers.mini: Instant exchange of key clues among all members of the search group. Everyone immediately sees what is important for solving the common task.
transformers.practical_application: Machine translation, voice assistants, and systems that understand long texts — from chatbots to automated reports.
transformers.description_popular: The Transformer is a neural network architecture where the entire sequence is processed in parallel. The word “bank” (meaning a financial institution or a bench) clarifies its meaning through connections with other words in the sentence, using the attention mechanism (dynamic importance weighting). This overcame the limitations of older models that got confused in long phrases. Similarly, a command center distributes tasks: each agent sees the big picture and identifies priority targets.
transformers.fun_fact_popular: Modern Transformers (like GPT) can contain hundreds of billions of trainable parameters — roughly the number of stars in a small galaxy.
transformers.description_simple: A search party simultaneously surveys the terrain. Each member (a separate computational unit) instantly sees what others have noticed and focuses on important details. Instead of reading sequentially, the sentence is processed as a whole. Each word sends queries to others (“what is important for me here?”), receives responses, and refines its meaning. Thus, several layers in succession build a complete picture. The Transformer is like a command center where everyone communicates simultaneously, not in a chain.
transformers.history_simple: First described in 2017 by the "Attention Is All You Need" team. It replaced previous approaches (recurrent networks that read text like a tape — letter by letter).
transformers.how_it_works_simple: Instead of reading sequentially, the Transformer looks at the entire sentence at once. Each word sends queries to others (“what is important for me here?”), receives responses, and refines its meaning considering the context. Thus, several layers in succession build a complete picture.
transformers.description:
The Transformer is a neural network architecture for processing sequences, based solely on the attention mechanism. By forgoing recurrent and convolutional layers, it uses multi-head self-attention, allowing each element of the sequence to interact with all others simultaneously. The architecture consists of an encoder and decoder with positional encoding, normalization layers, and residual connections. Scalability has enabled the creation of giant models that compress knowledge about the world into weights.

Imagine a search party in a vast forest. Instead of relaying information through a chain, each scout instantly shares observations with everyone else. The Transformer does the same: words cease to be isolated units and form a unified map of meanings. In the end, the squad gathers at headquarters with a complete understanding of the situation — just as the model produces a holistic representation of the sentence.
transformers.history: Proposed in the paper "Attention is All You Need" (2017) by Vaswani and colleagues at Google. The core idea of the attention mechanism dates back to work in the 1990s, but the Transformer established it as a self-sufficient building block. It first conquered machine translation, then generative models (GPT, BERT), computer vision, and even protein structure prediction.
transformers.how_it_works: The key element is self-attention: for the input sequence, matrices of queries (Q), keys (K), and values (V) are computed. Attention weights are obtained as the scaled dot product of queries and keys, followed by softmax. Formula: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T/√d_k)V, where d_k is the dimension of the keys. The encoder applies multi-head attention: several parallel heads project the input into different subspaces, then the results are concatenated. Positional encoding adds information about word order, since the model has no built-in notion of sequence.
key_problems: Quadratic complexity with respect to input length makes processing very long contexts difficult.
High memory and computational requirements when scaling.
Interpretation of internal functioning: how does the model arrive at conclusions?
transformers.fun_fact: Record-breaking models require training energy comparable to the annual consumption of several households, spurring the search for efficient architectures.

formulas.description: Self-attention mechanism
formulas.meaning: Q is the query matrix, K is the key matrix, V is the value matrix, d_k is the dimension of the keys (usually 64), softmax is a function that converts numbers into a probability distribution along the last axis, T denotes transposition.

weakly_supervised_learning.name: Weakly Supervised Learning
weakly_supervised_learning.mini: A detective pieces together a suspect's portrait from blurry photos and conflicting eyewitness accounts. Similarly, a machine learning algorithm learns to recognize patterns based on imprecise cues.
weakly_supervised_learning.practical_application: In medicine, this approach saves hours of manual work: a doctor merely brushes over a shadow on an image, and the program outlines the tumor boundaries for diagnosis.
weakly_supervised_learning.description_popular: In fully supervised learning, each training image comes with a pixel-perfect mask or label. Weakly supervised learning, in contrast, uses labels of lower quality: presence/absence of an object in the whole image, a coarse bounding box instead of exact contours, labels at the bag level (it is known that a set contains positive examples, but not which ones). The algorithm must infer details on its own by focusing on recurring features. For instance, if whiskers and a distinctive ear shape appear across a hundred images labeled 'cat,' the model associates them with the class without knowing precise locations.
weakly_supervised_learning.fun_fact_popular: Weak supervision has enabled models that classify documents into categories using only keywords for training, rather than full sentences.
weakly_supervised_learning.description_simple: Imagine a detective who, instead of a clear description like 'man in a blue coat, 180 cm tall,' is shown a crowd and told, 'somewhere in here there's a criminal.' The detective must find the one who stands out. Weakly supervised learning works similarly: the algorithm receives data but with general or imprecise labels. For example, on medical scans, a doctor might mark 'there is pathology in this square' without drawing exact boundaries. The program learns to identify patterns and produce a precise answer.
weakly_supervised_learning.history_simple: The first works appeared in the late 1990s, when researchers faced a shortage of labeled data. In the 2000s, methods of learning with partial teacher involvement gained popularity. Interest surged in the 2010s with the deep learning boom: powerful neural networks required massive datasets, and weak supervision allowed the use of existing data without costly manual labeling.
weakly_supervised_learning.how_it_works_simple: The algorithm acts like an investigator testing hypotheses. It proposes possible object locations in an image and checks them against a weak signal: 'did I get at least something right?' It then strengthens the internal connections that led to success and weakens those that caused errors. Over time, by accumulating statistics, it isolates details more accurately.
weakly_supervised_learning.description: Weakly supervised learning encompasses methods where the source of supervision provides not ideal but noisy, incomplete, or approximate target values. Three typical scenarios are distinguished: incomplete supervision (only part of the dataset has labels), inexact supervision (labels are coarser than desired, e.g., image-level instead of pixel-level segmentation), and inaccurate supervision (labels contain errors). Formally, the task reduces to constructing a mapping from input space to output space using a weak signal, often via the introduction of latent variables, optimization of empirical risk with regularization, or representation learning.
weakly_supervised_learning.history: The concept traces back to partially supervised learning works of the 1990s, but it gained wide recognition in the 2010s thanks to deep neural networks. In 2015, an influential paper "Weakly Supervised Learning with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks" showed how to train classifiers using only image-level labels, not object-level ones. Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) methods, which originated in the 1990s in the context of drug molecule activity, experienced a revival. Today, weakly supervised learning is a standard tool in medical imaging, natural language processing, and time series analysis.
weakly_supervised_learning.how_it_works: A typical approach: a neural network takes input X and produces intermediate predictions, which are then aggregated into a final answer that matches the weak label. For example, for pixel-level tumor segmentation, the model outputs an activation map, and averaging over all pixels is compared to the image-level label 'healthy/pathological.' Gradients propagate through the aggregation operation, forcing the model to highlight relevant regions. In MIL, the network learns to predict at the level of 'bags' (collections of instances): it is known that a bag contains at least one positive instance, and the model identifies it by maximizing the difference between bags. Additionally, Teacher-Student models are used, where weak labels are iteratively refined.
key_problems: How to assess the reliability of predictions with scarce labels?
Robustness to systematic errors in labeling.
Guaranteed quality as the proportion of accurate labels decreases.
Transfer of learning between types of weak signals.
weakly_supervised_learning.fun_fact: In 2017, a model trained on images with labels at the level of 'disease present/absent' detected barely perceptible microbleeds more accurately than a method trained on pixel-level annotations — because doctors manually missed tiny defects, while weak supervision inferred a statistical pattern directly from the diagnosis.

selfsupervised_learning.name: self-supervised learning
selfsupervised_learning.mini: A child learns to speak by listening to adults for years, without dictionaries or rules. Self-supervised learning works the same way — it finds patterns in piles of unlabeled examples.
selfsupervised_learning.practical_application: Speech recognition systems, machine translation, all modern large language models (like GPT), medical diagnostics from images without doctors' annotations.
selfsupervised_learning.description_popular: Self-supervised learning is a paradigm in which the model generates training signals by extracting them from the very structure of unlabeled data. Unlike unsupervised learning, which often focuses on clustering or dimensionality reduction, here surrogate (pretext) tasks are built that do not require human annotations. For example, in natural language processing, some words in an input sentence are masked, and the network learns to recover them from the context. In computer vision, contrastive methods are popular: two randomly distorted versions of the same image are brought closer in the representation space, while being pushed away from other images. This forms a visual concept reminiscent of how infants distinguish objects from the background.
selfsupervised_learning.fun_fact_popular: After self-supervised training on texts, the GPT-3 model turned out to be able to write poems, code, and scientific essays, although no one specifically taught it to do so.
selfsupervised_learning.description_simple: Usually, to train a computer, thousands of labeled images are needed: “this is a cat”, “this is a dog.” Self-supervised learning dispenses with such manual labor. It invents its own task — for example, guessing which part of the text is missing, or reconstructing a hidden part of a photograph. It’s like solving a crossword puzzle: the questions serve as hints, and the answers are the target labels. This way, the machine understands deep connections: that a face with whiskers and a tail typically occur together. Later, this skill is applied to any other task — from defect detection to movie recommendations.
selfsupervised_learning.history_simple: The methods emerged in the 2010s as a way to combat the high cost of data labeling. A turning point came in 2018–2020, when models like BERT and SimCLR showed that it is possible to learn from raw text and images, matching and sometimes exceeding supervised learning.
selfsupervised_learning.how_it_works_simple: The algorithm itself creates a “teacher” from the data. For example, it takes the sentence “The cat sits on the...”, removes a word, and learns to predict “mat.” Or it takes a photo, randomly rotates it, and learns to determine the rotation angle. These clever tasks force the neural network to truly delve into the structure of the world, not just memorize images.
selfsupervised_learning.description: Self-supervised learning (SSL) constructs auxiliary tasks (pretext tasks) from unlabeled data to obtain informative representations applicable to subsequent downstream tasks. Formally, let D = {x_i} be an unlabeled dataset. A pretext task is defined with automatic generation of pseudo-labels y_i = T(x_i), where T is a transformation without human involvement (e.g., rotation, cropping, token masking). The model f_θ is trained to predict y_i, in the process extracting internal patterns from x. In contrastive learning, the InfoNCE loss serves as the criterion: L = - log( exp(sim(z_i, z_j^+)/τ) / Σ_k exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ) ), where z_i is the representation of the anchor image, z_j^+ is a positive pair, z_k are from a negative pool, and τ is a temperature parameter. The success of SSL is evident in NLP (BERT, GPT) and CV (SimCLR, MoCo, MAE), where a linear classifier on frozen representations achieves about 90% accuracy on ImageNet without a single label.
selfsupervised_learning.history: Ideas of self-supervision can be traced to works on autoencoders (Hinton, 2006) and representation learning through reconstruction. The turning point was 2018 with the emergence of BERT (Devlin et al.), which uses word masking. For images, in 2020, the SimCLR method (Chen et al.) showed that a simple contrastive scheme with large batch sizes is comparable to supervised learning. Later, Vision Transformers combined with masked autoencoding (MAE) replicated the success of NLP, demonstrating scalability.
selfsupervised_learning.how_it_works: The general SSL scheme includes: 1) a pretext task — automatic generation of a target signal; 2) an encoder that extracts representations; 3) optionally, a projector for metric comparison; 4) a loss function that solves the specific pretext task. In NLP: masked language modeling (MLM) — the task of recovering hidden tokens. The model receives a sequence with [MASK] tokens and learns to predict the original words via cross-entropy. In CV: contrastive methods learn representations invariant to augmentations, using large batches and a momentum encoder mechanism for stabilization. Recent masked autoencoders (MAE) mask random patches of the image, and the decoder reconstructs the pixels, forcing the model to understand the global structure of objects.
key_problems: Generalization of pretext tasks to new domains without manual design
Potential collapse of representations in unsuccessful contrastive learning
Effective combination of SSL and supervised learning with limited labeled data
Theoretical explanation for the success of simple pretext tasks
selfsupervised_learning.fun_fact: Self-supervised learning enabled the creation of a medical imaging model that, using chest X-rays without diagnoses in training, learned to predict COVID-19 more accurately than experienced radiologists.

formulas.description: Contrastive loss function InfoNCE
formulas.meaning: zi — anchor representation, zj+ — positive sample (augmentation of the same source object), zk — other samples in the batch (negatives), sim — cosine similarity, τ — temperature, typically 0.1

fourier_analysis.name: Fourier analysis
fourier_analysis.mini: A tangled graph, like a dance of complex figures, can be broken down into smooth sine waves. Fourier analysis turns any oscillation — from sound to stock prices — into a set of simple waves and shows which frequencies are louder.
fourier_analysis.practical_application: Mobile communication, the internet, and JPEG image compression use Fourier analysis to transmit and store data in compressed form.
fourier_analysis.description_popular: Fourier analysis is not just a mathematical trick. It is a way to see through chaos. A stock chart that seems random may contain hidden cycles; an old film marred by scratches is restored by removing periodic noise. Even the shape of a musical instrument — a violin or a flute — is determined by the spectrum of harmonics it produces. In radio engineering, Fourier analysis allows hundreds of conversations to be superimposed on one carrier frequency and then separated again. And in computed tomography, doctors obtain a three-dimensional image of the body by processing X-ray detector signals using the fast Fourier transform.
fourier_analysis.fun_fact_popular: The human ear is a natural Fourier analyzer: the cochlea of the inner ear breaks down complex sound into individual frequencies, allowing us to distinguish voices in a noisy room.
fourier_analysis.description_simple: A musical note seems like a single sound, but in fact it consists of a fundamental tone and many overtones (additional frequencies). Fourier analysis is like separating a chord into individual strings. It takes a signal recorded over time (for example, a sound file) and converts it into a spectrum (frequency decomposition) — a graph where the horizontal axis is frequency (pitch) and the vertical axis is intensity. This allows us to see which frequencies dominate and filter out noise. The principle is universal: bridge vibrations, seismic waves, and X-ray images are analyzed in the same way.
fourier_analysis.history_simple: The French mathematician Jean-Baptiste Fourier in the early 19th century studied heat propagation in solids. He realized that any thermal distribution could be represented as a sum of simple trigonometric waves. His idea was initially met with skepticism, but later became the foundation of signal processing.
fourier_analysis.how_it_works_simple: The heart of the analysis is a formula that turns a signal recording into a frequency map. Essentially, we ask: 'How similar is my signal to a pure sine wave of a given frequency?' Multiplying the signal by a sine wave and averaging the result yields a number — this is the contribution of that frequency. Repeating this for all possible frequencies builds the spectrum. It's like trying many keys on a lock: each turn gives a measure of fit, and together they reveal the signal's structure.
fourier_analysis.description: Fourier analysis is a mathematical method of decomposing a function into a sum of trigonometric (sines and cosines) or complex exponential functions. The result of the Fourier transform is a complex-valued function of frequency, whose modulus gives the amplitude spectrum and argument gives the phase spectrum. For discrete signals (sequences), the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) and its fast algorithms (FFT) are used. Fourier analysis is based on the orthogonality of harmonic functions and the possibility of representing almost any function as an infinite series (Fourier series) or integral under certain conditions (e.g., Dirichlet conditions). It is widely used for solving differential equations, in spectroscopy, acoustics, communication systems, and computer vision.
fourier_analysis.history: In 1807, Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier presented a work on heat propagation to the Paris Academy of Sciences, where he claimed that any periodic function could be expanded into a trigonometric series. Leading mathematicians of the time (Lagrange, Laplace) were skeptical due to rigor; full convergence proofs came later (Dirichlet, Riemann). The fast Fourier transform (FFT), which made the algorithm practical, was independently discovered by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, though elements of the method go back to Gauss.
fourier_analysis.how_it_works: The forward Fourier transform of a function f(t) is defined by the integral: F(ω) = ∫ f(t) e^{-iωt} dt. The inverse: f(t) = (1/2π) ∫ F(ω) e^{iωt} dω. Physically, the quantity |F(ω)|² dω represents the fraction of signal energy in the frequency band [ω, ω+dω] (Parseval's theorem). In digital processing, the FFT is implemented, with complexity O(N log N) instead of O(N²) for direct DFT. Convolution in the time domain becomes multiplication in the frequency domain, which is convenient for filtering. The short-time Fourier transform adds time localization at the cost of frequency resolution — a compromise overcome by wavelets.
key_problems: Limited time localization for non-stationary signals
Sensitivity to noise at high frequency accuracy
Increasing computational efficiency for very long recordings
Analysis of signals on non-equidistant grids
fourier_analysis.fun_fact: Gauss developed an algorithm equivalent to the FFT as early as 1805 for astronomical data interpolation, but did not realize its universality.

formulas.description: Forward Fourier transform
formulas.meaning: f(t) — function in time domain, F(ω) — frequency spectrum, ω — angular frequency (ω = 2πν, ν — frequency), i — imaginary unit

formulas.description: Inverse Fourier transform
formulas.meaning: f(t) is recovered from the spectrum, factor 1/(2π) is normalization

natural_language_processing.name: Natural Language Processing
natural_language_processing.mini: You type 'breakfast with...' — and your phone suggests 'you'. It's not guessing; it reads billions of similar phrases. That's natural language processing.
natural_language_processing.practical_application: Voice assistants, text autocomplete, translators, spam filters — all rely on algorithms that understand human speech.
natural_language_processing.description_popular: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a field at the intersection of linguistics and machine learning, where algorithms learn to extract meaning from text and speech. At its core is the representation of words as vectors (numbers describing their meaning), and neural networks analyze sequences, capturing context. Modern models like GPT don't just cycle through rules — they absorb vast amounts of books, articles, dialogues and build a probabilistic picture of language: which word is most likely to appear after this phrase. This is how coherent text, translation, or an answer to a question is born.
natural_language_processing.fun_fact_popular: The largest language model has 'read' more texts than a person could in a thousand lifetimes — about 500 billion words.
natural_language_processing.description_simple: Natural language processing is when a computer learns to understand not commands, but ordinary human speech. Imagine you're explaining directions to a foreigner: you simplify, choosing familiar words. Similarly, a program breaks text into pieces, searching for connections between words and meaning. For example, to understand that 'apple' in one sentence is a fruit, and in another it’s a company. It looks at the neighbors of the word: if next to 'ate' — fruit, if 'stock' — business.
natural_language_processing.history_simple: The first attempts at machine translation began in the 1950s. In 1966, the famous chatbot Eliza appeared, pretending to be a psychotherapist. The real breakthrough came in the 2010s with the development of neural networks: they learned to memorize long sequences of words.
natural_language_processing.how_it_works_simple: Text is turned into numbers. Each word is encoded with a long list of digits — its semantic portrait. Words with similar meanings get similar numbers. Then the neural network reads the sentence word by word, guessing the next one. Given the input 'the cat sat on the...', the network recalls: after 'on' often comes something flat. From this, an answer, translation, or command is born.
natural_language_processing.description: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of artificial intelligence concerned with analyzing, understanding, and generating text and speech in human languages. Tasks include tokenization (splitting into words or subwords), parsing, part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, machine translation, and dialogue systems. Since the 2010s, neural network approaches have dominated: recurrent networks (LSTM), then the Transformer architecture with attention mechanism, enabling parallel text processing and capturing contextual dependencies between distant words. Models like BERT and GPT are pre-trained on unlabeled text corpora using self-supervised learning (predicting missing words or the next word). They are then fine-tuned for specific tasks. Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate emergent abilities: by slightly scaling up, they begin solving tasks for which they were not explicitly trained.
natural_language_processing.history: The idea of machine translation and text analysis dates back to the work of Alan Turing (1950) and the test named after him. In 1954, the Georgetown experiment — the first public machine translation from Russian to English — took place. In the 1960s-1970s, rule-based systems (grammars, dictionaries) dominated, but they broke down on language ambiguity. In the 1980s-1990s, statistical methods based on text corpora emerged. Neural networks sparked a revolution: in 2013, the word2vec model learned to obtain meaningful vector representations of words; in 2014, seq2seq with attention improved translation; and in 2017, the Transformer architecture became the basis for almost all modern NLP systems. The breakthrough of large language models began with BERT (2018) and GPT-3 (2020), showing that with increasing network size and data, a qualitative leap in language understanding occurs.
natural_language_processing.how_it_works: The key mechanism of modern NLP models is multi-head attention from the Transformer architecture. The input text is tokenized and converted into embeddings — fixed-size vectors. Then several layers of self-attention compute for each position a weighted sum of all other positions, allowing a word to gather context from the entire sentence. The attention formula: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √d_k)V, where Q, K, V are queries, keys, and values derived from the input embeddings. During pre-training, the model learns to predict missing tokens (as in BERT) or the next token (as in GPT), minimizing cross-entropy. After that, for specific applications, it is fine-tuned on a small labeled dataset. The model's output is a probability distribution over the vocabulary, from which the next token is chosen.
key_problems: Understanding true meaning and pragmatics (models often rely on patterns, not reasoning)
Eliminating biases and toxicity embedded in training data
Controlled generation of facts without hallucinations (models can invent names, dates, citations)
Efficient training without enormous computational costs
Incorporating common sense and causal reasoning
natural_language_processing.fun_fact: GPT-4 uses over a trillion parameters, and its pre-training required energy comparable to the annual consumption of hundreds of households.

formulas.description: Attention mechanism (scaled dot-product attention), underlying Transformer
formulas.meaning: Q — query matrix, K — key matrix, V — value matrix, d_k — dimension of keys; softmax turns similarity scores into probabilities

neural_networks.name: neural networks
neural_networks.mini: A child, looking at hundreds of pictures of animals, gradually learns to tell a cat from a dog. After hundreds of such examples, they can already name a new animal without error.
neural_networks.practical_application: Face recognition in photos, voice assistants, weather forecasting.
neural_networks.description_popular: Card by card, lion after lion, zebra after zebra — thousands of examples pass through the network. Each layer of artificial neurons extracts increasingly abstract features: first it catches edges and lines, then assembles them into parts of a face, then into a complete image. The final layer gives an answer — much like a child looks at ears, whiskers, and tail to say 'cat'.
neural_networks.fun_fact_popular: In 2012, the AlexNet network surpassed humans for the first time in an image recognition competition — it became clear then: the era of deep learning had begun.
neural_networks.description_simple: In the child's hand is a stack of cards with pictures of animals. They try to name each one, and an adult nods or corrects. Neural networks (programs that learn from examples) work in the same way. Card by card, small mistakes turn into the ability to recognize even new animals. Inside the program are layers of artificial neurons (simple computational cells). Each neuron processes a number and passes it on, multiplying by its weight (a number indicating the importance of the signal). Over time, all weights are adjusted so that the network gives the correct answer at the output.
neural_networks.history_simple: The idea was attempted back in the 1940s, when two scientists devised a simple electrical circuit imitating a nerve cell. The real breakthrough came in the 2010s, when powerful computers made it possible to train networks on millions of examples.
neural_networks.how_it_works_simple: A picture broken down into pixels is fed into the network's input. The first layer of neurons catches simple details — edges, brightness changes. The second layer assembles corners and arcs from them. Further layers combine these pieces into more complex shapes: ears, eyes, paws. The last layer decides what animal is in the photo, based on all the features found.
neural_networks.description: The child clutches a stack of cards in their hand. Over the summer, they've gone through thousands of images and now hardly make mistakes. A neural network is a computational model consisting of layers of artificial neurons (nodes) that transform input data (e.g., image pixels) into an output signal (class or number) through a series of weighted sums and nonlinear activation functions. Learning occurs by adjusting the connection weights based on the prediction error using the backpropagation algorithm. And in the end, clutching a stack of cards, the child looks at a new picture — and confidently says 'dog.' Having gone through millions of examples, the network does the same.
neural_networks.history: The concept of an artificial neuron dates back to the work of Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts (1943), who proposed a mathematical model of the neuron. In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt created the perceptron — the first trainable neural network. However, after criticism by Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert in 1969, interest waned. Revival began in the 1980s with the development of multilayer networks and the backpropagation algorithm (David Rumelhart et al.). In the 2000s, the availability of big data and GPU computing led to deep learning.
neural_networks.how_it_works: The input signal passes through layers: each neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs, adds a bias, and applies a nonlinear activation function (ReLU, sigmoid, etc.). Training minimizes a loss function via gradient descent; gradients are computed by the backpropagation method — from output to input, using the chain rule of derivatives.
key_problems: Overfitting requiring regularization
Interpretability of decisions — 'black box'
Need for large amounts of labeled data
Catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning
Vulnerability to adversarial attacks
neural_networks.fun_fact: The deepest network as of 2024 is not from architecture but from exploration: in one experiment, a network with 10,000 layers was trained to predict just a single pixel, demonstrating the potential redundancy of depth.

formulas.description: Output of a single artificial neuron
formulas.meaning: y — neuron output; φ — activation function (e.g., sigmoid); w_i — connection weights; x_i — input signals; b — bias

diffusion_models.name: Diffusion Models
diffusion_models.mini: Snowy 'noise' on a TV screen slowly transforms into a clear face. This is how diffusion models work—they remove randomness step by step until a meaningful image emerges.
diffusion_models.practical_application: Generating photographs from text descriptions, improving telescope images, designing new materials.
diffusion_models.description_popular: Diffusion models are a generative approach that transforms Gaussian noise into ordered data, such as a photo of a cat. The process resembles restoring a mosaic from memory: you have only a rough sketch, but you remember what similar works looked like, and you gradually recreate the pattern—from fuzzy patches to fine lines. The model contains a 'representation' of the world, learned from millions of examples, and thus can generate plausible new images. The key difference from other generative networks is iterativity: the picture is born not instantly but through a chain of small improvements.
diffusion_models.fun_fact_popular: Although diffusion seems slow, modern versions create an image in just half a second on a powerful graphics chip.
diffusion_models.description_simple: Diffusion models create an image from random points. Imagine fogged glass: at first nothing is visible—only gray smudges. The model, like an artist, adds details drop by drop, clarifying the contours. First an oval of a face appears, then eyes, mouth. It all starts with pure noise (a jumble of random numbers) that is processed hundreds of times. Each step slightly reduces the disorder, relying on what the model 'knows' about the structure of objects from analyzing thousands of real photographs.
diffusion_models.history_simple: The first ideas emerged in 2015 from the physics of non-equilibrium systems. In 2020, scientists from OpenAI and Google proved that this approach could surpass other methods in image quality. Today, diffusion powers DALL-E, Midjourney, and other tools.
diffusion_models.how_it_works_simple: Training is like a reverse game of telephone. First, take a real photo and repeatedly mix in random pixels—the image 'degrades', turning into noise. The model learns to guess what the picture was before distortion. After training, it is given pure noise—and, going backward, it 'develops' a new image that never existed before.
diffusion_models.description: Diffusion models in machine learning are a class of deep generative models based on the principle of gradual destruction and subsequent restoration of information in a random process. Fundamentally, they use a stochastic forward process that sequentially adds noise to data (e.g., to image pixels) according to a predefined schedule, and a reverse process trained by a neural network for denoising. Formally, the forward diffusion process is defined by a Markov chain that brings the distribution of real data to a standard normal distribution. The reverse process, also Markovian, is parameterized by a neural network that predicts the noise added at each step. Training involves minimizing the distance between the true and predicted noise. After training, new data can be sampled by inputting pure noise and applying the reverse process step by step. This approach does not use adversarial training like GANs, nor does it require variational inference like VAEs, which largely stabilizes training and improves generation quality.
diffusion_models.history: The method's roots go back to works on thermodynamics and statistical physics (e.g., the works of Langevin), but the modern embodiment was proposed in 2015 by Jascha Sohl-Dickstein as a stochastic generative model based on non-equilibrium thermodynamics. The breakthrough came after the 2020 publication of the paper 'Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models,' which demonstrated outstanding results on image synthesis tasks. Further improvements (accelerated sampling, conditional guidance) led to the creation of systems like DALL-E 2, Imagen, Stable Diffusion, which revolutionized the field of AI creativity.
diffusion_models.how_it_works: Forward process: to the original image x0, small amounts of Gaussian noise are added over T steps, obtaining a sequence x1, x2, ..., xT, where xT is practically indistinguishable from white noise. The transition at each step: q(xt|xt-1) = N(xt; sqrt(1-βt)·xt-1, βtI), where βt is the variance schedule. Reverse process: a neural network εθ(xt, t) learns to predict the noise added at step t, minimizing E[||ε - εθ(xt, t)||²]. During generation, one starts from xT ~ N(0, I) and iteratively applies xt-1 = (1/√(αt))·(xt - (1-αt)/√(1-ᾱt)·εθ(xt, t)) + σt·z, where z is noise. To speed up sampling, DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models) with step skipping is used. Conditional models augment the input with information about text, class, etc., guiding the reverse process.
key_problems: High computational cost of sampling without optimization
Difficulties in controlling rare concepts and precise instruction following
Potential generation of undesirable content and the need for filtering
Scaling to video and 3D data
diffusion_models.fun_fact: Training Stable Diffusion v2.1 used the LAION-5B dataset of 5.85 billion image-text pairs, and the model itself has around 860 million parameters.

formulas.description: Forward diffusion transition
formulas.meaning: xt — noisy data at step t, βt — noise drift coefficient, I — identity matrix

slam.name: SLAM
slam.mini: A robot enters an unknown maze and draws a plan on the fly, remembering where it has been. That's how SLAM works: simultaneously building a map and determining its own location on it.
slam.practical_application: A self-driving car doesn't drive blindly — it builds a 3D model of the street and knows where it is. Robot vacuums memorize the layout of an apartment so they don't miss corners.
slam.description_popular: SLAM is a mathematical framework that enables a moving platform (robot, drone, car) to simultaneously refine its own position in space and build a map of the environment. It is based on a probabilistic approach: the robot doesn't store a single exact position, but rather a whole fan of possible positions with varying degrees of confidence. Each new sensor measurement — from a laser rangefinder (lidar), inertial sensors, cameras — updates this distribution.
