The key idea is loop closure: when the robot returns to a previously visited place, it recognizes it and sharply reduces the accumulated error.
slam.fun_fact_popular: Some SLAM systems use multiple cameras and inertial sensors at once, similar to how a person orients themselves by looking with their eyes and sensing the tilt of their body.
slam.description_simple: When you wander in the dark in an unfamiliar room, you stretch out your hands and memorize the layout of the furniture. SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) allows a robot to do the same thing. It uses cameras or lasers (lidars) to measure distances to objects, and from this data it draws a map. At the same time, it continuously refines its own position so that the map lines don't diverge.
slam.history_simple: The first algorithms appeared in the 1980s for navigating submarines and military robots. Mass adoption began in the 2000s when fast processors and precise sensors became available.
slam.how_it_works_simple: The robot compares expected sensor readings with actual ones. If a wall turns out to be farther than it thought, the algorithm shifts its position on the map. Meanwhile, new details are added to the map. This is similar to the game 'hot or cold': the robot constantly makes mistakes and corrects itself.
slam.description: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is a computational problem from the field of mobile robotics, in which an agent (robot, drone) must build a model of an unknown environment and simultaneously estimate its trajectory within it. From a filtering perspective, this is a state estimation problem with partially observed dynamics: the state includes the robot's pose and the map parameters (often represented as a set of landmarks or grid cell occupancy). Observations come from sensors — lidars, cameras, odometry sensors, inertial measurement units. Mathematically, the problem reduces to maximizing the posterior probability of the trajectory and map given the data. Two families of solutions are common: based on particle filters (FastSLAM) and based on sparse nonlinear least squares (Graph SLAM). The loop closure problem is key: when the robot returns to a known place, the system must recognize it and redistribute the accumulated error over the entire trajectory, otherwise the map will be deformed.
slam.history: The concept of SLAM was formalized by Hugh Durrant-Whyte and John J. Leonard in 1991, although earlier works (e.g., Cheyne, 1986) had already tackled similar problems. Early implementations relied on the extended Kalman filter (EKF) and worked with radar or sonar data. A turning point came in 2002, when Montemerlo and Thrun introduced FastSLAM — a particle filter-based algorithm capable of processing thousands of landmarks in real time. Modern approaches, such as ORB-SLAM, use multi-sensor fusion and graph architectures, achieving high accuracy at large scales.
slam.how_it_works: Probabilistic SLAM models the joint distribution P(x_{1:t}, m | z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}), where x is the trajectory, m is the map, z are observations, and u are control inputs. Recursive Bayesian filtering is commonly used: prediction based on a motion model, correction using sensor data. In Graph SLAM, the problem is transformed into a sparse graph where nodes are robot poses and landmarks, and edges are constraints from odometry and observations. Optimizing the graph using Newton-Gauss or Levenberg-Marquardt methods yields the best estimate of the entire history. For loop closure, place recognition methods are used — often based on visual bags of words (BoW) for camera systems. Particle filters, in turn, represent the distribution with a set of hypotheses (particles), each with its own map; this approach is effective for nonlinear models and non-normal noise.
key_problems: Reliable loop closure in large spaces under changing lighting or weather conditions
Long-term storage and updating of the map during repeat visits
Collaboration of multiple robots with decentralized SLAM
Handling of dynamic objects and structural changes in the environment
slam.fun_fact: The FastSLAM 2.0 algorithm uses exactly one copy of the map per particle, making it computationally efficient — the number of operations depends logarithmically on the number of landmarks.

computer_vision.name: computer vision
computer_vision.mini: A baby, opening its eyes for the first time, learns to link patches of light to shapes and movement to objects. Computer vision does the same: it learns to see meaning in sets of pixels.
computer_vision.practical_application: A car recognizes road signs and pedestrians in real time to brake or alert the driver in time.
computer_vision.description_popular: Computer vision relies on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Their architecture mirrors the visual cortex: simple cells respond to lines at specific angles, complex cells to their combinations. A convolutional layer scans the image with a small window, multiplying it by a filter and producing feature maps. Several such layers sequentially build increasingly abstract representations: from edges and textures to object parts and entire faces. Modern systems also use attention mechanisms and transformers, treating the image as a sequence of patches.
computer_vision.fun_fact_popular: The Google Translate system can translate text on a menu photo in real time: you point the camera at foreign text, and it appears on screen in your language—all thanks to image recognition and understanding.
computer_vision.description_simple: Computer vision is the ability of programs to 'see': to receive an image from a camera and extract information from it. Imagine you look at a photo and describe it: 'a cat is sleeping on a rug.' The program, instead of eyes, uses a matrix of numbers—the brightness of each pixel (dot). It processes these numbers, finding patterns: where are the boundaries, what is the shape, what color. For this, neural networks are created—mathematical constructions resembling interconnected knots that learn from examples.
computer_vision.history_simple: It all began in the 1960s when scientists tried to teach a computer to distinguish simple geometric shapes. The first steps were difficult: Larry Roberts' program in 1963 was able to 'outline' the edges of a brick in a photo. Then for decades, edge detectors and segmentation were developed. The real breakthrough came in 2012: the neural network AlexNet won the ImageNet image recognition competition by a large margin, showing that deep neural networks could handle this task much better than previous methods.
computer_vision.how_it_works_simple: Training resembles a soccer goalkeeper's practice: the more balls he deflects, the better he predicts the trajectory. Similarly, the neural network processes millions of labeled images, each time guessing whether it's a cat or a dog. The error is calculated and sent back to adjust the weights—the sensitivity of each virtual 'neuron'—in tiny steps. Gradually, the network becomes an expert.
computer_vision.description: Computer vision is an interdisciplinary field combining signal processing theory, machine learning, robotics, and cognitive science, aimed at automatic extraction of meaningful information from images and video. It is defined by four classic tasks: classification (assigning a label), detection (localization and labeling), segmentation (pixel-wise labeling), and 3D structure recovery. Methods are divided into 'pre-deep learning' (SIFT, HOG, SVM) and 'post-deep learning' (CNN, Vision Transformers, diffusion models). Key benchmarks: ImageNet, COCO, Cityscapes.
computer_vision.history: The work of Hubel and Wiesel (1959) on the visual cortex is considered the starting point, inspiring hierarchical models. In 1963, Larry Roberts implemented the 'Blocks World' program, interpreting photos of cubes. In the 1970s, geometric methods developed rapidly. In the 1990s, the first effective edge detectors appeared. Convolutional networks were proposed by Yann LeCun in 1989 for digit recognition. The real revolution came in 2012 when Alex Krizhevsky and colleagues released AlexNet, using GPUs—accuracy on ImageNet jumped from ~74% to ~84%. In subsequent years, architectures deepened: VGG, ResNet (2015) solving the vanishing gradient problem through skip connections. Since 2020, Vision Transformers (Dosovitskiy et al.) brought self-attention to images, and models like DALL·E 2 and Stable Diffusion learned to generate new images from textual descriptions.
computer_vision.how_it_works: The main building block is convolution: a kernel of size k×k is multiplied element-wise with a patch of the image, and the result is summed. A pooling layer reduces resolution, emphasizing the most important. Fully connected layers take the final feature vector and output a prediction. Training is done via gradient descent with backpropagation. In modern systems, a large model is often pre-trained on large datasets (ImageNet-21k) and then fine-tuned for a target task (transfer learning). For image generation, autoencoders (VAE), generative adversarial networks (GAN), and recently diffusion probabilistic models are used, gradually removing noise from an initial random field until a clear picture emerges.
key_problems: Robustness in non-standard conditions (night, fog, unusual camera angles).
Interpretability: why did the model make that decision?
Dependence on labeled data and domain adaptation.
Ensuring privacy in face recognition.
Temporal consistency in video: absence of flickering artifacts from frame to frame.
Energy efficiency of inference on edge devices.
computer_vision.fun_fact: The ResNet-152 neural network in 2015 had 152 layers—the same as the number of neurons in one of the fully connected layers of its predecessor AlexNet.

large_language_models.name: Large Language Models
large_language_models.mini: A stranger thrown into a metropolis without knowing the language eventually learns to understand and respond by listening to conversations around them. Large language models work similarly—they absorb enormous volumes of text and then guess which word should come next.
large_language_models.practical_application: Such models write news, compose poems, generate programming code, answer customer questions in chats, and help doctors draft discharge summaries from medical histories.
large_language_models.description_popular: Modern large language models are neural networks with a 'transformer' architecture, featuring anywhere from hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions of parameters. Each parameter is a number that influences how the signal from one word is passed to another. The model doesn't store words but converts them into vectors of numbers—mathematical points in a high-dimensional space of meanings. Pre-training is carried out on an autocomplete task: the model fills in missing words or predicts the next word in a sequence. Afterwards, it can be fine-tuned on specialized examples to hold a dialogue, solve problems, or write code.
large_language_models.fun_fact_popular: GPT-3 can write an essay indistinguishable from a human-written one, as judged by a committee, in 2 seconds—the time it takes a person just to open a text editor.
large_language_models.description_simple: A large language model (LLM) is a program that learns language by reading billions of web pages, books, and articles. It doesn't understand meaning like a human but finds clever patterns in word combinations. Imagine a foreigner who has memorized a huge volume of phrases and each time, upon hearing the beginning, retrieves the most likely continuation from memory. That's how the model predicts word by word and constructs coherent text.
large_language_models.history_simple: The first attempts to create computer language models date back to the 1950s, but back then machines lacked memory and data. The real breakthrough came in the 2010s: engineers trained neural networks (programs mimicking the connections of neurons) on the texts of the entire internet. The most famous model, GPT-3 from OpenAI, appeared in 2020 and demonstrated that scale matters a great deal.
large_language_models.how_it_works_simple: The model works like a game of 'guess the next word.' It receives the beginning of a sentence and proposes dozens of possible continuations, estimating their probabilities. These probabilities are derived from the statistics of the texts it has read. Training is like tuning thousands of radio receivers: each parameter is adjusted to make the prediction more accurate. Inside the model, there are no grammar rules—only numerical weights that have self-organized into something resembling linguistic structures.
large_language_models.description: Large language models (LLMs) are probabilistic autoregressive models that operate on discrete sequences of tokens (subwords or characters). They are based on the transformer architecture, which uses the multi-head attention mechanism for weighted context aggregation. A key feature is scaling: increasing the number of parameters, the dimensionality of hidden representations, and the training corpus size leads to the emergence of qualitatively new abilities (in-context learning, reasoning without fine-tuning). Examples: GPT-4 (OpenAI), Llama (Meta), PaLM (Google).
large_language_models.history: The history began with statistical n-gram models (1950s), then neural network language models (Bengio et al., 2000s). The turning point was the paper Attention Is All You Need (2017), which proposed the transformer architecture. In 2018, OpenAI released GPT-1 with 117 million parameters, and in 2020, GPT-3 with 175 billion parameters demonstrated that a model without explicit training could translate, program, and reason simply by receiving instructions in natural language. Since then, the race has focused on both scaling up models and improving efficiency (Mixture-of-Experts, Chinchilla scaling laws).
large_language_models.how_it_works: The model receives a context window of n tokens as input. Each token is mapped to an embedding and encoded by self-attention layers, creating contextualized representations. At the output, a linear classifier predicts the probability distribution of the next token. Training minimizes the cross-entropy between the prediction and the true token. During generation, text is produced by sequential sampling of tokens (usually with top-p or top-k nucleus sampling). Key techniques: pre-training on unlabeled text, then instruction-based or RLHF fine-tuning to align with usefulness and safety. The attention mechanism computes similarity weights between queries and keys for each pair of tokens, allowing it to focus on long-range dependencies.
key_problems: Hallucinations: the model invents plausible but false facts.
Controllability and safety: generation of unwanted content.
High computational costs for training and inference.
Copyright issues regarding training data.
Difficulties with logical reasoning and mathematics.
Environmental footprint: the carbon footprint of a single training run is comparable to the lifecycle of several cars.
large_language_models.fun_fact: In 2020, GPT-3 consumed about 0.4 kWh to generate 100 pages of text—roughly equivalent to the energy used by a medium-brightness light bulb in 5 hours.

formulas.description: Key formula of the self-attention mechanism in transformers.
formulas.meaning: Q is the query matrix, K is the key matrix, V is the value matrix, d_k is the dimensionality of the keys, softmax is a function that converts numbers into probabilities. The output is a weighted sum of values, where the weights are determined by the similarity of queries and keys.

wavelet_transform.name: wavelet transform
wavelet_transform.mini: A zoom lens on a camera captures both the entire landscape and the pattern on a butterfly's wing. The wavelet transform similarly changes scale: it decomposes a signal into scaled copies of itself, allowing one to see both the overall shape and the tiniest jumps.
wavelet_transform.practical_application: Digital fingerprints and barcodes are compressed using wavelets. Instruments that search for defects in aircraft parts listen for crack echoes with wavelets.
wavelet_transform.description_popular: The secret of wavelets lies in compromise. Fourier analysis provides perfect frequency resolution but loses time information. The windowed Fourier transform fixes this but fixes the window size. Wavelets adjust the window width adaptively: for high frequencies, short windows are used; for low frequencies, long ones. This is like musical notation, where long notes represent bass sounds and short ones represent rapid trills. In practice, wavelets excel at image compression (JPEG 2000 format) and cleaning signals from noise without blurring sharp transitions—for example, in medical tomograms.
wavelet_transform.fun_fact_popular: Human vision is somewhat similar to wavelet analysis: we can discern both the overall shape of a chair in dim light and a fine inscription on its leg—the brain processes images at multiple scales simultaneously.
wavelet_transform.description_simple: Ordinary Fourier analysis shows which frequencies were present in a signal, but not when. It's as if someone told you that a symphony contains the note C, but not at what moment. The wavelet transform solves this problem: instead of endless sinusoids, it uses small waves—wavelets—that decay. The wavelet is applied to the signal and shifted along like a template. Changing the size of the template (scale) lets you see both broad features and fine details. This yields a map: time on the horizontal axis, scale on the vertical, and color indicating the strength of the match.
wavelet_transform.history_simple: Wavelets emerged in the 1980s when geophysicist Jean Morlet sought a way to extract weak reflected waves in seismic data. Together with physicist Alex Grossmann, he developed the continuous wavelet transform. Later, mathematician Ingrid Daubechies constructed elegant orthogonal wavelets with compact support, paving the way for fast algorithms.
wavelet_transform.how_it_works_simple: Take a short wave template (the wavelet). Compare it to a segment of the signal at the beginning—you get a similarity number. Shift the template slightly forward—another number. After sliding through the whole signal, you obtain a series of numbers for that template size. Then stretch the template (increase the scale) and repeat. A tiny template catches sharp peaks; a large one captures smooth curves. The collection of such series for different stretches is the wavelet spectrum.
wavelet_transform.description: The wavelet transform is a mathematical tool for time-frequency analysis of signals with adaptive resolution. The continuous wavelet transform (CWT) is defined as the convolution of a signal with scaled and shifted versions of a mother wavelet. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) uses multiresolution analysis to obtain a hierarchical set of coefficients—approximation and detail. Wavelets provide optimal localization in the time-frequency domain in the sense of the uncertainty principle, but with variable window width, unlike the fixed-window Fourier transform. They form a basis in function spaces and are used for denoising, compression, feature extraction, and solving differential equations.
wavelet_transform.history: The history of wavelets began with Haar's work (1909)—the simplest step-like system. From the 1930s to the 1980s, separate ideas emerged: the Littlewood–Paley function, quadrature mirror filters by Croisier, Esteban, and Galand. A coherent theory arose in the early 1980s from the work of geophysicist Jean Morlet and mathematician Alex Grossmann, who built the continuous wavelet transform for seismic signal analysis. Then Ingrid Daubechies (1988) created smooth orthogonal wavelets with compact support, enabling a fast transform. Later, Mallat and Meyer developed multiresolution analysis, linking wavelets to signal filtering.
wavelet_transform.how_it_works: The scaling function φ(t) and mother wavelet ψ(t) generate a basis such that {ψ_{j,k}(t) = 2^{-j/2} ψ(2^{-j}t - k)}. Any signal can be decomposed: f(t) = Σ_k a_{j0,k} φ_{j0,k}(t) + Σ_{j≥j0} Σ_k d_{j,k} ψ_{j,k}(t). The coefficients d are obtained by the fast Mallat algorithm using cascaded filtering. At each level, the signal passes through a pair of filters—low-pass (averaging) and high-pass (detailing)—followed by decimation. This is dual to a bank of quadrature mirror filters. The orthogonality condition of the wavelet basis requires the filters to satisfy certain relations. The analysis is flexible: the wavelet shape can be tailored to the data type.
key_problems: Automatic selection of a mother wavelet for a specific signal type
Efficient algorithms for multidimensional wavelet transforms
Wavelet analysis of nonlinear and nonstationary systems with fast chaotic dynamics
Improving reconstruction accuracy after heavy lossy compression
wavelet_transform.fun_fact: The FBI in the early 1990s chose wavelet compression for storing digital fingerprints: it preserves fine patterns much better than JPEG.

formulas.description: Continuous wavelet transform
formulas.meaning: f(t) — signal, ψ — mother wavelet, overline denotes complex conjugation, a — scale (a>0), b — shift, W(a,b) — wavelet coefficients

formulas.description: Signal decomposition into a discrete wavelet series
formulas.meaning: φ — scaling function, ψ — wavelet, j₀ — starting scale, a_{j₀,k} — approximation coefficients at level j₀, d_{j,k} — detail coefficients at level j

control_theory.name: control theory
control_theory.mini: Control theory helps maintain balance — like a cyclist subtly adjusting the handlebars to stay upright while moving.
control_theory.practical_application: Aircraft autopilots, household temperature control, camera stabilization systems in smartphones.
control_theory.description_popular: Control theory is the mathematics of maintaining order. It explains how to make a system do what you want despite wind, friction, and other whims of the real world. An engineer designs an algorithm (a controller) that continuously reads sensor data and doses commands to actuators to drive the difference between desired and actual values to zero.
control_theory.fun_fact_popular: The Hubble Space Telescope locks onto a star using three gyroscopes and six fine guidance sensors. Its control system holds the image steady with an accuracy equivalent to keeping a laser beam on a coin in New York from the distance of Los Angeles.
control_theory.description_simple: A tightrope walker balances with a long pole. He notices a tilt, quickly shifts the pole to the right, and straightens up. Control theory is the engineering science of how technical systems replicate the same trick: measuring a deviation and instantly correcting it.
control_theory.history_simple: The desire to tame steam and set flywheels in motion gave rise to a key question: how to restrain such unbridled power? Scottish engineer James Watt devised the centrifugal governor in 1788—spinning balls that spread apart as speed increased, throttling the steam supply. This became the first automatic controller.
control_theory.how_it_works_simple: Every control system works like the float in a toilet cistern. The float is a level sensor, the lever is a mechanism that compares the level to a setpoint, and the valve is an actuator. As soon as the water drops below the mark, the float sinks, the valve opens slightly, and the flow replenishes the loss. A thermostat, autopilot, or robotic arm works the same way.
control_theory.description: Control theory studies the behavior of dynamical systems and synthesizes controllers to achieve a desired goal. It is based on mathematical descriptions of objects in the form of differential or difference equations. It distinguishes between classical control (PID controllers, frequency-domain methods) and modern control (state-space, optimal, robust, adaptive). Key concepts: observability, controllability, Lyapunov stability, poles and zeros of the transfer function.
control_theory.history: The roots of the theory go back to Watt's governor (1788). James Clerk Maxwell laid the mathematical foundation in his paper 'On Governors' (1868), where he first analyzed the stability of a feedback system. In 1892, Russian-born Aleksandr Lyapunov introduced a rigorous definition of stability. The mid-twentieth century saw a flourishing of the field with contributions from Harry Nyquist, Hendrik Bode, Rudolf Kalman (for filtering and control problems), and Lev Semyonovich Pontryagin (the maximum principle). Today, control methods permeate aerospace, robotics, economics, and biology.
control_theory.how_it_works: The basic feedback loop: a sensor measures the current value y(t), a summing junction computes the error e(t) = r(t) – y(t) (where r(t) is the setpoint), and the controller produces a control input u(t) based on the error. The system's response is described by dynamical equations. For example, in a PID controller, u(t) = K_p e + K_i ∫ e dt + K_d de/dt. The proportional term responds to the current error, the integral term eliminates steady-state error, and the derivative term anticipates future deviations. For complex multivariable systems, the state equation is used: dx/dt = A x + B u, y = C x + D u, and controller synthesis often reduces to solving algebraic Riccati equations.
key_problems: Controlling nonlinear systems with delays and hysteresis
Robustness to parameter uncertainty and external disturbances
Decentralized control in large-scale networked systems (smart grids, drone swarms)
Synthesis of safe control algorithms for autonomous vehicles that guarantee collision avoidance
Reinforcement learning for control in the real world with high sample efficiency
control_theory.fun_fact: The most precise controller in history, the LISA Pathfinder system (2015), held test masses in free fall with a relative acceleration below 10⁻¹⁴ g, to demonstrate the technology for future gravitational-wave observatories.

formulas.description: The standard PID controller — the workhorse of industry.
formulas.latex: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int_{0}^{t} e(\tau) d\tau + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}
formulas.meaning: u(t) — control signal; e(t) — error (difference between setpoint and actual value); K_p — proportional gain; K_i — integral gain; K_d — derivative gain; t — time; τ — integration variable.

formulas.description: State equation — a generalized description of a linear dynamical system.
formulas.meaning: x(t) — state vector of the system (e.g., position and velocity); u(t) — control vector; A — system matrix, defining its internal dynamics; B — input matrix, showing how controls affect the state; the dot over x denotes the time derivative.

radar.name: radar
radar.mini: A bat in a night forest emits a squeak. The echo returns with a delay, drawing a map of branches in its brain. Radar is an artificial echo sounder that sees in the dark.
radar.practical_application: Radar measures the speed of your car, helps airplanes land in fog, and predicts thunderstorms by detecting raindrops hundreds of kilometers away.
radar.description_popular: Radar is an active radio-location system that emits electromagnetic waves and analyzes their reflections from targets. Modern radars use complex pulse sequences (chirps) with linear frequency modulation, allowing high range resolution (down to centimeters) at moderate peak power. The receiver measures the time of flight τ, amplitude, phase, and frequency of the returned signal, calculating range, size, speed, and even shape of the object. Doppler shift gives radial velocity, and beam steering (scanning) gives angular coordinates. Pulsed radars alternate transmission and reception; Doppler radars transmit continuously and filter the reflected signal from stationary clutter.
radar.fun_fact_popular: The radar installation at the Arecibo Observatory could measure the distance to the Moon with an accuracy of a few centimeters—that's like the thickness of a finger at a distance of 384,000 kilometers.
radar.description_simple: Radar (short for Radio Detection and Ranging) works on the principle of echo. An antenna emits a short radio pulse, which reflects off an object and returns. The delay time gives the distance: each microsecond of delay corresponds to 150 meters. The change in signal frequency (Doppler effect) measures the target's speed.
radar.history_simple: The first radar for aircraft detection was built by Scottish physicist Robert Watson-Watt in 1935. By 1940, a network of radars along the British coast helped win the Battle of Britain.
radar.how_it_works_simple: Imagine you shout toward a mountain: the shout reflects, and you hear an echo. The farther the mountain, the longer you wait. Radar does the same with radio waves, but much faster—the pulse lasts millionths of a second. The target's speed is found from the pitch of the returned signal: if a car approaches, the echo becomes “denser” (higher frequency).
radar.description: Radar (radio detection and ranging) is a device for detecting, measuring coordinates, and determining motion parameters of targets using radio waves. The cornerstone is the radar equation: received signal power P_r = (P_t G_t G_r λ^2 σ) / ((4π)^3 R^4), where σ is the target's radar cross-section, P_t is transmitter power, G are antenna gains, λ is wavelength, and R is distance. Modern radars use phased array antennas (AESA) for electronic beam scanning without mechanical rotation. Coherent processing (Doppler filtering) extracts moving targets against the background of the underlying surface. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is used to obtain radar images of terrain with sub-meter resolution.
radar.history: The idea of radar was proposed by Tesla as early as 1900, but practical implementation began in the 1930s simultaneously in several countries. Robert Watson-Watt in 1935 demonstrated aircraft detection at a distance of 27 km. The key invention was the cavity magnetron (1940, Boot and Randall), which enabled compact, powerful microwave radars. After the war, civilian applications—air navigation, meteorology, astronomy (radio telescopes)—came to the fore. The 1970s saw the introduction of digital signal processing, and the 21st century brought multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radars.
radar.how_it_works: Radar emits a coherent beam of electromagnetic waves (usually in the microwave band) and receives the reflected signal. The time delay Δt determines range: R = cΔt/2. Doppler frequency shift f_d = 2v/λ gives radial velocity v. Phased arrays steer the beam by changing the phase of the signal at each element, without moving the antenna. Pulse compression improves range resolution: a long chirp with frequency modulation is transmitted, and upon reception it is convolved with a matched filter to obtain a short response. In SAR, a moving platform (satellite, aircraft) uses its displacement to form an artificially synthesized aperture, whose length is proportional to the distance traveled, yielding resolution far better than a stationary antenna of real size.
key_problems: Detection of low-observable targets (stealth technology) against clutter
Improving resolution with limited aperture
Adaptive suppression of passive and active interference
Fusion of radar and optical data for accurate recognition
radar.fun_fact: The largest fully functional radio telescope with a 500-meter aperture (FAST) uses an active surface of 4,450 panels that can change shape to compensate for spherical aberration when tracking different parts of the sky.

formulas.description: Radar equation
formulas.meaning: P_r — received signal power, P_t — transmitter power, G_t, G_r — gain of transmitting and receiving antennas, λ — wavelength, σ — radar cross-section of the target, R — distance to the target, constant 4π from spherical front geometry

formulas.description: Range from delay
formulas.meaning: R — range, c — speed of light (c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s), Δt — delay time of the reflected signal, division by 2 accounts for the round trip

formulas.description: Doppler frequency shift
formulas.meaning: f_d — Doppler frequency shift, v — radial velocity of the target, λ — wavelength of the radiation

nmr_spectroscopy.name: NMR spectroscopy
nmr_spectroscopy.mini: Atomic nuclei in a magnetic field start spinning like tops and send out signals. NMR spectroscopy is a 'radio' for nuclei: it catches their response and from it learns which atoms are present and how they are arranged in the molecule.
nmr_spectroscopy.practical_application: MRI in hospitals is the very same NMR; this way doctors see soft tissues of the body without incisions. Chemists use NMR to determine the structure of new molecules, like a detective reconstructs a scene from clues.
nmr_spectroscopy.description_popular: NMR spectroscopy uses the magnetic properties of nuclei. Nuclei with non-zero spin (intrinsic angular momentum) possess a magnetic moment. In an external field, energy levels split (Zeeman effect), and transitions between them can be induced by radiofrequency radiation. The resonant frequency (Larmor frequency) is directly proportional to the field: for example, protons in a 9.4 T field resonate at 400 MHz. But nuclei in molecules are surrounded by electrons, which slightly shield the external field, so the frequency shifts — this is called chemical shift. From these shifts, the chemical environment of the atom is determined. Modern spectrometers obtain a spectrum by emitting a short pulse and recording the decaying signal (free induction decay), which is then converted to a frequency spectrum using Fourier transform.
nmr_spectroscopy.fun_fact_popular: The most sensitive NMR spectrometer can detect a signal from one millionth of a gram of substance. And in brain MRI, signals are collected from a glass of water, but with a resolution that allows discernment of individual neural pathways.
nmr_spectroscopy.description_simple: NMR spectroscopy is like eavesdropping on the conversations of atoms. The sample is placed in a strong magnet. Atomic nuclei, like tiny magnets, align along the field. Then they are nudged by a short radio pulse. The nuclei tilt, and when they return, they emit a weak radio signal. The frequency of this signal depends on the atom's neighbors in the molecule. Thus, one determines how many and what kinds of atoms are present, and how they are connected.
nmr_spectroscopy.history_simple: In 1946, Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell independently discovered nuclear magnetic resonance. They showed that nuclei can absorb and emit radio waves in a magnetic field. For this discovery, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1952. Later, the method became a principal tool for chemists.
nmr_spectroscopy.how_it_works_simple: Imagine that nuclei are tiny compasses. In a magnetic field, they point north. A radio pulse tilts the needles, and they begin to rotate around the field direction. The rotation speed (frequency) depends on the field strength and on what surrounds the nucleus. By measuring this frequency, one reconstructs the picture of the molecule. Each type of nucleus has its own characteristic frequency, like a radio station.
nmr_spectroscopy.description: NMR spectroscopy (nuclear magnetic resonance) is a method of studying matter based on the resonant absorption of radiofrequency radiation by nuclei in a strong magnetic field. Nuclei with spin I ≠ 0 possess a magnetic dipole moment μ = γℏI, where γ is the gyromagnetic ratio. In a field B₀, Zeeman splitting occurs into 2I+1 sublevels, with energy difference ΔE = γℏB₀. Under the action of an alternating field with frequency ν = γB₀/(2π) (Larmor frequency), transitions between sublevels arise. After pulsed excitation, the free induction decay (FID) is recorded. Fourier transformation of the FID yields a frequency spectrum, where line positions (chemical shift δ) reflect shielding of the nucleus by the electron shell, multiplet splitting reflects spin-spin interactions, and integral intensities indicate the number of equivalent nuclei. Two- and three-dimensional techniques (COSY, NOESY, HSQC, etc.) allow determination of the structures of complex macromolecules, including proteins, in solution.
nmr_spectroscopy.history: The prerequisites emerged in the 1930s when I. Rabi developed the method of magnetic resonance in molecular beams (Nobel 1944). In 1946, F. Bloch (measured induced electromotive force) and E. Purcell (radiofrequency absorption) simultaneously discovered NMR in solids and liquids, for which they received the Nobel Prize in 1952. In 1966, R. Ernst proposed the pulsed Fourier transform method, revolutionizing sensitivity. Further development of multidimensional spectroscopy (recognized with the 1991 Nobel Prize to Ernst) and stabilization of superconducting magnets pushed resolution to the sub-millihertz level. Today NMR is a standard structural analysis method in chemistry, biology, and medicine (MRI).
nmr_spectroscopy.how_it_works: Key Larmor equation: ω = γB₀ (where ω is angular frequency, γ is the gyromagnetic ratio). In liquids, due to rapid molecular motion, interactions are averaged, and narrow lines are observed, with positions characterized by chemical shift: δ = (ν_sample − ν_ref)/ν_ref · 10⁶, measured in parts per million (ppm). Shielding is described by the magnetic shielding tensor, which depends on the local electronic environment. Spin-spin coupling (J-coupling) between nuclei, transmitted through chemical bonds, splits lines into multiplets. A spectrometer consists of a superconducting magnet, radiofrequency generator, signal reception unit, and a computer for accumulation and Fourier transformation of the signal. Pulse sequences (gradient and multiplexed) allow encoding frequencies in multiple dimensions, extracting information about spatial proximity of atoms (nuclear Overhauser effect) and connectivity of the spin system.
key_problems: Low natural sensitivity for some nuclei (e.g., carbon-13)
Reducing experiment time without loss of resolution
Automatic signal assignment in complex spectra (macromolecules, mixtures)
Miniaturization and cost reduction of superconducting magnets for mass applications
nmr_spectroscopy.fun_fact: The noise recorded by an NMR spectrometer is so low that at room temperature, voltage fluctuations in the coil correspond to the thermal jitter of electrons — and this is the main source of interference. To reduce it, coils are cooled with liquid helium.
