formulas.meaning: ω — angular precession frequency (rad/s), γ — gyromagnetic ratio of the nucleus (for proton γ ≈ 2.675×10⁸ rad·s⁻¹·T⁻¹), B₀ — external magnetic field induction (T)

formulas.description: Chemical shift in parts per million
formulas.meaning: δ — chemical shift (dimensionless, ppm), ν_sample — resonance frequency of the nucleus in the sample (Hz), ν_ref — resonance frequency of the nucleus in a reference compound (e.g., TMS for 1H and 13C)

dynamical_systems.name: Dynamical Systems
dynamical_systems.mini: A pendulum swings, clouds drift, the heart beats. These are dynamical systems—everything that changes over time according to certain rules.
dynamical_systems.practical_application: Tomorrow's weather forecast, an airplane autopilot, epidemic spread models, the rhythm of the heart muscle—dynamical systems are at work everywhere.
dynamical_systems.description_popular: Wind stirs a wheat field, creating running waves. Each stalk obeys a simple rule, but together they give rise to a complex pattern. A dynamical system is a mathematical model of the evolution of a point in phase space (the space of all possible states). For continuous time, the law is given by a differential equation ẋ = f(x); for discrete time, by an iteration x_{n+1} = F(x_n). Linear systems are well studied and predictable. Nonlinear ones can surprise: bifurcations suddenly change the character of motion, limit cycles generate undamped oscillations, and chaos creates 'strange attractors'—bizarre sets toward which the system infinitely approaches without ever repeating its trajectory. The most famous strange attractor—the Lorenz attractor—arises from three simple equations modeling convection. Today, dynamical systems permeate science: from astrophysics to neurobiology. A wave of the hand—and the field freezes. Order and chaos are two sides of the same coin.
dynamical_systems.fun_fact_popular: The equations of general atmospheric circulation solved by meteorologists are so sensitive that the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil could, a week later, cause a tornado in Texas—that's chaos in action.
dynamical_systems.description_simple: A drop of paint falls into a glass of water and swirls into spirals. The trajectory of each colored thread depends on the current, and the current depends on the initial push. A dynamical system is a set of rules describing how something changes over time. The position of a pendulum, air temperature, population size—all are points moving along their own paths in an imaginary state space. Systems can be stable—returning to rest after a push—or chaotic, where the slightest error at the start leads to a completely different outcome. That very drop will never repeat its pattern.
dynamical_systems.history_simple: The French mathematician Henri Poincaré was the first to deeply study such systems at the end of the 19th century. He tried to understand whether the Solar System is stable and discovered that even three bodies attracting each other gravitationally can move unpredictably—chaotically.
dynamical_systems.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a ball on a slope. If it lies in a hollow, give it a push—it will roll back. The system is stable. But place the ball on a hilltop—the slightest gust of wind will carry it off who knows where. In mathematics, dynamics are written as equations where the rate of change of a quantity depends on its current value. Solving them allows us to look into the future of the system. If the equation has a sensitive point, an error in the initial measurement of a thousandth of a degree will, a month later, yield a forecast of rain instead of sun. The famous butterfly effect comes from this. Thus, a simple ball on a hill explains why the world is so complex.
dynamical_systems.description: In the Pantheon, Foucault's pendulum swings rhythmically, staying true to its plane of oscillation. This is a stable dynamical system. Formally, a dynamical system is an action of a semigroup T on a phase space M. For continuous time, T = {φ_t}_{t∈R} is a flow generated by a vector field f: ẋ = f(x). For discrete time, a diffeomorphism F: x_{n+1} = F(x_n). Qualitative theory studies the topology of the phase portrait: equilibrium points, periodic orbits, invariant sets. A bifurcation occurs when a parameter changes and the portrait changes its topological type (fold, pitchfork, Hopf). Chaotic dynamics is characterized by positive Lyapunov exponents—a measure of the exponential divergence of trajectories. Strange attractors have fractal dimension. Ergodic theory connects time averages and space averages. But bring a magnet close, and the measured motion turns into chaotic somersaults. The very essence of nonlinear dynamics lies in this juxtaposition of order and unpredictability.
dynamical_systems.history: Henri Poincaré laid the foundations of the qualitative theory of dynamical systems in the 1880s while investigating the three-body problem. He introduced the concepts of phase space, singular points, limit cycles, and Poincaré sections. In the 1920s, mathematicians developed ergodic theory, and in the 1960s, with the advent of computers, meteorologist Edward Lorenz discovered deterministic chaos in a simple convection model. Bifurcation theory took on a coherent form in the latter half of the 20th century through the work of many scientists.
dynamical_systems.how_it_works: The model is defined by a vector field or a map. Analysis includes linearization around equilibrium points and study of eigenvalues. The Grobman–Hartman theorem guarantees that local behavior is determined by the linearization for hyperbolic points. For global analysis, a Lyapunov function is constructed to prove stability. Chaos is detected by computing Lyapunov exponents and the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy. Numerical simulation remains the primary tool for most nonlinear systems. The superposition principle does not apply in nonlinear systems, which fundamentally distinguishes them from linear ones.
key_problems: Proof of the Ruelle–Takens conjecture on the onset of turbulence via a strange attractor
Rigorous description of phase transitions in non-equilibrium systems
Inverse problem of recovering equations from observational data
Prediction of long-term behavior of chaotic systems with limited accuracy
dynamical_systems.fun_fact: The Lyapunov exponent measures the rate of divergence of nearby trajectories. For large-scale atmospheric motions, it is about 1 bit per hour—meaning the error doubles every hour.

formulas.description: The logistic map—a classic example of a chaotic system
formulas.meaning: x_n is the population fraction in the n-th period (0 ≤ x_n ≤ 1), r is the growth parameter (r > 0). For r > 3.57, it exhibits chaos

recurrent_neural_networks.name: Recurrent Neural Networks
recurrent_neural_networks.mini: A person reads a book and remembers the plot to avoid confusing the characters. A recurrent network works the same way: it takes each new word without forgetting what came before, and predicts what will follow.
recurrent_neural_networks.practical_application: Text autocomplete on a phone, machine translation, smart speaker processing of long phrases.
recurrent_neural_networks.description_popular: The conductor's baton hangs in the air—the musician waits, remembering the previous motif. A recurrent network iterates over sequence tokens (characters or words) and after each updates the hidden state (a vector of numbers). This state is a compressed description of everything seen so far. Thanks to the feedback loop, the network can capture dependencies between distant elements: for example, case agreement in a long German sentence.
recurrent_neural_networks.fun_fact_popular: LSTM networks, created in 1997, remained the primary tool for machine translation for almost 20 years, until transformers supplanted them—yet they are still used in millions of smartphones for text autocomplete.
recurrent_neural_networks.description_simple: An old conductor remembers every note played, even when the orchestra is already playing a new bar. A recurrent neural network (a program that works with sequences) is like that conductor. It reads data step by step (letter by letter or word by word) while keeping a 'brief summary' of everything read in memory. This allows it to finish a phrase or translate a sentence.
recurrent_neural_networks.history_simple: The first recurrent networks were proposed in the 1980s, but those architectures quickly 'forgot' what had happened long before. In 1997, scientists invented LSTM—a special cell that learned to retain important information for a long time; this was a breakthrough for tasks like speech recognition.
recurrent_neural_networks.how_it_works_simple: At each step, the network receives a new input and its short-term memory (a vector of numbers describing what the network has remembered). It updates this memory by mixing new information with what it already knew and produces an output. For example, reading 'I love cats,' by the word 'cats' it already remembers that it's about me, not someone else.
recurrent_neural_networks.description: The conductor raises the baton. Each note builds on the previous one, holding the melody in memory. A recurrent neural network (RNN) is a class of architectures for processing sequential data where connections between elements can form directed cycles. Unlike feedforward networks, RNNs maintain a hidden state that is updated at each time step (h_t = f(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b)). This enables modeling dynamic processes and variable-length sequences. Modifications such as LSTM and GRU address the vanishing gradient problem. The conductor lowers the baton: the symphony is over. The recurrent network, remembering the entire context, writes the final word and falls silent.
recurrent_neural_networks.history: The foundations trace back to the work of John Hopfield (1982) and networks with feedback. In 1986, David Rumelhart et al. applied backpropagation to RNNs. Practical application was limited by the vanishing/exploding gradient problem. In 1997, Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber proposed LSTM (long short-term memory) with gated units—valves—solving long-term dependency issues. In 2014, Kyunghyun Cho et al. introduced GRU. Since the mid-2010s, RNNs have been gradually replaced by transformers but remain important in streaming tasks.
recurrent_neural_networks.how_it_works: At step t, the RNN receives the input vector x_t and the previous hidden state h_{t-1}, computes the new state: h_t = \tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t-1} + b). The vector h_t is fed to the output layer to predict y_t and passed to the next step. The parameters W_x, W_h, b are shared across all steps, enabling generalization to sequences of different lengths. Training is done by unfolding the network in time (backpropagation through time). LSTM adds a memory cell c_t and three gates: forget, input, and output, which regulate the flow of information.
key_problems: Vanishing/exploding gradient problem
Difficulty capturing long-term dependencies (partially solved by LSTM)
Sequential processing hindering parallelization
Difficulty training for very long sequences
Sensitivity to rare words in text processing
recurrent_neural_networks.fun_fact: In 2016, an LSTM-based RNN learned to generate text passages so similar to Tolstoy's style that literary scholars could not distinguish them from the original in 40% of cases.

formulas.description: Hidden state update in a recurrent network
formulas.meaning: h_t — hidden state at step t; x_t — input vector; W_{xh} — input weight matrix; W_{hh} — recurrent weight matrix; h_{t-1} — previous state; b_h — bias; tanh — hyperbolic tangent

optimization.name: optimization
optimization.mini: A delivery driver chooses the shortest route among dozens of streets. Optimization is the art of finding the best possible option, be it a route, a schedule, or the shape of a part.
optimization.practical_application: GPS navigators plot routes, airlines schedule flights, and engineers calculate streamlined shapes — all this is the work of optimization algorithms.
optimization.description_popular: An alpinist sees three ridges ahead, but he needs not the highest, but the lowest pass. Optimization mathematically seeks the minimum (or maximum) of an objective function — a numerical measure of solution quality. Constraints define the feasible region: you can't walk on air or steeper than 45 degrees. Linear programming deals with straight slopes, where the answer lies at a vertex. For smooth hills, gradient descent is used. If the terrain is cut by ravines and cliffs, evolutionary algorithms come into play — they launch a whole crowd of virtual alpinists, and the most successful routes are crossed and mutated. Thus, a path is found in multidimensional spaces where no map can be drawn. When the step becomes smaller than a millimeter, the search stops — the pass is conquered.
optimization.fun_fact_popular: The traveling salesman problem — visiting 100 cities by the shortest route — has more possible routes than there are atoms in the universe. Yet smart optimizers find a solution in seconds.
optimization.description_simple: You are baking cookies and want to get the maximum number of pieces from a given piece of dough. You can cut it in different ways: squares leave trimmings, hexagons leave almost no waste. Optimization is the search for a cutting method that squeezes every last crumb out of the dough, provided the cookies must be whole. The mathematical method simulates a clever pastry chef: it tries different layouts and picks the one with the least trimmings. A hundred options — and the shape is found. Cookies in neat rows fill the baking sheet with no gaps — problem solved.
optimization.history_simple: The first systematic techniques emerged in the 18th century during shipbuilding — how to choose hull lines so that a vessel sails faster under the same wind. Mass application began in the mid-20th century with the rise of computers, when manually sifting through thousands of combinations became impractical.
optimization.how_it_works_simple: A mountain range in the fog. The goal is to find the deepest depression. Standing at one point, you feel the slope and take a step downhill. This is gradient descent — step-by-step movement to where the function value (height) decreases. If a local dip is encountered on the way, the algorithm may get stuck there, never reaching the main valley. For complex landscapes, a 'shake' is added — occasionally jumping up to check if there is a deeper spot nearby. This is how modern global optimization methods work. The fog clears, and the bottom of the main basin is found.
optimization.description: A hanging chain naturally takes the shape that minimizes its potential energy. Similarly, optimization is the search for the state with the smallest value of a given function. Mathematically, it is formulated as a minimization problem of f: Rⁿ → R subject to constraints g_i(x)=0, h_j(x)≤0. Gradient methods use a linear approximation: x_{k+1} = x_k - α_k ∇f(x_k), where α_k is the step size. Convex problems guarantee global convergence. For non-convex problems, stochastic algorithms (simulated annealing, particle swarm) and metaheuristics are used. In unconstrained optimization, quasi-Newton methods (BFGS) approximating the Hessian are popular. Constrained optimization relies on Lagrange multipliers and the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions. In machine learning, stochastic gradient descent with momentum and adaptive step size (Adam) reigns. The chain freezes at the lowest point — the problem is solved.
optimization.history: Roots go back to the calculus of variations of the 17th–18th centuries, but the modern era began in the 1940s with the development of linear programming and the simplex method. The advancement of nonlinear optimization in the 1960s brought penalty methods and conjugate gradients. In the 1980s, interior-point algorithms emerged, revolutionizing the solution of large-scale problems. Today, optimization is the foundation of all machine learning technologies.
optimization.how_it_works: Most algorithms construct a sequence of points converging to the minimum. Gradient descent moves against the gradient. In machine learning, the gradient of the loss function is computed on a random subset of data (batch), enabling optimization of billions of parameters. Regularization adds penalties for complexity to avoid overfitting. For constrained problems, methods like the reduced gradient method or sequential quadratic programming are used. Global optimization employs Bayesian methods and search with decision trees.
key_problems: Overcoming local minima in non-convex problems
Computational complexity at large dimensionality (curse of dimensionality)
Guaranteed finding of the global optimum within acceptable time
Optimization under uncertainty and noise
optimization.fun_fact: Gradient descent with momentum is physically analogous to a ball rolling over a surface with inertia: it doesn't get stuck in shallow dips, passing over them due to speed.

formulas.description: Gradient descent step
formulas.meaning: x_t — current point, η — learning rate (step), ∇f(x_t) — gradient of f at x_t (vector of partial derivatives)

spectral_analysis.name: Spectral Analysis
spectral_analysis.mini: White light passing through a prism turns into a rainbow. Spectral analysis breaks down any signal—sound, radio waves, light from distant stars—into similar colored bands, telling us what it is made of.
spectral_analysis.practical_application: Astronomers use a star’s spectrum to learn what elements it is composed of. In medicine, tissue spectra help distinguish healthy cells from cancerous ones.
spectral_analysis.description_popular: Spectral analysis is a universal key. It doesn’t require touching the object; it’s enough to capture its emission. For example, light from a distant galaxy passing through a gas cloud loses very specific colors—they are absorbed by atoms. Such an absorption spectrum resembles a barcode: each dark line corresponds to a particular element. From the shift of these lines, one can even measure how fast the object is moving toward or away from us (the Doppler effect, a change in frequency due to motion). And in the radio range, spectral analysis ‘listens’ to molecular clouds, finding complex organic molecules.
spectral_analysis.fun_fact_popular: The spectrum is the only way to know the chemistry of distant objects: no space probe has ever visited the Sun, but we know for certain that it consists mainly of hydrogen and helium, thanks to spectral lines.
spectral_analysis.description_simple: A spectrum is like a musical chord: it is made up of many pure tones (simple vibrations). Spectral analysis is like being able to hear each individual note in the chord. Only instead of sound, we analyze light, radio signals, or even the pulsations of a distant star. The output is a graph showing how much energy is at each ‘note’ (frequency). Sharp peaks (‘notes’) reveal the presence of specific substances—like fingerprints.
spectral_analysis.history_simple: In 1814, German optician Joseph von Fraunhofer was the first to systematically describe the dark lines in the Sun’s spectrum. Later, scientists understood that each chemical element leaves its unique mark in the spectrum.
spectral_analysis.how_it_works_simple: A gas or heated body does not emit light of all colors, but only specific ones—those that resonate with its atoms. Passing this light through a prism or a diffraction grating (a plate with fine lines), we see individual bright lines against a dark background. Just as a guitar string sounds at its note, each atom glows at its own frequencies. By analyzing the positions of the lines, we learn what element we are looking at.
spectral_analysis.description: Spectral analysis is a set of methods for determining the composition and physical parameters of a substance from its spectrum. The spectrum is obtained by spatially separating the radiation by wavelength using dispersive elements (e.g., a diffraction grating). Depending on the nature of the light–matter interaction, emission (radiation), absorption, and Raman (scattering) spectra are distinguished. Each chemical element has a unique set of spectral lines corresponding to quantum transitions of its electrons. The width, intensity, and shape of the lines carry information about the temperature, pressure, velocity, and magnetic fields of the source. The method is fundamental to astrophysics, plasma physics, analytical chemistry, and medical diagnostics.
spectral_analysis.history: The origins of spectral analysis lie in 17th-century optics (Newton decomposed light with a prism). In 1802, Wollaston noticed dark lines in the solar spectrum. From 1814 to 1823, Joseph von Fraunhofer catalogued them, not knowing the cause. The decisive step was taken by Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen in 1859, who proved that each line is produced by a specific chemical element. Thus, the chemical analysis of radiation was born. Later, Johannes Rydberg (1890) derived a formula for hydrogen lines, and quantum mechanics explained spectra based on electron transitions.
spectral_analysis.how_it_works: Atoms absorb or emit photons of precisely defined energies equal to the difference between the energy levels of electrons. A transition from one level to another corresponds to a spectral line at frequency ν = ΔE/h. Spectra are classified into line spectra of atoms, band spectra of molecules (rotational and vibrational transitions), and continuous spectra of hot dense bodies (thermal radiation). For analysis, dispersive instruments (prism, diffraction grating), interferometers (high resolution), and photodetectors are used. Key characteristics: line position (wavelength), intensity, width, and line shape (Doppler and Lorentz broadening). The methods are applied across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to gamma rays.
key_problems: Increasing sensitivity for analyzing spectra of distant galaxies
Separation of overlapping lines in complex molecular mixtures
Detection of spectral signatures of dark matter
Real-time spectral analysis of fast processes
spectral_analysis.fun_fact: Using spectral analysis, astronomers discovered helium on the Sun (1868) before it was found on Earth. The element’s name comes from the Greek ‘helios’ (sun).

formulas.description: Planck–Einstein equation for photon energy
formulas.meaning: E — photon energy, h — Planck constant (h ≈ 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s), ν — radiation frequency

formulas.description: Rydberg formula for hydrogen-like atoms
formulas.meaning: λ — wavelength of the spectral line, R∞ — Rydberg constant (R∞ ≈ 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹), n₁ and n₂ — principal quantum numbers (n₂ > n₁)

reinforcement_learning.name: Reinforcement Learning
reinforcement_learning.mini: A dog gets a treat when it brings back a ball and remembers: doing so is beneficial. Reinforcement learning trains a program exactly the same way — through rewards and misses.
reinforcement_learning.practical_application: Game bots (chess, StarCraft), autonomous driving, optimization of factory processes, recommendation systems.
reinforcement_learning.description_popular: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a branch of machine learning where an agent independently learns optimal behavior through trial and error, interacting with an environment. Unlike supervised learning, there are no ready-made correct answers — only a reward signal, which can be rare and noisy. The agent has to balance between exploring new strategies (maybe they are better?) and exploiting known ones. This exploration–exploitation dilemma is the heart of RL. Modern algorithms, such as Deep Q-Networks and Proximal Policy Optimization, use deep neural networks to process complex visual input and control dozens of actions in parallel.
reinforcement_learning.fun_fact_popular: During training, AlphaGo Zero beat the version that defeated champion Lee Sedol 100:0 in three days, learning only through self-play, without access to human games.
reinforcement_learning.description_simple: In reinforcement learning, an agent program lives in its own world (for example, in a crossroads simulator). It sees the surrounding environment — the speed of cars, the traffic light. Its task is to take actions (turn the steering wheel, accelerate) to score as many points as possible. Points are awarded for success — reached the destination; penalties for accidents. The agent tries different moves, like a child learning to walk: fell — it hurts, got up and went on. After thousands of attempts, the strategy becomes ingrained.
reinforcement_learning.history_simple: The idea dates back to the mid-20th century when psychologists explained how animals learn through rewards. In the 1980s, algorithms emerged that could play backgammon at a human level, and in the 2010s, programs from Google DeepMind mastered Atari games and beat a Go champion.
reinforcement_learning.how_it_works_simple: The core scheme: the agent looks at the state, chooses an action, receives a reward. Gradually it builds a table or uses a neural network to remember which moves are more profitable in each situation. For example, in the game 'Snake', turning towards an apple gives points, while colliding with the tail is a penalty. Over time, the snake moves towards the goal almost flawlessly.
reinforcement_learning.description: Reinforcement learning is formalized as a Markov decision process (MDP), defined by the tuple (S, A, P, R, γ), where S is the state space, A is the action space, P(s'|s, a) is the transition dynamics, R(s, a) is the reward function, and γ ∈ [0,1] is the discount factor for future rewards. The goal is to find a policy π(a|s) that maximizes the expected discounted sum of rewards: J = E[Σ γ^t R_t]. Key concepts: the state value function V(s) = E[Σ γ^t R_t | s0 = s] and the action-value function Q(s, a). Algorithms are divided into value-based (Q-learning, DQN), policy-based (Policy Gradient, REINFORCE), and actor-critic (A2C, PPO) methods that combine both approaches. Deep RL uses neural networks to parameterize V, Q, or π, trained using variations of gradient descent and replay buffers to stabilize learning.
reinforcement_learning.history: The foundations of RL lie in psychological concepts of operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner). In AI, the first significant contribution was Minsky's dissertation on neural networks and reinforcement (1954). In the 1980s, Sutton and Barto laid the theoretical groundwork. The public breakthrough came in 2015, when DeepMind demonstrated a system playing 49 Atari games at human level. This was followed by AlphaGo (2016), AlphaZero (2017), and OpenAI Five (2019), proving viability in complex multi-agent environments.
reinforcement_learning.how_it_works: It is based on Bellman equations. For Q-learning: Q*(s, a) = E[R(s,a) + γ max_a' Q*(s', a')]. The algorithm updates the estimate: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max_a' Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]. In deep Q-learning, the Q-network minimizes the prediction error: L = E[(r + γ max_a' Q(s', a'; θ^-) - Q(s, a; θ))^2] using gradient descent methods, where θ^- are the parameters of a frozen target network. Policy gradient methods directly optimize J(θ) via the gradient: ∇θ J ≈ E[Σ_t ∇θ log π(a_t|s_t) · G_t], where G_t is the total reward. Modern actor-critic PPO limits policy change with a proximal penalty, ensuring stable updates.
key_problems: The exploration–exploitation dilemma without guarantees of optimal exploration
The problem of generalization to new, unseen states
Efficient learning in environments with very sparse rewards
Safety and predictability when deployed in the real world
reinforcement_learning.fun_fact: In a famous experiment teaching a robot to flip pancakes on a frying pan, an RL agent, unhappy with slow learning through real attempts, 'discovered' a way to rotate the pan at 50 Hz — which caused equipment wear but formally accomplished the task.

formulas.description: Bellman optimality equation for the Q-function
formulas.latex: Q^*(s, a) = \mathbb{E}\left[ R(s, a) + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^*(s', a') \right]
formulas.meaning: Q* is the optimal action-value function, s is the state, a is the action, R is the reward, γ is the discount factor (0 ≤ γ ≤ 1)

signal_processing.name: signal processing
signal_processing.mini: A guitar string vibrates 440 times per second. The ear hears the note A. Signal processing turns this vibration into numbers and breaks it down into pure tones, just as a prism decomposes light. Without it, a noisy ringtone would not become music in headphones.
signal_processing.practical_application: Noise cancellation in phones, music compression into MP3, medical tomographs, radars, data transmission over Wi-Fi — all of this works thanks to signal processing algorithms.
signal_processing.description_popular: Signal processing is a mathematical tool for working with information encoded in changes of a physical quantity (sound pressure, voltage, brightness). An analog signal is digitized: instantaneous values are measured at a given frequency, yielding a stream of samples. Then algorithms are applied for filtering (removing interference), compression (MP3 uses psychoacoustics to discard inaudible frequencies), and restoration (removing blur in photos). The central idea is the Fourier transform, which moves a signal from the time domain to the frequency domain: a graph of oscillations becomes a spectrum where the amplitude of each frequency component is visible. The entire telecommunications, audio recording, and medical imaging industries are built on this.
signal_processing.fun_fact_popular: The MP3 format discards about 90% of the data, yet to our ear the difference is almost imperceptible — the algorithm relies on how the brain masks weak sounds with loud ones at nearby frequencies.
signal_processing.description_simple: Signal processing is a way to extract useful information from a tangle of electrical, sound, or light vibrations. Take a noisy image: a face is visible but stripes interfere. The program decomposes the picture into waves of different frequencies and removes those resembling stripes. A clean portrait remains. Similarly, we clean up sound, align a radio signal, and predict earthquakes from seismic vibrations.
signal_processing.history_simple: It all began with sound analysis in the 19th century. Jean Fourier devised a way to break any wave into a sum of simple sinusoids. In the 20th century, with the development of radio and telephones, methods grew more complex, and with the advent of computers, processing became digital — signals turned into chains of ones and zeros.
signal_processing.how_it_works_simple: A signal, such as a voice recording, is measured thousands of times per second — a sequence of numbers is obtained. Then this digital footprint is decomposed by frequencies: we determine how much low sound (bass) and how much high sound (whistling) it contains. It's like a soup recipe: a cook tastes and says how much salt, pepper, vegetables there are. Knowing the recipe, you can remove the excess (noise) or compress the file, leaving only what the ear hears.
signal_processing.description: Signal processing is a broad engineering discipline that studies methods for analysis, modification, and synthesis of signals — time series, spatial distributions, or more general fields. Key operations: sampling (the Kotelnikov–Shannon theorem establishes the minimum sampling rate), quantization, filtering (linear and nonlinear), spectral analysis, statistical processing. It is applied in telecommunications (modulation, coding, compression), sonar and radar, seismology, audio and video processing, biomedical engineering (ECG, MRI). With the rise of neural networks, the field of deep learning on signals has emerged, where convolutional networks replace classical filters.
signal_processing.history: Its roots go back to the harmonic analysis of Jean Fourier (1822), though decomposition into trigonometric series appeared even earlier. In the 20th century, the works of Nyquist and Shannon on sampling gave an impetus, and then the digital revolution of the 1960s-1970s produced the Fast Fourier Transform algorithms (Cooley and Tukey, 1965), making spectral analysis fast. The development of integrated circuits allowed real-time processing — from CD players to cellular communications. In the 21st century, compression methods (JPEG, MPEG), wavelet transforms, and neural network approaches have expanded the capabilities of signal processing beyond recognition.
signal_processing.how_it_works: The basic cycle: an ADC converts the signal into a sequence of samples x[n]. Then a digital filter described by a difference equation is applied, e.g., y[n] = Σ b_k x[n-k] – Σ a_k y[n-k] (recursive filter). To analyze the frequency composition, the Discrete Fourier Transform is computed: X[k] = Σ x[n] e^{-j2πkn/N}. In practice, the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is used, reducing the complexity from O(N²) to O(N log N). For non-stationary signals (where frequencies change over time), the Short-Time Fourier Transform or wavelets, localized in both time and frequency, are used. Modern communication systems are built on Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM), which divides the channel into thousands of subcarriers to combat multipath fading.
key_problems: Blind signal processing: recovering the original signal without exact knowledge of channel characteristics
Processing of ultra-wideband signals at high frequencies (terahertz signals)
Robustness to interference at low signal-to-noise ratio
Energy-efficient algorithms for IoT devices
Extracting a signal from a mixture with unknown structure (cocktail party problem)
signal_processing.fun_fact: The Kotelnikov–Shannon theorem states: if the sampling frequency is twice the maximum signal frequency, the analog signal can be perfectly reconstructed. That is why the CD sampling rate — 44.1 kHz — covers the entire audible range up to 20 kHz.

formulas.description: Direct Fourier transform, moving the signal from the time domain to the frequency domain
formulas.latex: X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) e^{-j 2 \pi f t} dt
formulas.meaning: x(t) — original signal, X(f) — frequency spectrum, f — frequency

formulas.description: Discrete Fourier Transform for digital signals
formulas.latex: X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j 2 \pi k n / N}
formulas.meaning: x[n] — signal samples (n = 0...N-1), X[k] — spectrum coefficients at frequency k/N * sampling_rate

game_theory.name: game theory
game_theory.mini: Two street vendors stand across the road, setting prices for the same product. Each understands that their revenue depends on the other's decision.
game_theory.practical_application: Price formation in auctions, radio frequency allocation by operators, negotiation strategies, evolutionary models of animal behavior — all this is the arena of game theory.
game_theory.description_popular: In the auction room at Sotheby's, silence. Two bidders vie for a painting, each understanding that their bid depends on the opponent's behavior. Game theory models the interaction of rational agents striving to maximize their payoff function. Games are classified by the number of players, the possibility of agreements (cooperative or non-cooperative), and the sum of payoffs (zero-sum or non-zero-sum). The central concept is the Nash equilibrium: no player can increase their payoff by unilaterally changing their strategy. In dynamic games, the sequence of moves matters: the threat of punishment can deter defection in repeated interactions — this is how cartels and peace treaties work. Experiments show that real people do not always act as perfect egoists, hence the development of behavioral game theory and evolutionary models where strategies are selected according to Darwinian principles. Today, it is a tool in economics, political science, biology, cybersecurity, and the development of artificial intelligence for auctions and negotiations. When the gavel struck, both realized that equilibrium worked in the seller's favor.
game_theory.fun_fact_popular: The famous 'prisoner's dilemma' shows why two rational egoists can make a decision that worsens both their outcomes — exactly how companies often behave in price wars.
game_theory.description_simple: Saturday evening. You and a friend decide where to go: to the cinema or to a football match. Each writes their choice on a slip of paper without showing the other. If both choose the same, you go together and have a great time. If different, you stay home. Game theory studies precisely these situations: the outcome depends on the decisions of several people. Players can compete or cooperate. Mathematics seeks an equilibrium — a combination of moves where no one benefits from changing their choice alone. A payoff table will suggest the optimal strategy. That's exactly what you chose, writing 'cinema'.
game_theory.history_simple: In the mid‑20th century, mathematicians created an apparatus for analyzing conflict and cooperative situations. Key ideas took shape in works published in 1944 and quickly found application in economics.
game_theory.how_it_works_simple: Each player evaluates their payoffs under different combinations of moves. Take the 'prisoner's dilemma': two suspects are interrogated separately. If both remain silent — they each get one year in prison; both confess — three years each; one stays silent, the other betrays — the silent one gets ten years, the betrayer goes free. After calculating the options, each sees: betraying is more advantageous, no matter what the other does. In the end, both betray and get three years, even though they could have gotten away with just one. This is a conflict between personal gain and the common good. Mathematics unpacks such paradoxes for any game rules — from auctions to nuclear deterrence.
game_theory.description: A tennis match at Wimbledon — two players, each choosing the direction of their shot. Formally, a game is defined by a set of players N, for each i ∈ N a strategy set S_i, and a utility function u_i: S → R, where S = Π S_i is the strategy profile. A Nash equilibrium (in pure strategies) is a profile s* such that for all i: u_i(s*_i, s*_{-i}) ≥ u_i(s_i, s*_{-i}) ∀ s_i ∈ S_i. In games with incomplete information, player types and Bayesian equilibrium are introduced. Repeated games allow equilibria that support cooperation through trigger strategies. Nash's theorem guarantees the existence of a mixed equilibrium for finite games. Evolutionary game theory operates with replicator dynamics and evolutionarily stable strategies. Cooperative game theory analyzes payoffs using the core and Shapley values. The ball is out — the chosen strategy cost a point.
game_theory.history: Modern game theory emerged in the mid‑20th century. The first mathematical theorem was proved in 1928 for antagonistic games. In 1944, a seminal work systematized methods for analyzing strategic interactions and introduced the concept of expected utility. Later, the equilibrium concept was generalized to non‑cooperative games. Evolutionary game theory arose in the 1970s to explain behavior without assuming rationality. Today, this apparatus is one of the cornerstones of microeconomics and behavioral sciences.
game_theory.how_it_works: Analysis begins with constructing a payoff matrix or game tree. The solution is sought by eliminating dominated strategies, computing Nash equilibria, and in dynamic games, through backward induction for finite games with perfect information. Mixed equilibria are found by solving a system of nonlinear equations. For repeated games, the discount factor and observability of actions play a key role. Mechanism design (reverse game theory) constructs rules so that self‑interested agents arrive at the desired outcome.
key_problems: Accounting for irrational behavior and bounded rationality in complex environments
Development of efficient mechanisms for multi‑agent systems with incomplete information
Scaling methods to interactions of large populations (mean‑field games)
Empirical verification of theoretical models in real economic and social systems
game_theory.fun_fact: Braess's paradox: adding a new road to a transportation network can slow down overall traffic because each driver selfishly chooses the short route — a pure game situation where the equilibrium is worse than the optimal.

antennas.name: antennas
antennas.mini: The gramophone horn collected the faint sounds of the needle and directed them into the room. An antenna similarly captures radio waves and focuses them into an electric current.
antennas.practical_application: The antenna in your phone maintains a connection with the tower, the GPS receiver picks up satellite signals from 20,000 kilometers away, and the satellite TV dish receives broadcasts from space.
antennas.description_popular: An antenna is a transducer between electromagnetic waves and currents in the transmission line. The key characteristic is the radiation pattern: the directions in which the antenna radiates (or receives) most strongly. A simple dipole (two straight conductors each a quarter-wavelength long) radiates uniformly in the plane perpendicular to itself, but not along its axis. Parabolic reflector antennas (satellite dishes) concentrate energy into a narrow beam, like a searchlight. The size of any antenna is dictated by the wavelength: for transoceanic flights, vast fields of masts are built, while for cellular communication, antennas fit in the palm of your hand.
antennas.fun_fact_popular: Your credit card can be paid contactlessly thanks to a tiny antenna hidden inside the plastic—a loop of conductor that powers the chip with radio wave energy over a distance of a few centimeters.
antennas.description_simple: An antenna is a device that transmits or receives radio waves. In a transmitter, it works like a loudspeaker, converting an electric signal into waves, and in a receiver, like a microphone, catching waves and turning them back into current. The simplest antenna is a piece of wire cut in the middle: a generator or receiver is connected to the ends. The wire length must match the wavelength so that oscillations enter resonance.
antennas.history_simple: The first antennas were built by Heinrich Hertz in 1888 for his experiments with electric sparks. In 1895, Alexander Popov used a raised wire to detect lightning discharges, and later Guglielmo Marconi transmitted a signal across the Atlantic using an antenna.
antennas.how_it_works_simple: Electricity runs back and forth in the antenna, producing an alternating current. Around such a current, according to the laws of physics, oscillating electric and magnetic fields are born, which escape into space at the speed of light. During reception, it's the reverse: the incoming wave agitates electrons in the antenna, creating a weak current that the receiver amplifies.
antennas.description: An antenna is a device that provides radiation and reception of electromagnetic waves, matching the wave impedance of free space (377 Ω) to the impedance of the feeder line. Fundamental parameters: input impedance, bandwidth, directivity, gain (including losses), polarization. Types of antennas: wire (dipoles, monopoles, loops), aperture (horn, reflector), microstrip, phased array antennas. In transmit mode, the high-frequency current creates an alternating electromagnetic field, which in the far field (R > 2D²/λ) takes the form of a spherical wave; fields decay as 1/R, power decay rate is 1/R². In receive mode, the incident wave induces an EMF in the conductors.
antennas.history: The theoretical foundation was laid by James Clerk Maxwell in 1864, predicting electromagnetic waves. Experimental confirmation and the first dipole antennas—Heinrich Hertz, 1887–1888. In the 1890s, Oliver Lodge invented a tuned antenna with an inductive coil. Practical radio communication was established by Popov and Marconi using vertical wires. Sergei Nadenenko derived the formula for the radiation field in 1914. In 1926, Hidetsugu Yagi and Shintaro Uda created a multi-element directive antenna (now known as a Yagi–Uda antenna). The development of microwave technology in the 1940s led to the creation of waveguides and horns. The end of the 20th century was marked by the emergence of microstrip antennas and adaptive arrays with digital beamforming.
antennas.how_it_works: Antenna radiation is described by Maxwell's equations. The accelerated motion of charges in a conductor creates an alternating electromagnetic field that propagates as a wave. In the far field, the electric and magnetic fields are transverse to the direction of propagation and are related as E/H = Z₀ ≈ 377 Ω. For quantitative calculation, the vector potential is used: A(r) = (μ₀/4π) ∫ J(r') e^{-j k |r-r'|} / |r-r'| dV'. From A, the fields are found. In a receiving antenna, the wave induces a current distribution, which through the reciprocity theorem is related to the antenna's characteristics in transmit mode. Phased arrays sum signals from many elements with controlled phase, enabling beamforming and steering, as well as adaptive interference suppression (spatial filtering). Impedance matching is critical: mismatch leads to reflections and a drop in efficiency.
key_problems: Miniaturization of antennas while maintaining efficiency and bandwidth (Chu–Harrington limit)
Increasing capacity of MIMO systems: dozens of antennas in a limited volume with low mutual coupling
Terahertz antennas for future communication standards (6G)
Integration of antennas into flexible electronics and clothing
antennas.fun_fact: The record parabolic antenna in Goldstone (California) has a diameter of 70 meters and can communicate with Voyager 1 at a distance of 24 billion kilometers—the signal power from its 20 W transmitter reaches Earth at the level of 10^{-18} watts.

formulas.description: Far-field condition (Fraunhofer boundary)
formulas.meaning: R is the distance to the antenna, D is the maximum aperture dimension of the antenna, λ is the wavelength.

formulas.description: Power at the output of a receiving antenna (Friis transmission formula)
formulas.meaning: P_r is the received power, P_t is the transmitter power, G_t, G_r are the gains of the transmitting and receiving antennas, λ is the wavelength, R is the distance, 4π arises from spherical spreading.

information_theory.name: information theory
information_theory.mini: Each letter in this text is an act of choosing from 33 options. Information theory does not ask what the message is about; it counts how many surprises it contains: the more options there could have been, the more bits in each symbol.
information_theory.practical_application: Thanks to it, the internet, JPEG photo compression, and the recovery of scratched music on CDs work. Even DNA sequencing uses an information measure to assemble the genome.
information_theory.description_popular: The central concept is Shannon's information entropy: H = −∑ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ. It measures the average number of bits needed to encode one source symbol. If all symbols are equally likely, H is maximized. The redundancy of language allows lossless data compression (Shannon proved the compression limit in the source coding theorem). Another cornerstone is channel capacity: C = B log₂(1+S/N). If you encode a message at a rate lower than C, you can transmit it practically without errors, despite noise. These ideas work in all communication systems: from satellites to USB flash drives.
information_theory.fun_fact_popular: The phrase 'Hello, World!' in random English text would contain about 80 bits, but due to language redundancy it can be compressed to 40-50 bits. Shannon calculated that English text carries on average only 1.3 bits per letter.
information_theory.description_simple: Information theory is a mathematical accounting of uncertainty. Imagine a hat with notes. Pulling out a note, you get more information the less likely it was to draw it. The unit of information is the bit. One bit is a choice between two equally likely outcomes. All digital communication from the telegraph to Wi-Fi is built on this calculation: a message is more valuable the more uncertainty it removes.
information_theory.history_simple: Claude Shannon laid the foundations in 1948 while working at Bell Labs. He was looking for a way to transmit messages over a noisy telephone cable without interference. Shannon introduced the concept of information entropy—a measure of how unpredictable the message source is. His paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' paved the way for the digital age.
information_theory.how_it_works_simple: Each symbol in a message carries as much information as the uncertainty it removes. The Russian alphabet has 33 letters, so one letter gives almost 5 bits (since 2⁵=32). But letters occur with different frequencies: if the letter 'O' is ten times more frequent than 'Щ', its appearance is less surprising and carries fewer bits. A message can be compressed by assigning short codes to frequent letters — that's how Morse code and ZIP archives work.
information_theory.description: Information theory is a branch of applied mathematics, radio engineering, and computer science studying the quantitative laws of generation, transmission, storage, and processing of information. The foundational work is 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' by C. Shannon (1948). Basic concepts: 1) Information measure: the information of an event with probability p is I = −log₂ p bits. 2) Entropy of a discrete source: H(X) = −∑ p(x) log₂ p(x) — average uncertainty. 3) Mutual information: I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) — the amount of information Y contains about X. 4) Channel capacity: the maximum mutual information between input and output of the channel when optimizing the input distribution. Key theorems: source coding theorem (compression limit), noisy-channel coding theorem (achievable transmission rate). Development led to the creation of error-correcting codes (Hamming, Reed-Solomon, turbo codes, LDPC), compression algorithms (Huffman, arithmetic coding, LZW), and cryptography.
information_theory.history: Claude Shannon (1916–2001) formulated the mathematical theory in his secret wartime reports of the early 1940s and summarized it in the famous 1948 paper in the Bell System Technical Journal. He introduced the term 'bit' (suggested by J. Tukey) and linked information entropy with Boltzmann's physical entropy. Predecessors included H. Nyquist (studied telegraph transmission speed, 1924) and R. Hartley (proposed a logarithmic measure, 1928). Later, A.N. Kolmogorov developed an algorithmic approach to information (Kolmogorov complexity). In quantum information theory, von Neumann entropy generalizes Shannon entropy for mixed quantum states.
information_theory.how_it_works: Information is measured in bits as the logarithm of the number of possible states: I = log₂ N or −log₂ p. Entropy H = −∑ pᵢ log pᵢ reaches its maximum with a uniform distribution. When transmitted over a channel with capacity C (Shannon-Hartley formula: C = B log₂(1+S/N) for Gaussian noise), Shannon's theorem guarantees: if the coding rate R < C, then an arbitrarily low error probability can be achieved using sufficiently long block codes. In practice, the limit is approached using turbo and LDPC codes, which employ iterative decoding and prior probabilities. For lossless compression, the optimal code achieves an average length equal to entropy and is constructed using Huffman's algorithm or arithmetic coding. Information theory is also applied in machine learning (minimum description length principle, Bayesian methods) and bioinformatics.
key_problems: Computability of Kolmogorov complexity (non-computability in the general case)
Integration of semantics: how to measure the meaningfulness of information, not just its volume
Quantum information theory: overcoming classical channel capacity limitations through entanglement
Efficient coding methods for short packets in ultra-reliable systems (5G/6G)
information_theory.fun_fact: Claude Shannon built a mechanical mouse named Theseus, which explored a maze and remembered the path using relay logic. The mouse is considered one of the precursors of artificial intelligence. Shannon was also known for juggling on a unicycle and a device for playing roulette.

formulas.meaning: H — entropy (bit/symbol), p_i — probability of the i-th outcome, Σ — sum over all possible outcomes

formulas.description: Channel capacity with additive white Gaussian noise (Shannon-Hartley theorem)
formulas.meaning: C — capacity (bit/s), B — channel bandwidth (Hz), S/N — signal-to-noise power ratio (dimensionless)

photonic_crystals.name: photonic crystals
photonic_crystals.mini: Light darts among tiny towers, but the only way out is to reflect back. In a photonic crystal, rays enter a labyrinth of alternating layers, through which only waves of certain colors can squeeze through.
photonic_crystals.practical_application: Photonic crystals make LEDs brighter and lasers more efficient. They also hide in opals and butterfly wings, creating iridescent colors.
photonic_crystals.description_popular: A photonic crystal is a periodic structure with a contrast in refractive index (the ability to refract light). Alternating regions of high and low index create photonic band gaps — ranges of wavelengths that cannot propagate inside the crystal. An electronic analogy: just as band gaps in semiconductors block electrons, here they block photons. The typical lattice period is hundreds of nanometers, to match the wavelength of visible light.
photonic_crystals.fun_fact_popular: Natural photonic crystals are found in opals and butterfly wings. Their iridescent shimmering is not a pigment, but a play of light on periodic nanostructures.
photonic_crystals.description_simple: A photonic crystal is a tiny sponge for light. It consists of many identical cells, resembling a honeycomb. Each cell either transmits light or reflects it. Together they work like a sieve: one color slips through, another bounces back. The distance between cells (the lattice period) is chosen to control only the desired rays. The thickness of the layers is comparable to the wavelength of light — hundredths of the thickness of a hair.
photonic_crystals.history_simple: In 1987, Eli Yablonovitch and Sajeev John independently proposed creating materials that forbid light from moving in certain directions. Their idea grew out of work on Bragg gratings, where layers of different transparency reflect light selectively.
photonic_crystals.how_it_works_simple: Light is a wave. When a wave encounters an obstacle, it partially reflects. In a crystal, there are many such obstacles, and they are arranged strictly periodically. If the distance between them equals the wavelength, all the reflected waves add up in phase and amplify each other. As a result, light cannot pass — a spectral region (the band gap) appears, where the crystal acts as a mirror.
photonic_crystals.description: Photonic crystals are artificial or natural media in which the dielectric permittivity is periodically modulated in space with a period comparable to the wavelength of light. Such modulation leads to the appearance of photonic band gaps — spectral regions where the propagation of electromagnetic waves is suppressed. The phenomenon is based on Bragg diffraction: waves reflected from adjacent layers interfere constructively if the path difference is a multiple of the wavelength. In the band gap, the density of photonic states tends to zero, allowing control of spontaneous emission, light localization, and creation of waveguides with sharp bends. One-dimensional (Bragg mirrors), two-dimensional (hole lattices), and three-dimensional (structures like opals or “wells”) photonic crystals are distinguished. A complete three-dimensional band gap for visible light remains a technological challenge.
photonic_crystals.history: The concept of periodic structures for controlling waves dates back to Lord Rayleigh (1887), but the birth of photonic crystals is dated to 1987. That year, Eli Yablonovitch (USA) published a work on the suppression of spontaneous emission in three-dimensional dielectric lattices, and Sajeev John (Canada) on the localization of light in disordered media. Their ideas quickly grew into an active field: in 1991, the first three-dimensional photonic crystal for the optical range was demonstrated, and by the late 1990s, photonic crystal fibers appeared. Today, developments are applied in optoelectronics, quantum electrodynamics, and sensors.
photonic_crystals.how_it_works: Maxwell's equations for a periodic medium lead to an eigenvalue problem analogous to the Schrödinger equation for electrons in a crystal. The role of the potential is played by the periodic dielectric function. Solutions yield dispersion relations ω(k) — photonic bands. In certain directions and frequency ranges, solutions are absent: these are the band gaps. For a complete band gap, it must overlap for all directions and polarizations. The Bragg condition for a one-dimensional crystal: λ = 2d n_eff / m, where d is the period, n_eff is the effective refractive index, and m is an integer. In real structures, numerical methods (plane wave, FDTD) are used to calculate the band structure. The introduction of defects — i.e., breaking the strict periodicity — creates allowed levels within the band gap, enabling the localization of light in microcavities and the formation of waveguides.
key_problems: Creating three-dimensional photonic crystals with a complete band gap in the visible range
Integration of photonic crystals into silicon electronics
Control of spontaneous emission and creation of thresholdless lasers
Technological reproducibility of nanometer-scale periodic structures
photonic_crystals.fun_fact: The first three-dimensional photonic crystal for the optical range (wavelength ~1.5 µm) was fabricated in 1991 by Eli Yablonovitch and colleagues by drilling a system of holes in a silicon wafer at angles mimicking a face-centered cubic lattice.

formulas.description: Bragg reflection condition for a photonic crystal
formulas.meaning: λ — wavelength of light in vacuum, d — lattice period, n_eff — effective refractive index of the structure, m — integer diffraction order

graphs.name: Graphs
graphs.mini: Points connected by lines, like cities on a map with roads.
graphs.practical_application: Graphs help find the shortest path in a navigator and recommend new friends on social networks.
graphs.description_popular: A graph is a mathematical structure consisting of vertices and the edges connecting them. Unlike a geographical map, what matters here is not the shape of the lines but the presence of a connection and, possibly, its weight (for example, road length or travel time). This abstraction allows applying the same search algorithms to social networks, traffic flows, and even chemical reaction chains.
graphs.fun_fact_popular: In Facebook's social graph, the average distance between any two users is only 3.5 steps—this is the 'six degrees of separation' theory in practice.
graphs.description_simple: A metro map is a classic graph: stations serve as vertices (points), and track lines as edges (connections). On such a drawing, the curves of the line don't matter—only which points it connects. A graph turns the tangle of real connections into a clear pattern of circles and lines.
graphs.history_simple: The idea of graphs was born in 1736 when mathematician Leonhard Euler solved the puzzle of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg. He realized to look only at the landmasses and the bridges between them, ignoring distances.
graphs.how_it_works_simple: A graph works as a simplified model of connections. When you need to figure out how to get around traffic jams, the navigator turns streets into edges and intersections into vertices, and quickly iterates through options. The same logic finds friends of friends on a social network.
graphs.description: A graph is a mathematical object defined by a set of vertices and a set of edges (pairs of vertices). Distinguish between directed graphs (edges have a direction) and undirected ones. Additional structures are introduced: weighted graphs (each edge is assigned a weight), multigraphs (multiple edges allowed), etc. Graphs serve as the foundation for network analysis, algorithm theory, coding theory, and statistical physics. Complex systems break down into nodes and their interactions—just as the first navigator reduced the street maze to points and lines.
graphs.history: The birth of graph theory is linked to Leonhard Euler's work 'The solution of a problem relating to the geometry of position' (1736), where he demonstrated the impossibility of traversing all seven bridges of Königsberg without crossing one twice. The term 'graph' was introduced by K. König in 1936. In the 20th century, graph theory flourished thanks to problems in discrete optimization and computer science.
graphs.how_it_works: Graphs model systems of pairwise interactions. Analysis relies on adjacency and incidence matrices. Graph properties are studied through invariants: connectivity, cyclomatic number, chromatic number. Efficient algorithms on graphs (shortest path, maximum flow) are based on dynamic programming and greedy strategies. In physics, graphs are used in diagrammatic techniques (Feynman diagrams are directed graphs) and in the study of random media.
key_problems: The question of the equality of P and NP classes largely reduces to unsolved problems on graphs (Hamiltonian cycle).
The graph isomorphism problem: whether it belongs to the NP-complete or NP-intermediate class.
Existence of a strongly regular graph with certain parameters.
Exact exponential algorithms for intractable problems on graphs.
graphs.fun_fact: Feynman diagrams in quantum electrodynamics are directed graphs of a special kind, where each vertex corresponds to an interaction constant and edges to particle propagators. Computing the process amplitude reduces to summing over all possible graphs.
