formulas.description: Handshaking lemma
formulas.meaning: The sum of degrees of all vertices of the graph equals twice the number of edges; deg(v) is the degree of vertex v, |E| is the number of edges

bayesian_inference.name: Bayesian inference
bayesian_inference.mini: You update your beliefs upon seeing new evidence. A detective at a crime scene recalculates the suspects' odds with every new detail found.
bayesian_inference.practical_application: Spam filters learn from your markings, medical tests refine diagnoses based on new symptoms.
bayesian_inference.description_popular: Bayesian inference is a mathematical method for estimating the probability of a hypothesis based on new observations. It requires three components: a prior probability (initial degree of belief in the hypothesis), a likelihood function (how probable the data are given the hypothesis is true), and a normalization constant (the total probability of the data under all possible hypotheses). The result is the posterior probability—what you believe after considering the evidence. Unlike classical statistics, the Bayesian approach directly answers the question "What is the probability that the hypothesis is true given these data?" rather than "What is the probability of obtaining such data if the hypothesis is true?"
bayesian_inference.fun_fact_popular: British codebreaker Alan Turing used Bayesian methods to crack the Enigma code during World War II, assigning probabilities to various machine settings based on intercepted messages.
bayesian_inference.description_simple: Bayesian inference is a way to recalculate the probabilities of events when new data appears. Imagine you're unsure if there's chocolate in a box. You shake the box and hear a rattle—your confidence grows. Each new sound (evidence) changes your estimate. A detective works the same way: an initial version (e.g., 'the butler is guilty with a 20% chance') is refined after finding a glove or a fingerprint.
bayesian_inference.history_simple: The idea is named after Thomas Bayes, an 18th-century English clergyman who laid the foundation for updating probabilities. Later, Pierre-Simon Laplace developed it into a coherent theory.
bayesian_inference.how_it_works_simple: You start with an initial guess (how likely the hypothesis is before the experiment). Then you obtain evidence and look at how often such evidence occurs if the hypothesis is true, and how often if it is false. These two numbers are multiplied by the initial probability and give an updated estimate.
bayesian_inference.description: Bayesian inference is a fundamental framework of mathematical statistics, based on Bayes' theorem. It allows for quantitative assessment of uncertainty and updating beliefs in light of empirical data. The central concept is subjective probability as a measure of confidence. The process begins with a prior distribution over the space of hypotheses, which is then refined through a likelihood function reflecting the observed data. Computing the posterior distribution often requires high-dimensional integration, making practical implementation nontrivial. Bayesian methods naturally incorporate regularization through prior knowledge and provide interval estimates of parameters in the form of credible intervals. They are applied in machine learning (Bayesian networks, Gaussian processes), signal processing, econometrics, medical diagnostics, and cognitive sciences.
bayesian_inference.history: Bayes' theorem was first formulated in the posthumously published work of Thomas Bayes (1763), and later independently rediscovered and disseminated by Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1774. Laplace applied it to estimating the mass of Saturn and to demographic research. In the 20th century, interest revived thanks to the work of Harold Jeffreys, who introduced non-informative prior distributions, and Leonard Savage, who developed the axiomatics of subjective probability. With the advent of powerful computational methods such as the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm (1970) and Gibbs sampling, Bayesian inference became applicable to complex models in data science.
bayesian_inference.how_it_works: Inference relies on Bayes' theorem: P(H|D) = P(D|H) * P(H) / P(D), where H is a hypothesis, D is data. P(H) (prior) reflects the initial degree of belief, P(D|H) (likelihood) is the probability of obtaining data D if H is true, P(D) is the marginal probability of the data, serving as normalization. In practice, direct computation of the denominator, an integral over all hypotheses, is often impossible, and one resorts to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to approximate the posterior distribution. Modern packages such as Stan and PyMC automate these calculations.
key_problems: Choosing an objective prior distribution in the absence of knowledge.
Scalability of MCMC methods to models with millions of parameters.
Checking convergence of Markov chains in complex problems.
bayesian_inference.fun_fact: Bayes' theorem was published only after the author's death, and its importance was long unrecognized; even Laplace used his own formulation without knowing about Bayes' work.

formulas.description: Bayes' theorem
formulas.meaning: P(H|D) is the posterior probability of hypothesis H given data D, P(D|H) is the likelihood, P(H) is the prior probability of the hypothesis, P(D) is the marginal probability of the data

chaos_theory.name: chaos theory
chaos_theory.mini: A pendulum swings steadily, but push it a little harder and the trajectory becomes unpredictable. Chaos hides in simple systems.
chaos_theory.practical_application: Weather forecasts are inaccurate beyond two weeks due to the chaotic nature of the atmosphere, and encryption algorithms use chaos to protect data.
chaos_theory.description_popular: Chaos is not synonymous with disorder. It is orderly unpredictability. Look at the smoke rising from a cigarette: at first it flows in a smooth stream, but higher up it suddenly turns into billowing curls. The transition from laminar to turbulent flow is a typical scenario for the birth of chaos. The equations describing such processes are deterministic (containing no randomness), but so sensitive to initial data that the slightest rounding error grows and nullifies any forecast. This property is called exponential divergence of trajectories.
chaos_theory.fun_fact_popular: In 1961, Edward Lorenz, restarting a long computer weather calculation, entered 0.506 instead of 0.506127—and got a completely different climate. Thus was born the understanding that predictability even in simple systems is limited to a horizon of a few characteristic times.
chaos_theory.description_simple: Two pendulums, one suspended from the other. Gently push the upper one—and the motion of the lower becomes a whimsical dance that is impossible to repeat. Push a millimeter to the side—and the dance is completely different. Chaos is the behavior of systems where the tiniest difference at the start leads to completely different outcomes. Even if you know all the rules, you cannot predict the future beyond a certain horizon. In a room with the same setup, you will never see two identical motions—each time a unique pattern is born.
chaos_theory.history_simple: Henri Poincaré, studying the motions of three planets, realized that their orbits could be incredibly sensitive to initial conditions. The term 'chaos' was introduced by mathematician James Yorke in 1975, and the famous 'butterfly effect' was formulated by meteorologist Edward Lorenz.
chaos_theory.how_it_works_simple: Fold a sheet of paper in half, then again, and again. After 10 folds you get 1024 layers—that's exponential growth. In chaos, a small uncertainty multiplies just as rapidly, and after a few steps the prediction blurs. In a room with two pendulums on one suspension, the motion never repeats—each time a unique dance is born.
chaos_theory.description: Chaos theory is an interdisciplinary field studying the behavior of nonlinear dynamical systems that are extremely sensitive to initial conditions—a phenomenon known as the 'butterfly effect'. Chaotic dynamics are deterministic (described by unambiguous differential or difference equations without random terms), but practically unpredictable over long time intervals due to the exponential divergence of initially close trajectories. A quantitative measure of this unpredictability is provided by Lyapunov exponents. Chaos is often characterized by the presence of strange attractors—complex fractal sets with fractional dimension, on which motion never repeats but remains bounded. So it is with a pendulum: change the initial push by a hair, and instead of regular oscillations we get chaotic rotation.
chaos_theory.history: Although the first intuitive insights about the instability of certain motions were expressed by Henri Poincaré as early as the 1890s, modern chaos theory was born in the 1960s–1970s. Edward Lorenz of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology discovered chaos in a simplified model of atmospheric convection in 1963. Mathematician James Yorke and his student Tien-Yien Li introduced the term 'chaos' in 1975. Mitchell Feigenbaum in 1978 discovered universal patterns in the transition to chaos through a period-doubling cascade, linking them to constants named after him.
chaos_theory.how_it_works: The starting point is often the Lorenz system: three ordinary differential equations with two nonlinear terms of the xy and xz type. At certain parameter values (σ=10, ρ=28, β=8/3), the phase trajectories form a chaotic attractor—they endlessly wind around two regions, never intersecting or looping. The evolution of such a system has the property of mixing: any, even tiny, initial cloud of points eventually spreads uniformly over the attractor. Information about the initial state is irretrievably lost, although the equations themselves are reversible. This leads to the practical impossibility of long-term forecasting, despite determinism. Statistical methods, such as constructing return maps (Poincaré sections) and calculating the power spectrum, help distinguish chaos from periodic regimes and noise.
key_problems: Proof of the existence of a strange attractor in the Lorenz system remained an open problem until 2002 (solved by Warwick Tucker), but for many other systems rigorous analysis is lacking.
Prediction of bifurcations and regime shifts in climate models taking into account chaotic dynamics.
Using chaos for efficient mixing in microfluidic devices—understanding optimal parameters.
chaos_theory.fun_fact: The Lorenz system has symmetry: replacing (x, y) with (−x, −y) does not change the equations. Because of this symmetry, a trajectory can jump from one 'wing' of the attractor to the other at irregular time intervals, creating the effect of deterministic random switching, reminiscent of a coin toss.

formulas.description: Logistic map (discrete chaos)
formulas.meaning: x_n — population (in dimensionless units) at the nth generation, r — growth parameter (0 ≤ r ≤ 4)

variational_method.name: Variational Method
variational_method.mini: You estimate the length of a curved rope by replacing it with a broken line of straight segments. This trick helps to arrive at the exact answer when direct calculation is impossible.
variational_method.practical_application: Quantum chemists calculate molecular shapes this way, and engineers determine the optimal rocket trajectory with minimal fuel consumption.
variational_method.description_popular: The variational method is a powerful approximation technique widely used in physics and applied mathematics. Its essence is to minimize or maximize a functional — a rule that assigns a number to a function. In quantum mechanics, the functional is usually the average energy. You set up a trial wave function with adjustable parameters and find those parameter values that minimize the energy. According to the variational principle, the obtained energy is never lower than the exact ground state, so by deepening the trial function (increasing the number of parameters), one can approach the truth arbitrarily closely. A similar approach is used in elasticity theory, hydrodynamics, and machine learning, where variational autoencoders learn to compress and reconstruct data.
variational_method.fun_fact_popular: A path worn across a lawn by people is often the shortest route — a natural manifestation of the variational principle: the trajectory minimizes effort.
variational_method.description_simple: The variational method is a search for the best approximation when the exact solution is unknown. Imagine you need to measure the area of a whimsical lawn, but you have no formula. You lay a piece of cloth over the lawn and trim it along the contour — the more precisely you cut, the closer the area of the cloth to the lawn's area. Mathematicians do the same: they try different simple shapes (approximations) until they achieve minimal error. In quantum physics, this is how the distribution of electrons in atoms is found: the parameters of a trial wave function are varied until the computed energy drops to the lower limit.
variational_method.history_simple: The foundations of the calculus of variations were laid by Euler and Lagrange in the 18th century. In quantum mechanics, the method was introduced in 1928 by the German physicist Walter Ritz, who proposed a way to calculate atomic energies without complex equations.
variational_method.how_it_works_simple: A family of possible solutions is chosen, depending on several numbers (parameters). For each set of numbers, a certain quantity (for example, energy) is calculated. From all the options, the one that gives the smallest (or largest) value is selected, and this is considered the best approximation to the true solution.
variational_method.description: The variational method relies on the calculus of variations — a branch of mathematics that studies extrema of functionals. The main problem: find a function y(x) that yields an extremum of an integral of the form J[y] = ∫ L(x, y, y') dx, where L is the Lagrangian. The necessary condition for an extremum is given by the Euler-Lagrange equation. In quantum mechanics, the method is used for the approximate solution of the stationary Schrödinger equation. The energy functional E[ψ] = ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩ / ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ is minimized over trial functions ψ from a chosen parametric family. By the variational principle (Ritz method), the minimum value is an upper bound for the exact ground-state energy. For excited states, an orthogonality condition is applied. Variational approaches underlie the finite element method, the Hartree-Fock self-consistent field in quantum chemistry, as well as variational Bayesian inference in machine learning, where instead of the exact posterior distribution, one seeks the closest one from a chosen family of distributions (usually with a factorized form).
variational_method.history: The roots of the method go back to the 17th century — the brachistochrone problem solved by Johann Bernoulli. Systematic development of the calculus of variations was achieved in the works of Leonhard Euler and Joseph-Louis Lagrange. Walter Ritz in 1908 published a method of trial functions for solving boundary value problems, and in 1928 applied it to the quantum-mechanical helium atom, obtaining energy values close to experimental ones. Later, the method was generalized into a powerful computational tool with the advent of computers. In statistical physics, the variational approach was developed by Richard Feynman.
variational_method.how_it_works: For a quantum system, a trial wave function ψ(α; x) with variational parameters α = (α1, α2, ...) is set up. The functional E(α) = ∫ ψ* H ψ dτ / ∫ |ψ|^2 dτ is calculated, where H is the Hamiltonian. Then E(α) is minimized: ∂E/∂α_i = 0. The solution gives optimal α and an energy estimate E0 ≤ E_exact. Convergence is guaranteed by the completeness theorem: if the trial family is dense in the required functional space, then the limit of E_min coincides with the exact energy. In variational Bayesian inference, the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the approximation and the true posterior distribution is minimized.
key_problems: Choosing a suitable manifold of trial functions, especially for systems with strong correlations.
The problem of local minima in nonlinear variational problems.
The computational cost of variational Monte Carlo for solutions with nodal surfaces.
variational_method.fun_fact: Walter Ritz, who gave his name to the method, died at 31 from tuberculosis, but managed not only to create the Ritz method but also to formulate the combination principle in spectroscopy, which became the key to unraveling the structure of the atom.

formulas.description: Euler-Lagrange equation
formulas.meaning: L is the Lagrangian, depending on x, y, and the derivative y', y = y(x) is the desired function that yields an extremum of the functional

formulas.description: Variational principle in quantum mechanics
formulas.meaning: E_0 is the exact ground-state energy, E_0 ≤ the computed average value; H is the Hamiltonian of the system, ψ is any trial wave function

nonlinear_dynamics.name: nonlinear dynamics
nonlinear_dynamics.mini: In life, it's rarely a case of 'you get what you give.' Doubling your efforts might triple the result—or, conversely, barely change anything. That's nonlinearity at work.
nonlinear_dynamics.practical_application: Navigation systems account for nonlinear effects to achieve precise positioning, while engineers combat nonlinear vibrations in bridges and aircraft.
nonlinear_dynamics.description_popular: A linear relationship is like an ideal rubber band: elongation is strictly proportional to force. In reality, things are more complex: a bridge swaying in the wind can suddenly resonate and collapse; heart muscle can sometimes lapse into fibrillation. Nonlinear dynamics studies systems where the superposition principle breaks down—the effect is not the sum of independent causes. Here, feedback loops give rise to astonishing effects: self-organization, bifurcations (branching of states), and chaos.
nonlinear_dynamics.fun_fact_popular: The soliton—a solitary wave traveling down a channel without changing shape—was discovered in 1834 when engineer John Scott Russell spotted one on a canal and chased it on horseback for several kilometers. Solitons behave like particles and obey nonlinear equations.
nonlinear_dynamics.description_simple: You stretch a spring: as long as the force is small, it elongates exactly twice as much when you double the force. But cross a threshold and it stays deformed forever, breaking the link between force and extension. That's nonlinear dynamics—the science of systems where the response is not proportional to the input. Such systems are everywhere: from heart rhythms to stock market crashes. In a car's suspension, too much compression of a spring leads to bottoming out—and the impact is transmitted to the body far more harshly than expected. That's how nonlinearity turns a smooth motion into a sharp jolt.
nonlinear_dynamics.history_simple: Henri Poincaré in the late 19th century first noticed that even in simple celestial motions, small perturbations can cause catastrophic changes in orbits. Later, in the 20th century, computer modeling revealed the richness of nonlinear effects.
nonlinear_dynamics.how_it_works_simple: In a linear world, the result is the sum of its parts. In a nonlinear one, the parts influence each other, and the whole is greater than the simple sum. Picture a traffic jam: one car slows down, and a wave of stops ripples backward, intensifying with every kilometer. That's how feedback turns smooth flow into chaos.
nonlinear_dynamics.description: Nonlinear dynamics is a branch of mathematics and physics that studies systems whose evolution is described by nonlinear differential or difference equations. In such systems, the superposition principle does not hold: the response to a sum of inputs is not equal to the sum of responses to each input individually. Key concepts include attractors (sets toward which trajectories converge), bifurcations (qualitative rearrangements of the phase portrait when parameters change), stability, synchronization, and chaos. Nonlinearity gives rise to a rich spectrum of phenomena: self-oscillations, shock waves, solitons, turbulence, pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems. This explains why doubling the input energy can triple the output—or have almost no effect at all.
nonlinear_dynamics.history: Henri Poincaré in the late 19th century laid the foundations of the qualitative theory of differential equations, first realizing the complexity of behavior in celestial mechanics. In the 20th century, the work of Alexander Lyapunov, Andrey Kolmogorov, Vladimir Arnold, and Jürgen Moser (KAM theory) explained the conditions for the preservation of ordered motion in perturbed systems. Computer experiments by Lorenz, Feigenbaum, and others in the 1960s–1980s revealed universal scenarios for the transition to chaos and sparked an explosive growth of interest in nonlinear dynamics.
nonlinear_dynamics.how_it_works: The state of a nonlinear system is defined by a set of variables, and the rate of their change is given by nonlinear functions of these variables. Analysis often begins with finding equilibrium points and studying their stability according to Lyapunov. When a control parameter is varied, an equilibrium point may lose stability, and the system undergoes a bifurcation, switching to a new regime—for example, from a steady state to periodic oscillations (Andronov–Hopf bifurcation). With further parameter changes, a cascade of period-doubling bifurcations often leads to chaos—irregular, aperiodic motion with high sensitivity to initial conditions, characterized by positive Lyapunov exponents. Many phenomena, such as turbulence in fluids, are described by nonlinear partial differential equations (e.g., the Navier–Stokes equations), where the nonlinear term (v·∇)v is responsible for energy transfer between scales.
key_problems: The exact solution of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations for fully developed turbulence remains a Millennium Prize problem.
Prediction of bifurcations in high-dimensional systems, such as climate models or neural networks.
Understanding the mechanisms of self-organization and the emergence of complex structures in nonlinear distributed systems.
nonlinear_dynamics.fun_fact: In the mid-20th century, physicist Enrico Fermi, mathematician Stanisław Ulam, and programmer John Pasta numerically simulated oscillations of a chain of particles with nonlinear interactions, expecting rapid equilibration. Instead, they discovered recurrence—the system almost periodically returned to its initial state. This paradoxical behavior led to the discovery of solitons and a revision of ideas about thermalization in nonlinear systems.

stochastic_processes.name: stochastic processes
stochastic_processes.mini: A random process is a line drawn by luck: stock quotes, noise in a radio receiver, or Brownian motion of pollen.
stochastic_processes.practical_application: Predicting exchange rates, modeling traffic jams, and even generating realistic textures in computer games rely on random processes.
stochastic_processes.description_popular: A random process defines a probabilistic rule according to which a system transitions from one state to another over time. Unlike deterministic laws (like an apple falling), we can only talk about the probabilities of various trajectories. For example, radioactive decay of atoms is a Poisson random process: decay times are unpredictable, but the average number of decays per minute is stable.
stochastic_processes.fun_fact_popular: In 1905, Albert Einstein used a random process (Brownian motion) to prove the existence of atoms — he linked the chaotic movement of pollen to thermal jolts from molecules.
stochastic_processes.description_simple: A random process is a mathematical model of how a random variable changes over time. Take a temperature sensor that outputs a new value with error every second. The sequence of these values is a realization of a random process. An individual measurement cannot be predicted, but the process has statistical patterns and average behavior.
stochastic_processes.history_simple: The first random process was described by mathematician Louis Bachelier in 1900 while trying to predict prices on the Paris stock exchange. His work was long overlooked, but later it became the foundation of financial mathematics.
stochastic_processes.how_it_works_simple: Tossing a coin, you step left or right. After many tosses, your position will fall somewhere within a wide bell-shaped curve. This random walk is the simplest random process. Similarly, smoke particles move uncertainly as they collide with air molecules.
stochastic_processes.description: A stochastic process is defined as a family of random variables {X(t), t ∈ T}, indexed by parameter t (often time). Major classes include Markov processes, stationary processes, processes with independent increments, and martingales. Key characteristics are the distribution function, expected value, correlation function. The process is fully specified by finite-dimensional distributions. For continuous time, properties of sample paths are important: continuity, differentiability, variation. So the stock ticker quivers from second-by-second jumps to long-term trends — that is the imprint of this very process.
stochastic_processes.history: The formal theory of stochastic processes began to take shape in the early 20th century with the works of Louis Bachelier (1900) on Brownian motion and financial markets. Norbert Wiener in 1923 built a rigorous mathematical model of Brownian motion (Wiener process). Andrey Kolmogorov in 1931 laid the foundations of the axiomatic theory of random processes. The development of the theory was strongly motivated by problems in physics (diffusion), telecommunications (noise), and finance.
stochastic_processes.how_it_works: A stochastic process is described through transition probabilities between states. In discrete time, this can be a chain with given transition probabilities. In continuous time, the dynamics are given by stochastic differential equations (e.g., the Langevin equation for a Brownian particle). For analysis, the Chapman-Kolmogorov equation and the Fokker-Planck equation are often used. A key property — Markov property (the future depends only on the present) — leads to significant simplifications.
key_problems: Description of phase transitions in non-equilibrium stochastic systems
Exact solution of stochastic equations in strong fields
Modeling turbulence as a stochastic process
Exit time problem for multidimensional processes
stochastic_processes.fun_fact: In quantum field theory, the creation and annihilation of particles is described by a Poisson stochastic process. For example, quantum vacuum fluctuations can be modeled as a Wiener process in field space.

probability_theory.name: probability theory
probability_theory.mini: Flip a coin: heads and tails come up about equally often. Probability theory is a language for measuring such frequency, from dice games to rain forecasts.
probability_theory.practical_application: Insurance companies set policy prices, meteorologists report precipitation percentages, and doctors assess treatment risks — all based on probability calculations.
probability_theory.description_popular: Probability theory provides a way to measure uncertainty. It describes random phenomena — from pollen jittering in water (Brownian motion) to galaxy clusters. At its core is the probability space: a set of possible outcomes, each assigned a number from 0 to 1, and the sum of all equals 1. Conditional probability (the chance of an event given that another has occurred) refines our assumptions; Bayes' theorem flips the condition and updates probabilities with new data. This is the engine behind spam filters, medical diagnostics, and machine learning.
probability_theory.fun_fact_popular: Shuffle a deck of 52 cards, and the resulting order is almost certainly unique in history. The number of permutations is so vast (8×10⁶⁷) that even if every person on Earth had been shuffling a deck every second since the Big Bang, we would be nowhere near repeating a combination.
probability_theory.description_simple: Probability theory is a branch of mathematics that studies randomness and uncertainty. It provides rules for assigning numbers from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) to different events. Just as a cookbook helps bake a cake, probability combines chances: tossing two coins, the probability of two heads is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. When a weather app says '30% chance of rain', it means that out of 100 similar days, it rained about 30 times.
probability_theory.history_simple: In the 1650s, Blaise Pascal and Pierre Fermat began a correspondence about gambling problems, laying the foundations. Later, in the 1930s, Andrey Kolmogorov built a rigorous mathematical framework, turning probability into an exact science.
probability_theory.how_it_works_simple: Probability works by counting equally possible outcomes or observing frequency over long runs. For a fair die, each face has a chance of 1/6. In complex cases like disease spread, random numbers are used and patterns sought — much like guessing the shape of a forest from a few trees.
probability_theory.description: Probability theory is a mathematical discipline that, based on axioms and theorems, models random experiments and stochastic processes. Its foundations are Kolmogorov's axiomatics (1933): a probability measure on a σ-algebra of events must be non-negative, the total measure equals 1, and countable additivity holds. From these axioms, the concepts of random variable, expected value, distributions, independence, and conditional expectation are derived. Limit theorems (law of large numbers, central limit theorem) describe the stability of averages in long runs and the ubiquity of the normal distribution. Probability permeates statistical mechanics, quantum theory (Born rule), finance (stochastic calculus), information theory, and artificial intelligence.
probability_theory.history: The formal study of probability began in the 17th century with the correspondence of Pascal and Fermat in 1654. Jacob Bernoulli's posthumous work 'Ars Conjectandi' (1713) introduced the law of large numbers. Thomas Bayes (1763) and Pierre-Simon Laplace formulated the principle of inverse probability — Bayes' theorem. In 1933, Andrey Kolmogorov, in 'Foundations of the Theory of Probability', axiomatized it on the basis of measure theory, linking pure mathematics with experience.
probability_theory.how_it_works: Probability theory works by specifying a sample space of elementary outcomes and a probability function. Rules — additivity for mutually exclusive events, multiplication for independent ones — allow computing probabilities of complex events. The law of large numbers guarantees that as the number of trials grows, the sample mean tends to the expected value. The central limit theorem states that sums of independent random variables are asymptotically normal, justifying frequentist statistics. Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem provide a mechanism for updating knowledge with incoming information. The apparatus of measure theory formalizes distributions via distribution functions, densities, or characteristic functions.
key_problems: Justification of probability interpretation (frequentist vs Bayesian)
Quantum probability and its axiomatics
Computational complexity of Bayesian inference in large models
Problem of explaining probabilities in multiverse theories
probability_theory.fun_fact: The law of large numbers can be misleading: to state with 95% confidence that the proportion of heads in coin tosses lies between 49% and 51%, you need about 10,000 tosses. Most think a few hundred will suffice — this misconception is called the 'law of small numbers'.

electromagnetic_compatibility.name: electromagnetic compatibility
electromagnetic_compatibility.mini: In the morning, the toaster, phone, and Wi-Fi router turn on at the same time, but none of them interfere with each other. This is electromagnetic compatibility — the invisible conductor of the ether.
electromagnetic_compatibility.practical_application: Without it, a pacemaker would malfunction from a mobile phone, and aircraft navigation would fail in a thunderstorm.
electromagnetic_compatibility.description_popular: Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) is a branch of electrical engineering that ensures the coexistence of electronic systems without mutual interference. Any current-carrying wire, antenna, or microchip emits electromagnetic fields. If the level of these fields exceeds the sensitivity threshold of a neighboring device, a malfunction occurs — from crackling in speakers to a computer memory error. EMC solves two problems: reducing emissions from sources and increasing the immunity of receivers. In practice, this involves shielding, filtering, power decoupling, and line balancing. EMC standards are mandatory for all electronics, from children's toys to satellites.
electromagnetic_compatibility.fun_fact_popular: In an anechoic chamber where EMC is tested, you can hear the sound of your own blood in your ears — it's that quiet around you.
electromagnetic_compatibility.description_simple: 220 volts in the outlet, 2.4 gigahertz in Wi-Fi — every device throws invisible waves into space. Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) is the ability of all electronic devices to work side by side without creating mutual interference. Like in an orchestra, where violins shouldn't drown out the trumpets, and trumpets shouldn't overpower the flute. If one violin plays too loudly (interference), the others will falter. EMC sets the rules: each instrument (device) emits exactly as much as needed, and at the same time knows how to listen only to its own part, ignoring others' noise. Tests are conducted in anechoic chambers — rooms without reflections. Therefore, when you turn on the toaster, the phone doesn't crackle — the orchestra plays in harmony.
electromagnetic_compatibility.history_simple: The first problems arose with the spread of radio in the early 20th century. Engineers noticed that transmitters interfered with each other. Later, with the advent of computers and mobile phones, the issue became universal. The foundations were laid by James Maxwell, who described electromagnetic waves.
electromagnetic_compatibility.how_it_works_simple: Every device is both a source and a receiver of waves. To avoid chaos, developers reduce unwanted emissions (shielding wires, installing filters) and make devices immune to external interference (protected circuits). This is similar to soundproofing in an apartment: to sleep undisturbed by a neighbor's hammer drill, you need thick walls and earplugs.
electromagnetic_compatibility.description: Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) is a discipline that studies the unintentional generation, propagation, and reception of electromagnetic energy, with the aim of ensuring proper equipment operation in a common electromagnetic environment. It includes analysis of interference sources (natural, such as lightning, and man-made — switching power supplies, digital buses, radio transmitters), coupling mechanisms (galvanic, capacitive, inductive, radiation), and protection methods. Key concepts: radiated and conducted emission, susceptibility, immunity. EMC standards specify emission limits and minimum immunity levels for various device classes (CISPR, IEC, FCC).
electromagnetic_compatibility.history: The phenomenon of interference has been known since the experiments of Hertz and Popov. A systematic approach emerged in the 1930s with the growth of radio broadcasting and military communications. In 1933, the International Special Committee on Radio Interference (CISPR) began developing standards. James Clerk Maxwell made a significant contribution to the understanding of wave propagation, whose equations describe all electromagnetic interactions. In the second half of the 20th century, with the advent of microelectronics and digital systems, the problem intensified, leading to the creation of mandatory EMC standards in the 1990s.
electromagnetic_compatibility.how_it_works: Any alternating current creates an alternating electromagnetic field, which induces stray signals in neighboring circuits. According to Maxwell's equations, a changing electric field generates a magnetic field, and vice versa, forming a wave. To reduce emissions, shielding (reflection and absorption of waves), filtering (suppression of high-frequency components), and proper PCB layout (minimizing loop areas) are used. To increase immunity — differential signaling, galvanic isolation, and static suppression circuits.
key_problems: Accurate modeling of electromagnetic fields in complex systems (aircraft, automobile) with multiple emitters.
Ensuring EMC when transitioning to nanometer-scale processes, where interference becomes comparable in magnitude to useful signals.
Development of unified standards for new frequency bands (5G/6G, millimeter waves).
electromagnetic_compatibility.fun_fact: An electromagnetic wave from a lightning discharge 100 km away can induce a current of up to 100 A in a telephone line — more than enough to burn out the input circuits.

formulas.description: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction in Maxwell's form — the basis for the occurrence of induced interference
formulas.meaning: E — electric field strength, B — magnetic flux density, t — time.

finite_element_method.name: finite element method
finite_element_method.mini: Engineers test a bridge without building it: they break it into thousands of tiny pieces, like pixels, and calculate each one. The finite element method turns a complex shape into a mesh of simple pieces, where equations become solvable.
finite_element_method.practical_application: Without it, the design of safe airplanes, skyscrapers, and medical implants is impossible: virtual tests for strength, heat, and vibration weed out weak spots before production.
finite_element_method.description_popular: The finite element method is a mathematical strategy for approximate solution of differential equations on complex domains. The continuous problem is replaced by a discrete one: the domain is divided into simple subdomains (elements — triangles or tetrahedra), and the solution is approximated by piecewise polynomial functions. Engineers love it for its ability to handle irregular geometry and various materials. From car crash tests to blood flow in arteries — FEM turns elegant differential equations into computations that yield clear, useful results.
finite_element_method.fun_fact_popular: The largest FEM simulation of Earth's mantle convection uses a mesh of more than a billion elements and runs for months on supercomputers, helping to understand the movement of tectonic plates.
finite_element_method.description_simple: The finite element method (FEM) is a computer way of calculating the physics of objects with complex shapes. Imagine you want to know how a car's fender will bend in a crash. Instead of a whole curved panel, it is divided into thousands of small triangles or cubes (finite elements). Each piece follows simple rules, and the computer links them together and predicts the overall picture. It’s like building a sculpture from LEGO: each brick is simple, but together they create an accurate copy.
finite_element_method.history_simple: The method grew out of the needs of aircraft construction in the 1940s–50s. At first it was used to calculate airplane wings, and with the advent of digital computers in the 1960s it became a standard tool for strength and vibration problems.
finite_element_method.how_it_works_simple: First, a mesh is built — a scatter of points and shapes covering the object. At each point, the computer solves equations of motion or heat transfer using trial functions. Then everything is assembled into a giant system of equations; solving it reveals how each tiny fragment moves, stretches, or heats up. The finer the mesh, the more accurate the answer, but the heavier the calculation.
finite_element_method.description: The finite element method is a numerical technique for solving boundary value problems for differential equations. It originates in variational calculus: the solution minimizes a functional (energy) under constraints. FEM approximates the solution by a linear combination of basis functions with compact support, leading to a sparse linear system. Steps: (1) weak formulation of the PDE via integration by parts; (2) discretization by an element mesh; (3) assembly of the global stiffness matrix and load vector; (4) solution of the algebraic system. Error analysis relies on mesh refinement (h-version) or increasing polynomial degree (p-version). FEM is implemented in commercial (ANSYS, COMSOL) and open-source (FEniCS) packages.
finite_element_method.history: Early ideas date back to the 1940s: A. Hrennikoff used lattice analogies, and R. Courant used piecewise polynomials. The term 'finite element' was introduced by R. W. Clough in 1960. Rapid development took place at aerospace centers like Boeing and the University of California, Berkeley. The mathematical foundation (connection with Sobolev spaces, convergence proofs) was laid in the 1970s by Babuška, Brezzi, and others.
finite_element_method.how_it_works: FEM transforms a differential equation (e.g., from elasticity theory) into a weak form by multiplying by test functions and integrating. The domain is covered with a mesh, and the unknown field is approximated by a sum of shape functions on each element. Substitution into the weak form yields the system Ku = f, where K is the stiffness matrix (sparse, symmetric, positive definite in many problems). Boundary conditions are applied, and the system is solved iteratively or directly. Post-processing computes deformations, stresses, fluxes. Adaptive mesh refinement improves accuracy where gradients are large.
key_problems: Automatic generation of high-quality meshes for complex geometries
Stability and accuracy for high-speed problems with shock waves
Multiscale modeling: from atoms to structures
Integration with machine learning methods to accelerate computations
finite_element_method.fun_fact: The stiffness matrix of a three-dimensional elasticity problem with a million nodes contains on the order of 10^13 entries, but due to sparsity (almost all are zeros) only a few million numbers are stored and processed.

differential_equations.name: differential equations
differential_equations.mini: A speedometer shows speed at every moment. An odometer shows the distance traveled. Between them is an invisible thread connecting the moment with the total. This is the language of change.
differential_equations.practical_application: Differential equations describe how coffee cools, populations grow, and signals propagate in neurons.
differential_equations.description_popular: A differential equation is a compass for a moving world. It tells us not where we are, but where we are going and how fast, depending on our surroundings. Solving it means reconstructing the entire route from instantaneous clues. Such equations can be ordinary (with one independent variable, such as time) or partial (with many variables, as in describing a vibrating string). They underlie everything: from a ball's trajectory to the dynamics of galaxies.
differential_equations.fun_fact_popular: Schrödinger's equation is a differential equation that governs the behavior of quantum particles. It is as fundamental to the microworld as Newton's laws are to the planets.
differential_equations.description_simple: The speedometer needle quivers at 60 km/h. How far will you travel in an hour? 60 kilometers. But if the speed changes every second, the calculation requires adding up infinitely small pieces. That is exactly what differential equations do: they link what is happening now to what will happen a moment later. They take the instantaneous rate of change and reconstruct the whole story—just as an odometer computes distance from the speedometer's kilometers.
differential_equations.history_simple: In the 17th century, Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz created calculus—a tool for working with continuous change. Thus was born the language in which the laws of motion, heat transfer, and electromagnetism are formulated.
differential_equations.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a pool. Water drains through a hole. The flow rate depends on the water level, and the level changes due to the flow—a feedback loop. A differential equation describes this relationship and lets you calculate when the pool will be empty. It takes the instantaneous rate of change and reconstructs the whole story.
differential_equations.description: A differential equation is a mathematical relationship linking an unknown function with its derivatives. It sets a rule whereby the rate of change of a quantity at each point in space or time depends on the quantity itself. The order of the equation is determined by the highest derivative, and its degree of linearity depends on the presence of nonlinear combinations of the function and its derivatives. Equations can be ordinary (ODEs, one variable) or partial (PDEs, several variables). Solving a differential equation reconstructs the integral picture from the local law of change and requires setting initial or boundary conditions. Most fundamental laws of physics are formulated as differential equations. That is why the speedometer and odometer are not just instruments, but visible images of a profound mathematical connection.
differential_equations.history: The origins lie in the 17th century, when Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz independently created differential and integral calculus. Newton formulated the second law of motion as a differential equation. In the 18th century, Leonhard Euler, Joseph-Louis Lagrange, and Pierre-Simon Laplace developed methods for solving broad classes of equations, especially in celestial mechanics. The 19th century brought the theory of partial differential equations: Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier—the heat equation, James Clerk Maxwell—electrodynamics. In the 20th century, Henri Poincaré's qualitative theory and functional analysis made it possible to study solvability and stability even without explicit formulas.
differential_equations.how_it_works: Consider a first-order ODE dy/dx = f(x, y). Geometrically, this equation defines a direction field on the plane: at each point (x, y), the slope of a small segment equals f(x, y). An integral curve passing through a given initial point must be tangent to this field at every point. The simplest solution method is separation of variables, if f(x, y) factorizes. For linear ODEs with constant coefficients, solutions are sought as exponentials; multiple roots of the characteristic equation lead to resonant terms of the form x e^{λx}. Partial differential equations require more delicate techniques: separation of variables, Green's functions, Fourier transforms. The well-posedness of a problem (existence, uniqueness, stability of the solution) is established by theorems, such as the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem for analytic PDEs or the Galerkin method for weak solutions. Numerical methods (finite differences, finite elements) allow approximating solutions with controlled accuracy.
key_problems: For the Navier–Stokes equations in three dimensions, the existence of smooth solutions for arbitrary smooth initial data has not been proved (a Millennium Prize problem).
Development of efficient numerical schemes for stiff ODE systems where fast and slow time scales coexist.
Constructing analytical solutions for nonlinear PDEs describing turbulence and quantum field theory.
differential_equations.fun_fact: The Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation, describing long surface waves on shallow water, is a nonlinear third-order partial differential equation. It is remarkable for having an infinite number of conservation laws and being exactly solvable by the inverse scattering method, which gave rise to the whole field of integrable systems.

monte_carlo_methods.name: Monte Carlo methods
monte_carlo_methods.mini: You throw darts in a dark room to estimate the area of furniture by the number of hits. Randomness turns into precise calculation.
monte_carlo_methods.practical_application: Engineers use them to verify the reliability of bridges, financiers forecast stock prices, and physicists model nuclear reactions.
monte_carlo_methods.description_popular: Monte Carlo methods are a class of computational algorithms based on repeated random sampling. They allow numerical estimation of high-dimensional integrals, solving differential equations, and optimization problems. The key idea: instead of analytical calculation, one resorts to a statistical experiment. Convergence is slow (error decreases as 1/√N) but independent of dimensionality, making the methods indispensable in multidimensional space. In finance, for example, they estimate the value of complex derivative instruments, in biology they model population evolution, and in computer graphics they create realistic scene lighting (ray tracing).
monte_carlo_methods.fun_fact_popular: The most famous example is computing π: by throwing points into a square with an inscribed circle and counting the ratio of those that fall inside the circle to the total, one gets an approximation 4×(inside/total).
monte_carlo_methods.description_simple: Monte Carlo methods are a way to solve complex problems using random numbers. Imagine you need to find the area of a oddly shaped lake. You enclose it with a rectangle whose area you know, then scatter a handful of sand grains over the rectangle. By counting how many grains fell into the lake and knowing the total number of throws, you can roughly calculate its area. The more throws, the more accurate the result. Similarly, a computer 'throws' millions of random points in complex models—from molecular motion to stock market risks.
monte_carlo_methods.history_simple: The method was invented in the 1940s by scientists at the Los Alamos Laboratory working on the atomic project. Stanislaw Ulam formulated the idea, and John von Neumann connected it with computations. The name was given in honor of the Monte Carlo casino due to the role of chance.
monte_carlo_methods.how_it_works_simple: You set random input parameters for the problem, run the simulation many times, and see how often the result occurs. By aggregating these repetitions, you get an estimate of probabilities or average values that is difficult to compute with formulas.
monte_carlo_methods.description: Monte Carlo (MC) methods encompass a wide range of stochastic modeling techniques. The foundation is the law of large numbers: the arithmetic mean of random variables drawn from a sampling distribution converges to the expected value. To accelerate convergence, variance reduction methods are used (importance sampling, stratified sampling, control variates). In Bayesian inference, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is especially important, where a sequence of samples forming a Markov chain is generated, whose stationary distribution coincides with the target posterior. The most common are the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and Gibbs sampling. MC methods are also applied in quantum chemistry (diffusion Monte Carlo), particle physics (shower simulation), and reliability analysis.
monte_carlo_methods.history: The idea goes back to Buffon's needle experiment in the 18th century, but as a computational tool it took shape in the 1940s. Stanislaw Ulam, recovering from an illness, thought about solitaire games and realized that instead of complex combinatorial calculations, one could simply replay a random game many times and estimate the probability of winning. He discussed this with John von Neumann, and they applied the approach to neutron diffusion calculations. In 1953, the seminal paper by N. Metropolis et al. on the sampling algorithm appeared.
monte_carlo_methods.how_it_works: To estimate the integral I = ∫ f(x) dx, one introduces a probability density p(x) and generates N points xi ~ p(x). The approximation: I ≈ (1/N) Σ f(xi)/p(xi). In MCMC, a Markov chain is constructed with a transition kernel that ensures ergodicity and stationarity on the target distribution. For complex distributions, ensemble sampling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo are used, which utilizes gradients of the log-density.
key_problems: Slow convergence for rare events.
Diagnosing stationarity of the MCMC chain.
Choosing the optimal proposal distribution in the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.
monte_carlo_methods.fun_fact: Although the method is named after a casino, its creators worked under the strictest secrecy as part of the Manhattan Project; spreading ideas about 'roulette' or 'randomness' outside the laboratory was dangerous, as it could hint at nuclear research.

formulas.meaning: I is the true value of the integral, N is the number of samples, xi is a random point from distribution p(x), f(x_i) is the integrand function, p(x_i) is the density of the distribution from which the sample is drawn

computational_fluid_dynamics.name: computational fluid dynamics
computational_fluid_dynamics.mini: Air flows around a Formula 1 race car at 300 km/h — a digital wind tunnel slices the flow into millions of cells and computes the physics of shocks and eddies in each. Computational fluid dynamics turns the invisible dance of liquids and gases into a picture on the screen.
computational_fluid_dynamics.practical_application: It optimizes aircraft wings, forecasts weather and ocean currents, helps design quiet fans and heart valves — all without expensive prototypes.
computational_fluid_dynamics.description_popular: Computational fluid dynamics solves the conservation equations of mass, momentum, and energy on a discrete grid that describes the flow domain. These differential equations — Navier–Stokes — are notoriously nonlinear and turbulent. CFD methods (finite volume, finite element, spectral) approximate derivatives and advance the solution through iterations. Turbulence models (RANS, LES, DNS) handle the chaotic small scales. The result is a detailed map of velocities, pressures, and temperatures, allowing engineers to test designs virtually and scientists to study galaxy formation and blood flow.
computational_fluid_dynamics.fun_fact_popular: The first CFD calculation of an entire aircraft (F-16) was performed in 1983 on a Cray supercomputer with 8 million grid nodes. Today, toy CFD apps run on a smartphone.
computational_fluid_dynamics.description_simple: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is the simulation of liquid and gas motion on a computer. Just as a crowd simulation shows human flows around obstacles, CFD breaks air or water into a grid of small cells. Each cell is assigned velocity, pressure, and temperature, and the computer solves the equations linking them. Step by step, the whole flow picture emerges: vortices, drag, heat transfer.
computational_fluid_dynamics.history_simple: Flow calculations began in the 1960s in aerospace laboratories, when it became necessary to understand how spacecraft enter the atmosphere. Early computers could handle only simple two-dimensional flows. By the 1990s, CFD was used in designing cars, submarines, and even artificial hearts.
computational_fluid_dynamics.how_it_works_simple: First, a grid is built around the airplane or pipe. The fluid motion equations — the Navier–Stokes equations — are too complex for manual calculation, so the computer approximates them on each grid cell. Tiny corrections are recalculated step by step in time, like frames of a movie, until the entire flow is known. It resembles predicting the path of confetti in a drafty room — but with rigorous physical laws.
computational_fluid_dynamics.description: Computational fluid dynamics is the numerical simulation of liquid and gas flows and heat transfer by solving conservation laws (mass, momentum, energy) in the form of differential equations. The most common method is the finite volume method: the domain is divided into control volumes, and the equations are integrated over each, yielding algebraic relations for averaged quantities. Spatial schemes (upwind, central, TVD) and temporal integration (explicit, implicit) affect accuracy and stability. For turbulent flows, direct numerical simulation (DNS) resolves all scales but is often unfeasible; large eddy simulation (LES) and Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations with closure models are used instead. CFD is inseparable from mesh generation, high-performance computing, and visualization.
computational_fluid_dynamics.history: Ideas date back to the early 20th century and Lewis Fry Richardson's dream of a 'weather prediction factory' with human computers. True CFD emerged in the 1960s with the work of Francis Harlow at Los Alamos (particle-in-cell method) and panel methods in aerodynamics. In the 1980s, commercial codes FLUENT and CFX appeared, and in the 1990s, unstructured meshes and massive parallelization. Today, CFD is a pillar of engineering design and environmental sciences.
computational_fluid_dynamics.how_it_works: The Navier–Stokes equations for incompressible fluid: ∇·v = 0 and ρ(∂v/∂t + v·∇v) = -∇p + μ∇²v + f. They are discretized on a grid. In the finite volume method, fluxes through cell faces are computed for each cell using Gauss's theorem. Convective terms are treated with limiters to prevent spurious oscillations. The pressure–velocity coupling is resolved by algorithms like SIMPLE. The resulting large sparse linear systems are solved iteratively (multigrid, Krylov subspace methods). Boundary conditions specify inlets, walls, and far field. Postprocessing extracts forces, moments, and particle trajectories.
key_problems: Turbulence closure: no universal turbulence model exists
Grid convergence for high-Reynolds-number flows
Conjugate heat transfer and multiphysics modeling
Quantum computing to accelerate solving Navier–Stokes equations
computational_fluid_dynamics.fun_fact: The largest direct numerical simulation of turbulent channel flow used over 100 trillion grid points on the Fugaku supercomputer in 2022 and reproduced just a few seconds of real time.
