explainable_ai.name: Explainable AI
explainable_ai.mini: A black box that says 'trust me' — that's how ordinary neural networks work. Explainable AI opens the lid and shows: 'look, this is why I decided this way.'
explainable_ai.practical_application: The doctor sees not only the AI's diagnosis but also the image with the tumor highlighted to verify for themselves. The bank explains to the client why the loan was denied.
explainable_ai.description_popular: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is a field that makes the operation of machine learning models transparent to humans. Unlike traditional neural networks — 'black boxes', XAI provides an interpretation: why the model came to a particular conclusion, which features were important, and how reliable the prediction is. Approaches are divided into interpretable models (decision trees, linear models) and post-hoc explanations for already trained complex models (LIME, SHAP, gradient maps). This is critical in medicine, finance, and law, where an error can cost lives or freedom.
explainable_ai.fun_fact_popular: One of the XAI methods, SHAP, is named after Shapley from game theory — it fairly distributes the 'contribution' of each feature to the decision, like a bonus among team players.
explainable_ai.description_simple: A person brings test results, and the computer says: 'cancer.' Without explanations — it's scary. Explainable AI (XAI) turns a fortune-teller into a teacher. A neural network recognized a cat in a photo — XAI highlights the whiskers and ears that were decisive. It's as if a calculator not only showed '4' but also added: 'because 2+2.' Thus, AI ceases to be a black box and becomes a partner that says: 'look, I see this and this, so I think so.'
explainable_ai.history_simple: The problem arose in the 2010s when neural networks began making vital decisions, and no one could explain their logic. The first XAI methods emerged from model interpretation work. In 2018, the European Union introduced the right to explanation of algorithmic decisions (GDPR).
explainable_ai.how_it_works_simple: The simplest XAI method is LIME. It takes a complex model and builds a simple, understandable model around a specific example (e.g., a list of rules). Then it shows how the answer would change if details were substituted — as if we were covering parts of the image and checking whether the AI stops seeing the cat. Other methods look at which neurons in the network were most strongly activated.
explainable_ai.description: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is a research area at the intersection of machine learning, cognitive science, and human-computer interaction. The goal is to create models whose decisions can be understood and trusted by humans. Key concepts: interpretability (the degree to which internal mechanisms can be understood), explainability (the ability to provide understandable explanations), model transparency, and causality. Methods are divided into: 1) intrinsically interpretable (linear regression, decision trees, attention-based models), 2) post-hoc explanations (LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, Grad-CAM). Explanations are evaluated for reproducibility, accuracy, and consistency with human intuition.
explainable_ai.history: The black box problem intensified with the deep learning renaissance in 2012. Early work on model interpretation includes weight analysis in the 1990s, but XAI as a separate discipline took shape after 2016, when DARPA launched the Explainable AI program. The formal right to explanation of algorithmic decisions was established by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the EU.
explainable_ai.how_it_works: XAI is based on methods that approximate a complex decision function with a simple interpretable model in the local neighborhood of each example (LIME). SHAP uses game theory: the contribution of each feature is computed as its marginal contribution over all possible subsets of features. Gradient methods (Grad-CAM) visualize which parts of the input image most strongly activated the neurons of the last convolutional layer, using gradients of the target class. For text models (transformers), the attention mechanism allows highlighting important words.
key_problems: Lack of a unified metric for evaluating explanation quality.
Explanations can be misleading, creating a false sense of understanding (illusion of explanatory depth).
Trade-off between model accuracy and interpretability.
Social and legal aspects: who is responsible if a doctor makes an error by trusting the AI's explanation.
explainable_ai.fun_fact: Experiments have shown that people tend to trust even random but nicely presented explanations — this effect is called 'misleading interpretation'.

formulas.description: Shapley formula for SHAP: contribution of feature i
formulas.meaning: ϕ_i — contribution of feature i, N — set of all features, S — subset, f — model; computes the weighted average change in prediction when adding feature i to all possible subsets.

markov_chains.name: Markov chains
markov_chains.mini: A Markov chain is a random path where the next step depends only on the current position, without looking back at the past. Like in a board game where the square determines the next dice roll.
markov_chains.practical_application: Text autocomplete on your phone, Google's PageRank search algorithm, and epidemic spread models are all Markov chains.
markov_chains.description_popular: A Markov chain is a discrete random process with the Markov property: the conditional probability of the future given the present does not depend on the past. It is completely defined by an initial probability vector and a transition probability matrix P(i,j) — the chance of moving from i to j. For example, in the model of a tourist wandering along a pier, each step is random, but the direction depends only on the current spot. Chains can be ergodic (any state can be reached from any other) or absorbing (there are trap states).
markov_chains.fun_fact_popular: The PageRank algorithm, which made Google the search leader, treats the internet as a giant Markov chain, where pages are states and links are transition probabilities of an imaginary user.
markov_chains.description_simple: A Markov chain is a sequence of states (points on a diagram), where transitions between them are given by probabilities (numbers on arrows). The key condition: where the system goes next depends only on where it is now — previous steps have no influence. If it's rainy today, sunny tomorrow with a 70% chance — that's a Markov weather model.
markov_chains.history_simple: Andrey Markov, a Russian mathematician, invented these chains in 1906 while studying the alternation of vowels and consonants in Pushkin's poem “Eugene Onegin”. He calculated the transition probabilities from vowel to consonant and back.
markov_chains.how_it_works_simple: A Markov chain works as a sequence generator following probabilistic rules. Knowing the initial state and the transition table (probability matrix), you can repeatedly 'roll the dice' to determine the next step. After many steps, the chain often 'forgets' the start and settles into a stable distribution — as if a roulette wheel balances itself.
markov_chains.description: A Markov chain is a sequence of random variables {X_n} taking values in a discrete set of states, with the Markov property: P(X_{n+1}=j | X_n=i, X_{n-1}=i_{n-1}, ..., X_0=i_0) = P(X_{n+1}=j | X_n=i) = P_{ij}. If transition probabilities do not depend on n, the chain is homogeneous. Main objects of study: distribution after n steps, stationary distribution π satisfying π = πP, return time, period of a state. Fundamental theorem: for an irreducible, aperiodic, positive recurrent chain, there exists a unique stationary distribution to which distributions from any initial state converge. Just as a frog on lily pads, having forgotten its entire path, after many jumps ends up on each leaf with the same frequency.
markov_chains.history: Markov chains were introduced by A. A. Markov in 1906–1907 as a generalization of the law of large numbers to dependent trials. His motivation arose from a theoretical dispute with P. A. Nekrasov about the applicability of the central limit theorem. Markov analyzed a sequence of 20,000 letters from “Eugene Onegin” and showed that transitions between vowels and consonants are not independent. The theory was later developed by Kolmogorov, Doob, and others.
markov_chains.how_it_works: The dynamics of a Markov chain are described by powers of the transition matrix P. The distribution after n steps is μ_n = μ_0 P^n. In ergodic chains, as n→∞, μ_n → π regardless of μ_0, where π solves the system πP = π, Σ_i π_i = 1. The convergence rate is determined by the spectral gap (the difference between the unit eigenvalue and the second largest eigenvalue in modulus). For continuous time, continuous-time Markov chains are introduced with an intensity matrix Q. Applications: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms, hidden Markov models (speech recognition), DNA evolution models.
key_problems: General convergence rate for specific classes of large sparse chains
Mixing problem for spin glasses
Exact computation of stationary distributions in models with constraints
Connection with quantum Markov chains
markov_chains.fun_fact: Hidden Markov models underpin modern speech recognition systems and bioinformatics (gene finding). In them, the observed sequence is generated by a hidden Markov chain — like text corrupted by noise.

formulas.description: Stationary distribution equation
formulas.meaning: π is the row vector of stationary probabilities, P is the transition probability matrix, π_i is the probability of state i in equilibrium

formulas.description: Transition matrix over n steps
formulas.meaning: P^{(n)} is the matrix of transition probabilities between states over n steps, P is the one-step transition matrix (raised to the power n)

gamma_ray_burst.name: gamma-ray burst
gamma_ray_burst.mini: At a random point in the sky, a source flares up for an instant, a hundred times brighter than all the stars combined — the most powerful explosion since the Big Bang.
gamma_ray_burst.practical_application: Gamma-ray bursts help study the birth of black holes, and their radiation allows us to date the most distant galaxies and probe interstellar matter.
gamma_ray_burst.description_popular: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are divided into two classes: long (lasting over 2 seconds) — arising from the core collapse of a rapidly rotating massive star into a black hole, and short (under 2 seconds) — accompanying neutron star mergers. In both cases, the central engine is an accreting black hole that launches an ultra-relativistic jet, piercing the star or the ejected material shell. An observer sees a gamma-ray burst if the beam is directed toward Earth.
gamma_ray_burst.fun_fact_popular: The most distant known burst, GRB 090423, occurred 630 million years after the Big Bang — meaning its light traveled 13 billion years to reach us.
gamma_ray_burst.description_simple: A gamma-ray burst is a sudden, lasting from milliseconds to minutes, flash of gamma rays (the most energetic electromagnetic radiation), arriving from a random direction in the sky. It is the 'death cry' of a dying massive star or the merger of two neutron stars.
gamma_ray_burst.history_simple: The first gamma-ray bursts were accidentally detected in 1967 by the American Vela satellites, which were monitoring nuclear tests. For a long time their nature remained a mystery until the 1990s, when their cosmic origin was proven.
gamma_ray_burst.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a super-fast whirligig of hot gas spiraling into a black hole. Narrow jets of this gas, accelerated to near-light speeds, slam into the surrounding material and generate a flash visible across the entire Universe.
gamma_ray_burst.description: A gamma-ray burst (GRB) is a cosmic pulse of high-energy (tens of keV to tens of MeV) radiation, detected by gamma-ray observatories roughly once per day from random directions. Long GRBs (>2 s, average ~30 s) are associated with collapsars — hypernovae of type Ic-BL, where the core of a rapidly rotating massive star collapses into a black hole, forming an accretion disk and a relativistic jet. Short GRBs (<2 s, average ~0.3 s) arise from binary neutron star mergers (kilonovae). The afterglow in X-rays, optical, and radio persists for days to weeks, following a power-law decay.
gamma_ray_burst.history: Discovered on July 2, 1967, by the American Vela 4a satellite, which recorded a double flash of gamma rays. Initially thought to be signs of extraterrestrial civilizations. In 1997, the Italian-Dutch satellite BeppoSAX first measured the afterglow coordinates of GRB 970508, establishing its extragalactic nature. In 2017, the joint detection of GW170817 and GRB 170817A definitively confirmed the link between short bursts and kilonovae.
gamma_ray_burst.how_it_works: The central engine is a compact object (black hole or rapidly rotating neutron star — magnetar) surrounded by an accretion disk. Energy is extracted through neutrino cooling or the Blandford–Znajek electromagnetic mechanism, forming a collimated jet with a Lorentz factor >100. Internal shock waves within the jet produce the prompt gamma-ray emission, while the afterglow arises as the jet decelerates against the interstellar medium, according to the Bland–McKee model.
key_problems: Physics of relativistic jet generation and collimation
Nature of the central engine in particularly long (ultra-long) bursts
Origin of repeating and unusually soft bursts
Precise mechanism of energy transfer in the jet and conversion into gamma-ray emission
gamma_ray_burst.fun_fact: If a nearby gamma-ray burst exploded within a few thousand light-years, the radiation flux could sterilize Earth's surface, causing a mass extinction — such a scenario is considered a possible cause of one of the biosphere crises.

formulas.description: Amati relation: peak photon energy is proportional to the square root of the isotropic energy
formulas.meaning: E_{\text{p,i}} — peak photon energy in the burst spectrum, E_{\text{iso}} — isotropic equivalent energy emitted in the gamma-ray band

binary_star.name: binary star
binary_star.mini: Two suns chase each other against a purple sky. A gravitational waltz holds them on eternal orbits around an invisible center.
binary_star.practical_application: Binary stars serve as cosmic scales, allowing measurement of stellar masses and discovery of invisible objects like black holes. Their mergers generate gravitational waves and supernovae—forges of heavy elements.
binary_star.description_popular: A binary star is a system of two stars orbiting a common center of mass. Periods can range from hours to millions of years. Such pairs are often born together from a single gas cloud, becoming true twins. Their dance allows direct determination of stellar masses—a fundamental characteristic governing stellar evolution. Binaries come in visual (seen separately), spectroscopic (detected by Doppler shift—the change in light frequency due to motion), eclipsing (when one star periodically blocks the other), and astrometric (an invisible companion revealed by wobbles of the visible star).
binary_star.fun_fact_popular: The North Star, famously a guiding beacon, is itself a triple system: the bright supergiant is accompanied by two small companions.
binary_star.description_simple: A binary star is a pair of suns circling a common center of gravity (balance point). They are bound by gravity (the force of attraction between any masses). Like figure skaters holding hands, they spin without falling into each other. For instance, Sirius has a companion—a white dwarf, as heavy as the Sun but as compact as Earth. Most stars in the sky are not solitary; they live in such duets.
binary_star.history_simple: The first binary star was noticed in 1650 when Giovanni Riccioli saw Mizar split into two. A century later, William Herschel proved that pairs move in orbits. Today we know: there are more binary systems than single ones.
binary_star.how_it_works_simple: Two luminaries move, obeying the law of universal gravitation (the more massive and closer the bodies, the stronger the attraction). The faster the rotation, the stronger the bond. By measuring speed and distance, astronomers weigh stars—just as one can determine the mass of a weight by the tension of the rope used to spin it.
binary_star.description: A binary star is a system of two gravitationally bound stellar objects orbiting a barycenter. Classification includes visual, spectroscopic, eclipsing, and astrometric pairs. Component masses are determined via Kepler's third law in Newtonian form: the sum of masses is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis and inversely proportional to the square of the orbital period. In close systems, mass transfer is possible through the Roche lobe—an equipotential surface bounding each star's gravitational domain. Semi-detached and contact binaries exhibit accretion disks, common envelopes, and X-ray emission. Compact pairs (white dwarfs, neutron stars, black holes) upon merger become sources of gravitational waves and kilonovae. From swift pairs whose dance lasts hours to majestic duets stretched over millennia, each binary star remains a cosmic choreography where gravity writes notes audible across billions of years.
binary_star.history: The duality of Mizar was first recorded by Riccioli in 1650. In the late 18th century, William Herschel began systematic searches for binaries and proved their orbital motion. The 19th century brought computations of the first orbits. In the 20th century, spectroscopy unveiled invisible duets, and space telescopes allowed us to discern pairs in other galaxies. Today, the Gaia mission is building a three-dimensional map of billions of stars, revealing the architecture of binary systems in the Milky Way.
binary_star.how_it_works: Motion follows Newtonian mechanics (or general relativity for compact objects). Period and distance yield total mass. If the orbital plane lies along the line of sight, eclipses are observed with characteristic light curves. When the Roche lobe is filled, matter streams onto the accretor, forming a disk and a hot spot. This process explains cataclysmic variables, X-ray pulsars, and Type Ia supernovae. Mergers of neutron stars and black holes are detected by LIGO and Virgo detectors via gravitational-wave bursts. Kepler's third law plus spectroscopy unveil the masses of exoplanets in binary systems.
key_problems: How high is the fraction of multiple systems depending on mass and environment?
What mechanisms govern common-envelope evolution?
How do wide binaries survive in the tidal field of the Galaxy?
Why is there a mass gap for stellar-origin black holes?
binary_star.fun_fact: The system PSR J0737−3039 is a double pulsar, where both neutron stars emit radio pulses. It is a unique laboratory for testing general relativity: the measured periastron shift matches Einstein's calculations to within 0.05% accuracy.

formulas.description: Newtonian form of Kepler's third law for the sum of masses in a binary system
formulas.meaning: M_1, M_2 — component masses, a — semi-major axis, P — orbital period, G — gravitational constant (6.67430×10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²)

neutron_star_merger.name: neutron star merger
neutron_star_merger.mini: Two superdense stellar clumps, each the size of a city, crashed into each other on the galaxy's edge—and ejected clouds of incandescent metal, from which new planets will later form.
neutron_star_merger.practical_application: Such mergers are cosmic forges of gold, platinum, and uranium, without which many rare metals would not exist on Earth.
neutron_star_merger.description_popular: A neutron star merger is a rarest cosmic event where two compact objects lock in a dance, losing orbital energy through gravitational waves, and ultimately merge, forming a black hole or a massive neutron star. The process is accompanied by a short gamma-ray burst and a kilonova—the afterglow from radioactive decay of freshly forged nuclei.
neutron_star_merger.fun_fact_popular: The 2017 collision produced an amount of gold exceeding the mass of the entire Earth by 10 times—that's where the shine of your wedding ring comes from.
neutron_star_merger.description_simple: Neutron stars are ultra-dense remnants (mass of the Sun, size of a city) of exploded giant stars. When two such stars, orbiting, lose energy due to the emission of gravitational waves (ripples in spacetime), they spiral together and collide. The collision produces a kilonova—an explosion thousands of times brighter than a typical nova, momentarily outshining entire galaxies.
neutron_star_merger.history_simple: The first direct detection of a neutron star merger was in 2017 by the LIGO and Virgo detectors, simultaneously with telescopes that saw its light.
neutron_star_merger.how_it_works_simple: Imagine two magnets flying toward each other. Their superfluid interiors are torn apart by tidal forces, spilling neutron-rich material that instantly builds nuclei of heavy elements—like gold and platinum.
neutron_star_merger.description: A neutron star merger is the final stage of a binary system's evolution, whose inspiral is accelerated by gravitational wave emission. Upon contact, the ultra-dense (~10^14 g/cm³) objects deform, matter heats to billions of degrees, and the r-process (rapid neutron capture) forges half of the elements heavier than iron in the universe. The merger's outcome is either a supermassive neutron star that subsequently collapses into a black hole, or a direct collapse forming an accretion disk and an ultra-relativistic jet that pierces the shell of ejected material.
neutron_star_merger.history: The first detection of GW170817 on August 17, 2017, jointly by LIGO (USA) and Virgo (Italy) confirmed the nature of short gamma-ray bursts and launched the era of multi-messenger astronomy. The event was localized in the elliptical galaxy NGC 4993, and subsequent observations in optical, X-ray, and radio revealed details of the kilonova. Theoretical foundations were predicted as early as the 1970s (Clark, Early), but only the development of gravitational-wave observatories made direct detection possible.
neutron_star_merger.how_it_works: The inspiral is described by the gradual loss of energy through gravitational radiation according to general relativity. Tidal forces disrupt the neutron stars, ejecting neutronized material where rapid neutron capture (r-process) builds heavy-element nuclei. The resulting accretion disk, rotating with enormous angular velocity, collimates a relativistic jet, generating a gamma-ray burst. The thermal energy from radioactive decay in the ejected material powers the kilonova.
key_problems: Equation of state of neutron matter at supernuclear densities
Mechanism of launching a relativistic jet
Maximum mass of a neutron star and merger outcome (black hole or stable neutron star)
Exact nucleosynthetic efficiency and contribution to galactic enrichment
neutron_star_merger.fun_fact: The first signal detected since the start of gravitational-wave astronomy, GW150914, was from a black hole merger, while GW170817 was the first from neutron stars, and it was discovered just two days after Virgo came online, allowing almost immediate localization of the event.

formulas.description: Chirp mass characterizing the rate of frequency change of the gravitational signal
formulas.meaning: ℳ is the chirp mass, m₁, m₂ are the masses of the merging objects, measured in units of solar mass

topological_defect.name: topological defect
topological_defect.mini: Solidifying water cracks into fissures — just so the young Universe, cooling down, gave birth to eternal folds in its fabric.
topological_defect.practical_application: If such cosmic strings are found, they will explain anomalies in the microwave background and serve as natural gravitational lenses for distant galaxies.
topological_defect.description_popular: Topological defects are stable field configurations that cannot be smoothed out without breaking continuity. They arise in grand unified theories during symmetry breaking in the course of inflationary expansion. Three main types: domain walls (two-dimensional), cosmic strings (one-dimensional), and monopoles (point-like). The most promising for observation are strings — infinitely thin tubes of false vacuum with enormous linear density (~10^22 g/cm).
topological_defect.fun_fact_popular: A closed loop of cosmic string the size of a pea weighs as much as an entire mountain — and, trembling, emits powerful gravitational waves that future detectors could register.
topological_defect.description_simple: A topological defect is a ripple in spacetime that survived from the epoch when the Universe changed its 'aggregate state' (like the transition of water to ice) right after the Big Bang. At such junctions, defects arise: strings (threads of pure energy) or walls (flat membranes), left frozen while the rest of space became homogeneous.
topological_defect.history_simple: The idea was proposed by physicist Tom Kibble in 1976 while studying phase transitions in the early Universe. He realized that the cooling cosmic 'matter' must inevitably have formed such flaws.
topological_defect.how_it_works_simple: When water freezes, molecules align into a crystal lattice, but at the boundaries of differently aligned regions, defects emerge. Exactly the same in the early Universe: the fields that determine the forces of nature rearranged, and where the 'alignment' did not match up, tense threads or planes remained.
topological_defect.description: A topological defect is a stable non-trivial solution of field equations, arising from spontaneous symmetry breaking during kinetic phase transitions in the early Universe. Classification by inhomogeneity dimension: domain walls (co-dimension one), strings (line-like), monopoles (point-like), and textures (non-topological). Cosmic strings are described by the Nielsen-Olesen model as vortices in the Abelian Higgs model; their tension is on the order of Gμ ~ 10^{-6} (where G is the gravitational constant), leading to characteristic gravitational effects.
topological_defect.history: Tom Kibble in 1976 connected the mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking in quantum field theory with cosmological phase transitions. Subsequently, Yakov Zel'dovich and Alexander Vilenkin developed the theory of cosmic strings as gravitational lenses and sources of gravitational waves. The search for monopoles in the 1980s stimulated the development of inflation theory, which would 'inflate' the density of primordial defects to an unobservable level, but strings and walls can remain if the formation scale is below the Planck scale.
topological_defect.how_it_works: Spontaneous symmetry breaking leads to a degenerate ground state of the field. When the Universe cools below a critical temperature, uncorrelated vacua are randomly chosen in causally disconnected regions, creating a nontrivial field topology with a nontrivial homotopy class. For strings, this is a π_1 defect: upon circling around the string, the phase of the Higgs field winds, forming a closed loop that traps energy. Local stability is ensured by an energy barrier: to 'smooth out' the string, one would need to overcome the cost of flipping the field throughout the entire volume.
key_problems: Confirmation of existence: no direct observations
Contribution to the gravitational-wave background spectrum
Mechanism of formation of supermassive strings in inflationary scenarios
Exact value of string tension Gμ
topological_defect.fun_fact: A cosmic string 10^{-29} meters thick, stretched over billions of light-years, could, moving at about c, create characteristic double images of distant galaxies through gravitational lensing.

cosmic_reionization.name: Reionization
cosmic_reionization.mini: The Universe was a dark ocean. Suddenly countless beacons lit up, dispelling the fog. Reionization is the moment when the first stars and galaxies burned away the cosmic hydrogen fog.
cosmic_reionization.practical_application: It helps understand how galaxies formed. Modern telescopes search for this ancient light to map the early Universe.
cosmic_reionization.description_popular: The epoch of cosmic reionization is a phase transition of the intergalactic medium from neutral to ionized, triggered by the first luminous objects. Evidence: Gunn-Peterson absorption in quasar spectra (complete disappearance of radiation at wavelengths shorter than the Lyman-alpha line) and large-scale polarization of the cosmic microwave background measured by WMAP and Planck.
cosmic_reionization.fun_fact_popular: Reionization was not a single flash but lasted from about 150 million to 1 billion years after the Big Bang — like a summer dawn slowly flooding the sky with light.
cosmic_reionization.description_simple: After the Big Bang, the Universe filled with neutral hydrogen — a thick gaseous 'fog'. When the first stars ignited, their powerful ultraviolet light began to break hydrogen atoms apart (ionize them). Gradually the fog disappeared, and the Universe became transparent to light. This process took hundreds of millions of years.
cosmic_reionization.history_simple: In the 1960s, astronomers noticed something strange in the light of distant quasars (bright nuclei of early galaxies). The light carried traces of traveling through an environment that was once foggy and then cleared. Thus the idea of the reionization epoch was born. Key observations were made with the Sloan telescope and later the WMAP and Planck satellites.
cosmic_reionization.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a room full of steam. The first lamps (stars) emit hard radiation that breaks the steam molecules into transparent components. Similarly, ultraviolet light from the first sources ionized intergalactic hydrogen, making the cosmic 'room' clear. Ionization spread in bubbles around sources and then merged into a single transparent network.
cosmic_reionization.description: Cosmic reionization is the epoch when neutral hydrogen, which filled the Universe after recombination (z~1100), was ionized by ultraviolet radiation from the first astrophysical sources. Modern data indicate that the process began around z~15 and ended by z~6, with the main sources likely being stars in small galaxies, with a contribution from quasars at later stages. Reionization left an imprint on the cosmic microwave background in the form of optical depth τ ~ 0.054 according to Planck, and also in the suppression of small galaxy formation. A key observable marker is the Gunn-Peterson trough: complete absorption of radiation in the blue part of quasar spectra due to scattering on neutral hydrogen.
cosmic_reionization.history: The idea arose after the discovery of quasars by Maarten Schmidt in 1963. James Gunn and Bruce Peterson in 1965 predicted that intergalactic hydrogen should cause complete absorption of short-wavelength radiation from distant objects. In the mid-1990s, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey found quasars at z>6 exhibiting exactly this pattern, confirming the existence of a neutral medium at early times. Subsequent measurements of CMB polarization by the WMAP (2003) and Planck (2013) satellites allowed estimating the timing of reionization.
cosmic_reionization.how_it_works: Ultraviolet photons with energy above 13.6 eV ionize hydrogen atoms. Ionization spreads as expanding regions around sources, forming ionization fronts. Since the intergalactic medium is inhomogeneous, the process proceeded 'inside-out': regions with high galaxy density ionized first, then voids. The main sources are massive first-generation stars (Population III) and accreting black holes. Reionization heats the gas to ~10^4 K, which hinders the formation of new dwarf galaxies and explains their small number in the local Universe.
key_problems: Which sources contributed most to ionization — stars or quasars?
How exactly did the process proceed in space: from dense nodes to voids or vice versa?
What role did faint dwarf galaxies play, which are still invisible even to the best telescopes?
How did reionization affect the formation of dwarf galaxies and their dark halos?
cosmic_reionization.fun_fact: The epoch of reionization is often called the 'cosmic dawn' because it ended the 'dark ages' of the Universe. Interestingly, the cosmic microwave background carries information not only about recombination but also about reionization: scattering off free electrons leaves a characteristic polarization signal, which was first detected in 2002 by the DASI experiment.

large_scale_structure.name: large-scale structure
large_scale_structure.mini: A soap bubble three hundred million light-years across, its walls glowing with galaxies. The Universe is woven into a colossal foam of filaments and voids, where gravity has been gathering matter for billions of years.
large_scale_structure.practical_application: A map of the cosmic web is a chronicle of the Universe's growth. It tells of dark matter, dark energy, and the first moments after the Big Bang, and also serves as a compass for finding galaxy clusters.
large_scale_structure.description_popular: On scales of billions of light-years, the cosmos resembles a cellular network: galaxies, gas, and dark matter are stretched along filaments converging in rich clusters, outlining colossal voids. This 'cosmic web' is the largest known pattern of nature. Its contours are set by the distribution of dark matter, into whose gravitational wells ordinary matter collects. The structure is hierarchical: small halos formed first, then merged into more massive ones. Statistically, it is described by the two-point correlation function and the power spectrum of density fluctuations.
large_scale_structure.fun_fact_popular: The KBC void stretches over a billion light-years, and our Milky Way lies near its centre, so we live inside the emptiest region.
large_scale_structure.description_simple: The large-scale structure is the pattern formed by clusters and filaments of galaxies. Inside a void a billion light-years across, you wouldn't see a single galaxy with the naked eye. If you step back billions of light-years, it turns out that galaxies are not scattered randomly but are gathered into a sponge. The dense spots are cosmic cities (clusters), connected by filaments, with voids yawning between them. This foam grew from tiny inhomogeneities in the early Universe.
large_scale_structure.history_simple: Edwin Hubble in the 1920s proved that galaxies are separate islands beyond the Milky Way. In the 1980s, redshift surveys of thousands of galaxies revealed a foamy pattern. Vera Rubin showed that invisible dark matter governs the motion of galaxies and serves as the framework of this network.
large_scale_structure.how_it_works_simple: The young Universe can be imagined as an ocean with a gentle swell. Where the density was slightly higher, gravity drew in more matter. Over billions of years, the denser spots turned into galaxies and clusters, while the rarified spots became voids. Today the structure is expanding, but gravity continues to sculpt it according to Einstein's laws (general relativity).
large_scale_structure.description: The large-scale structure (LSS) covers the distribution of matter from tens to thousands of megaparsecs. Characteristic elements include voids, walls, filaments, and galaxy clusters, forming a foamy 'cosmic web'. The statistical measure of LSS is the spatial power spectrum P(k) and the correlation function. The seed perturbations, imprinted in the cosmic microwave background as temperature anisotropies, are amplified by gravitational instability and enter a nonlinear stage. The standard ΛCDM model (cold dark matter + cosmological constant) successfully reproduces the observed structure in numerical simulations. Baryon acoustic oscillations, frozen into the galaxy distribution, serve as a standard ruler for cosmological measurements. The wall of galaxies, the foam of voids—that is the very 'soap film' on the scale of the Universe, a cast of its infant irregularity, stretched by time and dark energy.
large_scale_structure.history: Hubble in the 1920s established the extragalactic nature of spiral nebulae and the linear law of redshift. The first redshift surveys (CfA, 2dF) in the 1980s–2000s laid bare the foamy morphology. The COBE satellite (1992) detected the primordial fluctuations—the seeds of the future structure. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) covered millions of galaxies, confirming ΛCDM. The contributions of Vera Rubin (rotation curves) and Fritz Zwicky (hidden mass in clusters) pointed to the dominance of dark matter in shaping the LSS.
large_scale_structure.how_it_works: Structure growth is governed by gravitational instability in an expanding background. In the linear approximation, the density contrast δ evolves as δ ∝ a in the matter-dominated era. After recombination, baryons fall into the potential wells of dark matter. The power spectrum bears the imprint of baryon acoustic oscillations—frozen sound waves from the primordial plasma. The nonlinear stage is described by the Vlasov-Poisson equations for collisionless dark matter and hydrodynamics for gas, taking into account feedback from star formation and active nuclei. Numerical models reproduce voids, filaments, and hierarchical clustering, creating virtual universes in the computer.
key_problems: What is the nature of dark matter and dark energy, which determine the dynamics of LSS?
How does baryonic physics (star formation, black holes) regulate the population of halos?
Can the neutrino mass be extracted from the suppression of small-scale power?
How did the first stars ignite and the first structures form in the dark ages?
large_scale_structure.fun_fact: The Sloan Great Wall—a filament of galaxies 1.37 billion light-years long—was long considered the record holder; but then the Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall was found, stretching ~10 billion light-years, which calls into question homogeneity on large scales.

formulas.description: Friedmann equation for a flat universe with matter and a cosmological constant
formulas.meaning: H is the Hubble parameter, H_0 is the Hubble constant (~70 km/s/Mpc), a is the scale factor, Ω_m is the relative density of matter, Ω_Λ is the relative density of dark energy

multi_messenger_astronomy.name: multi-messenger astronomy
multi_messenger_astronomy.mini: Astronomy where the sky is 'sensed' through multiple channels at once: light, gravitational ripples, particles — like a doctor diagnosing by pulse, temperature, and X-ray simultaneously.
multi_messenger_astronomy.practical_application: Early warning of neutron star collisions and understanding the processes that create gold and platinum.
multi_messenger_astronomy.description_popular: Multi-messenger astronomy combines electromagnetic radiation, gravitational waves, neutrinos, and potentially cosmic rays. Gravitational-wave detectors LIGO and Virgo register mergers of compact objects through oscillations of test masses with precision down to a thousandth of the proton diameter. Neutrino telescopes like IceCube scan a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice for Cherenkov radiation from high-energy neutrinos. Coordinated observations have made it possible to measure the speed of gravity — it matches the speed of light to within 10^−15 — and to determine that neutron star collisions do indeed produce heavy elements.
multi_messenger_astronomy.fun_fact_popular: On July 4, 2012, a supermassive black hole tore apart a star, and the IceCube detector recorded a neutrino with an energy of 200 TeV — 30 times higher than particles in the Large Hadron Collider; astronomers still debate whether it was connected to that event.
multi_messenger_astronomy.description_simple: Until recently, all information from space reached us only in the form of light — from radio waves to gamma rays. Multi-messenger astronomy adds two more 'senses' to this: gravitational wave detectors that capture ripples in spacetime, and neutrino observatories that register ghostly particles passing straight through planets. Together they create a three-dimensional picture of events — like a multi-track recording instead of a silent film.
multi_messenger_astronomy.history_simple: The first channel beyond light was neutrinos from supernova 1987A: the Japanese Kamiokande detector caught 11 particles. Gravitational waves were registered in 2015 by the LIGO facilities. And in 2017, for the first time, all three channels converged: from a neutron star merger, a gravitational wave, a gamma-ray burst, and an optical signal arrived simultaneously — the event was followed by thousands of astronomers.
multi_messenger_astronomy.how_it_works_simple: Each messenger tells its own story. Light shows what is heated and what substances are made of. Gravitational waves — like bass notes: they tell us the masses and speeds of the bodies involved. Neutrinos burst out from the very furnace where even light gets stuck, carrying information about thermonuclear reactions. By combining the evidence, scientists reconstruct the full scenario of the catastrophe, just as from a sound, a flash, and the smell of smoke we understand what burned in a fire.
multi_messenger_astronomy.description: Multi-messenger (multimessenger) astronomy is an approach to studying the Universe in which astrophysical sources are investigated simultaneously through several cosmic messenger channels: electromagnetic radiation (from radio to gamma rays), gravitational waves, neutrinos, and, in the future, cosmic rays. Each type of messenger carries complementary information about the processes underlying astrophysical phenomena. Gravitational waves allow us to 'hear' the dynamics of massive objects, neutrinos let us peer into dense regions where photons scatter, and electromagnetic observations provide context and localization. Data synthesis requires coordination of networks of ground-based and space-based observatories, global alert systems, and interdisciplinary analysis involving particle physics, nuclear astrophysics, and general relativity.
multi_messenger_astronomy.history: The idea of detecting cosmic neutrinos was discussed as early as the mid-20th century, but the first real event was the arrival of neutrinos from supernova SN1987A in 1987, recorded by the Kamiokande-II, IMB, and the Baksan Neutrino Observatory. Gravitational waves were predicted by Einstein in 1916, but direct detection occurred only in 2015 by the LIGO collaboration (Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne, Barry Barish — Nobel Prize 2017). The breakthrough of multi-messenger astronomy came on August 17, 2017, with the observation of the neutron star merger GW170817: the gravitational signal was registered by LIGO and Virgo, 1.7 seconds later a gamma-ray burst by the Fermi and INTEGRAL telescopes, and then hundreds of instruments worldwide tracked the optical, infrared, and radio emission from the kilonova. This event confirmed the link between kilonovae and the production of heavy elements (r-process).
multi_messenger_astronomy.how_it_works: Each messenger obeys its own physical laws. Gravitational waves are described by Einstein's equations and propagate at the speed of light, interacting extremely weakly with matter, which allows them to carry information about the most energetic processes, such as mergers of black holes and neutron stars. Neutrinos, having tiny mass and weak interaction, escape from practically any astrophysical crucible, for example, from the collapsing cores of supernovae, where densities are so high that photons are trapped. Electromagnetic waves provide a detailed picture of thermal and non-thermal processes, allowing us to reconstruct chemical composition, temperature, and magnetic fields. Joint analysis uses the arrival time, direction, and spectra of signals to build a complete model of the source. For instance, the gravitational-wave signal gives the distance and mass of the system, and optical identification gives the redshift, providing an independent measure of the Hubble constant.
key_problems: Creating a rapid global alert system that unites all types of detectors in real time
Developing methods for joint data processing with vastly different angular resolutions
Detecting common sources of high-energy neutrinos and gravitational waves to elucidate the nature of particle accelerators
multi_messenger_astronomy.fun_fact: The GW170817 signal lasted about 100 seconds and during that time radiated in gravitational waves an energy equivalent to converting roughly three solar masses into pure energy according to the formula E=mc².

filtering.name: Filtering
filtering.mini: Filtering separates the important from the background — just like a coffee filter mesh lets liquid through while keeping the grounds.
filtering.practical_application: Noise cancellation in headphones, cleaning CT scans from artifacts, extracting speech from recordings.
filtering.description_popular: Imagine a stream of water hitting a filter mesh. Only drops of a certain size slip through — the rest are broken up and rejected. Similarly, a digital filter lets through vibrations (frequencies) of a selected range, damping the others. The algorithm acts as a mathematical sieve: it multiplies each frequency by a transmission coefficient — from full approval to total rejection.
filtering.fun_fact_popular: Filters are everywhere: in Bluetooth headphones, active noise cancellation generates counter-sound to quiet the hum of an airplane. This is not a brute-force filter, but a clever one.
filtering.description_simple: Filtering is like making coffee. Coffee grounds are doused with boiling water, but the final drink must be clean. The mesh retains large particles, letting only the aromatic liquid through. Similarly, a data filter sifts out unwanted noise, leaving a useful signal — a conversation partner's voice, a melody, a sharp image.
filtering.history_simple: Simple filters have been known for thousands of years: people strained water through cloth. Mathematical methods of signal processing began to develop in the 19th century with the work of Jean Fourier.
filtering.how_it_works_simple: A filter works like a sieve with cells of a certain size. Fast changes in a signal (like crackling) pass through high frequencies, smooth ones — through low ones. By adjusting the cell size, you can let through only what you need.
filtering.description: Filtering in a broad sense is the process of selective transformation of a signal. In signal processing, a filter is understood as a device or algorithm that changes the spectrum of the input. A linear time-invariant filter is described by the convolution of the input signal with an impulse response, which in the frequency domain corresponds to multiplying the Fourier transforms. This allows cutting out interfering bands, smoothing noise, and extracting trends. In practice, filters with finite (FIR) and infinite (IIR) impulse responses are used, each with its own trade-offs in phase distortion and computational complexity.
filtering.history: The mathematical foundations were laid by Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier, who showed in 1807 that any periodic signal can be decomposed into a sum of sinusoids. The idea of spectral decomposition became a cornerstone. In the 1930s, with the advent of radio engineering, engineers such as Harry Nyquist and Claude Shannon formalized criteria for sampling and reconstructing signals. With the rise of digital computers in the second half of the 20th century, filtering methods became purely computational, giving rise to powerful algorithms like the fast Fourier transform (Cooley and Tukey, 1965).
filtering.how_it_works: Principle of convolution: the output signal y(t) is obtained as a sum of weighted past values of the input x(τ), where the weights are given by the impulse response h(t). In the frequency domain, this is equivalent to the product of complex spectra Y(f)=X(f)·H(f), where H(f) is the filter's frequency response. By shaping H(f), desired frequencies are attenuated or amplified. For example, a low-pass filter has H(f)≈1 for f<f_c and H(f)≈0 for f>f_c. Physically, in analog electronics this is implemented with RC circuits, digitally — with difference equations.
key_problems: Adaptive filtering of non-stationary signals with unknown statistics
Blind deconvolution: recovering the original signal without knowledge of the medium's impulse response
Nonlinear filtering to combat impulsive interference and non-Gaussian noise
Real-time filtering of ultra-high-resolution signals with low latency
filtering.fun_fact: Active noise cancellation in headphones uses an adaptive filter that, based on a microphone inside the earcup, generates 'anti-noise' with the same amplitude but shifted in phase by 180°. The system constantly adjusts to cancel engine hum even as flight altitude changes.

formulas.description: Convolution is the basis of linear filtering in the time domain.
formulas.meaning: y(t) — output signal; x(t) — input signal; h(t) — impulse response of the filter; τ — integration variable, delay time.

formulas.description: Multiplication of spectra in the frequency domain is equivalent to convolution.
formulas.meaning: Y(f) — complex spectrum of the output; H(f) — frequency response of the filter; X(f) — complex spectrum of the input; f — frequency.

hawking_radiation.name: Hawking radiation
hawking_radiation.mini: A black hole is a leaking bucket. Over an unimaginably long time, it loses energy drop by drop. This faint thermal glow is Hawking radiation.
hawking_radiation.practical_application: Shows that black holes are not eternal. Links gravity with quantum physics, a step towards a unified theory of nature.
hawking_radiation.description_popular: Hawking radiation arises from quantum effects at the horizon. The strong gravitational field tears apart virtual particle pairs, dooming one to fall in and letting the other escape. The escaping particle becomes real, carrying away energy. To a distant observer, the black hole emits a thermal spectrum with a temperature inversely proportional to its mass.
hawking_radiation.fun_fact_popular: A black hole with the mass of the Sun would evaporate in about 10^67 years — far longer than the age of the Universe.
hawking_radiation.description_simple: Stephen Hawking realized that black holes are not completely black. Right at the point of no return (the event horizon), pairs of particles are constantly born from the void (virtual particles). Sometimes one falls in and the other flies away. The escaping one carries away a tiny fraction of the black hole’s mass, causing it to shrink over time.
hawking_radiation.history_simple: In the 1970s, Hawking applied quantum mechanics to black holes. He was inspired by Jacob Bekenstein’s idea that black holes have entropy (a measure of disorder). Hawking’s calculations showed that black holes must emit radiation — a result that stunned physicists.
hawking_radiation.how_it_works_simple: Quantum uncertainty allows energy to briefly turn into particle pairs near the horizon. Usually they annihilate immediately, but if one particle falls into the hole and the other escapes, the hole loses mass and appears to glow. The smaller the hole, the hotter the glow.
hawking_radiation.description: Hawking radiation is a predicted quantum effect whereby a black hole emits a stream of particles with a blackbody spectrum. It arises from the evolution of the vacuum in the curved spacetime of a collapsing star: to a distant observer, the vacuum state appears as a state with a non-zero particle number. The radiation temperature of a non-rotating black hole of mass M is T = ħc³/(8πGMk_B), implying an entropy S = A/(4l_P²). The radiation leads to evaporation and entails the information paradox.
hawking_radiation.history: In 1971, Bekenstein proposed that the area of a black hole’s horizon is proportional to its entropy. Hawking was initially skeptical, but by 1974, applying quantum field theory in curved space (specifically, the Schwarzschild metric), he derived the existence of thermal radiation. This united thermodynamics and general relativity and gave rise to the information loss paradox, still debated today.
hawking_radiation.how_it_works: Near the horizon, the gravitational field gradient tidally separates virtual pairs. One particle acquires negative energy and falls in, reducing the hole’s mass; the other escapes as a real particle with positive energy. The energy spectrum is strictly Planckian with a temperature of about 6×10⁻⁸ K for a solar-mass black hole. For small primordial black holes, the temperature can be enormous, and the final stage of evaporation is an explosion. The process is universal and independent of the details of the collapse.
key_problems: Information paradox: does information falling into a black hole disappear, violating the unitarity of quantum mechanics?
Trans-Planckian problem: how do modes with ultra-high frequencies at the horizon produce low-energy radiation?
Final stage of evaporation: does the hole leave a stable remnant or disappear completely?
Observability: the radiation is too weak for known stellar-mass black holes, but could be detected from primordial black holes.
hawking_radiation.fun_fact: Hawking radiation means that a black hole is not entirely black. For a solar-mass black hole, the temperature is only about 60 billionths of a kelvin — colder than the cosmic microwave background, so today such holes grow by absorbing background photons rather than evaporating.

formulas.description: Hawking temperature for a non-rotating black hole of mass M
formulas.meaning: T — Hawking temperature, ħ — reduced Planck constant (ħ ≈ 1.0546×10⁻³⁴ J·s), c — speed of light (c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s), G — gravitational constant (G ≈ 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²), M — mass of the black hole, k_B — Boltzmann constant (k_B ≈ 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K)

microlensing.name: microlensing
microlensing.mini: A distant star suddenly brightens for several weeks and then fades back. This is an invisible lens—a dark sphere passing exactly in front of it—curving space and focusing the light like a magnifying glass.
microlensing.practical_application: Microlensing reveals 'invisibles': lone rogue planets, black holes, dark dwarfs. This is how dark matter is mapped and distant icy worlds are discovered.
microlensing.description_popular: Gravitational microlensing is a phenomenon where an unresolved massive object (with mass ranging from a planet to a star) temporarily magnifies a distant source. Light rays are deflected by the lens's gravity, forming two images that merge into one spot. Amplification depends on the alignment and mass of the lens, reaching a maximum at the smallest angular distance. The light curve has a characteristic symmetry, and when a planetary companion is present, it produces sharp spikes—caustics (sharp brightness peaks). The method does not require the lens itself to shine, making it ideal for searching for substellar bodies and dark clumps.
microlensing.fun_fact_popular: In 2017, microlensing revealed a lone planet the size of Jupiter wandering without a parent star through interstellar darkness.
microlensing.description_simple: Microlensing is nature's magnifying glass. A typical event lasts a month, and the star becomes several times brighter. When a massive object (star, planet) passes exactly between a distant star and Earth, its gravity bends the light rays. The distant star brightens for a while. From the shape of this brightening, astronomers determine the mass and distance of the lens, even if it does not shine itself.
microlensing.history_simple: Albert Einstein derived this effect in 1936, but thought it impossible to observe. It was not until 1993 that astronomers detected the first microlensing event: a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud brightened exactly as predicted by theory.
microlensing.how_it_works_simple: The gravity of a massive body warps the fabric of spacetime (the unified stage where events unfold). A passing ray goes around this warp. When the body, source, and observer align, an Einstein ring (a perfect circle of light) appears—so tiny that telescopes only see the total magnification. The rise and fall last for weeks—a unique signature of an invisible object.
microlensing.description: Microlensing is a transient regime of gravitational lensing with lens masses ranging from planetary to stellar (10²²–10³³ kg). The angular separation of images is on the order of microarcseconds, unresolvable directly; what is observed is a flux magnification. For a point lens, the light curve follows the Paczynski shape: A(u) = (u²+2)/(u√(u²+4)), where u is the angular source–lens distance in units of the Einstein radius. The Einstein radius θ_E = √[(4GM/c²)(D_ls/(D_l D_s))] sets the scale. Binary lenses and lenses with planets create caustic networks; when the source crosses a caustic, it produces sharp peaks that reveal the system's parameters. Microlensing is used for exoplanet statistics (including free-floating ones), searches for massive compact halo objects (MACHOs), and studying stellar atmospheres through chromatic effects. Thus a fleeting flash in the night becomes the signature of another world, momentarily caught in the focus of a gravitational lens.
microlensing.history: Einstein in 1936 calculated the magnification for a star lens, but considered the event incredibly rare. In the 1960s, Refsdal and others pointed out its observational potential. The first detection came in 1993 by the MACHO project: monitoring millions of stars confirmed dark compact bodies in the Milky Way's halo. Surveys like OGLE and MOA now record thousands of events per year, discovering exoplanets and placing constraints on dark matter.
microlensing.how_it_works: The lens equation relates the true and observed positions of the source. For a point mass, magnification is maximum at minimum u. The lens's motion relative to the line of sight gives a time-dependent u(t), producing a symmetric light curve of duration t_E. With a second mass (a planet), critical curves and caustics appear in the source plane; when the source crosses a caustic, the brightness changes sharply. Analysis of such anomalies yields the mass ratio and projected separation. Chromatic microlensing uses the absorption difference between the center and edge of the source disk, enabling reconstruction of the brightness profile of a distant star.
key_problems: What is the mass function of free-floating planets?
Can microlensing confirm or exclude primordial black holes as dark matter?
How to break degenerate parameters in complex events (mass–distance)?
Full characterization of orbital motion in binary lenses through continuous observations.
microlensing.fun_fact: The first planet discovered by microlensing—OGLE-2003-BLG-235/MOA-2003-BLG-53, a cold Jupiter orbiting a red dwarf at 17,000 light-years—was spotted through a 20-day anomaly in the light curve.

formulas.description: Angular radius of the Einstein ring for a point mass
formulas.meaning: θ_E — Einstein angular radius, G — gravitational constant (6.67430×10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²), M — lens mass, c — speed of light (299,792,458 m/s), D_l — distance to the lens, D_s — distance to the source, D_ls — distance from the lens to the source

eht.name: EHT
eht.mini: A telescope the size of Earth, assembled from antennas on different continents, captured the shadow of a black hole — like a bat's silhouette against the sunset.
eht.practical_application: Direct images of the event horizon and testing gravity theories under extreme conditions.
eht.description_popular: EHT uses the technique of Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). Eight observatories, from the South Pole to Greenland, are synchronized by atomic clocks, recording signals at a frequency of 230 GHz. This frequency corresponds to a wavelength of 1.3 mm – the submillimeter range where the superheated plasma near the black hole radiates. After years of processing on supercomputers, signal correlation achieved an angular resolution of 20 microarcseconds – equivalent to reading a newspaper from 500 km away.
eht.fun_fact_popular: The volume of data collected in one observing campaign exceeds the total daily Internet traffic; it was transported on hard drives by airplanes because network transmission would have taken years.
eht.description_simple: EHT is not a single instrument but a network of radio dishes across the planet. They simultaneously record signals from the same cosmic target, and then computers combine the data as if the antennas were a single giant mirror 10,000 kilometers in diameter. The image is assembled piece by piece, like a puzzle of a billion fragments.
eht.history_simple: The idea of linking distant radio telescopes emerged back in the 1960s, but data processing techniques only became available by the 2000s. The decisive step was taken by the team led by Sheperd Doeleman, publishing the first image in 2019.
eht.how_it_works_simple: Each pair of telescopes acts as an interferometer: waves arrive at different times due to Earth's rotation, and from the phase difference, the brightness of each point in the sky is reconstructed. The process resembles reconstructing a stereoscopic image — the brain builds a 3D picture from two flat images, but here thousands of pairwise combinations yield a detail a million times finer than the human eye.
eht.description: EHT is a global network of millimeter-wave radio telescopes operating on the principle of Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). Observations, starting in 2017, involve instruments such as ALMA, APEX, the IRAM 30-meter telescope, JCMT, SMA, SMT, SPT, and the Greenland Telescope. Joint synchronous recording of signals at frequencies around 230 GHz (wavelength 1.3 mm) and subsequent correlation processing of the data array enable image synthesis with an angular resolution determined by the maximum distance between telescopes (baseline) of about 10,000 km, yielding a diffraction limit of approximately 20 microarcseconds. This visual acuity is sufficient to discern the shadow of the black hole at the center of galaxy M87 or Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way. For the first time, it was possible to directly see the photon ring and event horizon, confirming the predictions of general relativity for the shadow shape under the Kerr metric.
eht.history: The concept of combining radio telescopes for interferometry dates back to the 1960s, when the first VLBI experiments were conducted. By the 1990s, advances in millimeter-wave receivers made it possible to consider observing compact sources such as Sgr A*. The EHT project began to take shape around 2009, and the first full observations were conducted in April 2017. After two years of data processing, the collaboration, involving more than 200 researchers from different countries, presented the image of the black hole shadow in M87 in 2019. In 2022, the image of Sgr A* – the black hole at the center of our Galaxy – was published.
eht.how_it_works: The telescopes record the amplitude and phase of incoming radio waves. Pairwise correlation of signals (product with delay) yields complex visibilities. Then image reconstruction algorithms, such as CLEAN or regularized maximum likelihood methods, translate the visibilities into a brightness map. The interferometer's resolution is given by the diffraction formula θ ≈ λ / D. With λ = 1.3 mm and D ≈ 10,000 km, we obtain θ ~ 20 μas (microarcseconds). The key challenge is achieving sub-nanosecond accuracy synchronization with hydrogen masers and accounting for atmospheric fluctuations. Due to Earth's rotation, the relative positions of the telescopes change, filling the UV-plane and improving image quality.
key_problems: Improve resolution for direct observation of the Kerr structure of the shadow and testing metrics of alternative gravity theories
Increase dynamic range and sensitivity for detecting faint jets and accretion flows
Create movies of event horizon evolution on timescales of hours, adding space antennas for continuous monitoring
eht.fun_fact: For synchronization, hydrogen masers were used – clocks that drift by one second every hundred million years. And to avoid phase loss in the atmosphere, telescopes were located at altitudes above 5000 meters, where the air is thin and relatively dry.

formulas.description: Diffraction resolution of the interferometer
formulas.meaning: θ — angular resolution (rad), λ — wavelength (1.3 mm), D — maximum distance between telescopes (baseline), D ≈ 10,000 km

quantum_gravity.name: quantum gravity
quantum_gravity.mini: Gravity and the quantum world are like water and oil. Quantum gravity tries to mix them into a unified picture of the universe at the smallest and most energetic scales.
quantum_gravity.practical_application: A successful theory will explain the first moment of the Big Bang and what is inside black holes, possibly leading to technologies that are currently hard to imagine.
quantum_gravity.description_popular: The main difficulty: standard methods of quantum field theory fail when applied to general relativity because gravity is non-renormalizable. Approaches: string theory replaces point particles with vibrating strings, naturally including a massless graviton (the quantum of gravity); loop quantum gravity breaks space down into discrete 'spin networks'.
quantum_gravity.fun_fact_popular: The Planck length, where quantum gravity effects become dominant, is about 1.6×10⁻³⁵ meters. If a hydrogen atom were enlarged to the size of the observable universe, the Planck length would be the thickness of a human hair.
quantum_gravity.description_simple: In the familiar world, gravity seems smooth, but at the smallest distances, space and time may be grainy and chaotic — like foam on a wave crest. Quantum gravity seeks to describe how the very fabric of spacetime obeys quantum rules.
quantum_gravity.history_simple: Einstein's general theory of relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime, but it doesn't mesh with the quantum theory that rules the world of atoms. In the mid-20th century, physicists realized that at the Planck scale (an incredibly small length) both theories must be taken into account. John Wheeler introduced 'quantum foam' — a seething structure of space.
quantum_gravity.how_it_works_simple: Imagine spacetime as an elastic fabric. Quantum uncertainty prevents us from precisely defining its shape at ultrasmall distances. The fabric bubbles and twists, creating a foam-like geometry. All particles and forces except gravity are described by quantum fields, and quantum gravity aims to make spacetime itself such a field.
quantum_gravity.description: Constructing a consistent quantum theory of gravity remains the most important unsolved problem in theoretical physics. The main candidates: string theory, where the fundamental objects are one-dimensional strings vibrating in higher-dimensional space, with one vibrational mode corresponding to a massless spin-2 particle (the graviton); loop quantum gravity, which directly quantizes geometry using spin networks and spin foams, yielding a discrete spectrum of areas and volumes; asymptotically safe gravity, causal dynamical triangulations, and ideas of emergent gravity, where spacetime is not fundamental. The theory must predict corrections to general relativity at short distances, quantum properties of black holes, and the early universe.
quantum_gravity.history: After the creation of general relativity (1916), attempts to quantize it began in the 1930s with the work of Rosenfeld, Pauli, and Fierz. In 1955, Wheeler introduced the concept of quantum foam. In 1967, Bryce DeWitt wrote the Wheeler-DeWitt equation. In the 1980s, string theory took shape (Green, Schwarz), and in the 1990s, loop quantum gravity (Rovelli, Smolin). Despite decades of effort, none of the approaches have yet received direct experimental confirmation.
quantum_gravity.how_it_works: At the Planck scale, quantum fluctuations of the metric become significant. Perturbative quantum gravity turns out to be non-renormalizable: an infinite number of counterterms is required. String theory solves this problem through the extended nature of objects, which softens ultraviolet divergences. The graviton emerges as a state of a closed string. In loop quantum gravity, the fundamental variables are holonomies of connections and fluxes, leading to discrete quantum geometry. Both approaches predict modified dispersion relations, possible violation of Lorentz invariance, and new effects in black hole physics.
key_problems: Non-renormalizability of general relativity: perturbative quantum gravity leads to infinities.
Problem of time: the Wheeler-DeWitt equation lacks a time variable, making interpretation difficult.
Background independence: how to formulate a theory without a fixed background geometry.
Lack of experimental evidence: the Planck scale is far beyond the reach of accelerators.
Consistency with black hole thermodynamics: resolving the information paradox requires a quantum-gravitational description.
Choosing between competing theories without a decisive experiment.
quantum_gravity.fun_fact: If you try to measure a particle's position with accuracy less than the Planck length, you'd need photons of such high energy that they would form a black hole and make the measurement impossible. This hints that spacetime ceases to be continuous.

formulas.description: The Planck length — the scale at which quantum gravity effects become dominant
formulas.meaning: l_P — Planck length (≈ 1.616×10⁻³⁵ m), ħ — reduced Planck constant (ħ ≈ 1.0546×10⁻³⁴ J·s), G — gravitational constant (G ≈ 6.674×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²), c — speed of light (c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s)

random_matrix.name: random matrix
random_matrix.mini: A crowd of people in a square moves chaotically, but the overall density at each point is predictable. A random matrix—a table of numbers governed by probabilistic laws—helps capture order in apparent disorder.
random_matrix.practical_application: Random matrices are used in signal processing: they separate important data from noise in radar and medical tomographs.
random_matrix.description_popular: A random matrix is a matrix whose elements are random variables with a given joint distribution. The best-known are the Wigner Gaussian ensembles: orthogonal (GOE), unitary (GUE), and symplectic (GSE), differing in symmetry under time reversal. The main result is the Wigner distribution for spacings between eigenvalues, which shows level repulsion: the probability of finding two very close values is small.
random_matrix.fun_fact_popular: The distribution of gaps between consecutive buses in some cities also resembles the Wigner distribution, because drivers tend to avoid bunching.
random_matrix.description_simple: A random matrix is a square table, each element chosen randomly but with overall constraints (e.g., mirror symmetry). The special numbers of such a matrix behave surprisingly uniformly across different systems—like average height in a group not depending on individual characteristics.
random_matrix.history_simple: The idea was proposed by physicist Eugene Wigner in the 1950s to describe the energy levels of heavy atomic nuclei, where exact calculations are impossible.
random_matrix.how_it_works_simple: Instead of calculating every interaction in a complex system (e.g., among all neutrons and protons in a nucleus), scientists replace them with random numbers, preserving only the overall symmetry properties. The distribution of the resulting numbers exactly matches experiment.
random_matrix.description: A random matrix is a matrix with random entries, studied in random matrix theory. The central object is the joint distribution of eigenvalues, which for Gaussian ensembles is proportional to exp(−β Σ λ_i^2) Π_{i<j} |λ_i − λ_j|^β with index β=1,2,4 for GOE, GUE, GSE, respectively. A key property is universality: in the large-size limit, many statistical characteristics of eigenvalues do not depend on the details of the entry distribution, but only on the symmetry class. This makes the theory applicable to atomic nuclei, financial correlations, and signal propagation in wireless networks.
random_matrix.history: In the 1950s, Eugene Wigner, while investigating resonance spectra of heavy nuclei, proposed replacing unknown elements of the Hamiltonian matrix with random numbers. Together with Dyson, Mehta, and others, he developed the statistical theory of spectra. Later, a deep connection emerged with eigenvalue distributions in numerical methods, number theory (distribution of zeros of the Riemann zeta function), and growth of random surfaces.
random_matrix.how_it_works: The eigenvalues of a random matrix behave like a distribution of charged particles on a wire repelling each other logarithmically. As a result, they are spaced unevenly: the probability of a small spacing s between them is proportional to s^β (β is the repulsion index). The spacing distribution is exactly described by the Wigner formula for GOE: p(s) = (πs/2) exp(−π s²/4). For comparison, a Poisson process (independent levels) would yield p(s) = exp(−s).
key_problems: Proof of universality for a wide class of correlated matrices.
Connection to quantum chaos and the Montgomery–Dyson hypothesis about zeros of the zeta function.
random_matrix.fun_fact: The eigenvalue distribution of certain random matrices coincides with the distribution of zeros of the Riemann zeta function on the critical line, which is part of the Montgomery–Dyson hypothesis.

formulas.meaning: s — spacing between neighboring levels, normalized so that the mean spacing is 1; p(s) — probability density

formulas.description: Joint distribution of eigenvalues for Gaussian ensembles
