effective_field_theory.name: Effective field theory
effective_field_theory.mini: The captain of an ocean liner charts a course on a map of currents, without thinking about water molecules. Effective field theory builds such a 'captain's' description of physics, discarding details unimportant at a given scale and leaving only the essential.
effective_field_theory.practical_application: Enables description of superconductors, calculation of gravitational waves from black holes, and construction of elementary particle models.
effective_field_theory.description_popular: Effective field theory (EFT) is a framework that describes phenomena at a given energy (or distance) scale without complete knowledge of a deeper microscopic theory. It is based on the idea of scale separation: low-energy physics is insensitive to the details of high-energy processes. The Lagrangian of such a theory is built from all possible interactions allowed by symmetries, arranged in descending order of importance as the scale increases. Heavy particles do not appear explicitly, but their virtual effects manifest in effective constants. Thus, the Standard Model of elementary particles itself is considered an effective theory, and EFT for gravity has allowed modeling black hole mergers without a complete quantum theory of gravity.
effective_field_theory.fun_fact_popular: The mass difference between the proton and neutron — a tiny 0.14% of their mass (like two almost identical balls, one slightly damp) — was calculated using chiral perturbation theory, which is an effective field theory for nucleons.
effective_field_theory.description_simple: The laws of physics look different up close and from afar. Effective field theory is a way to describe phenomena at one level of detail (for example, the size of an atom) without delving into the workings of much smaller or larger scales. It’s like describing a crowd: instead of each person, we introduce density and pressure. This approach simplifies calculations, replacing microscopic complexity with averaged rules (effective fields) and preserving the main thing — symmetries and conservation laws.
effective_field_theory.history_simple: The idea grew out of attempts to understand strong interactions in the mid-20th century. By the 1970s, it had crystallized into a general method, unifying particle physics and condensed matter physics.
effective_field_theory.how_it_works_simple: A car: to describe its motion, you don't need to know the chemistry of gasoline or friction in the pistons — just the steering wheel, pedals, and body aerodynamics. Effective field theory similarly coarsens the picture, keeping only those parameters that matter at the scale of interest. All small-scale processes are 'encoded' in a few numbers (effective constants) that can be measured experimentally.
effective_field_theory.description: Effective field theory (EFT) is a quantum field theory describing the low-energy dynamics of a system when high-energy degrees of freedom (heavy particles) have been integrated out. The Lagrangian contains a set of all local operators that respect the symmetries, with coefficients suppressed by the cutoff scale Λ: L_eff = L_dim≤4 + Σ_i c_i O_i / Λ^{d_i-4}, where d_i is the operator dimension. The theory is renormalizable in the Wilsonian sense: ultraviolet divergences are absorbed by renormalization of a finite set of parameters at each order of the expansion. EFT yields systematically improvable predictions by including contributions from operators of ever higher dimension.
effective_field_theory.history: The formalism of effective field theories took shape in the 1970s in the work of Kenneth Wilson on the renormalization group. In the 1990s, a language was created for building models of physics beyond the Standard Model. John Archibald Wheeler introduced the concept of effective action in quantum gravity, and Kip Thorne with colleagues constructed the effective one-body (EOB) approach for gravitational-wave sources, successfully used by LIGO.
effective_field_theory.how_it_works: The key principle is scale hierarchy. Integrating out heavy fields generates an effective Lagrangian that at low energies can be expanded in local operators. The renormalization group governs the 'running' of effective constants as the scale changes. For example, in quantum electrodynamics, the Heisenberg–Euler effective Lagrangian describes photon–photon scattering via virtual electron loops at energies much lower than the electron mass. Thus, effective field theories, like navigational charts for physicists, allow us not to get bogged down in details and to predict phenomena from superconductors to galaxy collisions.
key_problems: The mass hierarchy: why is the electroweak scale (100 GeV) so far from the Planck scale (10^19 GeV)?
Dark energy: the cosmological constant as a dimension-zero operator in the EFT of gravity.
Constructing a UV-complete theory (e.g., quantum gravity) from low-energy data.
effective_field_theory.fun_fact: The effective one-body (EOB) approach, based on EFT, has made it possible to analyze black hole mergers via gravitational waves in real time — without it, LIGO detectors would not have been able to extract signals from the noise.

formulas.description: Effective Lagrangian
formulas.meaning: 𝒪_i are operators of dimension d_i, c_i are dimensionless coefficients, Λ is the cutoff scale (the energy at which the effective description breaks down).

fractal.name: fractal
fractal.mini: The coastline of an island becomes infinitely long if measured with tiny rulers. This is not a trick — many natural forms are structured this way: mountains, clouds, blood vessels.
fractal.practical_application: Fractal antennas in mobile phones receive signals over a wide frequency range, and computer graphics create realistic landscapes.
fractal.description_popular: A fractal is a set with a fractional dimension and self-similarity at all scales. For example, the Koch snowflake is constructed by replacing each line segment with a broken line, and after infinite steps its length is infinite but its area is finite. The fractal dimension quantitatively describes how densely an object fills space.
fractal.fun_fact_popular: Human lungs pack about 100 m² of surface area into a volume of a few liters thanks to the fractal structure of the bronchial tree.
fractal.description_simple: A fractal is a self-similar structure: each part, when scaled down, repeats the whole. Much like a fern frond, where each tiny branch looks like the entire leaf. Instead of ordinary length, fractals are assigned a fractional dimension (a number like 1.5 — more than a line, less than a plane).
fractal.history_simple: The term was coined by Benoit Mandelbrot in 1975. He noticed that the length of a country's borders depends on the map's precision — the more precise, the longer.
fractal.how_it_works_simple: When you zoom into a fractal, it remains equally detailed. In nature, this arises from simple repetition rules: for instance, a river channel branches, and each branch resembles the entire river network.
fractal.description: A fractal is a geometric figure with nontrivial structure at all scales and usually has a fractional Hausdorff–Besicovitch dimension. The rigorous definition includes the property of self-similarity (exact, approximate, or statistical). Many natural objects — coastlines, clouds, trees, blood vessel networks — exhibit fractal properties over a limited range of scales. Mathematically, fractals are often generated by iterating simple mappings; for example, the Mandelbrot set is defined by the recurrence relation z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c.
fractal.history: The term 'fractal' (from Latin fractus, meaning 'broken') was coined by Benoit Mandelbrot in 1975, but its origins lie in the work of Pierre Fatou and Gaston Julia (early 20th century), who studied iterations of complex mappings. Lewis Fry Richardson noticed in 1961 that the length of country borders increases as the measurement standard becomes smaller. Mandelbrot generalized these ideas, describing the fractal geometry of nature in his 1982 book.
fractal.how_it_works: The fractal structure arises from the recursive application of a simple rule. For example, the Koch curve: each straight segment is replaced by four segments forming a protrusion. After an infinite number of steps, the length of the curve grows without bound, and its dimension is log 4 / log 3 ≈ 1.26. The fractal dimension d is defined by the power law N(ε) ∝ ε^{−d}, where N(ε) is the minimum number of balls of radius ε needed to cover the object (box-counting dimension).
key_problems: Creating a unified theory of fractals that describes nonequilibrium systems.
Linking fractal dimension to the physical properties of materials.
fractal.fun_fact: The Mandelbrot set has a finite area (about 1.5), but its boundary is infinitely wiggly and is itself a fractal with dimension 2.

formulas.description: Dimension of a self-similar fractal
formulas.meaning: d — fractal dimension; N — number of identical parts into which the object is divided when the linear size is reduced by a factor of s (s — scaling coefficient)

formulas.meaning: z_n — complex number at step n (starting with z_0 = 0); c — complex parameter corresponding to a point on the complex plane

spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.name: spontaneous symmetry breaking
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.mini: A ball on a hilltop rests in equilibrium, but the slightest breath sends it rolling into one of the valleys. Spontaneous symmetry breaking is when the laws are symmetric, yet the world chooses one of many equally possible states.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.practical_application: Thanks to this mechanism, particles gain mass, magnets stick to refrigerators, and superconducting magnets work in tomographs.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.description_popular: Spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) occurs when the ground state (vacuum) of a system is less symmetric than the equations describing it. The classic model is the 'Mexican hat' potential: the energy minimum is not at the center but on a circle of equally possible states. By randomly choosing one, the system generates massless excitations (Goldstone bosons). In gauge theories such as the electroweak theory, these bosons are 'eaten' by fields, becoming their longitudinal components and giving them mass (the Higgs mechanism). In a ferromagnet, rotational symmetry is broken, and the Goldstone bosons are magnons—magnetization waves.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.fun_fact_popular: In the expanding Universe, spontaneous symmetry breaking could have produced cosmic strings—filament-like defects as thin as a proton but millions of light-years long. The search for them continues through light distortions from distant galaxies.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.description_simple: Symmetry in physics means laws remain unchanged under rotation, translation, or particle exchange. But often symmetry disappears in the observable world. A coin on its edge: the situation is symmetric with respect to falling heads or tails, but a slight puff is enough for it to fall and the symmetry to vanish. In physics, such 'spontaneous' disappearance of symmetry is called spontaneous symmetry breaking. It is responsible for magnetism, superconductivity, and even why particles have mass.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.history_simple: The idea was born in the theory of magnetism in the early 20th century, but its real blossoming came in the 1960s when it was applied to quantum field theory. This led to the creation of the Higgs mechanism and the explanation of the masses of W and Z bosons.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.how_it_works_simple: A person balancing on tiptoes—the symmetry is perfect, but a fall inevitably chooses one side. Similarly, atomic magnets in a piece of iron: at high temperature their arrows are disordered and symmetric; upon cooling they suddenly align in a single direction, creating a magnet. The direction is random, but once it appears, it 'freezes' in. In the quantum world, a similar process causes the Higgs field to fill the vacuum and give particles mass.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.description: Spontaneous symmetry breaking is a phenomenon where the Lagrangian of a system is invariant under the action of a group G, but the vacuum state (lowest-energy state) is invariant only under a subgroup H ⊂ G. According to Goldstone's theorem, each broken generator corresponds to a massless particle (Goldstone boson). The potential of a typical model is given by V(φ) = -μ^2 φ^2 + λ φ^4 with μ^2 > 0; at φ = ±v = ±√(μ^2/λ) the energy is minimal. In quantum field theory, realistic models include complex scalar doublets that break SU(2)×U(1) symmetry down to U(1) of electromagnetism. SSB explains ferromagnetic transition, superfluidity, Bose-Einstein condensation, and mass generation in the Standard Model.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.history: The idea of spontaneous symmetry breaking goes back to Werner Heisenberg's theory of ferromagnetism in the 1920s and Lev Landau's theory of phase transitions (1937). In 1961, Yoichiro Nambu and Giovanni Jona-Lasinio built a model of chiral symmetry breaking in hadrons. In 1964, Peter Higgs, as well as François Englert and Robert Brout, showed how to combine SSB with gauge invariance, solving the problem of gauge boson masses. Emmy Noether had earlier in 1918 proved the fundamental connection between symmetries and conservation laws, which formed the basis for understanding broken symmetries.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.how_it_works: Consider the Lagrangian L = (∂_μ Φ)* (∂^μ Φ) - V(Φ) with the potential V(Φ) = -μ^2 |Φ|^2 + λ |Φ|^4. The minima lie on the circle |Φ| = v = √(μ^2/(2λ)). Choosing a specific direction for the vacuum expectation value ⟨Φ⟩ = v breaks the U(1) symmetry. Parameterizing Φ = (v + h) e^{iθ/v} reveals a massive field h (the Higgs particle) and a massless field θ (the Goldstone boson). In the presence of a gauge field A_μ, the covariant derivative D_μ Φ = ∂_μ Φ - i e A_μ Φ leads to the field θ being absorbed, becoming the longitudinal mode of A_μ, which acquires the mass m_A = e v. Thus, like a ball rolling into one of the valleys, the vacuum chooses a specific state, and this choice determines the properties of elementary particles.
key_problems: The nature of the Higgs field and the stability of its vacuum up to the Planck scale.
Spontaneous supersymmetry breaking and the mechanism of its transmission to the visible sector.
The origin of the cosmological constant as a consequence of supersymmetry breaking.
spontaneous_symmetry_breaking.fun_fact: In superfluid helium-4, spontaneous U(1) symmetry breaking manifests as quantized vortices. When the container is rotated, they form a regular lattice visible to the naked eye—frozen mini-tornadoes about a millimeter in diameter.

formulas.description: Potential 'Mexican hat'
formulas.meaning: φ — scalar field, μ^2 — positive mass parameter (μ^2 > 0), λ — self-interaction constant (λ > 0). Minima at φ = ±v, where v = √(μ^2/λ).

quasiparticle.name: quasiparticle
quasiparticle.mini: In a football stadium, a wave of standing fans circles the bowl. No one runs a lap — only the pattern moves. Similarly, in a solid, collective atomic vibrations give rise to particle-like energy clumps.
quasiparticle.practical_application: Quasiparticles explain semiconductor conductivity and superconductivity: without the concept of holes — empty places that behave like positive particles — no transistor would work.
quasiparticle.description_popular: A quasiparticle is an elementary excitation of a condensed medium (solid, liquid) that possesses particle-like properties: energy, momentum, angular momentum, charge. Examples: phonons (sound quanta), magnons (spin waves), excitons (bound electron-hole pair). Quasiparticles do not exist outside the medium — they are a collective mode. Landau proposed the concept of a Fermi liquid, where fermions turn into weakly interacting quasiparticles with renormalized mass.
quasiparticle.fun_fact_popular: Without considering hole quasiparticles, it's impossible to understand how solar cells work: it's the movement of holes that creates the current.
quasiparticle.description_simple: A quasiparticle is not an independent particle like an electron, but a coherent excitation of many interacting particles. For example, when a sound wave runs through a crystal, its quantum is called a phonon. A phonon is like a particle of sound. Another example is a hole in a semiconductor: the absence of an electron behaves like a positive charge.
quasiparticle.history_simple: The idea was introduced by Soviet physicist Lev Landau in 1941 while describing liquid helium. He realized that complex collective motions can be simplified to particle-like excitations.
quasiparticle.how_it_works_simple: In a solid, particles continuously interact. Instead of tracking each one, physicists replace the system with a set of almost independent quasiparticles that carry energy, momentum, and even charge. This is similar to describing a crowd by density and flow velocity, rather than the movements of individual people.
quasiparticle.description: A quasiparticle is a quantum of collective excitation of a many-body system. In the formalism of second quantization, creation and annihilation operators describe the generation and absorption of such excitations. They are classified by statistics: fermions (electronic quasiparticles in metals) obey the Pauli principle; Bose quasiparticles (phonons, plasmons) do not. Properties (effective mass, charge, dispersion) are determined by the medium. The concept is critically important for solid-state theory, superfluidity, and superconductivity — Cooper pairs in BCS theory form bosonic quasiparticles responsible for the superconducting current.
quasiparticle.history: Lev Landau introduced the term in 1941 while constructing the theory of superfluidity of helium-II. In 1956, Landau generalized the idea to Fermi liquids. Independently, similar approaches were developed by Eugene Wigner for crystals. Experimental confirmation came through measurements of effective mass in metals by cyclotron resonance and neutron spectroscopy of phonons.
quasiparticle.how_it_works: At low energies, the Hamiltonian of a many-particle system transforms into a sum of independent quasiparticle modes: H = Σ ε_k γ_k^† γ_k, where γ_k are creation/annihilation operators of quasiparticles with momentum k. The interaction of the original particles manifests in the renormalization of the spectrum ε_k and residual weak interaction between quasiparticles. In metals, the lifetime of an electronic quasiparticle grows as 1/T² as temperature decreases, and the energy obeys the Pauli principle: occupancy does not exceed 1.
key_problems: A consistent description of quasiparticles in strongly correlated systems (strange metals, high-temperature superconductivity).
Explaining the breakdown of the Fermi liquid picture in some materials.
quasiparticle.fun_fact: Some quasiparticles can possess fractional charge (for example, in the fractional quantum Hall effect) and even fractional statistics — anyons, which is impossible for ordinary particles in three dimensions.

formulas.meaning: m* — effective mass; ħ ≈ 1.05×10⁻³⁴ J·s — reduced Planck constant; E — energy as a function of wave vector k

zeta_function.name: zeta function
zeta_function.mini: The zeta function is a mathematical lens that turns scattered prime numbers into a tidy picture. Through it, we see how often twin primes occur.
zeta_function.practical_application: Testing the reliability of cryptographic keys, analyzing random processes, quantum chaos — wherever we need to look into the depths of numerical disorder.
zeta_function.description_popular: The Riemann zeta function is defined for complex s with real part greater than 1 as ζ(s) = ∑ 1/n^s and analytically continues to the entire complex plane except s=1. Its zeros are divided into trivial ones (at negative even integers) and non-trivial ones. The Riemann Hypothesis states that all non-trivial zeros have real part 1/2. The zeta function factors into the Euler product over primes, linking it to number theory. The distribution of its zeros governs deviations in the prime number theorem. A deep connection with matrices: in the 1970s, Hugh Montgomery discovered that the pair correlation of zeros matches that of eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices, giving rise to the conjecture of a link with quantum chaos.
zeta_function.fun_fact_popular: The famous millennium problem — proving the Riemann Hypothesis — is directly related to the security of modern cryptosystems, since a proof could accelerate unveiling the distribution of prime numbers.
zeta_function.description_simple: The zeta function is not just a formula, but a sensitive instrument. If you plug a complex number (a number with an imaginary part, like a shadow) into it, it yields a result that 'senses' prime factors. The most interesting part is its zeros, the points where the value vanishes. The location of these zeros controls how smoothly the primes are distributed.
zeta_function.history_simple: Leonhard Euler in the 18th century noticed that the sum of reciprocal powers of all natural numbers equals the product over primes. Bernhard Riemann in 1859 extended this idea to complex numbers and discovered that all non-trivial zeros probably lie on the critical line with real part ½. This hypothesis remains unproven to this day.
zeta_function.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a sieve that sifts out composite numbers. The zeta function is like an X-ray of this sieve: each bright streak on the image (a zero of the function) corresponds to a cluster of primes. If the zeros lie strictly on one line, then the primes are distributed as chaotically as possible — as if scattered by a random wind.
zeta_function.description: The Riemann zeta function ζ(s) is a meromorphic function on the complex plane with a single simple pole at s=1. For Re(s)>1 it is given by the absolutely convergent Dirichlet series or the Euler product over primes: ζ(s) = ∏_{p} (1 - p^{-s})^{-1}. Analytic continuation is achieved via the functional equation linking ζ(s) and ζ(1-s) with involvement of the gamma function. Riemann Hypothesis: all non-trivial zeros lie on the critical line Re(s)=1/2. Verified for the first tens of billions of zeros. The distribution of zeros is described by the Montgomery–Odlyzko formula, and their connection with the spectrum of random matrices (universality) points to a possible explanation via quantum chaos. Generalizations: Dirichlet L-functions, Dedekind zeta functions, elliptic curves.
zeta_function.history: Euler in 1737 derived the product over primes, establishing the fundamental connection. Riemann in 1859 introduced analytic continuation and formulated the hypothesis. In the 20th century, Hardy proved the infinitude of zeros on the critical line, Selberg proved that a positive proportion of zeros lie on it. In 1972, Montgomery identified statistical regularities of zeros, and Odlyzko confirmed them numerically on a huge scale.
zeta_function.how_it_works: The functional equation ζ(s) = 2^s π^{s-1} sin(πs/2) Γ(1-s) ζ(1-s) is symmetric about the critical line. The explicit Riemann–von Mangoldt formula expresses the sum over prime powers in terms of the sum over non-trivial zeros of ζ(s). This means each prime 'contributes' to the oscillations of ζ(s), and each zero modulates the deviations in the distribution of primes from the main term. The density of zeros at height T grows as (T/2π) log(T/2πe). The Prime Number Theorem is equivalent to the absence of zeros on the line Re(s)=1. Through this lens, we see how primes, like keys, fit the locks of cryptography.
key_problems: The Riemann Hypothesis — proving that all non-trivial zeros lie on the critical line
Clarifying the connection with quantum chaos and the operator approach (does a self-adjoint operator exist whose eigenvalues are the imaginary parts of the zeros?)
The Lindelöf Hypothesis on the growth of ζ(s) on the critical line
zeta_function.fun_fact: The first 10^{13} non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the critical line, but this is not a proof.

elliptic_curve.name: elliptic curve
elliptic_curve.mini: An elliptic curve is like a smooth, curved lock whose latch points combine to form a secret combination. It’s what keeps your online banking safe.
elliptic_curve.practical_application: HTTPS protocols, cryptocurrency wallets, digital signatures—anywhere a fast and secure digital lock is needed.
elliptic_curve.description_popular: An elliptic curve is defined by the equation y² = x³ + ax + b. Its graph is a smooth, symmetric curve without self-intersections. On the set of its points (including the point at infinity) one can define an addition operation, turning the curve into a commutative group. This means addition follows the same laws as ordinary numbers: there is a 'zero', an inverse element, and associativity. But the geometry of addition is unusual: to add two points, we draw a secant line through them, find the third intersection with the curve, and reflect it across the x-axis. In cryptography (e.g., the Diffie–Hellman protocol on elliptic curves), security relies on the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem: given an initial point P and an endpoint Q = n·P, computing the number n is virtually impossible.
elliptic_curve.fun_fact_popular: Perhaps the most famous elliptic curve is the one connected to Fermat's equation. Andrew Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem by establishing a link between elliptic curves and modular forms.
elliptic_curve.description_simple: Imagine a lock with many positions, but shaped as a smooth curve. An elliptic curve is defined by a mysterious equation, but the key is that its points can be 'added': draw a line through two points and you get a third. It's like trying combinations in a multi-digit code, only instead of numbers you have geometric steps.
elliptic_curve.history_simple: First noticed by 19th-century mathematicians, these 'locks' only saw their true potential for secrecy in 1985, when digital signatures on them were invented.
elliptic_curve.how_it_works_simple: To lock a message, you take a public generator point (like a well-known lock base) and a secret multiplier. By repeatedly 'turning' the point, you derive a key. An attacker would need to guess the multiplier—like trying an astronomical number of combinations by feel.
elliptic_curve.description: An elliptic curve over a field K is a smooth projective curve of genus 1 with a distinguished point (usually O, the point at infinity). Such a curve is given by a Weierstrass equation: y² = x³ + ax + b, with 4a³ + 27b² ≠ 0. Over the real numbers, the graph consists of one or two components. The key property is the ability to define a group operation on the set of curve points with O as the identity. Geometrically, addition P + Q is formed by drawing a line through P and Q (tangent if P=Q), finding its third intersection R with the curve, and reflecting that point across the x-axis to obtain R' = -R. This group is finite over a finite field and infinite over the rationals, and its rank is a deep arithmetic invariant. Elliptic curves have become central to the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, modern algebraic geometry, and cryptography.
elliptic_curve.history: The study of elliptic curves began with elliptic integrals in the works of Abel and Jacobi in the first half of the 19th century. The term 'elliptic' arose from their connection to computing the arc length of an ellipse. Henri Poincaré contributed to the study of algebraic curves and their groups. In 1985, Neal Koblitz and Victor Miller independently proposed using elliptic curves in cryptography, leading to the widespread ECC systems used today. The link to modular forms, established by Wiles and Taylor, resolved Fermat's Last Theorem.
elliptic_curve.how_it_works: The group law on an elliptic curve forms an abelian group. For a curve over a finite field F_p, this group has order about p+1, and the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem in this group underpins cryptographic security. In protocols like ECDSA, a message is signed using a secret key—a multiplier n—and verified with the public key Q = n·P. Computing n from Q and P is the ECDLP, for which no subexponential algorithms are known in general. Additionally, elliptic curves over the rationals carry a rich structure: by the Mordell–Weil theorem the group of rational points is finitely generated, and its rank and regulator are linked to the L-function of the curve via the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. Thus, the mathematical lock of a smooth curve guards our digital borders.
key_problems: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture on the link between the rank of an elliptic curve and the behavior of its L-function
Constructing elliptic curves with a prescribed rank
Quantum attacks on ECDLP (Shor's algorithm)—the need to transition to post-quantum cryptography
elliptic_curve.fun_fact: The largest known group of rational points on an elliptic curve has rank at least 28, found by N. Elkies in 2006.

formulas.meaning: y and x are coordinates of a point on the curve, a and b are coefficients determining the curve's shape
