formulas.latex: a \cdot (b + c) = a \cdot b + a \cdot c
formulas.meaning: a, b, c are elements of the ring; '+' and '·' are the addition and multiplication operations in the ring

potential_energy.name: potential energy
potential_energy.mini: A boulder on top of a hill. It is motionless, but inside there is tension, ready to turn into a rapid descent. This hidden force is potential energy, the reserve of position.
potential_energy.practical_application: Hydroelectric power plants convert water's potential energy into electricity. Any object at height stores energy ready to do work — from a clock weight to a hanging chandelier.
potential_energy.description_popular: The energy hidden in stationary objects is called potential by physicists. It comes in different forms: gravitational (associated with height in a gravitational field), elastic (compression or stretching of materials), electrical (charges in a field). All these types share a principle: the work that a system can perform is determined by its configuration. When a stone falls down, its potential melts away, turning into speed. On cosmic scales, gravitational potential energy is the main source of starlight: as a gas-dust cloud contracts, it heats up and ignites a thermonuclear furnace.
potential_energy.fun_fact_popular: A tablespoon of neutron star matter, if it fell to Earth, would release as much energy as a powerful atomic bomb — thanks to the enormous gravitational potential energy.
potential_energy.description_simple: The drawn bowstring freezes. Muscles are tensed, but there is no motion. Energy seems to sleep. This is potential energy — a reserve created by position or state. A stone on a mountain slope, a compressed spring, clouds above the plain — they all store the capacity to act, just waiting for a push. When equilibrium is broken, hidden power flows into visible motion — the rotation of a turbine, the flight of an arrow. So too the boulder from the top: rolling down, it can smash an obstacle, spending all the potential accumulated by height.
potential_energy.history_simple: People guessed about hidden energy since ancient times: water flows downhill, a stone falls. But the scientific concept was formalized in the 19th century by engineer William Rankine. Later, Emmy Noether showed that the energy reserve is linked to the symmetry of time — her theorem explained why energy does not disappear, but only changes form.
potential_energy.how_it_works_simple: Potential energy depends on the object's location in a force field. In Earth's gravity field, it increases with height: a kilogram weight on a table stores more energy than on the floor. Falling, it accelerates — potential energy transforms into kinetic energy (the energy of motion). Similarly, water falling from a dam spins a turbine.
potential_energy.description: Potential energy is a scalar physical quantity that characterizes the ability of a system to do work by virtue of its position or configuration. It is introduced only for conservative forces (those whose work does not depend on the path but on the initial and final states). Mathematically, the change in potential energy equals the negative of the work done by the conservative force. For gravitational interaction in Newtonian mechanics, U = -GMm/r, and near the Earth's surface U = mgh. The elastic potential energy of a spring is proportional to the square of deformation: U = kx^2/2. The energy of electrostatic interaction of point charges is computed from Coulomb's law and is also potential energy. In deeper theories, such as general relativity, there is no strict concept of gravitational potential energy because gravity is described by spacetime curvature, and the energy of the gravitational field is not localizable.
potential_energy.history: The term 'potential energy' was introduced in 1853 by the Scottish engineer and physicist William Rankine. However, the roots of the idea go back to Galileo and Leibniz, who spoke of 'living force' (vis viva) and 'dead force'. Lagrange and Hamilton embedded potential into analytical mechanics, making it the foundation of describing motion. In 1915, Emmy Noether proved that the law of conservation of energy (and hence the rigorous definition of potential function) follows from the homogeneity of time. Today, potential energy remains a key concept from quantum mechanics to cosmology.
potential_energy.how_it_works: In mechanics, the change in potential energy dU is related to the work dA done by a conservative force: dU = -dA = -F·dr. The potential is defined up to an arbitrary constant; only potential differences have physical meaning. In the Earth's gravitational field, U = mgh, where h is measured from a chosen reference level. In general, the gravitational potential of a point mass M is φ = -GM/r, and the potential energy of a test body of mass m is U = mφ. In electrodynamics, the scalar potential φ and vector potential A form a four-dimensional potential that determines field strengths. Quantum mechanics uses the potential energy operator in the Schrödinger equation. The gravitational potential energy of a uniform sphere (e.g., a star) determines its internal thermal history and stability.
key_problems: The impossibility of localizing gravitational energy in general relativity
The nature of potential energy in quantum gravity
potential_energy.fun_fact: Earth's gravitational potential energy (negative) is comparable in magnitude to the energy the Sun radiates in a week.

harmonic_oscillator.name: harmonic oscillator
harmonic_oscillator.mini: A swing, pushed very gently, always returns to the same rhythm. This is a harmonic oscillator — a system that sways back and forth around a rest point with an unchanging beat.
harmonic_oscillator.practical_application: A quartz crystal in a wristwatch vibrates exactly 32,768 times per second, setting the pace for the hands. The same law gives lasers their pure color and keeps bridges steady when wind blows over them.
harmonic_oscillator.description_popular: The harmonic oscillator is the basic model for almost all of physics. It appears in mechanics (pendulum, spring), acoustics (strings, air columns), optics (light as an oscillating electric field), and quantum theory (vibrations of atomic bonds). The reason for this universality is simple: near a stable equilibrium, the potential energy curve of any system resembles a parabola — and that is the 'signature' of an oscillator. The restoring force grows in direct proportion to the displacement, giving rise to sinusoidal motion.
harmonic_oscillator.fun_fact_popular: Surgeons use a harmonic scalpel vibrating 55,500 times per second. It cuts soft tissue and simultaneously seals blood vessels — coagulation without excess heat.
harmonic_oscillator.description_simple: The pendulum of a clock swings smoothly and predictably. A harmonic oscillator is anything that, when displaced from a comfortable position, receives a restoring force pulling it back, and by inertia overshoots, starting a cycle. Imagine a mass on a spring: stretch it — the spring pulls back; the mass gains speed — overshoots and compresses the spring from the other side. Energy dances between stored tension and motion. Every oscillator has a favorite rhythm — its natural frequency. Push it in time, and it will ring louder.
harmonic_oscillator.history_simple: Galileo noticed a swaying chandelier in a cathedral and realized that the period of a pendulum depends only on its length. Later, Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, making timekeeping tens of times more accurate.
harmonic_oscillator.how_it_works_simple: A swing has its own frequency — the round-trip time. Frequency is determined by two things: how strongly the restoring force 'springs' back and how heavy the oscillating object is. A heavy child on long ropes swings more slowly than a light one on short ropes. In a car, the springs and shock absorbers are also an oscillator, but they dampen vibrations to make the ride smooth.
harmonic_oscillator.description: A classical harmonic oscillator obeys the equation d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0, its solution being x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ). Energy alternates between kinetic and potential, remaining constant in the absence of friction. In quantum mechanics, this is one of the few exactly solvable problems. The Hamiltonian is H = p²/(2m) + ½mω²x², energy levels are quantized: E_n = ℏω (n + ½). The fraction ½ℏω is the zero-point energy, which does not disappear even at absolute zero. The ladder operators a and a† raise and lower the quantum number n — the entire quantum field theory is built on this language.
harmonic_oscillator.history: In 1602, Galileo described the pendulum, initiating the quantitative study of oscillations. Euler and Bernoulli later formulated the linear oscillator equation. In 1900, Max Planck used the quantization of oscillator energy to derive the blackbody spectrum — this step began the quantum era. Erwin Schrödinger solved the quantum harmonic oscillator in 1926, and the algebraic method with creation and annihilation operators was proposed by Paul Dirac. Ludwig Boltzmann applied the classical oscillator to molecular heat capacity, linking atomic motion to temperature.
harmonic_oscillator.how_it_works: Near the stable equilibrium point x₀, the potential V(x) is expanded in a Taylor series: V(x) ≈ V(x₀) + ½k(x−x₀)², where k = V''(x₀). The force F = −kV'(x) = −k(x−x₀) is linear, and the oscillation frequency ω = √(k/m). In the quantum case, position and momentum become operators; the Schrödinger equation yields eigenfunctions expressed via Hermite polynomials. The equidistant energy spectrum is the reason why fields in physics can be represented as a set of independent oscillators for each mode.
key_problems: Real nano- and micro-oscillators are nonlinear at large amplitudes, which limits the precision of compact clocks.
Cooling macroscopic oscillators to the ground state to test the quantum-classical transition.
Suppressing thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors, where test masses are suspended as oscillators.
harmonic_oscillator.fun_fact: Laser cooling can bring an ion to nearly zero oscillations in a harmonic trap. Such a quantum pendulum simultaneously exists in several positions — the atom becomes blurred, like a cloud, proving that even a pendulum behaves like a wave.

uniform_convergence.name: uniform convergence
uniform_convergence.mini: When a sequence of functions approaches the limit so uniformly that the maximum difference over all points tends to zero, that is uniform convergence. It does not allow any 'lagging' points.
uniform_convergence.practical_application: When designing an airplane wing, engineers expand flows into Fourier series; uniform convergence ensures that the approximation is equally good at all points of the profile.
uniform_convergence.description_popular: A sequence of functions fn converges to f uniformly on a set E if for any ε>0 there exists N such that for all n≥N and all x∈E, |fn(x) - f(x)| < ε. This is stronger than pointwise convergence, where N may depend on x. Uniform convergence implies the limit function is continuous if the fn are continuous, and allows termwise integration on a finite interval.
uniform_convergence.fun_fact_popular: The Fourier series of a continuous function can converge non-uniformly, and before Weierstrass's work, many believed this was impossible. The mistake cost several false proofs.
uniform_convergence.description_simple: Imagine you are smoothing a road: you lay layer after layer of asphalt. If after each layer the depth of potholes decreases equally everywhere, the paving is uniform. If some potholes remain while other areas are already smooth, the convergence is non-uniform. In mathematics, it's the same: a sequence of functions has uniform convergence when, for any given error ε, all function values after a certain index differ from the limit by less than ε across the entire considered region.
uniform_convergence.history_simple: Karl Weierstrass in the mid-19th century realized that without uniformity, the sum of an infinite series of continuous functions could be discontinuous. This discovery brought order to analysis.
uniform_convergence.how_it_works_simple: Uniform convergence preserves good properties: if each approximation was continuous, then the exact solution will be continuous. Without uniformity, the limit can 'jump'. That is why all physical calculations where solutions are approximated by series require a check for uniformity.
uniform_convergence.description: Uniform convergence is a type of convergence of a function sequence, defined via the sup-norm: ‖fn - f‖∞ → 0, where ‖g‖∞ = supx∈E |g(x)|. It is stronger than pointwise convergence and weaker than convergence in Lp norms on infinite spaces. Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence: the sequence {fn} is fundamental in the uniform norm. Theorems: the uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous; if fn converge uniformly to f on an interval and each fn is Riemann integrable, then f is integrable and ∫f = lim∫fn; with an additional condition on the convergence of derivatives, one can interchange limit and derivative.
uniform_convergence.history: The rigorous definition appeared in 1870 in the works of Eduard Heine, based on Weierstrass's lectures. Weierstrass showed that the series ∑bk cos(akπx) for certain ak, bk converges uniformly, but its sum is nowhere differentiable — this shattered intuition about the connection between smoothness and convergence. Henri Poincaré in the 1880s used uniform convergence in the theory of automorphic functions and differential equations, and later the concept became part of the foundation of functional analysis through spaces C(X) with the uniform norm.
uniform_convergence.how_it_works: The key tool is estimation of the supremum. Weierstrass M-test: if |fn(x)| ≤ Mn and ∑Mn converges, then ∑fn converges uniformly (and absolutely). Uniform convergence is closely related to compactness: on a compact set, a pointwise convergent sequence may not be uniform, but from any uniformly bounded and equicontinuous sequence one can extract a uniformly convergent subsequence (Arzelà–Ascoli theorem). In numerical methods, uniform convergence ensures stability of approximation under parameter variation.
key_problems: Effective estimates of the rate of uniform convergence for neural network approximations of multivariate functions
Uniform convergence of spectral expansions of non-equilibrium physical systems (e.g., for non-normal operators)
Criteria for uniform convergence for non-smooth domains in homogenization problems
uniform_convergence.fun_fact: There exist sequences that converge uniformly on every compact set but not on the entire real line — for example, fn(x)=x/n. Such convergence is called 'uniform on compacts' and is typical for power series.

formulas.meaning: f_n, f are functions on a set E; sup denotes the supremum; the limit is zero, meaning the maximum deviation tends to zero

luminosity_distance.name: photometric distance
luminosity_distance.mini: A lantern and a candle at a distance can shine equally. Photometric distance is a way to determine how far a source is by comparing its apparent brightness with its true power.
luminosity_distance.practical_application: The method is used to measure distances to Type Ia supernovae, which led to the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe. Without it, modern cosmology would lose its ruler.
luminosity_distance.description_popular: Photometric distance D_L relates the observed radiation flux F to the true luminosity L via the formula F = L / (4π D_L²). It includes a correction for the expansion of the universe: photons lose energy due to redshift (wavelength increases), and the time between the arrival of successive photons also stretches. As a result, D_L = (1+z) D_M, where z is the redshift, and D_M is the comoving transverse distance. For nearby objects, D_L ≈ D_M, but for distant galaxies (z ~ 1 and higher) the difference becomes significant. D_L is precisely what is measured using standard candles—objects of known luminosity, like Type Ia supernovae.
luminosity_distance.fun_fact_popular: Looking at a galaxy with redshift z=1, we receive light dimmed by a factor of four just due to the expansion of space—the photometric distance turns out to be twice the comoving distance.
luminosity_distance.description_simple: Photometric distance is not a distance you can measure with a tape measure. It says: 'If the source looked this dim in ordinary empty space, it would have to be this far away.' It is calculated by how much the light from a distant star or galaxy has weakened. But space itself expands and can further dim the light—so the photometric distance is larger than the geometric distance.
luminosity_distance.history_simple: The concept began to take shape in the 1920s when Edwin Hubble investigated the relationship between redshift and distance. The modern meaning crystallized with the advent of standard candles—sources with known luminosity. In 1998, two teams of astronomers, using Type Ia supernova explosions, discovered through photometric distance that the universe is expanding at an accelerating rate.
luminosity_distance.how_it_works_simple: Imagine an inflating balloon with light bulbs stuck on it. Bulbs of the same power dim not only because they move away but also because space stretches, 'smearing' the light. Photometric distance accounts for both effects: dimming due to geometric dispersion and additional dimming due to cosmological redshift.
luminosity_distance.description: Photometric distance D_L in cosmology is defined through the relation between the absolute luminosity L of a source and the measured bolometric flux F: D_L ≡ √(L / (4πF)). In an expanding universe, this distance is larger than coordinate or angular distance because the energy of each photon decreases by a factor of (1+z), and the interval between photon arrivals is further lengthened by another factor of (1+z), giving a factor of (1+z)² for the flux and consequently D_L = (1+z) D_M. D_M is the transverse comoving distance, which depends on the model: in a flat ΛCDM cosmology, D_M = (c/H₀) ∫_0^z dz' / E(z'), where E(z') = √(Ω_m(1+z')³ + Ω_Λ). Measuring D_L with standard candles such as Type Ia supernovae is the foundation of the cosmological distance scale and led to the discovery of dark energy.
luminosity_distance.history: The concept originates from the work of Edwin Hubble, who in 1929 established the proportionality of redshift to distance. The formula for photometric distance in relativistic cosmology was derived within the framework of the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric. The Supernova Cosmology Project (Saul Perlmutter) and the High-Z Supernova Search Team (Brian Schmidt, Adam Riess) in 1998 used Type Ia supernovae as standard candles and discovered a deviation of D_L from the linear law, which indicated accelerated expansion. This became direct observational evidence for the existence of dark energy. Adam Riess and Saul Perlmutter are present in the list of scientists.
luminosity_distance.how_it_works: The relationship between apparent magnitude m and absolute magnitude M is given by the distance modulus: m − M = 5 log₁₀(D_L / 10 pc). For an object with known absolute luminosity (standard candle), measuring the peak apparent magnitude yields D_L. Within general relativity, D_L is expressed through solutions to the Friedmann equations, which follow from Einstein's equations for a homogeneous isotropic universe. The value of D_L depends on the densities of matter Ω_m, dark energy Ω_Λ, curvature Ω_k, and the Hubble constant H₀. Therefore, measuring D_L for a set of objects at different z allows placing constraints on cosmological parameters, in particular on the equation of state of dark energy w.
key_problems: Systematic uncertainties in standardizing Type Ia supernovae (metallicity, dust, population evolution).
The influence of possible gray dust and lensing effects on the measured flux.
Calibration of the local distance scale and the tension between H₀ values from the early and late universe.
luminosity_distance.fun_fact: If the universe were expanding uniformly without acceleration, D_L would increase linearly with z, but due to dark energy, for z=1, D_L is about 20% larger than predicted by the simple model.

formulas.description: Relationship between photometric distance and redshift
formulas.meaning: D_L — photometric distance; z — redshift of the observed radiation; D_M — comoving transverse distance (distance in coordinates that move with the expansion of the universe).

formulas.description: Definition of photometric distance via flux
formulas.meaning: F — observed energy flux (energy per unit area per unit time); L — absolute luminosity of the source (total emitted power); D_L — photometric distance; 4πD_L² — area of the sphere over which the energy is distributed in static space.

fermion.name: fermion
fermion.mini: In a crowded bus, everyone needs their own seat—no one will sit on your lap. A fermion is a tiny particle that follows the same rule: two identical fermions can never occupy the same state.
fermion.practical_application: Electrons are fermions. Their stubbornness prevents atoms from collapsing and creates all the diversity of chemistry. Without this rule, there would be no solid table, nor your palm.
fermion.description_popular: Fermions are divided into leptons (electron, neutrino) and quarks (which make up protons and neutrons). They share a spin-½, which forces them to follow Fermi–Dirac statistics—a mathematical expression of the exclusion principle. When a gas of fermions is cooled, all lower energy levels are filled up to a boundary—the Fermi energy. This Fermi surface explains the electrical conductivity of metals: only electrons near the boundary can move. The pressure of degenerate fermions prevents white dwarfs from collapsing under their own gravity—stars are held up by the exclusion force.
fermion.fun_fact_popular: The human body contains about 7×10²⁷ fermions (electrons and quarks). If the Pauli principle vanished, all these particles would clump into a single point—and you would shrink to the size of a grain of sand.
fermion.description_simple: The entire familiar world is built from fermions. Electron, proton, neutron—these are fermions. Each such particle has an intrinsic property—spin, akin to an internal compass needle. But spin is tricky: its value is always half-integer (½, 3/2…). Because of this half-integer spin, fermions obey a strict rule: two identical fermions are forbidden to be in the same place with the same spin direction. That is why electrons in an atom occupy different shells and do not all fall onto the nucleus—the spots are already taken. This exclusion was discovered by Wolfgang Pauli, and it is responsible for the strength of a brick and the opacity of matter.
fermion.history_simple: In 1925, Austrian physicist Wolfgang Pauli introduced the “exclusion principle” to explain why electrons in atoms occupy different levels. Soon after, Paul Dirac combined quantum mechanics with relativity and discovered that every fermion must have an antiparticle twin—for example, the positron for the electron.
fermion.how_it_works_simple: Imagine a row of chairs in a lecture hall. Each chair is one state with a certain height, position, and spin orientation. The first electron takes any free chair; the next is forced to take another. Filling proceeds from bottom to top, by energy. If you try to shove an extra electron onto an already occupied chair, the atom will strongly resist—this is the solidity of any body.
fermion.description: In quantum field theory, fermions are quanta of excitation of fermionic fields. They satisfy anticommutation relations: {ψ(x), ψ†(y)} = δ(x−y). The spin-statistics theorem rigidly links half-integer spin with antisymmetry of the wave function under particle exchange. The Dirac equation (iγ^μ ∂_μ − m)ψ = 0 describes a free fermion and inevitably predicts antiparticles. The Standard Model contains 12 fundamental fermions: six quarks (u, d, c, s, t, b) and six leptons (electron, muon, tau, and their neutrinos). Quarks carry color charge and are confined inside hadrons by the strong interaction.
fermion.history: The name “fermion” honors Enrico Fermi, who together with Paul Dirac in 1926 developed the statistics for particles with half-integer spin. A year earlier, Wolfgang Pauli formulated the exclusion principle by analyzing atomic spectra. The Dirac equation (1928) combined quantum mechanics and special relativity for the electron and led to the discovery of the positron by Carl Anderson in 1932. The quark model, proposed by Gell-Mann and Zweig in 1964, organized the zoo of strongly interacting particles.
fermion.how_it_works: The Pauli principle is a consequence of the antisymmetry of the wave function of a fermion system: Ψ(…,x_i,…,x_j,…) = −Ψ(…,x_j,…,x_i,…). When coordinates and spins coincide, the wave function vanishes. In a free electron gas at zero temperature, all levels below the Fermi energy E_F are filled, and those above are empty, according to the Fermi–Dirac distribution f(E) = 1/(e^{(E−μ)/k_B T} + 1). The degeneracy pressure of nonrelativistic fermions p ∝ n^{5/3} supports white dwarfs, while in the relativistic regime the Chandrasekhar limit restricts their mass.
key_problems: Why exactly three generations of fundamental fermions?
Colossal mass range: neutrinos lighter than 1 eV, t‑quark at 173 GeV.
Are neutrinos Majorana fermions (particle = antiparticle)?
Mechanism for the origin of matter–antimatter asymmetry in the universe.
fermion.fun_fact: The Dirac equation deduced spin as a direct consequence of relativity, but along the way it gave birth to antimatter—a mirror world where every particle has an antipode. The positron, predicted purely mathematically, was found in a cloud chamber by a track twisted the “wrong” way by a magnetic field.

magnetic_field.name: magnetic field
magnetic_field.mini: A fridge magnet holds a note as if by an invisible hand. That's the field at work — a web of force that permeates the space around the magnet and deflects a compass needle thousands of kilometers from the pole.
magnetic_field.practical_application: Magnetic fields spin the rotors of electric motors, focus the beam in old TV sets, confine incandescent plasma in reactors, and shield Earth from the harmful solar wind.
magnetic_field.description_popular: The magnetic field is a vector field that manifests through force on moving charges and magnetized bodies. In classical electrodynamics its measure is the magnetic induction B. The sources of the field are electric currents and changing electric fields (Maxwell's equations). The field lines are always closed: no magnetic monopoles have been found in nature. Materials react differently to the field: paramagnets (aluminum) slightly enhance it, diamagnets (water) repel it, and ferromagnets (iron) create a huge intrinsic field due to parallel alignment of electron spins. Earth's magnetic field (~50 µT) deflects the solar wind to the poles, generating auroras; without it the atmosphere would be swept into space.
magnetic_field.fun_fact_popular: A neutron star's magnetic field is hundreds of millions of times stronger than Earth's — such a field would evaporate a person at the atomic level faster than a nerve impulse reaches the brain.
magnetic_field.description_simple: The magnetic field is a special form of matter created by moving electric charges. A compass needle senses it, and any moving charge experiences a force within it. Earth is a giant magnet: molten iron in its core generates a field that makes a compass point north. A current in a wire is wrapped in a ring-shaped magnetic field — any electric motor is based on this. Even a tiny neodymium magnet creates a field that can affect electrons flying nearby.
magnetic_field.history_simple: Lodestone fragments attracted iron back in antiquity. But James Clerk Maxwell gave the unified picture in the 19th century: he proved that electricity and magnetism are two sides of the same coin. Earlier, Ørsted noticed that a current deflects a compass needle, and Faraday discovered that a moving magnet induces a current in a coil. Since then, the magnetic field has been a working tool of civilization.
magnetic_field.how_it_works_simple: Around any moving charge, a magnetic field immediately arises. In a permanent magnet, microscopic circular currents — electron orbits — add up to a common field. The lines of force exit the north pole, arc through space, and enter the south pole, closing inside. If you place a current-carrying conductor in this field, a force acts on it that can spin a rotor.
magnetic_field.description: The magnetic field is a component of the electromagnetic field tensor F_μν, and is relative: in different frames of reference, the division into electric and magnetic components varies. In vacuum B = μ₀(H + M) = μ₀H; in matter the relationship is nonlinear and depends on history. Maxwell's equations: ∇ × H = j + ∂D/∂t, ∇ · B = 0. The absence of magnetic charges is an experimental fact, though grand unified theories predict monopoles. Quantum electrodynamics describes the magnetic field as an exchange of virtual photons. In astrophysics, magnetic fields govern the dynamics of accretion disks, the generation of relativistic jets, and the structure of galaxies. Type I superconductors completely expel the field (Meissner effect), while type II form a vortex lattice. Technologically, strong fields are produced in superconducting solenoids (MRI, accelerators) and pulsed systems (up to 100 T).
magnetic_field.history: William Gilbert published the first scientific treatise on magnets in 1600, proposing that Earth is a large magnet. Hans Christian Ørsted discovered the magnetic effect of an electric current in 1820. André-Marie Ampère promptly built a mathematical theory. Michael Faraday introduced the concept of lines of force. James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s created a complete classical theory of the electromagnetic field, predicting light as a wave. Hendrik Lorentz later derived the force acting on a charge in a field. Quantum magnetism arose from the works of Pauli (spin-statistics theorem), Heisenberg (exchange interaction), and Dirac (equation with magnetic moment). Today, magnetic field research extends from cosmology to quantum computers.
magnetic_field.how_it_works: The magnetic field is generated by conduction currents and displacement currents: the Ampère–Maxwell equation ∇ × H = j + ∂D/∂t. The Biot–Savart law gives the field of a current element. The Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B) explains the motion of charged particles in the field. In matter, microscopic magnetic moments (orbital and spin) align, creating magnetization M. Ferromagnetic ordering is described by the Heisenberg exchange integral; domains are separated by Bloch walls. The magnetic field can do work, for example, rotate a current-carrying loop — the principle of electric motors. In a plasma, the field is frozen into the matter, leading to the dynamo effect in the liquid cores of Earth and the Sun. The quantum Aharonov–Bohm effect demonstrates that field potentials are more fundamental than field strengths. Relativistic particles in a magnetic field emit synchrotron radiation, visible in radio galaxies and supernova remnants.
key_problems: Experimental detection of magnetic monopoles
Origin and evolution of large-scale magnetic fields in the Universe
magnetic_field.fun_fact: The record pulsed magnetic field produced in a lab is 1200 tesla; it lasted millionths of a second and destroyed the setup. For comparison, Earth's field is 0.00005 tesla.

lens.name: lens
lens.mini: A dewdrop on a leaf turns the veins into a sharp map. That is a lens—a transparent curve that gathers light into an image.
lens.practical_application: Lenses in phone cameras and in telescopes catching distant galaxies. Tiny lenses also live in the eye, focusing the world onto the retina.
lens.description_popular: A lens is typically a transparent body with two spherical surfaces. Its curvature together with the refractive index (how much the material slows light) determines the focal length—the distance from the lens to the camera sensor when focused at infinity. A camera objective contains several lenses made of different glasses, because a single lens produces rainbow fringes and blurriness at the edges. The human eye is an amazing example: its crystalline lens changes thickness, focusing without a single moving part.
lens.fun_fact_popular: The largest objective lens ever made—the Yerkes Observatory telescope (1897)—has a diameter of 102 centimeters. It is so heavy that the glass sags under its own weight, which is why modern telescopes use mirrors.
lens.description_simple: A puddle, with ripples gathering a sunbeam on the bottom, does the same as a lens. A glass or plastic disc with a smoothly curved surface redirects light rays, making them converge at one point. When you use a magnifying glass, light from the page changes direction twice—upon entering and exiting the lens. The curvature causes all rays from one point of a letter to arrive at one point in your eye, making the font appear larger. The lens works like a traffic controller for photons, lining them up in orderly rows to draw a sharp image on the retina or sensor.
lens.history_simple: The first ground glasses aiding vision appeared around the year 1000, but craftsmen from Italy in the 13th century created wearable spectacles.
lens.how_it_works_simple: A convex lens (thicker in the middle) gathers rays like a bowl gathers raindrops. A concave lens (thinner in the middle) scatters them like a falling drop creates circles on water. The shape and material determine the distance at which the rays converge into focus.
lens.description: An ideal lens converts a spherical wave from a point source into a converging spherical wave that collapses to a point on the image plane. Real lenses suffer from distortions: spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, chromatic aberration. Modern objectives are composed of multiple elements made of different types of glass, which mutually cancel out these errors. Metalenses—flat arrays of nanostructures—can focus light without a curved surface, paving the way for ultrathin optics.
lens.history: The earliest lenses made of ground rock crystal date back to 700 BCE, Assyria. The scientific approach to lens systems began with Newton's invention of the reflecting telescope (to avoid the rainbow fringe) and the subsequent development of achromatic doublets by Chester Moore Hall in the 1730s. In 1665, Robert Hooke, using a compound microscope assembled from several lenses, first revealed the cellular structure of living matter in his 'Micrographia'.
lens.how_it_works: The law of refraction (Snell's law) n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2, when light hits a curved boundary, gives different ray slopes at different points. For a thin lens, the lens formula works: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, where f is the focal length, u is the object distance, v is the image distance. In the wave picture, the lens introduces a spatial phase delay proportional to the square of the distance from the axis, and thereby uses diffraction to turn a diverging wavefront into a converging one.
key_problems: Overcoming the diffraction limit for large lenses.
Eliminating chromatic dispersion without multi-lens designs.
Creating adaptive lenses with liquid or elastic surfaces for instant correction.
lens.fun_fact: The glass of the largest refractor lens (Yerkes Observatory, 102 cm) sags by only 0.1 mm, but that's enough to make the image 'drift'. That is why astronomers switched to reflecting telescopes: the mirror can be supported from behind.

dislocation.name: dislocation
dislocation.mini: Atomic railway with a switch. The train pushes one car — and the entire line shifts thousands of times easier than dragging the whole train at once.
dislocation.practical_application: Forging metal, rolling steel, and the strength of alloys rely on the skillful management of dislocations — without them, an aluminum fuselage would crack rather than bend.
dislocation.description_popular: The crystal lattice is a three-dimensional pattern of atoms. A dislocation disrupts this pattern: it is the edge of an incomplete atomic plane wedged between full layers. Around the dislocation line, the crystal is strained. This stress allows the dislocation to move under load, rearranging atomic rows step by step. Thus the metal flows rather than cracks. In fact, any piece of metal contains billions of dislocations per square centimeter; their tangled movement is plasticity.
dislocation.fun_fact_popular: The yellow color of gold is partly due to dislocations, which affect light absorption. Without them, gold might be silvery, like most metals.
dislocation.description_simple: The interior of a crystal resembles perfectly stacked rows of bricks. A dislocation is an extra half-plane of atoms inserted between rows, as if an unfinished row appeared in a wall. The edge of this extra plane — the break line — is the dislocation. Under load, it slides between adjacent rows, switching atomic bonds one by one. The entire crystal deforms gradually, rather than breaking immediately.
dislocation.history_simple: The idea emerged in 1934 when three scientists — Taylor, Orowan, and Polanyi — independently realized that real crystals bend much more easily than the theory of an ideal lattice predicted. Later, in 1956, Peter Hirsch and colleagues first observed dislocations in an electron microscope.
dislocation.how_it_works_simple: Imagine moving a heavy carpet across the floor: dragging the whole thing is difficult, but creating a fold and pushing it along is easy. A dislocation works like that fold. Atoms rearrange bonds not all at once, but locally along the dislocation line. The resistance drops by orders of magnitude.
dislocation.description: A dislocation is a linear defect of the crystal lattice that determines the mechanisms of plastic deformation. There are edge (extra atomic half-plane) and screw (spiral distortion) dislocations. The Burgers vector b characterizes the magnitude and direction of distortion. The stress field around a dislocation extends over several interatomic distances and interacts with other defects. The motion of dislocations (glide and climb) controls yielding, hardening, and fracture of materials. The density of dislocations in annealed metal is ~10⁶–10⁸ cm⁻², increasing to 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻² after severe deformation. The interaction of dislocations with impurities, precipitates, and grain boundaries underlies all methods of alloy strengthening.
dislocation.history: The concept of dislocations was introduced in 1934 by Geoffrey Taylor, Egon Orowan, and Michael Polanyi to resolve the paradox of the low strength of real crystals compared to theoretical estimates. In the 1940s, Jacques Friedel developed the theory of dislocation networks. Direct observation of dislocations in a transmission electron microscope was achieved by Peter Hirsch and colleagues in 1956. Subsequently, William Lawrence Bragg contributed to the understanding of dislocation structure using X-ray diffraction.
dislocation.how_it_works: Under shear stress, a dislocation moves in the slip plane, sequentially breaking and reforming interatomic bonds. The Peierls–Nabarro stress determines the lattice resistance to motion. Schmid's law relates the critical resolved shear stress to the plane orientation. When dislocations meet, they can interact elastically, form Lomer–Cottrell barriers, or annihilate. The Orowan equation relates the plastic strain rate to the density of mobile dislocations, their velocity, and the Burgers vector: dε/dt = ρ_m b v. With increasing temperature, dislocation climb becomes possible through vacancy diffusion, which is essential for creep.
key_problems: Predicting the collective behavior of dislocations under large strains and cyclic loading.
Modeling the nucleation of dislocations from defect-free regions of a crystal.
The influence of dislocations on thermal conductivity, electronic and optical properties in nanoscale structures.
dislocation.fun_fact: In silicon, dislocations can serve as channels for hopping conduction, which is being explored for radiation detectors.

heat_capacity.name: heat capacity
heat_capacity.mini: A cast iron skillet heats slowly on the flame and cools down for a long time. An aluminum one flares up with heat almost instantly. Heat capacity is a measure of how stubbornly a substance resists heating.
heat_capacity.practical_application: The high heat capacity of water moderates the climate: oceans accumulate daytime heat and release it at night. In engineering, the low heat capacity of copper allows radiators to quickly dissipate heat.
heat_capacity.description_popular: Heat capacity C defines the relationship between the heat absorbed ΔQ and the temperature change ΔT: C = ΔQ/ΔT. Specific heat capacity c is normalized per kilogram of substance. Gases, liquids, and solids differ by orders of magnitude. Monatomic gas (argon) has a molar heat capacity of about 12.5 J/(mol·K), diatomic oxygen — 20.8 J/(mol·K), and crystals — approximately 25 J/(mol·K) (Dulong–Petit law). Water breaks records: 4.2 kJ/(kg·K), twice as high as one might expect — colossal energy goes into overcoming hydrogen bonds between molecules. That is precisely why tea cools in a quarter of an hour, while milk — in five minutes.
heat_capacity.fun_fact_popular: If the oceans had the heat capacity of sand, at night the planet would freeze down to minus one hundred degrees, and during the day it would heat up to plus one hundred.
heat_capacity.description_simple: Heat capacity is the amount of heat that must be transferred to a body to raise its temperature by one degree. A sponge with fine pores soaks up a lot of water, while a dense stone — only a drop. Heat capacity is the same sponge, but for heat. Water is 'spongy': it takes a huge amount of energy to shift its degree. Iron is 'stony': it heats up quickly. A cast iron skillet full of soup stores heat for tens of minutes, but at night it still warms the cooling house for a long time. That is why the climate of coastal countries is mild — water, like a giant battery, smooths out temperature jumps.
heat_capacity.history_simple: In the 18th century, Scottish chemist Joseph Black first separated the concepts of 'heat' and 'temperature'. Observing how differently iron and water heat up, he introduced the term 'heat capacity'. Later, James Joule and William Thomson proved: heat is the motion of microscopic particles.
heat_capacity.how_it_works_simple: Heating makes atoms tremble, rotate, or rush around faster. The more ways microscopic particles have to move (degrees of freedom), the more heat is required to set this ‘dance’ in motion, and the higher the heat capacity. Water is complex: its molecules not only move but also break the tenacious hydrogen bonds — hence its record appetite for heat.
heat_capacity.description: Heat capacity is a thermodynamic response function characterizing the change in internal energy U (or enthalpy H) with temperature: C_V = (∂U/∂T)_V, C_p = (∂H/∂T)_p. For an ideal gas, C_p - C_V = R. Quantum theory of solids (Debye model) predicts C_V ∼ T³ for T ≪ θ_D and approaching the classical limit of 3R at high T. In real crystals, anharmonicities must be taken into account; in metals, the electronic contribution C_el = γT. During second-order phase transitions, heat capacity experiences a jump or logarithmic divergence. At the liquid–gas critical point, an anomalous increase in C_V is observed. Experimental methods: differential scanning calorimetry, relaxation method, adiabatic calorimetry.
heat_capacity.history: Joseph Black in the 1760s, studying the heat of fusion of ice, noticed that different bodies require different amounts of 'fire' for the same heating, and called this 'capacity for heat'. Dulong and Petit in 1819 formulated the empirical law of constant atomic heat capacity (~6 cal/(mol·K)). Ludwig Boltzmann in 1871 gave the first statistical explanation via equipartition of energy among degrees of freedom. Albert Einstein in 1907 applied the quantum hypothesis to atomic vibrations in a crystal, and Peter Debye in 1912 refined the theory by accounting for the full spectrum of phonon modes. Today, heat capacity measurements are a standard tool for investigating phase transitions, superconductivity, and topological materials.
heat_capacity.how_it_works: Statistical mechanics connects heat capacity with fluctuations of internal energy: C_V = (⟨U²⟩ - ⟨U⟩²)/(k_B T²). In a classical ideal gas, C_V = (f/2)R, where f is the number of quadratic degrees of freedom. Debye model: C_V = 9R (T/θ_D)³ ∫_0^{θ_D/T} (x⁴ e^x)/(e^x-1)² dx. For metals, the contribution of the degenerate electron gas is significant: C_el = (π²/2)(k_B²/g(ε_F)) T, which at low temperatures becomes C_V = γT + βT³ — a formula used to determine the density of states at the Fermi level and the Debye temperature. Magnetic materials exhibit heat capacity peaks at magnetic transitions (λ-anomalies). In glasses and amorphous solids, an excess low-temperature heat capacity is observed due to tunneling two-level systems. The heat capacity of a black hole, computed by Bekenstein and Hawking, is negative (in the sense of stability).
key_problems: Incomplete theory of heat capacity of liquids over a wide range of temperatures and pressures
Nature of low-temperature anomalies of heat capacity in glasses (boson peak problem)
heat_capacity.fun_fact: At temperatures of millionths of a kelvin, the heat capacity of helium-3 changes by ten orders of magnitude due to the transition of nuclear spins into an ordered state.

brown_dwarf.name: brown dwarf
brown_dwarf.mini: A star that missed one heartbeat. In its core, lithium flared up—and went out, leaving a warm gas ball to slowly cool over billions of years.
brown_dwarf.practical_application: Brown dwarfs serve as natural laboratories for studying the atmospheres of giant planets and stars—they have intermediate temperatures and the same molecules: methane, water vapor, carbon monoxide.
brown_dwarf.description_popular: Brown dwarfs fill the gap between giant planets and true stars. Their masses range roughly from 13 to 75 Jupiter masses. Unlike planets, they can briefly fuse deuterium early in life, but hydrogen fusion is beyond their reach. The atmospheres of these objects are quite cool (300 to 2500 K), where dust grains of silicates and iron condense. Spectra divide them into classes from L (hot, with metal lines and dust) to T (cooler, with methane bands) and further Y—the faintest, with temperatures below 500 K.
brown_dwarf.fun_fact_popular: The first discovered brown dwarf, Gliese 229 B, has a temperature of only about 950 K—cooler than a candle flame, though it shines not in visible light but in infrared.
brown_dwarf.description_simple: A brown dwarf is an object heavier than the largest planet but lighter than the lightest star. It is born like a star, from a collapsing gas cloud, but its interior never heats up enough to ignite steady hydrogen burning. A brief flash of lithium or deuterium fusion provides a little heat, after which the dwarf simply cools for tens of billions of years, glowing faintly in the infrared.
brown_dwarf.history_simple: The idea emerged in the 1960s, when astronomer Shiv Kumar calculated that objects with less than 0.07 solar masses could not sustain thermonuclear fusion. The first candidate, discovered in 1995, Gliese 229 B, turned out to be a small, dim companion to a red dwarf.
brown_dwarf.how_it_works_simple: Gravity compresses the gas. If the mass is too low (less than ~75 Jupiter masses), the central temperature reaches only a few million degrees. The hydrogen furnace never ignites, but deuterium (a hydrogen variant with an extra neutron) and lithium can react briefly. Once they burn out, the object loses its energy source and fades over decades, like a cooling ember.
brown_dwarf.description: A brown dwarf is a substellar object with a mass of 13–75 M_J (about 0.012–0.072 M_⊙), unable to sustain the stationary ppI chain or CNO cycle of hydrogen burning. In the core, deuterium fusion (D + p → ³He + γ) can occur briefly at masses above ~13 M_J, and lithium fusion (⁷Li + p → ⁴He + ⁴He) above ~65 M_J. Effective temperatures range from ~300 to 2800 K, with the bulk of emission in the infrared. Spectral classification includes classes L, T, Y; the transition from L to T is marked by the appearance of methane absorption bands, while class Y features the disappearance of alkali lines and the dominance of ammonia. Internal structure is described by equations of state for partially degenerate electron gas; central densities reach 10²–10³ g/cm³. Many brown dwarfs exhibit rapid rotation (periods of hours) and magnetic activity up to X-ray flares.
brown_dwarf.history: The theoretical prediction was made by Shiv Kumar in 1963, who introduced the term 'black dwarf' for objects with mass less than 0.07 M_⊙. In 1975, Jill Tarter proposed the name 'brown dwarf.' The first confirmed discovery took place in 1995: Tad Owen and colleagues detected Gliese 229 B at the Palomar Observatory. Later, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar made a fundamental contribution by calculating the limiting mass for degenerate bodies—the Chandrasekhar limit, which, although higher than brown dwarf masses, laid the foundation for describing their internal structure.
brown_dwarf.how_it_works: The object forms like a star, from the fragmentation of a molecular cloud and accretion. As it contracts, the core temperature rises; if the mass is below the threshold, electron degeneracy sets in before the pp-chain temperature (~3×10⁶ K) is reached. Further contraction is slowed by the pressure of degenerate electrons. Any thermonuclear reactions ignited during the deuterium or lithium phase quickly deplete their fuel because the temperature drops as the core expands. Thereafter, the object's luminosity is sustained only by the release of gravitational energy and gradual cooling. Cooling curves are described by solutions of the stellar structure equations with a degenerate equation of state; the characteristic cooling time is tens of billions of years.
key_problems: Detailed chemical differentiation of brown dwarf atmospheres and formation of dust clouds.
Mechanisms of magnetic field generation and flare activity in fully convective interiors.
Population statistics: the fraction of brown dwarfs at the boundary between planets and stars and their formation mechanisms.
brown_dwarf.fun_fact: Some brown dwarfs have atmospheric temperatures at which clouds of molten iron and silicate particles form—essentially, it rains rocks.
